0.title: The LORD Fights for His People: The Book of Joshua
0.overview:
The message. Joshua is the story of God keeping his word. Centuries earlier he had promised Abraham a land; now, under Joshua, he brings Abraham’s children across the Jordan, fights their battles, gives them the land and divides it. The walls of Jericho fall to a shout, and at the end the old general tells the people, “it is the LORD your God who has fought for you” (23:3). Grace comes first, then the call to answer it: be strong, keep God’s word, choose whom you will serve. Its summit is one verse: “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass” (21:45).

Background: the man. Joshua son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, had served as Moses’ assistant since his youth. Among the twelve spies, he and Caleb alone urged the people to trust God, and of that generation only they lived to enter the land (Numbers 14:6–9, 30). His name had been Hoshea until Moses called him Joshua (Numbers 13:16), which means “the LORD saves”. In Greek it is Iēsous: Jesus. The book opens with Moses dead and God saying to Joshua, “Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan” (1:2).

The writer. The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition credited Joshua himself, and he did write down the covenant at Shechem (24:26), but his death (24:29–33) was plainly recorded by someone else. Notes that things remain “to this day” point to a time soon after: Rahab, or at least her family, still living in Israel (6:25), and the Jebusites still in Jerusalem (15:63), which David took about 1000 BC. Many modern scholars think it was shaped centuries later, in the exile, as part of one history running from Deuteronomy to Kings. This commentary takes the book to rest on records from Joshua’s own day, with some later inspired notes, and leaves the date of its final form open.

When and where. If the exodus was about 1446 BC (1 Kings 6:1), Israel crossed the Jordan about 1406 BC; many believing scholars prefer a date nearly two centuries later, and this commentary, as in Exodus, leaves the date open. Canaan was then a patchwork of small city-states, each with its own king; chapter 12 lists thirty-one. Letters found at Amarna in Egypt, from the fourteenth century BC, show these kings, Egypt’s vassals, quarrelling and begging Pharaoh for help against raiders. Their religion centred on Baal, the storm god, and on fertility rites, and Scripture says that “they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods” (Deuteronomy 12:31).

The kind of writing. The Hebrew Bible places Joshua first among the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings), history told as God’s dealings with his people. Its long lists of borders and towns are not padding but title deeds: every family could find its inheritance written down. Its summary statements, such as “So Joshua took the whole land” (11:23), describe the breaking of the Canaanite kings’ power, not the settling of every town, for the same book says that “there remains yet very much land to possess” (13:1) and names cities Israel did not take (15:63; 16:10). The archaeology of Jericho and Ai is disputed, and the digging neither proves nor disproves it; this commentary reads the book as true history, as the New Testament does (Hebrews 11:30–31).

How the book makes its case. Entering (chapters 1–5): God charges Joshua three times to “be strong and courageous” (1:6, 7, 9); Rahab, a Canaanite prostitute, hides the spies and confesses that “the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath” (2:11); the Jordan parts; and Israel meets the commander of the LORD’s army. Taking (chapters 6–12): Jericho falls to trumpets and a shout; Achan’s hidden theft brings defeat at Ai until it is dealt with (chapters 7–8); the Gibeonites trick Israel into a treaty (chapter 9); and two campaigns break the kings, “because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel” (10:42). Dividing (chapters 13–21): the land is shared out by lot, with old Caleb claiming the giants’ hill country (chapter 14), cities of refuge (chapter 20) and towns for the Levites, whose inheritance is the LORD himself (chapter 21). Serving (chapters 22–24): Joshua’s farewells call Israel to cling to the LORD, and at Shechem he sets the choice before them: “choose this day whom you will serve … But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (24:15). The order is the message: God gives before he asks, and every command rests on a gift.

The violence of Joshua. Hardest of all is the command to devote whole cities to destruction (herem), which at Jericho meant “both men and women, young and old” (6:21). It must not be softened or hurried past. Critics call it ethnic slaughter, or legend. Scripture itself sets the command in a frame. The judgment was announced centuries ahead and delayed in patience, “for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis 15:16). Israel was told it was “not because of your righteousness” (Deuteronomy 9:5), and warned that the land would vomit Israel out too for the same sins (Leviticus 18:28), as in time it did. It was never about ancestry, for Rahab’s household walked out of Jericho alive because she believed. And it was one command for one time and place, never applied by any apostle. This commentary’s view is that it was God’s just judgment on long-persistent wickedness, never a pattern or licence for violence today. That does not make verse 21 easy, but this commentary trusts the Judge of all the earth to do right with every child (Genesis 18:25), and notes that in the end judgment fell, at the cross, on the one man who did not deserve it.

Where it leads: to Christ. Joshua points to Christ chiefly by pattern and by the need it exposes. The angel told Joseph, “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21): the same name, and a far greater rescue. Joshua brought Israel into the land but could not change their hearts, and told them plainly, “You are not able to serve the LORD” (24:19). Hebrews draws the conclusion: “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on. So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:8–9). It is found in the one who says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The commander of the LORD’s army, who receives Joshua’s worship (5:13–15), is best read, this commentary holds, as the Son himself before his incarnation. Rahab, the outsider saved by faith, stands in Matthew’s family tree of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). And the promise-keeping of 21:45 finds its fullest answer in him, for “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

For us. We take no land by the sword, for “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4). Yet Joshua’s courage rests outside us: God told Joshua, “I will not leave you or forsake you” (1:5), and Hebrews gives it to every believer: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). The seven tribes slow to take land already given them (18:3) warn that we can believe all the right things and still not lay hold of what God has given us in Christ. And Rahab shows that no one is too far outside for grace. So be strong and courageous, and choose this day whom you will serve.

1.title: The Commissioning of Joshua
1.text: <sup>1</sup>After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' assistant,<sup>2</sup>"Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel.<sup>3</sup>Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, just as I promised to Moses.<sup>4</sup>From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun shall be your territory.<sup>5</sup>No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.<sup>6</sup>Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.<sup>7</sup>Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go.<sup>8</sup>This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.<sup>9</sup>Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."<sup>10</sup>And Joshua commanded the officers of the people,<sup>11</sup>"Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, 'Prepare your provisions, for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.'"<sup>12</sup>And to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said,<sup>13</sup>"Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, 'The LORD your God is providing you a place of rest and will give you this land.'<sup>14</sup>Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan, but all the men of valor among you shall pass over armed before your brothers and shall help them,<sup>15</sup>until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you, and they also take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them. Then you shall return to the land of your possession and shall possess it, the land that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise."<sup>16</sup>And they answered Joshua, "All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go.<sup>17</sup>Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses!<sup>18</sup>Whoever rebels against your commandment and disobeys your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Only be strong and courageous."
1.overview:
Where we are. The book opens where Deuteronomy ended: Moses is dead, Israel is camped east of the Jordan, and the land promised to Abraham lies across a river in flood. The man who brought them to the border could not take them over it, and the charge passes to his assistant.

The message. God’s promise does not die with God’s servants. The land is already given (v. 3), and the God who was with Moses will be with Joshua, so the new leader is to be strong and courageous: not because he is a brave man, but because the outcome is sworn, the word is sure and the LORD goes with him. Courage is commanded, and it rests on a gift given first.

Why it was said. The first hearers stood at a hinge of their history: a great leader gone, an untested successor, walled cities ahead, and a nation whose parents had lost their nerve at this very border (Numbers 14). Later readers, losing the land, needed to hear again that it was God’s gift (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God speaks to Joshua (vv. 1–9). Moses is dead, so cross; the land is given; “I will not leave you or forsake you” (vv. 1–5). Then the command comes three times, each with its own anchor: the oath to the fathers (v. 6), the Book of the Law (vv. 7–8) and God’s presence (v. 9). Joshua speaks to the people (vv. 10–15): prepare food for the crossing (vv. 10–11), and the tribes settled east of the river must fight for their brothers until all have rest (vv. 12–15). The people answer, giving God’s own words back to their leader (vv. 16–18).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Joshua bears the name of Jesus and leads God’s people into the inheritance Moses could only see, yet the rest he gave was not the last rest (Hebrews 4:8–9). Christ is the greater Joshua: the one man who kept the Book without turning to the right hand or the left, who left his own rest to fight for his brothers, and whose last word to his people repeats this chapter’s best promise: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

For us. Every Christian stands where Joshua stood: an inheritance already given in Christ, and real battles still ahead. Courage does not come from temperament but from what God has sworn, from a Bible kept open, and from a Saviour who goes with us; and no one’s comfort excuses him from his brothers’ fight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s first word after Moses’ death is a marching order resting on a gift. Moses is dead but the promise is not, so Joshua must arise and lead the people over the Jordan (vv. 1–2). The land is spoken of as already given, with borders as wide as the oath to Abraham (vv. 3–4), and God promises his presence: as with Moses, so with Joshua, never leaving or forsaking him (v. 5). Then the command comes three times, each time anchored outside Joshua: be strong, for the outcome is sworn (v. 6); be very courageous in keeping the Book of the Law, meditating on it day and night (vv. 7–8); do not be frightened, for the LORD is with you wherever you go (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Grace arrives before duty and grounds it. The land is given in verse 3 and fought for from chapter 6 onwards, which is the pattern of the whole Bible: God announces the accomplished gift and then calls his people to walk into it. Israel does not fight to earn Canaan; they fight because it is already theirs.
verseByVerse.examples: The middle command is the surprising one. The most courageous thing required of a general on the eve of a war is not to storm a wall but to keep a book: to meditate on it day and night and not turn from it to the right hand or to the left (vv. 7-8). Before a single battle plan is drawn, God says the campaign will depend on what happens in the heart of the man who reads.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' assistant,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is dead and the work is unfinished, but God is not silent: he speaks at once to the man he has spent forty years preparing.

After the death of Moses. The book is hinged on a grave. The man who spoke with God “as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11) is gone, and the land is not yet entered. Yet there is no anxious pause: Moses dies and God speaks. There is no power vacuum in the kingdom of God, because the King does not die.

The servant of the LORD … Moses’ assistant. The writer sets the two titles side by side on purpose. Moses is “the servant of the LORD”, among the highest titles the Old Testament gives anyone. Joshua is “Moses’ assistant”, as he had been “from his youth” (Numbers 11:28). He led the fighting in the valley while Moses held up his hands on the hill (Exodus 17:9–13). He stayed in the tent of meeting after Moses had gone back to the camp (Exodus 33:11). He stood with Caleb against ten frightened men and a nation ready to stone him (Numbers 14:6–10). None of it made him famous. All of it made him ready.

Joshua the son of Nun. His name matters more than the chapter says aloud. Joshua is Yehoshua, “the LORD saves”, later shortened to Yeshua, and in Greek Iēsous: the name that would be given to a carpenter’s son in Nazareth (see the introduction). Hebrews makes the connection and marks the limit: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later of another day (Hebrews 4:8). This man will bring them into the land; he cannot bring them into the lasting rest with God that only Jesus gives.

The hidden years. Ours is an age of the platform. We measure significance by visibility, followers and titles. Joshua’s life runs the other way. For some forty years he was the second man, and God was not wasting those years. Hidden faithfulness is not a waiting room for real life; it is where a person is made into someone who can bear being seen. The pattern runs through Scripture, from David with the sheep to Paul in Arabia (Galatians 1:17), and above all in the Son of God, who spent about thirty years in a carpenter’s workshop in a village nobody respected before he preached a single sermon (Luke 3:23; John 1:46). If the eternal Word could be hidden that long without loss, nobody’s unseen years are wasted. The gospel frees us from needing a platform, because the only audience that finally counts has said of Christ, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and says the same of all who are in him.
verseByVerse.note: Joshua means “the LORD saves.” The book covers Israel’s entry into Canaan and the division of the land, probably in the late 1400s or 1200s BC.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel. Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, just as I promised to Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names the loss honestly and then sends Joshua on, because the land is already given: every battle to come will be fought on ground God has deeded to Israel, and faith takes possession by setting its foot on the promise.

Moses my servant is dead. God himself says it: the grief is neither denied nor hurried. But the next word is “arise”, and it is the right word to a man who has spent thirty days in mourning (Deuteronomy 34:8). Some losses persuade us that the story has stopped. It has not. God’s answer to a funeral, here, is a task: a river to cross.

I have given to you. The tense drives the whole book. Not “I will give you” but “I have given to you”: before a single Israelite has crossed the water, the land is deeded over. Every battle in the next eleven chapters is fought on ground that already belongs to them.

Every place that the sole of your foot will tread. Yet the gift has to be walked on. The promise is the title deed, and setting foot on the land is taking possession. Faith is the foot set down on the promise. A man may own a field for years and never walk it, and some hold God’s promises that way.

In the Christian life. Nobody fights sin in order to become a child of God; the fighting is what a child of God does on territory the Father has already put in his name (Colossians 3:3–5).

verseByVerse.quote: From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun shall be your territory. No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land God gives is as wide as his oath to Abraham, and the promise behind every battle is not exemption from fighting but the presence of God, who will never leave or forsake his servant.

As far as the great river. The borders are those God swore to Abraham (Genesis 15:18), and they are enormous, reaching the Euphrates. They were never fully occupied. Chapter 13 opens with God telling the aged Joshua that very much land remains, and something near the fullest extent was reached only briefly, centuries later, under Solomon (1 Kings 4:21). The book is honest about the gap between what was promised and what was held, and the gap is not a failure in the promise but a signpost to something larger (see below).

No man shall be able to stand before you. Verse 5 is the bedrock of the chapter, and it is worded with care. Not “no one will attack you”, but no one will be able to stand. Not “I will make it easy”, but “I will be with you”. The promise is presence, not exemption.

I will not leave you or forsake you. Hebrews hands this sentence to ordinary Christians worried about money: “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” The conclusion it draws is courage: “So we can confidently say, ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear’” (Hebrews 13:5–6).

Where Christians differ. Does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people and to the modern state of Israel? Dispensationalists hold that it does: God’s promise to Abraham’s physical descendants remains literal, borders included, and awaits a future fulfilment. Others note that Joshua itself says “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed” (21:45), and that the New Testament widens the promise: Abraham was to be “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs looked for “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16). Many hold the dispensational view out of a desire to honour every word God spoke, and both sides agree that the promises stand because God keeps his word.

This commentary’s view. The land promise was fulfilled in Joshua’s day and points beyond itself to the whole new earth that Christ’s people will inherit: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). The modern state of Israel is not the fulfilment of these promises, though Christians should love the Jewish people and pray for their salvation.

Uncertain wording. Exactly what “all the land of the Hittites” means here is not certain. The Hittite empire, centred in Anatolia (modern Turkey), had once ruled northern Syria, and later Assyrian records still called the lands west of the Euphrates “Hatti”; most take the phrase to mean that northern region. Others connect it with the Hittites who lived in Canaan itself (Genesis 23). Either way the point is clear: the promised borders reach far to the north.
verseByVerse.note: “The great sea” is the Mediterranean.

verseByVerse.quote: Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua’s courage is commanded, and it can be commanded because the outcome is already sworn: he will lead Israel into the land God promised their fathers.

Be strong and courageous. This is the first of the three commands. Courage here is not a temperament some are born with; it is commanded, so it must be available to whoever is commanded to have it.

You shall cause this people to inherit. What makes it available is the clause attached. Joshua is not told to attempt the conquest and hope. He is told he “shall” cause this people to inherit, because God swore it to their fathers. The outcome is settled before the courage is required, and the courage is simply the fitting response to a settled outcome. Most fear works the other way round: we wait to see how a thing will turn out and take our courage from the evidence. God reverses it: here is how it turns out; now be strong.

That I swore to their fathers. The oath reaches back through Moses to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, across centuries. God’s word does not expire with those who first heard it. Joshua leads as the trustee of a promise much older than himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go. This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bravest thing asked of Joshua is to keep God’s word exactly, speaking it, pondering it day and night and doing it, for that is the road to the success of his commission.

Only be strong and very courageous. The second command raises the temperature, “very” courageous, and attaches it not to the walls of Jericho but to the law. A leader in a long campaign will be pressed off the road both ways: the shortcut on one side, the compromise on the other.

You shall meditate on it day and night. Three things are involved, in an instructive order: the mouth, the mind and the hands. The book is to be spoken, chewed over and done. The word for meditate, hagah, is a low muttering, the word Isaiah uses of a lion that “growls over his prey” (Isaiah 31:4). It does not mean emptying the mind. The book is not to depart from the mouth, so this is a man reading half-aloud to himself, turning the words over day and night like the blessed man of Psalm 1:2.

Then you will have good success. The sentence is often quoted badly. The Hebrew word behind “good success” also means acting wisely, and the success promised is the success of this commission: bringing a people into a land God had sworn to give them. It is not a formula for turning devotions into money. What the verse does teach, on the eve of a war when there seems least time for reading, is that the campaign will be won or lost long before the army forms up, in the quiet of one man’s reading.

Only one has kept this book. No one but Christ has kept this book without turning to the right or the left. He did it for us, and his obedience is counted ours (Romans 5:19); and the Spirit he gives writes the same word on our hearts and moves us to walk in it (Ezekiel 36:27). So a believer who has turned aside comes back by confession, and opens the book again as a child, not as a hired servant.

How do I meditate on it? Meditation is not a technique for experts; it is reading slowly enough for the words to stay with you. Take a little, not a lot. One paragraph read twice does more than three chapters skimmed. Say it. Read it half-aloud, or write it on a card by the kettle or on the dashboard, and turn it over at the red light or when you wake at 2 a.m. Ask it questions. What does this show me about God? About myself? What does it ask of me today? Look for him in it. On the Emmaus road, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). The law Joshua muttered over is fulfilled in the one who kept it for us, so we read it not to earn God’s favour but to know the one through whom it has already been given. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (Colossians 3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third command comes as a reminder of orders already given, and it rests on the best ground of all: the LORD himself goes with Joshua wherever he goes.

Have I not commanded you? The third command opens with a question that lands like a hand on the shoulder: Joshua is being reminded that he has orders.

Do not be frightened. This puts fear in an uncomfortable light. If courage is commanded, then settled fear is not only a weakness of the nerves; it is a way of not taking God at his word. Scripture is full of frightened people handled gently, and God does not shout at the trembling. But it does mean that fear is answerable to something, and that a believer may argue with his own dread rather than obey it.

Wherever you go. The last words are the best in the chapter. Not “wherever I send you”, which would cover obedient errands only, but “wherever you go”, including the places Joshua would choose badly: the valley at Ai, the day he believed the Gibeonites without asking the LORD (chapters 7 and 9). The promise is hammered three times because it will need to be remembered three hundred.

God with us. The New Testament gives these words a face. A child is born and called Immanuel, “God with us”, and the last thing the risen Christ says on a hillside, to men about to be scattered across the world, is “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 1:23; 28:20). The promise made to one soldier at a river has become the permanent arrangement for all Christ’s people. For the Christian the presence is nearer still, for the Spirit of Christ lives in us, and he gives the courage the command asks for (2 Timothy 1:7).

How do I argue with my fear? Name it. Say exactly what you are afraid of: the scan result, the redundancy meeting, the son who has stopped ringing. A named fear can be brought to God. Answer it with what he has said. Fear says you are on your own. God says, “I will not leave you or forsake you” (1:5). Speak back, as the psalmist did: “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (Psalm 56:3). Pray it, specifically. “In everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). Then take the next step anyway. Courage is making the phone call while still shaking. Where fear has hardened into constant anxiety or panic, talk to a pastor or biblical counsellor and see a doctor too; the body matters, and medicine is no failure of faith. And remember why the argument can be won. God has already given the costliest thing he had: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The one who went into the deepest darkness for us will not desert us in a smaller one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — The Charge to the People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God said to Joshua in private, Joshua turns at once into orders, and the people take them up. The officers tell the camp to prepare provisions, for in three days they will cross into the land the LORD is giving (vv. 10–11). The tribes already settled east of the Jordan are held to their promise: their fighting men must cross armed and help their brothers until every tribe has rest (vv. 12–15). The people answer with a full pledge on one condition, that the LORD be with Joshua as he was with Moses, and they end by giving God’s own words back to their leader: “Only be strong and courageous” (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: No tribe rests while its brothers are still fighting, and the new leader's authority rests on God's presence, not on his own.
verseByVerse.examples: When we repeat God's promises to a tired leader or a frightened friend, as Israel does in v. 18, we give them nothing of our own and nothing less than God's word.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua commanded the officers of the people, "Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, 'Prepare your provisions, for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua turns God’s word into orders at once, and the first order is wonderfully ordinary: pack food, for in three days they cross into the land God is giving.

Joshua commanded the officers. There is no gap between hearing God’s word in private and giving the order in public. Obedience that waits for better feelings has already begun to be disobedience.

Prepare your provisions. God has given the land, and the people are to pack food: faith gets ready for what God has promised. Divine sovereignty and human effort are not rivals sharing out the work between them; the certainty of the outcome is what makes the preparation confident rather than anxious.

The end of the manna. There is a quiet change of era in this instruction. These people have eaten manna every morning for forty years and have never had to think about supplies. Within a fortnight of this order the manna will stop (5:10–12). God’s provision does not become less; it stops being miraculous and starts being a harvest, which is how he feeds nearly everybody.

verseByVerse.quote: And to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said, "Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, 'The LORD your God is providing you a place of rest and will give you this land.' Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan, but all the men of valor among you shall pass over armed before your brothers and shall help them, until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you, and they also take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them. Then you shall return to the land of your possession and shall possess it, the land that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribes already settled east of the Jordan must leave their homes and fight for their brothers until every tribe has its rest: no one’s inheritance excuses him from his brother’s battle.

Remember the word. Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh had been granted the land east of the river on one condition (Numbers 32), and Joshua now holds them to it. These men already have their inheritance. They are told to leave all of it and cross a river to fight a war of some seven years (14:7, 10) for land that not one of them will ever own.

Until the LORD gives rest to your brothers. The term of service is not a number of years: they go home when everyone else is home. “Rest”, secure and settled life in God’s land, is a key word of the book, given at the end (21:44) and taken up by Hebrews for the rest that remains in Christ (Hebrews 4:8–9).

Someone greater than Reuben. Someone greater is faintly visible here. Christ, who was at rest, at home and in possession of everything, crossed over armed into a war he had no need to fight, for the sake of an inheritance that would belong to his brothers (Philippians 2:6–8; Hebrews 2:11).

My brother’s battle. Here is the principle: my inheritance does not excuse me from my brother’s battle. It is entirely possible to be settled, provided for and spiritually comfortable while people you are bound to are still fighting for their lives, and this chapter treats that arrangement as a debt, not a blessing. Paul says it in four words, “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2), and this is what it looks like with boots on.

verseByVerse.quote: And they answered Joshua, "All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses! Whoever rebels against your commandment and disobeys your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Only be strong and courageous."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people pledge full obedience on one condition, that God be with Joshua as he was with Moses, and they send him into the work with God’s own words: “Only be strong and courageous.”

All that you have commanded us we will do. The pledge is total, but it hangs on something they cannot give him: God’s presence. Joshua’s authority is borrowed, and their one concern about the new leader is not whether he is able but whether the LORD is with him.

Shall be put to death. The clause is severe. In a covenant nation crossing into war, rebellion against God’s appointed leader was rebellion against God, and the penalty shows how seriously the arrangement was meant. Here the Old Testament feels a long way from a Sunday morning, and the distance is real: the mediator now is not a man with an army but a Son with a cross, and to reject him is a graver thing, not a lighter one (Hebrews 10:28–29).

Only be strong and courageous. The last words of the chapter are God’s own. He said them to Joshua three times, and now the people say them back to him. That is how courage travels. It begins in the mouth of God, is spoken over one frightened man, and comes back to him from the people he is to lead. When we repeat God’s promises to a tired leader or a frightened friend, we give them nothing of our own and nothing less than God’s word.

1.theology:
Grace before duty. The land is given in verse 3 before a foot has touched it. That order is never reversed in Scripture, and it is the whole difference between obedience and bargaining.

The sufficiency of God's presence. The promise of verses 5 and 9 is the foundation of the book: presence, not exemption.

The Word as the source of strength. Meditation is commanded before strategy (v. 8), and the 'good success' promised is the success of this commission.

No one rests alone. Being settled does not excuse us from a brother’s battle (v. 15).
1.examples:
Then: A nation stood at a river with its leader newly buried and walled cities ahead, with no army to match Canaan's, only a sentence spoken over them: I have given to you (1:3).

Now: The cure for fear here is not a change of circumstances but a presence and a book. When a person dies, a job ends, or a diagnosis lands, the promise is not that the river will be easier but that the same God will be on both banks. If you are waiting for a change in the facts before you will be at peace, this chapter offers something else, and calls it better.

keyVerse.quote: Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.
keyVerse.note: The third and fullest form of the chapter’s command gives its deepest ground: not Joshua’s strength, nor even the promised outcome, but the LORD’s presence wherever he goes. It is the promise Christ makes to all his people (Matthew 28:20), and it turns courage from a temperament into an act of faith.

1.reflection:
Joshua spent some forty years as “Moses’ assistant” before God called him to lead. What hidden or unnoticed seasons has God used in your life, and how does the example of Christ’s thirty quiet years change the way you see them?

God says “I have given” (v. 3) before Israel has fought a single battle. How does knowing that our standing with God is already given in Christ change the way we fight against sin or face hard tasks?

The command to be courageous is tied to keeping and meditating on God’s word (vv. 7–8). What helps or hinders you in taking God’s word in slowly, and what one step could you take this week?

The eastern tribes had to fight “until the LORD gives rest to your brothers” (v. 15). Who in your church or circle is still in a battle while you are settled, and what would it mean to cross the river for them?

2.title: Rahab and the Spies
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun sent two men secretly from Shittim as spies, saying, "Go, view the land, especially Jericho." And they went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab and lodged there.<sup>2</sup>And it was told to the king of Jericho, "Behold, men of Israel have come here tonight to search out the land."<sup>3</sup>Then the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, "Bring out the men who have come to you, who entered your house, for they have come to search out all the land."<sup>4</sup>But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. And she said, "True, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from.<sup>5</sup>And when the gate was about to be closed at dark, the men went out. I do not know where the men went. Pursue them quickly, for you will overtake them."<sup>6</sup>But she had brought them up to the roof and hid them with the stalks of flax that she had laid in order on the roof.<sup>7</sup>So the men pursued after them on the way to the Jordan as far as the fords. And the gate was shut as soon as the pursuers had gone out.<sup>8</sup>Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof<sup>9</sup>and said to the men, "I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.<sup>10</sup>For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and Og, whom you devoted to destruction.<sup>11</sup>And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.<sup>12</sup>Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that, as I have dealt kindly with you, you also will deal kindly with my father's house, and give me a sure sign<sup>13</sup>that you will save alive my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and deliver our lives from death."<sup>14</sup>And the men said to her, "Our life for yours even to death! If you do not tell this business of ours, then when the LORD gives us the land we will deal kindly and faithfully with you."<sup>15</sup>Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was built into the city wall, so that she lived in the wall.<sup>16</sup>And she said to them, "Go into the hills, or the pursuers will encounter you, and hide there three days until the pursuers have returned. Then afterward you may go your way."<sup>17</sup>The men said to her, "We will be guiltless with respect to this oath of yours that you have made us swear.<sup>18</sup>Behold, when we come into the land, you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down, and you shall gather into your house your father and mother, your brothers, and all your father's household.<sup>19</sup>Then if anyone goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood shall be on his own head, and we shall be guiltless. But if a hand is laid on anyone who is with you in the house, his blood shall be on our head.<sup>20</sup>But if you tell this business of ours, then we shall be guiltless with respect to your oath that you have made us swear."<sup>21</sup>And she said, "According to your words, so be it." Then she sent them away, and they departed. And she tied the scarlet cord in the window.<sup>22</sup>They departed and went into the hills and remained there three days until the pursuers returned, and the pursuers searched all along the way and found nothing.<sup>23</sup>Then the two men returned. They came down from the hills and passed over and came to Joshua the son of Nun, and they told him all that had happened to them.<sup>24</sup>And they said to Joshua, "Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands. And also, all the inhabitants of the land melt away because of us."
2.overview:
Where we are. Joshua has received his charge and the camp is preparing to cross the Jordan (chapter 1). Now two spies go to Jericho, and the story turns from an army to one house in the city wall.

The message. Before God gives Israel a single city, he saves a Canaanite prostitute who believes. The judgment coming on Jericho is real, but so is the door of mercy: whoever hears what the LORD has done, fears him, confesses him and takes refuge under his promise will be spared. The conquest of Canaan opens with a conversion.

Why it was said. Israel was about to fight peoples whose wickedness had ripened for judgment (see the introduction), and could easily have concluded that God’s favour ran along lines of blood. Rahab shows that it never did. In chapter 7 an Israelite, Achan, will perish while this Canaanite is brought in, because what matters is faith in the LORD.

How the chapter makes its case. The spies lodge in Rahab’s house, and when the king demands them she hides them under flax on her roof and sends his men towards the fords (vv. 1–7). On the roof she confesses that the LORD has given the land and that “the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath” (vv. 8–11). She asks for her family’s lives, and the spies pledge theirs for hers (vv. 12–14). She lets them down the wall, and they set the terms: a scarlet cord in the window, the family inside, no one going out (vv. 15–21). The spies return with a report that repeats God’s own word (vv. 22–24).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by the character of God the chapter reveals and the need it exposes. Rahab had no claim on God. She asked for his loyal covenant love and received it, and Matthew writes her into the family tree of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), a Canaanite woman among the ancestors of the Saviour of the nations. Her rescue follows the shape of the gospel: judgment certain, a sign on the house, refuge in one place only, and a life pledged for hers. “By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient” (Hebrews 11:31).

For us. No one is too far outside, too stained or too late to call on the name of the LORD. Faith hears what God has done in Christ, believes it and takes refuge under his promise without waiting for the walls to fall; and its first prayers reach for the people under its own roof.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Spies Sheltered and Hidden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith acts before the crisis, and it acts at a cost. Joshua sends two spies quietly to Jericho, and they lodge in the house of a prostitute named Rahab (v. 1). Their arrival is reported at once, and the king’s men come to her door to demand them (vv. 2–3). She has already hidden them under stalks of flax on her roof, and she sends the pursuers off towards the fords of the Jordan while the city gate shuts behind them (vv. 4–7). Rahab had chosen her side before the knock came: away from her king, towards a God she had only heard about.
verseByVerse.theology: Rahab is not improvising under pressure: she had chosen a side while there was still time to choose the other one (see v. 6).
verseByVerse.examples: Whatever is said about her lie (see below), what is beyond dispute is the direction she moved: away from her king, towards a God she had only heard about.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua the son of Nun sent two men secretly from Shittim as spies, saying, "Go, view the land, especially Jericho." And they went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab and lodged there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua sends two spies quietly to Jericho, and they come to the house of a prostitute named Rahab: the one door in the city behind which somebody was ready to believe.

Sent two men secretly … as spies. The last time Israel sent spies into this country there were twelve of them, their report was made in public, and it cost the nation forty years (Numbers 13–14). Joshua was one of the two who came back telling the truth, and he has learned that a scouting report is for the leader’s ears, not the crowd’s. Jericho is named above the rest because of where it stood: at the foot of the passes that climb from the Jordan valley into the hill country, so that no army could go up into the land with that city left behind it.

A prostitute whose name was Rahab. Where they end up is the surprise, and the narrator says it flatly, without euphemism and without a sneer. Some ancient Jewish interpreters softened the word to “innkeeper”, but the Hebrew is the ordinary word for a prostitute, and the New Testament keeps it.

Why this house. There were practical reasons. A house where strangers came and went at night attracted no attention, and a house built into the city wall had a window on the outside (v. 15). But the practical explanation runs out quickly: of all the doors in Jericho, these two men walked through the only one behind which somebody was ready to believe.

How Scripture remembers her. Scripture never tidies her up. Both New Testament writers who praise her keep the word: “Rahab the prostitute” (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). And the genealogy of Jesus names her, without explanation, as the wife of Salmon and mother of Boaz (Matthew 1:5). Taken as written, that makes this woman David’s great-great-grandmother (ancient genealogies sometimes skip generations, so there may be more links than are written) and an ancestor of Christ. The Son of God was not ashamed to have Rahab in his family.
verseByVerse.note: Shittim lay on the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho, some miles east of the river.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was told to the king of Jericho, "Behold, men of Israel have come here tonight to search out the land." Then the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, "Bring out the men who have come to you, who entered your house, for they have come to search out all the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king hears of the spies within hours and demands them from Rahab, forcing on her a choice between her city and a God she has only heard about.

It was told to the king of Jericho. The king’s information is good and fast. The spies have been in the city a matter of hours and the king already knows the house. Jericho is a frightened city watching its own gates, and frightened cities are observant.

Bring out the men. The demand comes straight to Rahab, and it puts her in an impossible position. Handing over two foreigners costs her nothing and is what any loyal citizen would do. Refusing is treason, and treason inside a walled city expecting attack has one penalty.

What she had to weigh. On one side: her city, her king, her neighbours, her livelihood and the roof over her family’s heads. On the other: reports about a God she has never seen, whose people are camped across the river and have not yet won a single battle on this side of it. Everyone in Jericho had the same information; the whole city had heard about the Red Sea. What separates Rahab from her king is not that she knew more, but what she did in the ten seconds after the knock.

verseByVerse.quote: But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. And she said, "True, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from. And when the gate was about to be closed at dark, the men went out. I do not know where the men went. Pursue them quickly, for you will overtake them." But she had brought them up to the roof and hid them with the stalks of flax that she had laid in order on the roof. So the men pursued after them on the way to the Jordan as far as the fords. And the gate was shut as soon as the pursuers had gone out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rahab hides the spies and sends the king’s men the wrong way, having settled her loyalty before they ever knocked.

She had brought them up to the roof. Verse 6 is told out of order on purpose: “she had brought them up” means the decision was not made under questioning but earlier, when there was still time to make the other one. Faith that survives a crisis is nearly always faith that settled the question before the crisis arrived.

The stalks of flax. Flax stalks were spread on flat roofs to dry before being worked into linen: ordinary household work in progress. She had two grown men under it before the soldiers came; she had planned the hiding place beforehand.

The lie. Then she deceives the king’s men in detail, with a false direction and a note of urgency. This is the honest difficulty of the chapter, and Christians have answered it in two ways.

Where Christians differ. Augustine and Calvin held that every lie is sin, which God may forgive and overrule: Scripture commends Rahab’s faith and her protection of the spies (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25), never her words, and God accepted the genuine service of a believer a few days old without approving every part of it, a mercy the rest of us live on. Others hold that deceiving those bent on murder is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids, which is false witness against a neighbour.

This commentary’s view. The second view is the more likely. Rahab owed no truth to men coming to kill God’s servants, as the Hebrew midwives owed none to Pharaoh (Exodus 1:19), and Christians who hid Jews from the Gestapo stood where she stood. Ordinary life is another matter: “Do not lie to one another” (Colossians 3:9).
verseByVerse.note: Once dried, flax stalks were soaked and beaten to free the fibres spun into linen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Confession on the Roof
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith comes by hearing, and here is what it sounds like when hearing is all there is. On the roof Rahab tells the spies what she knows: the LORD has given them the land (v. 9). She gives her evidence, the drying of the Red Sea and the defeat of Sihon and Og, and admits that Jericho’s heart, her own included, has melted (vv. 10–11). Then she confesses the LORD as God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath, and asks for an oath of kindness for her whole family (vv. 11–13). The spies pledge their own lives for hers (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: She has no Scripture, no covenant, no priest and no temple, and out of a rumour she has reached a conclusion that half of Israel had failed to reach in the wilderness. Faith comes by hearing, and this is what it sounds like when the hearing is all there is.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who feels they have no claim on God may ask what Rahab asked, and on the same terms: not merit, but mercy promised on oath.

verseByVerse.quote: Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof and said to the men, "I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rahab says with certainty what God had told Joshua, that the land is already given, and she calls Israel’s God by his own name, the LORD.

I know that the LORD has given you the land. She cannot wait until morning. “I know”: not “I suspect” or “I have heard it said”. And what she knows is what God said to Joshua a chapter earlier (1:3). A Canaanite on a roof in Jericho and the LORD on the far bank of the Jordan are using the same sentence.

The LORD. She also uses the covenant name. Not “your god” or “the god of the Hebrews”, as everyone else in the region would speak, but the LORD, the name given to Moses at the bush. When the ESV prints LORD in capitals, it stands for God’s own name, YHWH, which he explained when he gave it: “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14). A name means he can be known, spoken to and called on, and that he has bound himself to people by promise. See Lord in the Theological Dictionary.

All the inhabitants of the land melt away. Her reading of the situation is more accurate than her king’s, and she gives the reason without flattering the men in front of her. It is not the Israelite army that has frightened the country; Israel has been wandering for forty years. What has fallen on Jericho is “the fear of you”, and behind it stands the song Israel sang at the Red Sea: “all the inhabitants of Canaan have melted away. Terror and dread fall upon them” (Exodus 15:15–16). She is watching that song come true, as one of those it was sung about.

Call him by his name. Most people think of God the way Jericho did, as a vague power out there, to be feared or kept at a distance. Rahab grasped that she was not bargaining with a force but asking a Person who keeps his word. And the name came, in the end, to wear a face. Jesus said, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), and the apostles gave the prophet’s promise to him: “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). Nobody has to be the right kind of person to use that name, as a woman in the wall of Jericho found. So when you pray, do not aim your words at “someone up there”. Call him by the name he gave, and ask him to be to you what he said he is.

verseByVerse.quote: For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and Og, whom you devoted to destruction. And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rahab heard the same news as everyone in Jericho and was as frightened as everyone else, but she drew the right conclusion: the LORD is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.

For we have heard. Her evidence has two items, one forty years old and hundreds of miles away, the other recent and local: the drying of the Red Sea, and the defeat of Sihon and Og east of the Jordan (Numbers 21:21–35). Both had been carried up the trade routes by men with no interest in converting anybody.

Our hearts melted. This clause is often misquoted, as if Jericho melted in terror while Rahab melted in faith. The verse does not say that. She says “our hearts melted”, and “there was no spirit left in any man”; she is inside that description, not outside it. That settles what faith is and is not. Faith here is not a steadier nervous system or a braver temperament; it is what one melted heart did with its melting. Everyone else in that city took the same terror and locked the gate. She took it upstairs and asked for mercy.

He is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath. Then the summit of the chapter, and one of the great confessions of the Old Testament. It is not a compliment paid to a strong local deity; it denies that there is any other god, in heaven or on earth. It is almost word for word what Moses had told Israel to know and lay to heart (Deuteronomy 4:39). She had never read Deuteronomy and nobody had taught her, yet she reached the truth that Israel, with all its privileges, still had to be persuaded of.

Is changing your faith a betrayal of your people? Many feel that it is. Religion, we assume, is part of where you come from, like a language or a cuisine, and leaving your family’s gods looks like disloyalty. By Jericho’s lights Rahab was a traitor, and she knew it. But notice what she actually leaves. Not her family: she spends the next verses trying to bring every one of them with her. Not her name or her past: Scripture keeps both, and Matthew writes her, a Canaanite, into the family of the Messiah. What she leaves is a god who could not save her city and a king who was about to fall. The gospel has always worked this way. It does not ask anyone to stop being a Canaanite, a Greek or an Englishman; it asks them to stop worshipping what cannot save, and it promises that the kings of the earth will one day bring “their glory” into the city of God (Revelation 21:24). Conversion is not trading one tribe for another. It is coming home to the Maker of every tribe, and bringing your people with you if you can.
verseByVerse.note: “Devoted to destruction” means set apart to the LORD for destruction (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that, as I have dealt kindly with you, you also will deal kindly with my father's house, and give me a sure sign that you will save alive my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and deliver our lives from death." And the men said to her, "Our life for yours even to death! If you do not tell this business of ours, then when the LORD gives us the land we will deal kindly and faithfully with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rahab’s confession turns at once into a plea for mercy for her whole family, and the spies answer by pledging their own lives for hers.

Please swear to me by the LORD. Confession turns immediately into asking, which is the order faith always runs in. She has said who God is; now she asks him for something, and it is her family’s lives.

As I have dealt kindly with you. The word behind “deal kindly” is hesed, one of the great words of the Old Testament: loyal love, the settled kindness of someone bound by covenant. It is what God shows Israel. Rahab asks a God who was foreign to her for the love he gives his own family, and she asks it as a Canaanite with no claim on him whatever.

My father and mother, my brothers and sisters. The request is wide. Her first instinct is to get everyone she is related to under the same roof; salvation in this chapter is never a private arrangement, and a believer’s first prayers still run the same way.

Our life for yours even to death! The oath is startling. Two Israelite soldiers pledge their own lives as the guarantee of a Canaanite prostitute’s: if she dies, they die.

Answered with a life laid down. A woman with no standing asked for mercy and was answered with a life pledged as the price of hers. Many Christians have heard in that room an echo of the gospel, in which Christ laid down his own life for people who had no claim on him. The text does not make the spies a picture of Christ, and they had no idea of any such thing; but the echo is a fair one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The terms of mercy are simple and exact, so that no one need guess how to be safe. Rahab lets the spies down through her window in the city wall and tells them to hide in the hills for three days (vv. 15–16). They set the conditions of the oath: the scarlet cord tied in that window, her whole family gathered inside, and no one stepping out into the street; and she must keep their business to herself (vv. 17–20). She agrees without bargaining, sends them away and ties the cord in the window at once (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The terms are precise, and the precision is a mercy, not meanness: with one sign, one house and one condition, nobody is left guessing how to be safe.
verseByVerse.examples: Rahab's first thought was for her household, and a believer's first prayers still run the same way: for the people under our own roof.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was built into the city wall, so that she lived in the wall. And she said to them, "Go into the hills, or the pursuers will encounter you, and hide there three days until the pursuers have returned. Then afterward you may go your way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rahab lets the spies down from her house in the wall and gives them sound advice: hide in the hills, away from the search, until it is over.

She lived in the wall. The detail is given because the story needs it twice: once now, for the escape, and once later, when the city falls and her house is the one the spies come back to (6:22–25). Houses built into a town wall were probably where the poor and the disreputable lived, which tells you something of where Rahab stood in Jericho. The place that put her on the edge of society is the place that made her useful to God.

Go into the hills. Her advice is not pious. She does not tell the spies that God will protect them. She tells them to go the opposite way, into the hills west of the city, not towards the Jordan where the search has gone, and to sit still for three days until the patrols give up. Faith in this chapter thinks carefully: she has worked out how long a search party stays out and where it will not look. Trusting God has never meant declining to think, and the newest believer in the story is giving sound advice to trained soldiers.
verseByVerse.note: The same house is the one the spies return to when the city falls (6:22–25).

verseByVerse.quote: The men said to her, "We will be guiltless with respect to this oath of yours that you have made us swear. Behold, when we come into the land, you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down, and you shall gather into your house your father and mother, your brothers, and all your father's household. Then if anyone goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood shall be on his own head, and we shall be guiltless. But if a hand is laid on anyone who is with you in the house, his blood shall be on our head. But if you tell this business of ours, then we shall be guiltless with respect to your oath that you have made us swear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spies set three exact terms for Rahab’s rescue: the scarlet cord in the window, the whole family inside the house, and no one going out.

This scarlet cord. The cord may well be the rope she has just used to lower them, the working equipment of the escape left hanging where anyone could see it. With one sign, one house and one condition, nobody is left guessing how to be safe; the precision is a mercy, not meanness.

His blood shall be on his own head. The line is drawn at the doorway. Inside, the spies carry the responsibility; outside, a man carries his own. The arrangement is that of the Passover: a sign on the house, the family indoors, no one to go out, judgment passing over (Exodus 12:22–23).

Salvation with an address. On the day, the only question is which side of a doorway a person is standing on. Grace is free, but it is found in one place. A man who preferred the street was not lost for want of mercy on the day the walls came down; he was simply not in the house. So the gospel still says that salvation is found in Christ and nowhere else (Acts 4:12), and invites everyone in.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for “cord”, tiqvah, appears in this sense only here (vv. 18, 21), and it is spelled exactly like the common word for “hope”. Most scholars think these are two different words that happen to sound alike, the cord being something “stretched”, so the link should not be pressed. But a Hebrew reader could hardly miss the echo: what hung in that window was a line of hope.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said, "According to your words, so be it." Then she sent them away, and they departed. And she tied the scarlet cord in the window.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rahab accepts the terms without bargaining and ties the cord in the window that very day, then waits on the promise while life in Jericho goes on.

According to your words, so be it. She asks for no amendment. Not one clause is negotiated, though she is handing her entire family’s survival to two foreign soldiers on the strength of their word.

She tied the scarlet cord in the window. Then the point of the whole scene: she tied the cord in the window. Not on the morning the trumpets started, not when the dust of an approaching army appeared on the road, but at once, while the spies were still climbing into the hills.

The days of waiting. Consider the days that followed. Jericho carries on. The market opens, the king’s men patrol, and in a window in the wall hangs a red rope that everybody can see and nobody understands. She has to leave it there, and persuade a household of relations, who may well think she has lost her mind, to come indoors and stay there. Every believer knows something of those days: the sign is given, the promise is made, and the world goes on as if nothing had been said.

The rope held. Rahab of Jericho, whose name was a byword in her own street, hung a rope in a window on the strength of a God she had heard about twice, and it held. She walked out of the falling city alive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Same land, same walls, same enemies as forty years before; the difference is in the men who report them. The spies follow Rahab’s advice, wait out the search in the hills and return to Joshua with everything that had happened (vv. 22–23). Their report contains no military facts, only a verdict about who owns the country: “Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands” (v. 24). It is the sentence God spoke to Joshua and Rahab spoke on her roof, and the opposite of the report that once kept Israel out of the land.
verseByVerse.theology: Same land, same walls, same giants as forty years before; the difference is not in the facts but in the men who report them.

verseByVerse.quote: They departed and went into the hills and remained there three days until the pursuers returned, and the pursuers searched all along the way and found nothing. Then the two men returned. They came down from the hills and passed over and came to Joshua the son of Nun, and they told him all that had happened to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spies escape by following Rahab’s advice and tell Joshua everything, and their account of her is why her household will be remembered when the city falls.

Found nothing. Two men on a mission from Israel’s leader take their orders from a Canaanite prostitute and are kept safe by them. The narrator notes that the search found nothing and does not comment further; the chapter is not laying down a rule about lying.

All that had happened to them. This matters more than it looks. The only thing recorded from three days inside enemy territory is not a survey of the defences but a conversation on a roof. That is why, when the city falls, Joshua knows the name of one household and sends the same two men to bring them out (6:22–25). The report saved her family a second time.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to Joshua, "Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands. And also, all the inhabitants of the land melt away because of us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spies’ report contains no military facts, only a verdict of faith: the LORD has given the land, and its people are already beaten in heart.

Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands. There is no estimate of walls or garrison, just a verdict about who owns the country. It is what God said to Joshua (1:3) and what Rahab said on the roof (2:9): the same sentence has travelled from God to a Canaanite to Israel’s scouts unchanged.

Two reports compared. Set it beside the report the last generation brought back from the same country: “We are not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are”, and “we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers” (Numbers 13:31, 33). Same land, same walls; a generation had died in the desert learning the difference.

God at work before Israel came. The LORD who dried a sea forty years before had been working on Jericho ever since, without an army, without a preacher and without a word of written Scripture inside it. By the time Israel arrived, the walls were still standing but the hearts behind them had already given up. He had a woman in that town before he had a soldier on that side of the river.

2.theology:
Grace reaching outside the covenant. Rahab has no claim of any kind. She is the wrong nationality, in the wrong trade, in a city under sentence, and she says out loud what God had said to Joshua, in almost his own words. If the conquest were a story about a deserving nation dispossessing an undeserving one, this chapter could not have been written. That is why it stands where it does, at the front.

A faith that acts, and a faith that is afraid. Rahab is the rare figure cited by Hebrews for faith (11:31) and by James for works (2:25), and both specify the same actions: she welcomed the messengers and sent them out another way. Neither commends the lie. And verse 11 makes her good company for everyone who has ever been frightened: faith here is not the absence of fear but what a melted heart does next.

The cord, the house, and the line at the door. The text never calls the scarlet cord blood and never mentions the Passover, so the connection should be made the way the text makes it, by the shape of the arrangement. A marked house, a family gathered inside, an instruction that no one go out, a judgment passing over: every element recurs. The Passover blood itself pointed to Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19), and many Christians have heard in the scarlet cord an echo of that blood. It is a fair echo so long as it stays an echo: the text's own point is the shelter of a marked house, and it never explains the cord's colour.

The conquest is God's before it is Israel's. No Israelite preached in Jericho, and no army had yet crossed the river, yet the city's courage was already spent (v. 24).
2.examples:
Then: A woman in a doomed city heard what God had done at a sea she had never seen, believed it, hid two enemy soldiers on her roof, and hung a red rope in her window. Then she lived under it for weeks, in a town going about its business, arguing her relatives indoors on the word of two men who had gone away and promised to come back.

Now: That is the position of every Christian between the promise and its keeping — living under a sign, in a world carrying on as normal, on the word of someone who has left and said he will return. Rahab's evidence was two pieces of news about what God had done in history; ours is a tomb that did not stay shut. She was saved not by her courage but by the mercy she asked for, and the same mercy is held out to us in Christ. If you are still waiting for more before you will trust him, remember that she had less information than anyone reading this, and she tied the cord that night.

keyVerse.quote: And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.
keyVerse.note: Rahab’s confession is the summit of the chapter. She was as frightened as the rest of Jericho, but she drew the conclusion they refused: the LORD is the only God, in heaven and on earth. Out of a report and a melted heart came saving faith, the faith Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25 remember.

2.reflection:
Everyone in Jericho heard the same news about the LORD, yet only Rahab acted on it (vv. 9–11). What makes the difference between knowing about God and turning to him? Where have you seen fear lead people towards God or away from him?

Scripture keeps calling her “Rahab the prostitute”, even while praising her faith, and Matthew puts her in the family line of Jesus. What does this teach us about God’s grace, and about how we see people with a past, including ourselves?

Rahab’s first request was for her family (vv. 12–13). Who are the people under your roof or in your circle you most long to see safe in Christ, and how could we pray for them together?

The terms of rescue were simple: one sign, one house, stay inside (vv. 17–20). How does this picture help us explain to someone that salvation is found in Christ alone, and why is that good news rather than narrow?

3.title: Crossing the Jordan
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Joshua rose early in the morning and they set out from Shittim. And they came to the Jordan, he and all the people of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over.<sup>2</sup>At the end of three days the officers went through the camp<sup>3</sup>and commanded the people, "As soon as you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you shall set out from your place and follow it.<sup>4</sup>Yet there shall be a distance between you and it, about 2,000 cubits in length. Do not come near it, in order that you may know the way you shall go, for you have not passed this way before."<sup>5</sup>Then Joshua said to the people, "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you."<sup>6</sup>And Joshua said to the priests, "Take up the ark of the covenant and pass on before the people." So they took up the ark of the covenant and went before the people.<sup>7</sup>The LORD said to Joshua, "Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.<sup>8</sup>And as for you, command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, 'When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan.'"<sup>9</sup>And Joshua said to the people of Israel, "Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God."<sup>10</sup>And Joshua said, "Here is how you shall know that the living God is among you and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, and the Jebusites.<sup>11</sup>Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you into the Jordan.<sup>12</sup>Now therefore take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, from each tribe a man.<sup>13</sup>And when the soles of the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the LORD, the Lord of all the earth, shall rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off from flowing, and the waters coming down from above shall stand in one heap."<sup>14</sup>So when the people set out from their tents to pass over the Jordan with the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people,<sup>15</sup>and as soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water (now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest),<sup>16</sup>the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan, and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off. And the people passed over opposite Jericho.<sup>17</sup>Now the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan.
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1 and 2 prepared for the crossing. Now, after three days on the bank, Israel faces the Jordan in flood, the last barrier between the wilderness and the promise.

The message. The God who brought his people out is the God who brings them in. He goes ahead of them, in the ark of his covenant, into water nobody could cross; the river stops the moment the priests’ feet touch it, and the ark stays in the riverbed until the whole nation is over. The crossing proves that “the living God is among you” (v. 10), the Lord of all the earth, and that he will keep his promises to the last name on the list.

Why it was said. Forty years earlier their parents had walked through the Red Sea on dry ground. This generation had only heard the story, and was following a new leader into a land of walled cities (see the introduction). They needed to know that their parents’ God was theirs, and that Joshua was his man, before they faced Jericho.

How the chapter makes its case. Israel camps by the river and is told to follow the ark at a distance and to consecrate themselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders (vv. 1–6). God promises to exalt Joshua, and Joshua tells the people what the crossing will prove: the living God is among them, and the ark of the Lord of all the earth is going ahead of them (vv. 7–13). Then, in the harvest flood, the priests’ feet touch the water, the river stands in a heap far upstream, and all Israel crosses on dry ground while the priests stand firm in the middle (vv. 14–17).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. The ark, the sign of God’s throne and covenant among his people, goes first into the waters and stays there until every last one is across. So the Son of God went ahead of his people into the deep waters of death, and lost none of those the Father had given him (John 18:9). Christians have long sung of the Jordan as a picture of death, and not without reason: our great high priest has gone through ahead of us (Hebrews 4:14).

For us. We are often asked to walk a road we have never walked before (v. 4). We are not required to see the way, only to keep Christ in view, to step out on his word before the water parts, and to trust that he will not leave the river until the last and slowest of his people are safely over.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people are not asked to know the route, only to keep the ark in sight. Joshua leads Israel from Shittim to the bank of the Jordan, where they wait three days within sight of a river they cannot cross (vv. 1–2). Then the officers give the order: when the priests carry the ark of the covenant, set out and follow it, keeping a distance of about 2,000 cubits so that everyone can see the way, “for you have not passed this way before” (vv. 3–4).
