The people are to consecrate themselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders (v. 5), and the ark goes out ahead of them all (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The people were not asked to know the route; they were asked to keep the ark in sight.
verseByVerse.examples: A believer facing a road never walked before, a new country, a bereavement, an illness, is not required to know the way, only to keep the Lord in view.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua rose early in the morning and they set out from Shittim. And they came to the Jordan, he and all the people of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over. At the end of three days the officers went through the camp and commanded the people, "As soon as you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you shall set out from your place and follow it. Yet there shall be a distance between you and it, about 2,000 cubits in length. Do not come near it, in order that you may know the way you shall go, for you have not passed this way before."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel waits three days by the river and is then told to follow the ark at a distance, because nobody has walked this road before and everyone must be able to see where God is going.

Lodged there before they passed over. They camp on the bank, and the order to move comes only “at the end of three days” (v. 2). These days, the three of 1:11 and the spies’ three days in the hills (2:22) probably overlap; the writer does not stop to fit them together. Whatever faith this generation had, it had to survive those days within sight of a river it could not cross.

The ark of the covenant of the LORD your God. The ark was the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law: the sign of God’s covenant, his binding promise to Israel and his claim on it, and of his throne among them. It is carried by the Levitical priests.

Follow it … for you have not passed this way before. This is the tender reason in the chapter. Nobody in that column knew the road, and there was no veteran to ask. They are not told to work it out. They are told to keep something in sight and walk after it.

About 2,000 cubits. The gap, about half a mile (see Cubit), is the detail nobody would invent, and it does two jobs. It keeps the ark visible to every family in a long column: the person at the back can see where God is going. And it keeps everyone well out of arm’s reach of it. Near enough to follow, far enough to fear: that is the whole life of faith, close to God and in awe of him.
verseByVerse.note: Two thousand cubits is about 1,000 yards, a little over half a mile.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua said to the people, "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you." And Joshua said to the priests, "Take up the ark of the covenant and pass on before the people." So they took up the ark of the covenant and went before the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The night before the crossing is given to holiness, not planning, because God has promised to act tomorrow; then the ark, the sign of his throne, goes first towards the water.

Consecrate yourselves. Before the river, a wash. Consecration probably meant what it had meant at Sinai (Exodus 19:10, 14–15): garments washed, households put in order, a night spent getting ready to meet God. As military preparation it is startling.

Tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you. Joshua does not say “may” but “will”, and puts a date on it in front of the whole nation. The consecration answers a promise; it does not buy one.

Pass on before the people. The most protected object in Israel, normally screened behind a curtain, goes first, towards the water. God does not send his people anywhere he has not gone, and the order of march is the order of the gospel: God’s presence goes in front, and his people follow onto ground they have never walked, as Christ goes before his sheep (John 10:4).

What this looks like. The washing was for Israel’s camp, but the New Testament carries the principle over: “Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God” (2 Corinthians 7:1). Notice the order: promises first, then cleansing. Get ready the night before. Before Sunday, or a hard decision or conversation, give time to God and not only to preparation. Put things in order. Confess the sin you know about, send the apology, delete what should not be on the phone: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24). Expect him to act. Consecration is getting ready for a promise, not bargaining for one. And the cleansing itself is a gift: we come “with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22), because “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The Living God Among You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the miracle, God says what it will mean. He will begin to exalt Joshua, so that Israel may know he is with him as he was with Moses (v. 7), and the priests carrying the ark are to walk into the river and stand still (v. 8). Joshua gathers the people to hear God’s word: the crossing will show that the living God is among them and will drive out every nation of Canaan (vv. 9–10). The ark of “the Lord of all the earth” goes first, twelve men are chosen, and the promise is made exact: when the priests’ feet rest in the water, the river will stop and stand in one heap (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The title in verses 11 and 13, the Lord of all the earth, settles the question the whole book raises: by what right does Israel take this land?
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 13 asks for the first step to be taken before anything has changed, which is where faith is usually tested.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Joshua, "Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. And as for you, command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, 'When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan.'" And Joshua said to the people of Israel, "Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God." And Joshua said, "Here is how you shall know that the living God is among you and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, and the Jebusites. Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you into the Jordan. Now therefore take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, from each tribe a man. And when the soles of the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the LORD, the Lord of all the earth, shall rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off from flowing, and the waters coming down from above shall stand in one heap."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the miracle God tells Israel what it will prove: that he is with Joshua as he was with Moses, that the living God is among them, and that as Lord of all the earth he will keep every promise about the land.

That they may know. The exaltation is not for Joshua’s benefit; it is so that “they may know”. A nation that had followed Moses through one body of water now has to learn to follow somebody else, and God gives them the evidence before he asks for the trust.

You shall stand still in the Jordan. The priests are not told to cross but to walk into a flooding river and stop. Standing still in the bed of a river in spate, holding the ark, while a nation files past, is a harder assignment than running across.

The living God … the Lord of all the earth. Neither title is decoration. “The living God” is set against the gods of the land they are entering, which are carved and carried and can do nothing (Isaiah 44:9–20). “The Lord of all the earth” answers the question the conquest raises. If Israel’s God were a regional deity, this would be one tribe taking another’s land. But he owns the earth, so the conquest, hard as it is to read, is not theft: it is the owner’s judgment on those who lived in his land. The seven peoples named in verse 10 are the standard roll of Canaan’s inhabitants (Deuteronomy 7:1), and the crossing is a pledge that the promise will be kept down to the last name on the list.

Take twelve men. Their task is not explained until 4:1–8. God is already planning the memorial before the miracle has happened.

Unlike the Red Sea. The difference from the Red Sea is stated in advance so that nobody can miss it. At the sea, Moses stretched out his hand, the water divided, and then Israel walked in (Exodus 14:21–22). At the Jordan the water goes on flowing until there are feet in it.

Joshua and Jesus. Hebrews sets Joshua beside Jesus (Hebrews 4:8), and sets Moses beside Christ too, who is faithful over God’s house “as a son”, not as a servant (Hebrews 3:5–6). The God who exalted Joshua at the Jordan has “highly exalted” the greater Joshua, raised from the dead and seated at his right hand (Philippians 2:9).

In everyday life. The promise comes first and the path second, and between them is a step taken with nothing under it but God’s word. That is not a special demand made of priests. It is the ordinary shape of obedience: the evidence usually arrives after the foot goes down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — The Waters Stood in a Heap
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God does exactly what he said, at the worst possible time of year. The people set out behind the ark, and the priests step into a Jordan swollen over its banks with the harvest floods (vv. 14–15). At once the water stops, piling up far upstream at Adam, and the flow down to the Dead Sea is cut off, so that the people cross opposite Jericho (v. 16). The priests stand firm on dry ground in the middle of the riverbed until the whole nation has passed over (v. 17). The crossing echoes the Red Sea, so that a new generation will know that the same God is with them.
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle is dated to the worst possible week of the year, and it echoes the Red Sea so that Israel will know the same God is with them.
verseByVerse.examples: The slowest in the column were not hurried or left: the people who feel they are always at the back are the ones verse 17 was written for.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the people set out from their tents to pass over the Jordan with the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people, and as soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water (now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest), the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan, and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off. And the people passed over opposite Jericho. Now the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the harvest flood, the moment the priests’ feet touch the water, the Jordan stops far upstream, and the priests stand firm in the riverbed until every last Israelite has crossed.

The Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest. The narrator mentions the river’s condition only now, in brackets. God brought them to the river in spring, at the barley harvest, when the snowmelt from the north swells it beyond wading; at other times it could be forded, as the fords of 2:7 show. The timing is not bad luck; it removes every other explanation.

At Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan. The geography is exact enough to check: the water stopped far upstream, and everything below Adam ran on to the Dead Sea, “the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea”, leaving the bed dry for miles. This is a story with a place name in it.

Rose up in a heap. The picture echoes the song Moses sang at the Red Sea: “the floods stood up in a heap” (Exodus 15:8). Their fathers sang about it. They walked on it.

Until all the nation finished passing over. Everything in the chapter has been building to verse 17. The ark does not go across and wait on the far side. It stays until “all the nation” has passed: not most, not the strong and the quick. The priests hold their ground while the last of the people straggle by: the old, the pregnant, the children, the man with the lame leg who has been at the back of the column all his life. The people who feel they are always at the back are the ones this verse was written for.

I have lost not one. The throne of God went down into the riverbed and would not come up until everyone was across. Many Christian hymns have heard in the Jordan a picture of death, and the New Testament gives them a Priest to match. Christ, “a great high priest who has passed through the heavens” (Hebrews 4:14), went down into death itself and keeps every last one the Father has given him: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one” (John 18:9).

Natural causes and the miracle. Some explain the crossing by a landslide damming the Jordan upstream near Adam, as has happened in later centuries. Even if God used such a means, the timing is the miracle: the water stopped the moment the priests’ feet touched it, in flood season, and returned the moment they came out (4:18).

Uncertain wording. Adam is usually identified with Tell ed-Damiyeh, near where the Jabbok joins the Jordan, some sixteen miles (about 25 km) upstream. Zarethan, named to locate it, appears again near Succoth (1 Kings 7:46), but its site is unknown. The sense is clear: the water was held back a long way north.
verseByVerse.note: Adam was probably Tell ed-Damiyeh, a town about 16 miles upstream.

3.theology:
The presence goes first. The ark leads, and the reason given is that the people do not know the way (v. 4).

The step before the sight. The promise is exact and it is conditional on a movement: when the soles of the priests' feet rest in the waters, the Jordan shall be cut off (v. 13). Had they waited on the bank for the river to open first, they would still be there.

The Lord of all the earth. The title is given twice at the crossing (vv. 11, 13), before a single Canaanite city falls, and the rightness of the whole conquest rests on it. The owner may give or judge as he wills, and Scripture adds that he waited centuries before judging (Genesis 15:16).

The ark in the riverbed. The priests hold the ground until the slowest child is across (v. 17), and in them Christians hear a greater Priest who loses none of his own.
3.examples:
Then: A nation stood on a bank in the barley harvest, looking at a river in flood, with no boats and no bridge, and was told to follow a gold box into it.

Now: Much of what God asks of a Christian is asked at that spot, and the difficulty is the order of events: we would like the river opened and then to walk. The step is not taken alone: the God who has gone ahead in Christ goes with us by his Spirit, and when we have hung back on the bank, his mercy calls us again rather than leaving us there. The water moved when there were feet in it, and not one moment sooner.

keyVerse.quote: Now the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter builds to this verse. God’s presence, carried in the ark, did not cross and wait on the far side but stood in the riverbed until the last Israelite was over. It is a picture of the Saviour who goes into the waters ahead of his people and loses none of them (John 18:9).

3.reflection:
Israel was told to follow the ark “for you have not passed this way before” (v. 4). What unfamiliar road are you facing now, and what does it mean in practice to keep Christ in view rather than to know the whole route?

The night before the crossing was given to consecration, not planning (v. 5). Why does God call his people to holiness before he acts for them, and how does 2 Corinthians 7:1 put the promise before the cleansing?

The priests had to step into the flooding river before it stopped (vv. 13, 15). Can you think of a time when you had to obey God before you could see how things would work out? What happened?

The ark stayed in the riverbed until “all the nation finished passing over” (v. 17). How does this picture comfort those who feel they are always at the back, and how does it point to Christ’s care for his people in life and in death?

4.title: The Twelve Memorial Stones
4.text: <sup>1</sup>When all the nation had finished passing over the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>2</sup>"Take twelve men from the people, from each tribe a man,<sup>3</sup>and command them, saying, 'Take twelve stones from here out of the midst of the Jordan, from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly, and bring them over with you and lay them down in the place where you lodge tonight.'"<sup>4</sup>Then Joshua called the twelve men from the people of Israel, whom he had appointed, a man from each tribe.<sup>5</sup>And Joshua said to them, "Pass on before the ark of the LORD your God into the midst of the Jordan, and take up each of you a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel,<sup>6</sup>that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?'<sup>7</sup>then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it passed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. So these stones shall be to the people of Israel a memorial forever."<sup>8</sup>And the people of Israel did just as Joshua commanded and took up twelve stones out of the midst of the Jordan, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel, just as the LORD told Joshua. And they carried them over with them to the place where they lodged and laid them down there.<sup>9</sup>And Joshua set up twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there to this day.<sup>10</sup>For the priests bearing the ark stood in the midst of the Jordan until everything was finished that the LORD commanded Joshua to tell the people, according to all that Moses had commanded Joshua. The people passed over in haste.<sup>11</sup>And when all the people had finished passing over, the ark of the LORD and the priests passed over before the people.<sup>12</sup>The sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh passed over armed before the people of Israel, as Moses had told them.<sup>13</sup>About 40,000 ready for war passed over before the LORD for battle, to the plains of Jericho.<sup>14</sup>On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they stood in awe of him just as they had stood in awe of Moses, all the days of his life.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>16</sup>"Command the priests bearing the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan."<sup>17</sup>So Joshua commanded the priests, "Come up out of the Jordan."<sup>18</sup>And when the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up from the midst of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests' feet were lifted up on dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and overflowed all its banks, as before.<sup>19</sup>The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped at Gilgal on the east border of Jericho.<sup>20</sup>And those twelve stones, which they took out of the Jordan, Joshua set up at Gilgal.<sup>21</sup>And he said to the people of Israel, "When your children ask their fathers in times to come, 'What do these stones mean?'<sup>22</sup>then you shall let your children know, 'Israel passed over this Jordan on dry ground.'<sup>23</sup>For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over,<sup>24</sup>so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever."
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 ended with the priests standing in the dry riverbed until the whole nation had crossed. Chapter 4 tells the crossing again with a new emphasis: before Israel moves against Jericho, God has a memorial built.

The message. What God does for his people is to be remembered and retold, so that every generation knows it was done for them and fears the LORD for ever. Twelve stones from the riverbed, set up at Gilgal, will make children ask, and the answer will be a story with their own name in it: the God who dried up the Red Sea for their parents dried up the Jordan for them. And the purpose reaches beyond Israel, “so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty” (v. 24).

Why it was said. Israel’s besetting sin was forgetting. The generation that saw the Red Sea complained at the first thirst, and Moses had charged parents to tell their children what God had done (Deuteronomy 6:20–25). Within a lifetime of Joshua’s death “there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel” (Judges 2:10).

How the chapter makes its case. Twelve men, one from each tribe, carry stones from where the priests stood, so that children will ask what they mean, and Joshua sets up a second twelve in the riverbed itself (vv. 1–9). The people hurry across, the eastern tribes keep their word, the LORD exalts Joshua, and when the ark comes out last the river returns to flood (vv. 10–18). On the tenth day of the first month Israel camps at Gilgal, the stones go up, and Joshua gives the answer for the children, joining the Jordan to the Red Sea and turning the memorial outward to the nations (vv. 19–24).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern. The ark went into the river first and came out last, so that God’s presence stood between his people and the waters until all were safe; Christ has gone through death ahead of us and will not leave his people in it. And the church has its own Gilgal. The Lord’s Supper is a memorial that makes children ask, and its answer is the greatest crossing of all: “as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26).

For us. Faith is kept alive by remembering. Mark what God has done, tell it to your children as their story too, and let the memory produce not nostalgia but lasting reverence, and a witness that reaches the people around you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Twelve Stones Out of the Riverbed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The battle waits while a monument is built, because what God has done must not be forgotten. As soon as the nation is across, God tells Joshua to have twelve men, one from each tribe, take twelve stones from the very place where the priests’ feet stood in the riverbed and carry them to that night’s camp (vv. 1–5). They are to be a sign: when children ask what the stones mean, they will be told how the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark (vv. 6–7). The people obey (v. 8), and Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, where the priests had stood (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The battle waits while a monument is built: the first order after the miracle is not to advance but to remember.
verseByVerse.examples: Every Christian has some stones of this kind: a mercy that would be forgotten unless it were marked. Name yours, and keep them where you will pass them.

verseByVerse.quote: When all the nation had finished passing over the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua, "Take twelve men from the people, from each tribe a man, and command them, saying, 'Take twelve stones from here out of the midst of the Jordan, from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly, and bring them over with you and lay them down in the place where you lodge tonight.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as the nation is across, before a single soldier moves on Jericho, God orders a memorial: twelve stones from the very spot where the priests stood in the riverbed.

When all the nation had finished passing over. The enemy city is a few miles off, and God’s first instruction is about rocks. What calls for the pause is the human memory. A wonder like this will be vivid for a month, argued about for a year and gone in a generation unless something is done about it, so the first act of Israel in the promised land is to remember the last thing God did.

Take twelve stones from here out of the midst of the Jordan. Not from the bank, which would have been easier, but “from the very place where the priests’ feet stood firmly”: out of the middle of the riverbed, from ground that was dry only because God was standing on it.

From each tribe a man. Each of twelve men carries his own stone on his own shoulder (v. 5). So every tribe in Israel has a man with a wet stone on his back, and nobody in the nation can look at that heap later and say it was somebody else’s deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua called the twelve men from the people of Israel, whom he had appointed, a man from each tribe. And Joshua said to them, "Pass on before the ark of the LORD your God into the midst of the Jordan, and take up each of you a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel, that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?' then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it passed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. So these stones shall be to the people of Israel a memorial forever." And the people of Israel did just as Joshua commanded and took up twelve stones out of the midst of the Jordan, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel, just as the LORD told Joshua. And they carried them over with them to the place where they lodged and laid them down there. And Joshua set up twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The stones are meant to make children ask, so that parents can tell them what God did; and a second set, left in the riverbed, stands where only God can see it.

When your children ask in time to come. The monument is there to start a conversation that has not yet happened: a child not born at the crossing, asking his father what the stones are for. The stones teach nothing on their own; they provoke a question, and a parent answers it. Moses had provided for the same thing: “When your son asks you in time to come, ‘What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the LORD our God has commanded you?’” (Deuteronomy 6:20).

A memorial forever. The answer is short and centres on one thing: the waters were cut off “before the ark of the covenant of the LORD” (v. 7). The stones do not commemorate Israel’s courage or Joshua’s leadership, but God’s presence going ahead of them.

Twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan. The second set nobody will see again: within the hour the flood closes over them. They stand under a running river with nobody but God to look at them, and the narrator’s aside, “they are there to this day”, is written by a man who knows they are invisible and knows they are there.

In everyday life. Much of the evidence in most Christian lives is hidden like those stones: prayers answered that nobody else heard about, sins put to death that nobody knew were alive, a marriage still standing for reasons never explained to anyone. The water goes back over it, and it is still there.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 9 most naturally describes a second set of stones in the riverbed itself, and the ESV and the ancient Greek translation (the Septuagint) read it so. Some translations take it as the stones from the riverbed being set up at Gilgal, making only one set. Either way, the Gilgal stones (v. 20) are the ones meant for the children.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s presence went into the water first and comes out last. The priests stand in the river until everything God commanded is done, and the people hurry across (v. 10); only then does the ark pass over (v. 11). The eastern tribes keep their promise, about 40,000 armed men crossing for battle (vv. 12–13), and the LORD exalts Joshua as he said he would, so that Israel reveres him as it revered Moses (v. 14). Then at God’s command the priests come up, and the moment their feet touch dry ground the river returns and floods its banks as before (vv. 15–18).
verseByVerse.theology: God's presence goes in first into the water (3:6) and comes out last, behind the people (v. 11).
verseByVerse.examples: Because the ark led them in and stayed to see them out, at no point was anybody the last one in the river. Christ's people are never left alone in the water.

verseByVerse.quote: For the priests bearing the ark stood in the midst of the Jordan until everything was finished that the LORD commanded Joshua to tell the people, according to all that Moses had commanded Joshua. The people passed over in haste. And when all the people had finished passing over, the ark of the LORD and the priests passed over before the people. The sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh passed over armed before the people of Israel, as Moses had told them. About 40,000 ready for war passed over before the LORD for battle, to the plains of Jericho. On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they stood in awe of him just as they had stood in awe of Moses, all the days of his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people hurry across while the priests hold their place, the ark comes out last, the eastern tribes keep their word, and God exalts Joshua as he had promised.

The people passed over in haste. With water standing in a heap upstream, every family crossed as fast as it could. The event was glorious and frightening, and the writer lets both stand.

The ark of the LORD and the priests passed over. Only after everyone had crossed did the ark come up, so God’s presence stood between his people and the river until the last was clear. It went into the water first (3:6) and came out last, and nobody was ever the last one left in the river. Christ’s people are never left alone in the water either (Isaiah 43:2).

Passed over armed. The eastern tribes keep the promise they made in chapter 1 (1:16): men who already had their land cross to fight for somebody else’s, and it cost them years.

The LORD exalted Joshua. What God said he would begin (3:7) he did, and the verb is the one to notice: the LORD exalted Joshua. Joshua did not exalt himself; he obeyed an instruction about a river and God did the rest. Peter tells suffering Christians the same: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you” (1 Peter 5:6).

Why only 40,000? The two and a half tribes numbered over 110,000 fighting men (Numbers 26:7, 18, 34). These were picked troops; the rest stayed east of the Jordan to guard families and flocks (1:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, "Command the priests bearing the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan." So Joshua commanded the priests, "Come up out of the Jordan." And when the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up from the midst of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests' feet were lifted up on dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and overflowed all its banks, as before.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The river returns to full flood the instant the priests step out, so the crossing is plainly God’s act, and the way back to the wilderness is closed behind them.

Come up out of the Jordan. God speaks to Joshua; Joshua repeats it to the priests, adding nothing. It is a small picture of leadership in this book: passing on God’s word without altering it.

The waters of the Jordan returned to their place. The river does not seep back over hours. It stopped when feet went in (3:15) and returned at the instant they came out: not an ebb that happened to coincide with a crossing, but a thing that started and stopped on command.

No way back. Then look at what the returning flood does to the way home. Behind them is a river in full flood. The wilderness is now out of reach: every complaint about Egypt, every proposal to go back, every option but forward has been closed by God himself, and he waited to close it until every last one of them was safely on the other side.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — What Do These Stones Mean?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The crossing is dated and explained so that it will never be forgotten. Israel comes up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, the day the Passover lamb was chosen in Egypt, and camps at Gilgal, where Joshua sets up the stones (vv. 19–20). He gives the answer parents are to give when their children ask: Israel crossed this Jordan on dry ground, because the LORD dried it up just as he dried up the Red Sea (vv. 21–23). The purpose looks both outward and inward: that all the peoples of the earth may know his mighty hand, and that Israel may fear the LORD for ever (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: The date links the entry to the Passover, and the stones join two crossings, forty years apart, into one story.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 24 keeps the whole event from turning inward: what God does for his people is meant to be heard about by others.

verseByVerse.quote: The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped at Gilgal on the east border of Jericho. And those twelve stones, which they took out of the Jordan, Joshua set up at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel enters the land on the tenth day of the first month, the day the Passover lamb was chosen in Egypt, and the memorial stones go up in the middle of the camp at Gilgal.

On the tenth day of the first month. The date is not a filing detail. On the tenth day of the first month in Egypt the lamb was chosen, four days before its blood went on the doorframes (Exodus 12:3–7). Forty years later the nation walks into the land on that day, and four days later it keeps the Passover there (5:10). The calendar of their slavery becomes the calendar of their inheritance.

They encamped at Gilgal. The stones go up at Gilgal, on Jericho’s doorstep: not on a hilltop or at a shrine, but in the middle of the camp, where the washing is done and the children play and everyone walks past them a dozen times a day.
verseByVerse.note: The first month is Abib, later called Nisan, in early spring.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the people of Israel, "When your children ask their fathers in times to come, 'What do these stones mean?' then you shall let your children know, 'Israel passed over this Jordan on dry ground.' For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over, so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The stones are to be explained to children as their own story, the Jordan joined to the Red Sea, so that the nations may know God’s mighty hand and Israel may fear him for ever.

What do these stones mean? The question comes round a second time, and now the Red Sea is in the answer. Watch the pronouns, for they carry the point. The Jordan was dried up “for you”; the Red Sea was dried up “for us”. Joshua was a grown man at both. Before a nation most of whom were not born when the sea opened, he puts the two events in one sentence, so that no child grows up thinking God did something for his grandparents and something else, unrelated, for him. The people who came out and the people who came in are one people, and the God who did the one did the other.

So that all the peoples of the earth may know. The last verse turns the monument outward before it turns it inward. The river was dried up so that the news would travel, as it already had to a woman in Jericho (2:10). And the right response to a memorial is not nostalgia but awe, “that you may fear the LORD your God forever”.

The hand of the LORD is mighty. The hand that stopped a flooded river at a town far upstream, held it, and let it go at the moment the last priest stepped out, is mighty. He arranged the whole thing so that a child not yet born would ask a question, and so that a stranger in a foreign country would hear the story and be saved by it. Two rivers, forty years apart, and one hand over both.

How a family teaches faith. Not by handing on a doctrine alone but by handing on a story with the child’s own name in it. Christian parents are given the same charge: “bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). The stones suggest how. Keep your own stones. Write down answered prayers and hard providences, with dates. Welcome the question. “Why do we pray before tea?” or “Why do you go to church when you’re tired?” is not an interruption; it is the moment the stones were for. Tell it as their story. Not only “God helped Grandad” but “This is what Jesus did, and he did it for people like you and me.” Let them see the meal. The Lord’s Supper is the church’s Gilgal: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). A child who watches it and asks what it means is being told of the greatest crossing of all, the one Christ made through death for us.

4.theology:
Memory is commanded, not assumed. God halts a military campaign to build a heap of stones. The same concern runs through the whole Bible and comes at last to the Lord’s Supper: do this in remembrance of me (1 Cor. 11:24-25). Christian memory is not nostalgia; it is a practice with physical objects attached: water, bread, wine, stones.

Faith is handed on in conversations. The arrangement here puts the next generation's faith in the hands of parents answering questions. Moses had made the same provision, and the psalmist describes the chain running four generations deep so that children not yet born would set their hope in God (Ps. 78:4-7). A generation that falls silent puts the next at risk, though God is not limited to parents, as a Canaanite in Jericho shows.

One work, two waters. Joshua puts the Red Sea and the Jordan in the same sentence (v. 23), and the date makes the same point (v. 19). The God who brings people out of slavery and the God who brings them into the inheritance are not two Gods with two projects. Paul reads the sea crossing as a kind of baptism into Moses (1 Cor. 10:1-2), and the same pattern holds for the church: the Saviour who brings his people out of sin's slavery is the one who will bring them into an inheritance kept in heaven for them (1 Peter 1:4).

Salvation aimed at the nations. The stated purpose reaches further than Israel: that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty (v. 24). This is not a private deliverance with a religious souvenir. It is a public act meant to travel.
4.examples: In Israel the story survived because a child asked about a heap of stones and a parent answered beside a cooking fire. The question still has to be answered by somebody who knows the story for himself. What do the children and younger believers around you know of God's deeds: what he did at the cross, and what he has done in your house? The telling is not a burden laid on us to keep the faith alive by our own effort; God gave the question and the answer, and his Spirit uses ordinary words. Most Christians have a Gilgal, a mercy worth marking, that they have never described to anyone, and it is not too late to begin.

keyVerse.quote: so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever.
keyVerse.note: The chapter ends by naming the purpose of the miracle and its memorial, and it faces two ways: outward, so that the nations hear of God’s mighty hand, and inward, so that his people revere him for ever. Remembering what God has done is never meant to end in nostalgia, but in worship and witness.

4.reflection:
God stopped the campaign to have a memorial built before Israel fought a single battle (vv. 1–3). Why do you think remembering mattered so much at that moment? What would your own “stones” be, the mercies of God you most need not to forget?

The stones were meant to make children ask, “What do these stones mean?” (vv. 6, 21). What questions do the children and young people around us ask about our faith, and how can we answer them with a story that includes them?

The second set of stones was hidden under the river, seen only by God (v. 9). What hidden evidences of God’s faithfulness are there in your life, and why might it matter that some witness is seen by God alone?

Joshua joined the Jordan to the Red Sea: “for you” and “for us” (v. 23). How does the Lord’s Supper join Christ’s death long ago to our lives today, and how should verse 24 shape the way we tell others what God has done?

5.title: Circumcision, Passover, and the Commander of the LORD's Army
5.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as all the kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan to the west, and all the kings of the Canaanites who were by the sea, heard that the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan for the people of Israel until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them because of the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>At that time the LORD said to Joshua, "Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time."<sup>3</sup>So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth.<sup>4</sup>And this is the reason why Joshua circumcised them: all the males of the people who came out of Egypt, all the men of war, had died in the wilderness on the way after they had come out of Egypt.<sup>5</sup>Though all the people who came out had been circumcised, yet all the people who were born on the way in the wilderness after they had come out of Egypt had not been circumcised.<sup>6</sup>For the people of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the nation, the men of war who came out of Egypt, perished, because they did not obey the voice of the LORD; the LORD swore to them that he would not let them see the land that the LORD had sworn to their fathers to give to us, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>7</sup>So it was their children, whom he raised up in their place, that Joshua circumcised. For they were uncircumcised, because they had not been circumcised on the way.<sup>8</sup>When the circumcising of the whole nation was finished, they remained in their places in the camp until they were healed.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you." And so the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day.<sup>10</sup>While the people of Israel were encamped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening on the plains of Jericho.<sup>11</sup>And the day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain.<sup>12</sup>And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.<sup>13</sup>When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man was standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. And Joshua went to him and said to him, "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?"<sup>14</sup>And he said, "No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come." And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped and said to him, "What does my lord say to his servant?"<sup>15</sup>And the commander of the LORD's army said to Joshua, "Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so.
5.overview:
Where we are. Israel has crossed the Jordan on dry ground and set up the twelve memorial stones at Gilgal (chapter 4). The army is camped on the plains within sight of Jericho, and the kings of Canaan have just heard what happened at the river.

The message. Before God gives his people a single city, he makes them his own again. The covenant sign is restored, the shame of the past is rolled away, the Passover is kept, and the LORD’s own commander appears with a drawn sword. The conquest will rest not on Israel’s strength or readiness but on Israel belonging to God, and on God leading his own war.

Why it was said. This generation stood at the border where their parents had refused to go in (Numbers 14), without the covenant sign and with forty years of disgrace behind them. Later readers, facing the loss of the land, needed to hear that it is held only by a people who belong to the LORD (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The enemy’s courage melts (v. 1), and in that very week God makes his own army defenceless: every man born in the wilderness is circumcised (vv. 2–8), and God declares the reproach of Egypt rolled away (v. 9). The first Passover in the land is kept, and the manna stops the day after Israel eats the land’s grain (vv. 10–12). Then Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword who refuses to take sides, takes command, receives worship and tells him to remove his sandals (vv. 13–15).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and, this commentary holds, by his own appearing. Circumcision and Passover, the two signs restored here, are both fulfilled in him: believers receive “a circumcision made without hands” (Colossians 2:11), and “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The manna gives way to the land’s grain, as it gives way at last to Jesus, the true bread from heaven (John 6:32–35). And the commander of the LORD’s army is best read as the Son himself before his incarnation: the one who takes command at Jericho is the one who later fought the decisive battle alone, at the cross.

For us. God marks his people as his before he sends them into any battle, and he deals with their shame himself. Christians do not fight in order to become his; we fight as those already circumcised in heart and fed by Christ, under a Commander who is not on our side but asks whether we are on his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Knife Before the Battle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God makes Israel his covenant people again before he gives them a single city, and he does it in the week when they are least able to defend themselves. The kings of Canaan hear of the Jordan and lose all courage (v. 1). Then God orders flint knives: the generation born in the wilderness had never received the covenant sign, for their fathers’ disobedience had left the nation under God’s sentence (vv. 2–7). The whole army lies helpless in the camp until it heals (v. 8), and God declares that he has rolled away the reproach of Egypt, which gives Gilgal its name (v. 9). The covenant is renewed and the shame removed, entirely by God’s hand.
verseByVerse.theology: A generation grew up belonging to God by promise and carrying nothing in their bodies to say so, and the first thing God does with them in the land is put the mark back on.
verseByVerse.examples: When obedience leaves us weak, we are not thereby left unguarded: the God who asks it is also at work in the hearts of those we fear.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as all the kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan to the west, and all the kings of the Canaanites who were by the sea, heard that the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan for the people of Israel until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them because of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
News of the dry riverbed drains every king in Canaan of courage before Israel has struck a blow, in the very week God is about to make his own army helpless.

Their hearts melted. The wording is Rahab’s, almost word for word, from her roof three chapters earlier: “our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you” (2:11). What she reported of her own city has now happened to every king in the land, the Amorites of the hill country and the Canaanites along the coast. Israel has fought no one west of the river: there has been only a river that stopped for an afternoon, and the news travelling faster than the army (compare Exodus 15:14–16).

Weak in the same week. Within days Israel will circumcise every fighting man and lie helpless in the camp. The one week in which a determined attack could have wiped Israel out is the week in which no king in Canaan can bring himself to move. That is how this book says the conquest was won: God empties the enemy of courage in the same week that he empties his own army of strength.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the LORD said to Joshua, "Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time." So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth. And this is the reason why Joshua circumcised them: all the males of the people who came out of Egypt, all the men of war, had died in the wilderness on the way after they had come out of Egypt. Though all the people who came out had been circumcised, yet all the people who were born on the way in the wilderness after they had come out of Egypt had not been circumcised. For the people of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the nation, the men of war who came out of Egypt, perished, because they did not obey the voice of the LORD; the LORD swore to them that he would not let them see the land that the LORD had sworn to their fathers to give to us, a land flowing with milk and honey. So it was their children, whom he raised up in their place, that Joshua circumcised. For they were uncircumcised, because they had not been circumcised on the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s first order in the land is for a knife, not a sword: the generation born in the wilderness must receive the covenant sign their fathers’ unbelief had left undone, because Israel must belong to God before it fights for him.

Make flint knives. Flint, not metal: this is the ancient blade, as when Zipporah took a flint and circumcised her son (Exodus 4:25), the old rite performed the old way. It is the sign God gave Abraham that he and his offspring belonged to God under his covenant (Genesis 17:10–14). A second time does not mean cutting men already circumcised; it means doing again, for the generation born on the journey, what had been done for the generation that came out of Egypt (v. 5).

This is the reason why. The writer does not say exactly why the rite was not kept on the journey, but he sets the lapse beside the reason for the journey: their fathers “did not obey the voice of the LORD”, and God swore they would not see the land (v. 6). It seems the sign lapsed with them, and for forty years Israel was fed and led by God without it. Now the children God “raised up in their place” (v. 7) receive what their parents’ unbelief had left undone.

What this order cost. Think what this costs with Jericho a few miles away. When the men of Shechem were circumcised, Simeon and Levi came on the third day, while they were sore, and killed every male in the city (Genesis 34:25). God tells his army to do to itself, in sight of an enemy stronghold, what once left a whole town defenceless. The conquest will not rest on Israel’s readiness: God will have a people marked as his before he has a people fit to fight.

Belonging before battle. A Christian, likewise, does not fight sin to become God’s; he fights because he already is, sealed by the Spirit as Christ’s own (Ephesians 1:13).
verseByVerse.note: “Gibeath-haaraloth” means “the hill of the foreskins” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: When the circumcising of the whole nation was finished, they remained in their places in the camp until they were healed. And the LORD said to Joshua, "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you." And so the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the whole army lies helpless, God himself declares the disgrace of Israel’s past removed, and the place is named for what he did: Gilgal, “rolling”.

The reproach of Egypt. An entire army lies still in enemy country, and God speaks not about strength but about shame. The disgrace that clung to them from Egypt is the whole weight of what they had been: slaves, and a people whose God had, on the evidence, brought them into a desert and left them there for forty years to die. Moses had twice warned that the Egyptians would say exactly that (Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13–16).

Called Gilgal to this day. Gilgal sounds like the Hebrew for “to roll”. The picture is of a weight the size of a millstone rolled off a nation, in one day, and by God: I have rolled it away. Israel did not answer the taunt; they were not required to. That is the pattern of everything God does about shame: the people concerned lie still, unable to do anything at all, and the weight is moved from outside by someone else.

The circumcision of Christ. The New Testament carries both halves of this scene to Christ. Believers receive “a circumcision made without hands”, the circumcision of Christ (Colossians 2:11), worked in the heart by the Spirit (Romans 2:29). And it speaks of the reproach Christ bore when he “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood”, and calls us to go out to him and “bear the reproach he endured” (Hebrews 13:12–13). The shame that matters most is rolled away by one who bore shame himself.

Uncertain wording. What exactly “the reproach of Egypt” refers to is not certain. Many take it as the Egyptians’ taunt (Exodus 32:12), silenced now that Israel stands in the land as God’s marked people; others think of the disgrace of slavery, or of the unbelieving generation whose sentence ends here. The readings overlap, and the point is plain: a shame that clung to Israel since Egypt is ended by God’s act.
verseByVerse.note: Gilgal became Israel's base camp for the early campaigns (9:6; 10:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — Passover, and the Last Morning of Manna
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel now eats as a people at home, and the God who fed them in the desert feeds them from the land. Four days after the crossing they keep the Passover on the plains of Jericho, the first ever kept in the land (v. 10), remembering the night of rescue from Egypt in the country that rescue was for. The next day they eat unleavened cakes and parched grain from fields they never sowed (v. 11), and the following morning the manna stops, after forty years, for good (v. 12). The miracle ends only when the harvest is already in their hands: God’s care has changed its form, not its faithfulness.
verseByVerse.theology: The first four days in the land follow the Passover calendar, and the order in verse 12 is exact and kind: the new food comes before the old supply stops.
verseByVerse.examples: The provision had not failed; it had changed form, because the land had arrived, and the manna had only ever been given for the journey there.

verseByVerse.quote: While the people of Israel were encamped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening on the plains of Jericho. And the day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain. And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel keeps its first Passover in the land and eats its first meal from the land’s harvest, and the manna that fed them for forty years stops: God’s care changes its form, not its faithfulness.

They kept the Passover. Israel came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month (4:19), the day the lamb was chosen in Egypt (Exodus 12:3); now it is the fourteenth, the night the lamb was killed. The first days in the land follow the Passover calendar exactly. And since “no uncircumcised person shall eat of it” (Exodus 12:48), the knife had to come before the meal. This Passover is eaten in the land itself, in sight of the first city Israel must take. Every Passover looked beyond itself, as the New Testament says plainly: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Unleavened cakes and parched grain. Parched grain, new grain held over a fire and eaten in the hand, comes here with the unleavened bread of the feast that follows Passover. What makes it remarkable is whose field it came from: grain they did not sow, as Moses had promised them cities they did not build and vineyards they did not plant (Deuteronomy 6:10–11).

And the manna ceased. One sentence ends forty years. Every adult in the camp had found breakfast on the ground every morning of his life, and then one morning there was nothing. The order of events is the mercy: the harvest was in their hands before the miracle ended.

In everyday life. Hold onto that when a form of God’s care leaned on for years comes to a stop: a job, health, a person, a season of nearness in prayer. The manna ending was not the withdrawal of God’s kindness. It was the arrival of what the manna had been standing in for.

The true bread. It was always standing in for something. Jesus told a crowd who wanted the bread miracle repeated, “Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died”, and said that he himself was the living bread from heaven, which a man may eat and live for ever (John 6:49–51). The manna stopped at Gilgal because the land had come. It stopped for good because the true bread had.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–15 — The Commander of the LORD's Army
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The battle for Canaan belongs to the LORD, and Joshua must learn that before he hears one word about Jericho. Near the city he meets a man with a drawn sword and asks the soldier’s question, “Are you for us, or for our adversaries?” (v. 13). The answer is “No”: the man is the commander of the LORD’s army, and he has come to lead, not to be enlisted. Joshua falls on his face in worship and asks for orders (v. 14). The only order given is the one Moses heard at the burning bush: take off your sandals, for the place is holy (v. 15). The God of the bush is the Captain of the war.
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua offers two options and is told neither. God does not join sides in this book; he takes command of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The orders for Jericho come in the next chapter. This encounter settles who is in charge before anything is planned.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man was standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. And Joshua went to him and said to him, "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?" And he said, "No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come." And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped and said to him, "What does my lord say to his servant?" And the commander of the LORD's army said to Joshua, "Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua meets the commander of the LORD’s army, who will not take sides but takes command, receives worship and makes the ground holy: Israel’s war is the LORD’s war, and its Captain is the LORD himself.

Are you for us, or for our adversaries? Joshua goes straight up to an unknown man with a drawn sword and asks the only question a soldier can think of. It is a reasonable question and the wrong one, and the answer says so in one word: “No”. Neither option applies.

I am the commander of the army of the LORD. God does not enlist; he commands. The question refused is the one we bring to God about anything difficult: is he on my side in this argument, this decision, this dispute? The refusal lifts the matter higher. The right question was never whether God had joined Israel’s war. It was whether Israel had joined his.

Fell on his face to the earth and worshiped. Joshua bows down in worship and is not stopped. The Hebrew word can mean simply bowing low before a superior, but it is telling: when John falls at the feet of an angel, the angel will not have it: “You must not do that! … Worship God” (Revelation 22:9). This one receives it.

Take off your sandals from your feet. Israel had heard this sentence before, almost word for word, when God spoke out of the burning bush to Moses (Exodus 3:5). The voice that commissioned Moses is standing outside Jericho. A field at the edge of a Canaanite city is holy because of who is standing on it, the only thing that has ever made any ground holy, and the LORD’s general takes off his sandals.

Now I have come. No battle orders are given here; the scene ends with Israel’s general in the dirt with his shoes in his hand. The commander came with his sword already drawn, not to be recruited but to take command. Every wall in the country was already his, and the man he was speaking to would not swing a sword for seven days. The orders for Jericho follow at 6:2, where the speaker is simply “the LORD”.

The Commander who came. The one who took command at Jericho later took flesh and fought the decisive battle alone, triumphing over the powers of evil at the cross (Colossians 2:15), not with a drawn sword but with his own body given up. He still does not join our causes; he calls us into his.

Where Christians differ. Who is the commander? Some take him as a high angel, like Michael, “one of the chief princes” (Daniel 10:13), speaking for God. Others see the LORD himself: he receives worship, the ground is holy because he is there, and the words about Jericho that follow come from “the LORD” (6:2).

This commentary’s view. The commander is best read as the Son appearing before his incarnation (a theophany, a visible appearing of God), the same one who appears elsewhere as the angel of the LORD.

Uncertain wording. “Now I have come” is abrupt in Hebrew, and its exact sense is uncertain. It may mean that he has now arrived to take command, or the sentence may be broken off as Joshua falls down, with the orders following at 6:2. Either way, the LORD’s Captain arrives before the battle.

5.theology:
Consecration before conquest. The order of this chapter is the argument of the book. Circumcision, then Passover, then worship on holy ground, and only then a battle. The conquest never rested on Israel's readiness, and while Israel lay helpless God emptied the kings of Canaan of courage (v. 1).

The reproach rolled away. The taunt that God had brought a nation into a desert to die is removed in a day, by God, while the people concerned lie still. Shame is lifted from outside, by someone else.

When the manna stops. The provision that had defined a generation ends the morning after the first harvest is eaten (v. 12), and nothing is wrong. God does not take away an old kindness before the new one is in his people’s hands, and the manna itself pointed to the true bread from heaven.

He does not take sides. Joshua's question assumes two armies and asks which one this man belongs to. The answer is No. The commander of the LORD's army, most likely the LORD himself (see vv. 13-15), gives no instructions at all. The encounter exists to settle who is in charge, which is the question every believer is tempted to get the wrong way round.
5.examples: Joshua's question is the one nearly everybody brings to God in a conflict: are you for me in this argument, this church split, this decision I have already made? The answer outside Jericho was No, and an invitation to ask a better question: what does my lord say to his servant? We can ask it without fear, because the Lord who will not take our side has already given himself for us.

keyVerse.quote: No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come.
keyVerse.note: The commander refuses to take Israel’s side and takes command instead, and Joshua falls down and worships. Everything that follows in the book rests on this: the battles are the LORD’s and he leads them, and this commentary reads the Captain as the Son himself.

5.reflection:
God ordered the circumcision of the whole army before a single battle, in the week Israel was most exposed. Why does God insist that his people belong to him before they serve him, and how does that change the way you think about your own service?

“Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you” (v. 9). What shame from the past still clings to you or to people you know, and what difference does it make that Christ bore reproach “outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12)?

The manna stopped only when the harvest was already in Israel’s hands. When has a familiar form of God’s care come to an end in your life, and how did he go on providing?

Joshua asked, “Are you for us, or for our adversaries?” and was told “No”. Where are you tempted to ask God to take your side, and what would it look like to ask instead whether you are on his?

6.title: The Fall of Jericho
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jericho was shut up inside and outside because of the people of Israel. None went out, and none came in.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "See, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valor.<sup>3</sup>You shall march around the city, all the men of war going around the city once. Thus shall you do for six days.<sup>4</sup>Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets.<sup>5</sup>And when they make a long blast with the ram's horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat, and the people shall go up, everyone straight before him."<sup>6</sup>So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests and said to them, "Take up the ark of the covenant and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD."<sup>7</sup>And he said to the people, "Go forward. March around the city and let the armed men pass on before the ark of the LORD."<sup>8</sup>And just as Joshua had commanded the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the LORD went forward, blowing the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD following them.<sup>9</sup>The armed men were walking before the priests who were blowing the trumpets, and the rear guard was walking after the ark, while the trumpets blew continually.<sup>10</sup>But Joshua commanded the people, "You shall not shout or make your voice heard, neither shall any word go out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you shall shout."<sup>11</sup>So he caused the ark of the LORD to circle the city, going about it once. And they came into the camp and spent the night in the camp.<sup>12</sup>Then Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD walked on, and they blew the trumpets continually. And the armed men were walking before them, and the rear guard was walking after the ark of the LORD, while the trumpets blew continually.<sup>14</sup>And the second day they marched around the city once, and returned into the camp. So they did for six days.<sup>15</sup>On the seventh day they rose early, at the dawn of day, and marched around the city in the same manner seven times. It was only on that day that they marched around the city seven times.<sup>16</sup>And at the seventh time, when the priests had blown the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, "Shout, for the LORD has given you the city.<sup>17</sup>And the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall live, because she hid the messengers whom we sent.<sup>18</sup>But you, keep yourselves from the things devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted them you take any of the devoted things and make the camp of Israel a thing for destruction and bring trouble upon it.<sup>19</sup>But all silver and gold, and every vessel of bronze and iron, are holy to the LORD; they shall go into the treasury of the LORD."<sup>20</sup>So the people shouted, and the trumpets were blown. As soon as the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they captured the city.<sup>21</sup>Then they devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword.<sup>22</sup>But to the two men who had spied out the land, Joshua said, "Go into the prostitute's house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her."<sup>23</sup>So the young men who had been spies went in and brought out Rahab and her father and mother and brothers and all who belonged to her. And they brought all her relatives and put them outside the camp of Israel.<sup>24</sup>And they burned the city with fire, and everything in it. Only the silver and gold, and the vessels of bronze and of iron, they put into the treasury of the house of the LORD.<sup>25</sup>But Rahab the prostitute and her father's household and all who belonged to her, Joshua saved alive. And she has lived in Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.<sup>26</sup>Joshua laid an oath on them at that time, saying, "Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. "At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates."<sup>27</sup>So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.
6.overview:
Where we are. Israel is camped at Gilgal, newly circumcised and eating the produce of the land, and its general has just met the commander of the LORD’s army (chapter 5). Jericho, the first city west of the Jordan, stands shut in front of them.

The message. The LORD gives the city, and he gives it in a way that leaves nobody else any credit. Israel’s part is to believe and obey a word that makes no military sense, and the walls fall to faith, not force. In the same act God judges a city ripe for judgment and saves the one household inside it that believed.

Why it was said. A generation about to spend years fighting walled cities needed to learn at the first wall that the land is taken by trusting God’s word. Later Israel needed to remember both why Canaan was judged and the warning that the same judgment could fall on them (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God declares Jericho already given and lays down the plan: six days of marching, then seven circuits, a long blast and a shout (vv. 1–7). Israel obeys for six days with nothing to show for it (vv. 8–14). On the seventh day the shout goes up, the city is devoted to the LORD, the wall falls flat and the city is destroyed (vv. 15–21). Rahab and her household are brought out alive as the spies swore, Jericho is burned and cursed, and the LORD’s presence with Joshua is confirmed (vv. 22–27).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. Jericho’s fall previews the last judgment, which a trumpet will announce (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and Rahab’s rescue previews the gospel: a condemned sinner saved by faith because of a promise (Hebrews 11:31). The God who is both just and merciful at Jericho is fully revealed at the cross, where judgment fell on the one man who did not deserve it, so that people like Rahab could walk out alive. She stands in the family tree of Jesus himself (Matthew 1:5).

For us. Our walls do not fall by technique, and obedience often looks for long stretches like walking in circles. God’s people walk on his word, wait for his day, and keep the door open for anyone, however far outside, who will trust the greater Joshua.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Plan No General Would Write
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jericho is already the LORD’s gift, and the plan he gives for taking it is designed so that no one but God can take the credit. The city is shut tight against Israel (v. 1), yet God speaks of it in the past tense: “I have given Jericho into your hand” (v. 2). Then comes the strangest battle plan ever given: march around the city once a day for six days, with seven priests carrying rams’ horns before the ark, and on the seventh day march round seven times, blow a long blast and shout, and the wall will fall flat (vv. 3–5). Joshua passes on the orders exactly as given, adding nothing and improving nothing (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: What is asked of Israel at Jericho is not strength, courage or tactics. It is a week of doing something that cannot possibly work.
verseByVerse.examples: Jericho falls not to the noise of an army but to the sound of Israel's worship, carried round the walls before the ark.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jericho was shut up inside and outside because of the people of Israel. None went out, and none came in. And the LORD said to Joshua, "See, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jericho is locked tight against Israel, but God speaks of it as already handed over: the city, its king and its soldiers are his gift before a single step is taken.

Shut up inside and outside. From the ground, Jericho is in total lockdown: none went out, and none came in.

See, I have given Jericho into your hand. From heaven, the city is already handed over, in the past tense as at 1:3, king and best troops included. Walls keep out armies; they have never kept out God. Faith learns to see a situation first as God describes it.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall march around the city, all the men of war going around the city once. Thus shall you do for six days. Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets. And when they make a long blast with the ram's horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat, and the people shall go up, everyone straight before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s plan for Jericho has no military content at all, only priests, horns, days of marching and a shout, so that when the wall falls nobody can say Israel brought it down.

You shall march around the city. No army has been given a plan like it: no ladders, no ram, no assault on the gate. Paul, writing of God’s habit of choosing what looks foolish, gives the reason: “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God” (1 Corinthians 1:29). Jericho is that sentence acted out over a week.

Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets. Seven priests, seven horns, seven days, seven circuits on the last: the Bible’s number of completeness is stamped over all of it.

Trumpets of rams’ horns. These are not war trumpets but rams’ horns, the instrument of Israel’s worship, carried by priests before the ark. The sound going round Jericho is a sound of worship before it is a sound of war, and inside the city there is a woman with a scarlet cord in her window (2:18) for whom it will mean release.

The wall of the city will fall down flat. The outcome is told in advance, including the manner: not breached but flattened, so that “the people shall go up, everyone straight before him”.

Uncertain wording. The word behind “rams’ horns” is yobel, which is rare; most take it to mean “ram”. The same word gave the Year of Jubilee its name, the year of release announced by the horn (Leviticus 25:9–10). Whether the writer means us to hear that note at Jericho is uncertain, and nothing should be built on it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests and said to them, "Take up the ark of the covenant and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD." And he said to the people, "Go forward. March around the city and let the armed men pass on before the ark of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua passes on God’s strange orders exactly as given, and the ark, the sign of God’s presence, goes at the centre of the column in full view of the walls.

Take up the ark of the covenant. Joshua changes nothing. A soldier who has fought since the battle with Amalek (Exodus 17:8–13) is handed a plan with no military content, and there is no record of a question. A general who has been face down before the commander of the LORD’s army (5:14) is in no hurry to improve on the instructions.

Before the ark of the LORD. The shape of the column matters: armed men first, then priests with horns, then the ark, then the rear guard. The ark is in the middle, exactly where it was in the riverbed. The presence of God is not kept out of harm’s way behind the lines but carried in the centre of the formation, in full view of the walls.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Obedience here means six days of doing exactly what God said with nothing to show for it. The procession forms with the armed men in front, then the priests with their horns, the ark at the centre and the rear guard behind, and the horns sound continually (vv. 8–9). But the people themselves must stay silent until Joshua tells them to shout (v. 10). They circle the city once and go back to camp (v. 11), and the same thing is done the next morning and every morning for six days (vv. 12–14). Each evening the wall stands exactly as it stood. Faith is walking on God’s word when nothing on the ground has moved.
verseByVerse.theology: The wall is exactly as high on the sixth evening as it was on the first morning, and the only instruction is to come back tomorrow and do it again.
verseByVerse.examples: There are seasons when the faithful thing is to keep walking and say nothing back.

verseByVerse.quote: And just as Joshua had commanded the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the LORD went forward, blowing the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD following them. The armed men were walking before the priests who were blowing the trumpets, and the rear guard was walking after the ark, while the trumpets blew continually.
