But Joshua commanded the people, "You shall not shout or make your voice heard, neither shall any word go out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you shall shout." So he caused the ark of the LORD to circle the city, going about it once. And they came into the camp and spent the night in the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The procession circles the city with the horns sounding and the people silent, then returns to camp: the first day of obedience looks like a wasted day.

The trumpets blew continually. The horns do not stop, and the writer repeats the trumpets blew continually until the reader begins to hear them.

You shall not shout. Joshua adds an order of absolute silence, and it is the hardest part of the week. Thousands of men walk within earshot of a wall lined with defenders, and whatever may be shouted down from the ramparts, no Israelite may answer it. The instinct when mocked is to reply, and the reply always feels like strength. Israel is to walk past the insult with a closed mouth, because the answer is coming on a day God has chosen, and not before.

They came into the camp. Day one ends with nothing. This is what obedience looked like on the first evening, and it looked like a wasted day.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the LORD. And the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD walked on, and they blew the trumpets continually. And the armed men were walking before them, and the rear guard was walking after the ark of the LORD, while the trumpets blew continually. And the second day they marched around the city once, and returned into the camp. So they did for six days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel does the same thing for six days with nothing to show for it, and this, rather than the seventh day, is the part of the chapter most believers actually live in.

So they did for six days. The writer repeats the formation for day two and covers four more days in one line. By then the defenders may well have found it funny. Israel had no way of explaining what they were doing, because the only explanation was a sentence from God.

In everyday life. The dramatic seventh day gets preached; the six days are where the years go: praying for the same person, turning up to the same duty, keeping the same promise, and seeing the wall unchanged. Six days of obedience with no visible result is not failure. It is what the seventh day is made of. Israel knew there would be a seventh day, but not what it would bring. They walked on the word alone, and the God who gives the word keeps his people walking by his Spirit when their own resolve runs out (Galatians 6:9; Philippians 2:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — The Wall Fell Down Flat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the seventh day the LORD gives what he promised, and the judgment that falls on Jericho is total. Israel rises at dawn and marches seven times around the city (v. 15). At the seventh circuit Joshua gives the order to shout, and with it the terms: the city is devoted to the LORD for destruction, Rahab’s household alone is to be spared, and no one may take anything devoted, for its silver and gold belong to the LORD’s treasury (vv. 16–19). The people shout, the wall falls flat, and Israel goes straight in (v. 20). The writer then records, without softening and without celebration, that everything living in the city was destroyed (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The order of Joshua's sentence in verse 16 is the point of the chapter: not "shout, and the LORD will give you the city", but shout, FOR the LORD has given.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 18 plants a warning in the middle of a victory, and one man in the crowd, Achan, is about to ignore it (chapter 7).

verseByVerse.quote: On the seventh day they rose early, at the dawn of day, and marched around the city in the same manner seven times. It was only on that day that they marched around the city seven times. And at the seventh time, when the priests had blown the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, "Shout, for the LORD has given you the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the seventh day, after seven circuits, Joshua lets the people shout, and the reason he gives is that the LORD has already given them the city.

Seven times. Seven circuits in armour is most of a day’s work, and nothing suggests the last will differ from the others.

Shout, for the LORD has given you the city. The silence of six days ends in one word, and the reason attached is the heart of the chapter: shout, for the LORD has given you the city. The gift comes first, as something already done, exactly as in verse 2 and at 1:3. The shout is not the cause of anything. It is the response of people who have been told that a thing is settled and are finally allowed to say so out loud.

In the Christian life. So it is with the gospel. We do not praise God in order to be accepted; we praise him because in Christ we have been.

verseByVerse.quote: And the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall live, because she hid the messengers whom we sent. But you, keep yourselves from the things devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted them you take any of the devoted things and make the camp of Israel a thing for destruction and bring trouble upon it. But all silver and gold, and every vessel of bronze and iron, are holy to the LORD; they shall go into the treasury of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jericho, the first city of the land, is devoted wholly to the LORD: everything living in it is to be destroyed except Rahab’s household, its metals go to his treasury, and anyone who takes what is devoted brings the same sentence on Israel.

Devoted to the LORD for destruction. This is the hardest thing in the book, and it must not be hurried past. The word is herem: something handed over to God entirely and taken permanently out of human use. Jericho is the first city in the land, the firstfruits of the conquest, and like every firstfruit it belongs to God, not to the people. Nobody profits from this city: its silver, gold, bronze and iron are “holy to the LORD” and go into his treasury (v. 19).

Keep yourselves from the things devoted. Then a warning is dropped into the middle of the victory: take any of it, and the same sentence of destruction falls on you, and you “make the camp of Israel a thing for destruction and bring trouble upon it” (v. 18). The whole of the next chapter comes out of this verse.

What it meant. Verse 21 states what the ban meant without softening: men and women, young and old. Children died at Jericho, and that must be said plainly. What the Bible itself puts around it can be taken in order.

Announced in advance. First, the judgment was announced centuries in advance, and the delay was mercy. God told Abraham his descendants would not receive the land for four generations, “for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis 15:16). Judgment came late, not early, and it came on a culture that was burning its own children to its gods, the practice Scripture names again and again as the reason (Leviticus 18:21–25; Deuteronomy 12:31).

Not Israel’s righteousness. Second, and decisively, Israel is told at length that none of this is because they are better. “Not because of your righteousness”, says Moses, three times in three verses, for “you are a stubborn people” (Deuteronomy 9:4–6). The land is said to vomit out its inhabitants for what they do, and Israel is warned in the same breath that it will vomit them out too if they do the same (Leviticus 18:26–28). That warning was kept, through Babylon.

Not about ancestry. Third, the ban was never about ancestry, and this chapter is the proof. A Canaanite household walks out of Jericho alive, not because of nationality or morality, both against her, but because she believed what she had heard of God and acted on it. The door out of the judgment was open, and one household went through it.

Not a pattern to repeat. Fourth, this was a specific, dated, limited command, and Scripture never treats it as a pattern. No prophet urges Israel to repeat it elsewhere, and no apostle applies it to the church, whose weapons “are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4). Anyone who has used Joshua to justify violence has had to ignore the whole New Testament to do it.

Does that close the question? No. Verse 21 still says young and old, and no argument makes that easy, nor should it be made to feel easy. The Westminster Confession (10.3) teaches that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ; Scripture says no more about which children those are, and this commentary, with many Christians, trusts the Judge of all the earth to do right with every child (Genesis 18:25), a Judge more merciful than we are. And the God who did this is the God who, in the same chapter, took a prostitute out of the condemned city and put her name in the family tree of his own Son.

The judge we want and the judge we fear. Why does this chapter trouble us so much? We want someone to deal with the trafficker, the tyrant and the man who burns children, and we are rightly outraged when they die comfortably in their beds. What we do not want is a judgment that might one day reach us. And the instinct that recoils at verse 21, that the weak and the young matter as much as the strong, did not come from nowhere. Much of the ancient world did not share it; it grows from the Bible’s first page, where every human being bears the image of God (Genesis 1:27). So we stand inside the Bible’s own conscience to accuse the Bible’s God. Scripture does not wave that outrage away; it answers it where nobody expected. Judgment fell, in the end, on the one man who deserved none of it. On the cross the Son became “a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), handed over and forsaken (Matthew 27:46), so that a world of Jerichos could be offered what Rahab was offered: a door, and a house that would stand.

Where Christians differ. Some evangelical scholars read phrases such as “both men and women, young and old” as the stock language of ancient war reports, meaning total victory rather than the death of every person. Others hold that at Jericho, at least, the words mean what they say, since this city was singled out as the firstfruits and Rahab’s household is the one exception named.

This commentary’s view. At Jericho the account is to be taken at its word: a unique, God-commanded judgment on long-persistent wickedness, never a pattern or licence for violence today.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people shouted, and the trumpets were blown. As soon as the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they captured the city. Then they devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the shout the wall falls flat, Israel goes straight in, and the city is devoted to destruction as God commanded, recorded flatly and without celebration.

The wall fell down flat. A week of walking, and one sentence. The wall is not broken through at one point; it drops where it stands, so the whole circumference becomes the way in, and no fighting is recorded at the wall.

By faith. Hebrews puts this on its list of what faith has done, and words it carefully: “By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days” (Hebrews 11:30). Not by shouting, but by faith, and faith in that verse is thirteen laps of a city by people who had no idea what walking was supposed to achieve.

Young and old. Verse 21 is written flatly: nothing is celebrated or described in detail. Jericho had heard for forty years what this God had done at the sea (2:10), as Rahab had, and only one household acted on it.

Why kill the animals too? Under the ban everything was given wholly to God, and none of it was taken for Israel’s gain (vv. 17–19).

Was it just? The fuller answer is given on verses 17–19: a judgment on sin ripened over centuries, a unique command, and no pattern for any later war, nation or church, for Christ’s kingdom is “not of this world” (John 18:36).

How did Rahab’s house survive? Rahab’s house was built into the wall (2:15). The text does not say how it survived; perhaps her stretch of wall was spared. It says only that her family came out alive (vv. 22–23).

Does archaeology support it? The evidence is disputed. Excavations at Tell es-Sultan in the 1950s concluded that the city had been destroyed long before Joshua; a later reassessment of the pottery argued for a destruction, with fallen walls and burned stores of grain, around 1400 BC, which fits the earlier date for the exodus (see the introduction). Erosion on an exposed mound has removed much. The digging neither proves nor disproves the account; Christians receive it as history because Scripture does (Hebrews 11:30).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — Rahab Brought Out, and the City Cursed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the judgment God keeps his promise of mercy. Joshua sends the two spies to keep their oath, and they bring out Rahab with her father, mother, brothers and all who belong to her, setting them outside the camp (vv. 22–23). The city is burned, and its metal goes into the LORD’s treasury (v. 24). Rahab is saved alive and lives in Israel “to this day” (v. 25). Joshua lays a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho, a word fulfilled centuries later (v. 26), and the chapter closes as the book began, with the LORD keeping his promise to be with Joshua (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The one household that walked out of that city alive is not a footnote to the judgment; it is the writer’s way of showing that mercy was open to whoever believed.
verseByVerse.examples: Jericho was left a ruin as a monument, so that every traveller on that road could see how the conquest began: by God's hand, not Israel's.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the two men who had spied out the land, Joshua said, "Go into the prostitute's house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her." So the young men who had been spies went in and brought out Rahab and her father and mother and brothers and all who belonged to her. And they brought all her relatives and put them outside the camp of Israel. And they burned the city with fire, and everything in it. Only the silver and gold, and the vessels of bronze and of iron, they put into the treasury of the house of the LORD. But Rahab the prostitute and her father's household and all who belonged to her, Joshua saved alive. And she has lived in Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the judgment Joshua keeps the spies’ oath, and Rahab’s whole household is brought out alive, first to the edge of the camp and in the end into Israel itself.

As you swore to her. The city is coming down, and Joshua stops to keep someone else’s promise: two soldiers pledged their lives on a roof (2:14), and their commander treats that oath as binding on the whole nation. Every name she asked for, father, mother, brothers and all who belonged to her, is read back as a list of survivors.

Outside the camp of Israel. The last clause of verse 23 is honest about the awkwardness. A Canaanite family at the edge of Israel, ceremonially unclean, alive but not yet belonging: grace got them out of the fire before it got them a tent.

She has lived in Israel to this day. Outside the camp is not where the story ends; she ended inside the nation. Whether the writer means Rahab herself, still alive when he wrote, or her family after her depends on when the book was written, and that is uncertain (see the introduction).

Rahab the prostitute. The narrator keeps calling her the prostitute to the last line, not from cruelty but because he will not tidy up the person grace actually saved. Matthew does the same when he writes her into the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), so that the Redeemer of Israel has a Canaanite in his family tree, and the record says out loud what she used to be. Hebrews and James both hold up her faith (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). No one is too far outside for grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua laid an oath on them at that time, saying, "Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. "At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates." So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua lays a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho as a fortified city, a word fulfilled centuries later, and the chapter ends with the LORD’s promise to be with Joshua kept.

Cursed before the LORD. Jericho is to stay down, and the curse was not empty words. Centuries later, in the reign of Ahab, a man called Hiel of Bethel rebuilt the city, and the historian records the price in one grim sentence: he laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, “according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun” (1 Kings 16:34).

The LORD was with Joshua. The chapter closes by recording, in a single line, that the promises of 1:5 and 3:7 were kept. Joshua had done nothing a soldier would put on his record; his fame came entirely from the LORD being with him.

A door held open until then. The Commander with the drawn sword took a fortified city without Israel drawing a blade. He did it slowly, in daylight, to the sound of rams’ horns, and carried out of the ruin only a household that had believed him. That is the shape of the judgment the New Testament still announces: a day fixed, a trumpet sounding (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and a door held open until then for anyone who will trust the greater Joshua, Jesus, who carries his people safely through the judgment because he bore it for them (Romans 5:9).

Uncertain wording. “At the cost of his firstborn” is literally “with” or “by” his firstborn. It may mean the builder’s sons would die under God’s judgment as the work went on, or that he would offer them as foundation sacrifices, a pagan practice. 1 Kings 16:34 does not say which; either way, the word came true.
verseByVerse.note: The site was not left wholly empty meanwhile (18:21; Judg. 3:13); the curse fell on rebuilding it as a fortified city.

6.theology:
The gift comes before the shout. The city is spoken of as already given before anything happens (vv. 2, 16). Every act of Christian obedience has that order: God gives first, then we act.

The six days. The faith Hebrews commends is not the shout on the last morning but the walking on the first six, when nothing whatever happened. Obedience without visible result is not a failure of faith; it is most of what faith consists of.

The ban, faced honestly. Verse 21 says men and women, young and old. The commentary on verses 17–19 sets out what Scripture puts around it, and admits that none of it closes the question.

Judgment and mercy in the same morning. The writer sets them side by side without comment: a city devoted to destruction, and a household walked out of it (v. 25). Grace in this chapter is not a softening of the judgment. It is a door held open in the middle of it.
6.examples: Jericho was promised to Israel, on a named day. God has not promised that the wall in your marriage or your prayers will fall on a timetable. He has promised to be with his people, that labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Cor. 15:58), and that in Christ they will enter the inheritance Joshua's victory pointed to. So keep walking in the six days. And if you stopped walking long ago, the way back is not to make up the lost laps but to return to the Lord, who runs to meet those who come home (Luke 15:20).

keyVerse.quote: See, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valor.
keyVerse.note: Before a single step is marched, God speaks of the city in the past tense. Everything Israel does in the chapter, the six silent days, the seven circuits and the shout, is the response of faith to a gift already given, which is why Hebrews can say the walls fell “by faith” (Hebrews 11:30).

6.reflection:
God gave Israel a plan for Jericho that made no military sense (vv. 3–5). Why do you think he chose a way that left no room for human credit, and where might he be doing something similar in your life or church?

Israel walked round the city for six days and saw nothing change. What “six days” are you living in now, and what keeps you walking when the wall looks the same?

The destruction of Jericho (v. 21) is one of the hardest things in Scripture. How do Genesis 15:16, Deuteronomy 9:4–6 and the cross help you face it honestly, without explaining it away or turning away from God?

Rahab, still called “the prostitute”, is saved and lives in Israel (v. 25), and Matthew names her among Jesus’ ancestors. What does her story say about who can be saved, and is there anyone you have quietly written off?

7.title: Achan's Sin and the Defeat at Ai
7.text: <sup>1</sup>But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is near Beth-aven, east of Bethel, and said to them, "Go up and spy out the land." And the men went up and spied out Ai.<sup>3</sup>And they returned to Joshua and said to him, "Do not have all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and attack Ai. Do not make the whole people toil up there, for they are few."<sup>4</sup>So about three thousand men went up there from the people. And they fled before the men of Ai,<sup>5</sup>and the men of Ai killed about thirty-six of their men and chased them before the gate as far as Shebarim and struck them at the descent. And the hearts of the people melted and became as water.<sup>6</sup>Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the LORD until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads.<sup>7</sup>And Joshua said, "Alas, O Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hands of the Amorites, to destroy us? Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!<sup>8</sup>O Lord, what can I say, when Israel has turned their backs before their enemies!<sup>9</sup>For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?"<sup>10</sup>The LORD said to Joshua, "Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?<sup>11</sup>Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them; they have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen and lied and put them among their own belongings.<sup>12</sup>Therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies. They turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become devoted for destruction. I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.<sup>13</sup>Get up! Consecrate the people and say, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow; for thus says the LORD, God of Israel, "There are devoted things in your midst, O Israel. You cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the devoted things from among you."<sup>14</sup>In the morning therefore you shall be brought near by your tribes. And the tribe that the LORD takes by lot shall come near by clans. And the clan that the LORD takes shall come near by households. And the household that the LORD takes shall come near man by man.<sup>15</sup>And he who is taken with the devoted things shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has, because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD, and because he has done an outrageous thing in Israel.'"<sup>16</sup>So Joshua rose early in the morning and brought Israel near tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was taken.<sup>17</sup>And he brought near the clans of Judah, and the clan of the Zerahites was taken. And he brought near the clan of the Zerahites man by man, and Zabdi was taken.<sup>18</sup>And he brought near his household man by man, and Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken.<sup>19</sup>Then Joshua said to Achan, "My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me."<sup>20</sup>And Achan answered Joshua, "Truly I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and this is what I did:<sup>21</sup>when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent, with the silver underneath."<sup>22</sup>So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent; and behold, it was hidden in his tent with the silver underneath.<sup>23</sup>And they took them out of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the people of Israel. And they laid them down before the LORD.<sup>24</sup>And Joshua and all Israel with him took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver and the cloak and the bar of gold, and his sons and daughters and his oxen and donkeys and sheep and his tent and all that he had. And they brought them up to the Valley of Achor.<sup>25</sup>And Joshua said, "Why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today." And all Israel stoned him with stones. They burned them with fire and stoned them with stones.<sup>26</sup>And they raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. Then the LORD turned from his burning anger. Therefore, to this day the name of that place is called the Valley of Achor.
7.overview:
Where we are. Jericho has fallen, Rahab is safe, and the last chapter ended in triumph: “the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land” (6:27). Israel turns to the next town, Ai.

The message. Hidden sin among God’s people is not a private matter. It breaks the covenant, robs the whole community of God’s help, and must be confessed and removed. God is utterly serious about sin, yet even in judgment he draws the sinner to confession, and the valley named for the trouble will one day become a door of hope.

Why it was said. Israel had just been warned to keep away from the devoted things (6:18), and the first hearers needed to learn at once that the conquest rested on obedience as well as on promise. Later Israel, losing the land for its unfaithfulness, could read here why God’s help is withdrawn (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The narrator tells the reader what Israel does not know: Achan has taken devoted things, and God is angry (v. 1). A confident small force goes up against Ai and is routed, and Israel’s heart melts (vv. 2–5). Joshua falls before the ark in anguished prayer (vv. 6–9). God tells him to get up: Israel has sinned, and God’s presence is withdrawn until the devoted things are removed (vv. 10–15). The lot narrows to Achan, who confesses that he saw, coveted, took and hid (vv. 16–21). The goods are dug up, Achan and all that is his are stoned and burned, and the place is named the Valley of Achor, “trouble” (vv. 22–26).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by contrast. Achan of the tribe of Judah brought trouble on Israel and died for his own sin; Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, took his people’s trouble on himself and died for sins not his own (2 Corinthians 5:21). God promised through Hosea to “make the Valley of Achor a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15), and the cross is where that happens. Because Christ bore the judgment, confession now leads not to stones but to forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

For us. Sin hidden in a life or a church is never as private as it feels, and the cure is not more praying around it but confessing it and digging it up. Come early, be specific, and come to a God who has already given the one who bore our trouble.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The reader is told at once what Israel does not know: one man’s theft has put the whole nation under God’s anger. Achan of the tribe of Judah has taken some of the devoted things from Jericho, and the LORD’s anger burns against Israel (v. 1). Unaware, Joshua sends scouts to Ai, who come back confident that two or three thousand men will be plenty (vv. 2–3). The three thousand flee, about thirty-six are killed on the slope below the town, and the hearts of the people melt like water (vv. 4–5), as the hearts of Canaan had melted before them. Without God, Israel is no stronger than its enemies.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel assumed that yesterday’s victory guaranteed today’s, and the hidden sin was doing its work unseen.
verseByVerse.examples: Success is often more dangerous to faith than failure, because it makes asking God feel unnecessary.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One man takes some of the devoted things from Jericho, and God counts it as the unfaithfulness of the whole nation, though no one else in the camp yet knows anything is wrong.

But. One word turns the book over. The last chapter ended with Joshua’s fame filling the land; this one begins with God angry. And nobody knows: Israel wakes the next morning under the anger of God, and the whole camp is entirely unaware of it.

The people of Israel broke faith. The sentence says that the people of Israel broke faith, though the man who did it was Achan. The devoted things were the goods of Jericho handed over wholly to God (the Hebrew word is herem), to be destroyed or given to his treasury (6:17–19).

One and many. That offends a modern reader, who thinks of himself as a separate unit responsible for his own actions alone. Scripture consistently does not. A family, a church, a nation is treated as a body, and what one member does affects all of it. The cases are not identical, for Achan did not stand for Israel as its representative, as Adam stands for the human race and Christ for his people (1 Corinthians 15:22). But the principle that people are bound together, so that one person’s act reaches those who belong with him, is the same one; and if it were simply unjust, no one could be saved by one man’s obedience (Romans 5:19).

Son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah. The writer gives Achan’s line, three generations back, before anything else about him. He is not an anonymous thief. He is somebody’s son and somebody’s grandson, from the tribe of Judah, and every one of those names will matter before the chapter is finished.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is near Beth-aven, east of Bethel, and said to them, "Go up and spy out the land." And the men went up and spied out Ai. And they returned to Joshua and said to him, "Do not have all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and attack Ai. Do not make the whole people toil up there, for they are few." So about three thousand men went up there from the people. And they fled before the men of Ai, and the men of Ai killed about thirty-six of their men and chased them before the gate as far as Shebarim and struck them at the descent. And the hearts of the people melted and became as water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without asking God, Israel sends a small force against Ai and is routed: thirty-six men die, and Israel’s heart melts as Canaan’s once did.

Go up and spy out the land. The scouting is competent. What is missing is the whole of chapter 6: nobody asks God anything. At Jericho every detail came from outside; here the plan is assembled by men looking at a hill and doing arithmetic. It is not rebellion. It is something more ordinary and far more common: a victory so complete that praying about the next one felt unnecessary.

For they are few. Israel has started counting the enemy. The week before, the size of the opposition had been the least relevant fact on the field.

About thirty-six of their men. It is a small number for a battle and an enormous one for this book, because until now Israel has not lost a single soldier. Somebody had to carry that news back into thirty-six homes. They died for a sin they did not commit and never heard about. That is the ugliest fact in the chapter, and the writer does not soften it: this is what hidden sin does, and it does not stop at the person who committed it.

The hearts of the people melted. The last sentence is an echo. The hearts of the people melted and became as water recalls what Rahab said of her own city (2:11) and what happened to the kings of Canaan when they heard about the Jordan (5:1). Israel has caught the enemy’s condition. The terror that had been fighting on their side has changed sides.

Where was Ai? It is usually identified with et-Tell, which seems to have been unoccupied in Joshua’s time; others identify it with a nearby site such as Khirbet el-Maqatir, where remains of a fortress of the right period have been found. The question is open, and it does not touch the truth of the account.

Uncertain wording. “As far as Shebarim” may be a place name, or an ordinary word meaning “the quarries” or “the breaks”, perhaps the broken, rocky ground below the town. Either way, Israel was chased down the hillside and struck “at the descent”: a rout on steep ground.
verseByVerse.note: Ai means “the ruin.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua takes the defeat to God, honestly and badly at first, and then well. He and the elders tear their clothes, put dust on their heads and lie before the ark until evening (v. 6). His prayer begins with the old wilderness complaint, wishing they had stayed beyond the Jordan (v. 7), and with bewilderment that Israel has turned and run (v. 8). But it ends on solid ground: the Canaanites will hear and wipe out Israel’s name, “And what will you do for your great name?” (v. 9). Scripture records the prayer without polishing it, and the plea it lands on is the one that never depends on the person praying.
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua's prayer begins badly and ends well, and Scripture prints both halves.
verseByVerse.examples: Under enough pressure a believer can find himself saying the very thing he once stood against. God does not cast him off for it; he answers, and sets him on his feet.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the LORD until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads. And Joshua said, "Alas, O Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hands of the Amorites, to destroy us? Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan! O Lord, what can I say, when Israel has turned their backs before their enemies! For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua and the elders lie before the ark in grief, and Joshua prays an honest, faltering prayer that ends on the one plea that does not depend on him: God’s great name.

Joshua tore his clothes. Torn clothes and dust on the head are the signs of mourning, and Joshua and the elders hold that posture from morning to evening. And this is not a good prayer, yet Scripture prints it. In effect Joshua says that God brought them over the Jordan only to destroy them. Those are almost exactly the words of the wilderness generation at Kadesh: “Why is the LORD bringing us into this land, to fall by the sword? … Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?” (Numbers 14:3). Joshua had stood up in front of that crowd and contradicted them, and nearly been stoned for it.

The old complaint. Forty years later, one bad afternoon, and the man who opposed the complaint is making it. Scripture records it without excusing or condemning him: God can bear his servants’ bewildered prayers.

What will you do for your great name? Then the prayer turns. Joshua does not say Israel deserves better; he has just watched thirty-six men die and has no idea why. He says that God’s own reputation is bound up with what happens to Israel. It is exactly how Moses prayed when God offered to destroy the nation and start again: not a word about Israel’s merits, only “Why should the Egyptians say …?” (Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13–16).

In everyday life. That is the one plea in prayer that does not depend on the person making it. A believer with nothing to say for himself can still say, “Your name is on this, and I am asking for your sake and not mine.” Christians pray in Jesus’ name for the same reason: our plea rests on his record, not ours, and the Father is glorified in answering it (John 14:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Joshua’s prayer by telling him to stop praying and act. “Get up!” (v. 10). The problem is not that God has abandoned Israel but that Israel has sinned: devoted things have been taken, stolen, lied about and hidden among their goods (v. 11). Until they are removed Israel cannot stand, and God will be with them no more (v. 12). The people are to consecrate themselves, and in the morning the LORD will point out the guilty man by lot, tribe by tribe, clan by clan, household by household, man by man (vv. 13–14). The one taken is to be burned with all he has, for he has broken the covenant and done an outrageous thing in Israel (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The presence of God has been the basis of everything in the book since 1:5. Verse 12 says it can be withdrawn, and names the condition. Sin in the camp does not merely displease God; it removes the one thing Israel had going for it.
verseByVerse.examples: When God puts his finger on a hidden sin, it is not to crush us but to free the whole household of faith, and the way out is the way Joshua points: tell the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Joshua, "Get up! Why have you fallen on your face? Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them; they have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen and lied and put them among their own belongings. Therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies. They turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become devoted for destruction. I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you. Get up! Consecrate the people and say, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow; for thus says the LORD, God of Israel, "There are devoted things in your midst, O Israel. You cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the devoted things from among you." In the morning therefore you shall be brought near by your tribes. And the tribe that the LORD takes by lot shall come near by clans. And the clan that the LORD takes shall come near by households. And the household that the LORD takes shall come near man by man. And he who is taken with the devoted things shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has, because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD, and because he has done an outrageous thing in Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Joshua to get up and deal with the sin: Israel has broken the covenant by stealing and hiding devoted things, and God will not go with them until those things are removed and the guilty man is found.

Get up! God’s first word to a man who has been praying all day is to stop. Prayer is not usually the thing that needs interrupting, but there is a kind of praying that is a substitute for obedience: agonising before God about a situation he has already told us how to put right. Joshua is asking why God has abandoned Israel. God’s answer is that no one has abandoned anyone, and there is a man in the camp with stolen property under his tent.

They have stolen and lied. Four verbs, and each is a step further down. Taken is the act. Stolen names what kind of act it was. Lied is what had to happen next, because Achan has been walking round the camp for days behaving normally. And put them among their own belongings is the settled state: the thing is in the tent now, and life has arranged itself around it.

I will be with you no more. Verse 12 is one of the most frightening sentences in the book. Everything since chapter 1 has rested on one promise: I will be with you. Here God says that his help in battle can be withdrawn, and states the condition. He does not say Israel will be forgiven when they feel worse about it. He says the devoted thing has to go. There is no route round the object itself, and a great deal of religious distress is the attempt to find one: genuine grief, genuine prayer, genuine resolve, and the thing still under the floor of the tent.

The tribe that the LORD takes by lot. The detection is deliberately slow. God knew the name on the first day; instead the lot walks toward Achan in four public stages, over a morning, in front of everybody. Four times he watches it come nearer, and four times he could have stood up. The process that exposes him is also, to the last moment, an invitation.

An outrageous thing in Israel. The word is used of gross, shameless sins that betray the whole community (as in Genesis 34:7). The sentence of burning matches the crime: the man who took what was devoted to destruction has made himself devoted to destruction (6:18).

What it does not mean. The lot was God’s appointed means in Israel, and “its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). It is not a pattern for guidance today: God now guides his people chiefly through his word, prayer, wisdom and godly counsel, and believers should not cast lots or demand signs.

Does this contradict 1:5? God’s promise to fight for Israel as a nation depended on its faithfulness, and the nation could forfeit his help in battle. That is different from the bond with each believer in Christ, who promises, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). A Christian can grieve the Spirit and lose the sense of God’s help, but not lose God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — I Saw, I Coveted, I Took, I Hid
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The search narrows slowly to one man, and when it reaches him he tells the truth. In the morning the lot takes Judah, then the clan of the Zerahites, then Zabdi’s household, then Achan (vv. 16–18). Joshua speaks to him as “My son” and calls him to give glory to God by confessing (v. 19). Achan answers plainly: he saw a beautiful cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver and a bar of gold, coveted them, took them and hid them in the ground inside his tent (vv. 20–21). His four verbs trace the path of every temptation, from the eye to the heart to the hand to the hiding place.
verseByVerse.theology: Achan's four verbs, saw, coveted, took, hid, are the oldest sequence in the Bible: the steps of the first sin (Gen. 3:6-8).
verseByVerse.examples: What we hide is usually small. Its smallness is what makes it easy to keep, and costly to everyone near us.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua rose early in the morning and brought Israel near tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was taken. And he brought near the clans of Judah, and the clan of the Zerahites was taken. And he brought near the clan of the Zerahites man by man, and Zabdi was taken. And he brought near his household man by man, and Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken. Then Joshua said to Achan, "My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me." And Achan answered Joshua, "Truly I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and this is what I did: when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent, with the silver underneath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lot narrows step by step to Achan, Joshua gently urges him to give glory to God by confessing, and Achan admits the whole sequence: he saw, coveted, took and hid.

Of the tribe of Judah. The pedigree is read out again in public. The tribe is Judah: the royal tribe, the one Jacob blessed with the sceptre (Genesis 49:10), the tribe the Messiah would come from. The first recorded sin in the promised land is committed by a man of the line that produces the King.

My son. Joshua’s first two words are the surprise of the chapter. He is speaking to a man who has cost thirty-six lives and is about to be executed, and he addresses him as a father would.

Give glory to the LORD God of Israel. Notice how he describes confession: telling the truth is giving glory to God. Not clearing the record, or getting it off one’s chest, but agreeing with God about what happened, which honours him. So there is still one good thing Achan can do with his life. Whether his confession was the repentance that brings life, Scripture does not say; it was at least true, and the God who heard a dying thief (Luke 23:42–43) can be trusted with him.

I coveted them and took them. Four more verbs, and every one of us has used them in that order: I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid. It is Eve at the tree, who saw, took, and then hid (Genesis 3:6–8); it is David on his roof, seeing Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:2–4); and it is James’s account of how sin grows: desire conceives and gives birth to sin, and sin when fully grown brings forth death (James 1:15).

A beautiful cloak from Shinar. Shinar is the plain where men once said, “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower” (Genesis 11:4); it is the Bible’s name for Babylonia, and the cloak was an expensive import. In the first week of the conquest, a man of Judah smuggled a piece of Babylon into the camp of God and buried it under the place where he slept.

200 shekels of silver. The inventory is pitifully small: a coat, about five pounds of silver and a bar of gold he could hold in one hand (a shekel was about two-fifths of an ounce). For that, thirty-six men are dead and his own family is finished.

Isn’t wanting more just ambition? We have a kinder word for what Achan felt, aspiration, and whole industries exist to keep it alive. Coveting is the one commandment of the ten that concerns only what happens inside, and it is the one a modern economy has learned to treat as a virtue. Achan’s verbs show why the Bible will not. He saw, then he wanted, and the wanting did not rest until the thing was his; then it had to be hidden, and a man who had walked through the Jordan on dry ground was living on top of a hole in his floor. Coveted things promise to make us somebody, and they end up owning us. Jesus put it plainly: “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15). The cure is not to want nothing but to want something greater, and to see it given: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). A heart that has that wealth can leave the cloak where it lies.

How do I confess? Do not wait for the lot. Achan watched it come nearer four times; confession is better made early, before anything forces it. “Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). Be specific. Achan named the cloak, the silver and the gold. Tell God what you actually did, the lie to your manager, the money, the words to your wife, not “I haven’t been very good”. Dig it up. Confession that leaves the thing under the tent is not finished: return what was taken, delete what was hidden, put right what you can, as Zacchaeus did (Luke 19:8). Tell someone where it helps. “Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16), above all the person you wronged. And confess to a God who has already dealt with it. Achan had no one to stand between him and the stones; we do, for Christ bore the judgment himself. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
verseByVerse.note: A shekel was about 2/5 ounce: Achan took about 5 pounds of silver and over a pound of gold.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What was buried in the dark is brought into the light, and the trouble Achan brought on Israel comes back on him. Messengers run to the tent, find everything as he said, and lay it out before the LORD (vv. 22–23). Achan, the stolen goods, his children, his animals and all he had are taken to a valley, where all Israel stones them and burns them (vv. 24–25). A great heap of stones is raised over him, the LORD turns from his burning anger, and the place is named the Valley of Achor, “trouble” (v. 26). The name stands, but the prophets would later promise that God would make this valley of trouble a door of hope.
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment is carried out in the open and before God, and the valley's name keeps the memory.
verseByVerse.examples: No one reading this is beyond the reach of the God who turns valleys of trouble into doors of hope.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent; and behold, it was hidden in his tent with the silver underneath. And they took them out of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the people of Israel. And they laid them down before the LORD. And Joshua and all Israel with him took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver and the cloak and the bar of gold, and his sons and daughters and his oxen and donkeys and sheep and his tent and all that he had. And they brought them up to the Valley of Achor. And Joshua said, "Why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today." And all Israel stoned him with stones. They burned them with fire and stoned them with stones. And they raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. Then the LORD turned from his burning anger. Therefore, to this day the name of that place is called the Valley of Achor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The stolen goods are brought into the light, Achan and all that is his are stoned and burned, and God turns from his anger; the place is named Trouble, but God would later promise to make it a door of hope.

They ran to the tent. What was buried in the dark under a man’s bed is dug up, carried across the camp and spread out on the ground in the open, in front of everybody, before God. That is what happens to everything in the end: nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known (Luke 12:2). The only question about any concealed thing is whether it is brought into the light by confession or by exposure.

The LORD brings trouble on you today. Joshua’s words play on the name of the valley: Achor means “trouble”, and the verb is the same. Achan troubled Israel, and the trouble comes back on him. 1 Chronicles 2:7 remembers him as “the troubler of Israel”.

His sons and daughters. The list in verse 24 is meant to be long: everything he owned and everyone he loved goes up that valley with him. The death of his children is the second hard thing in this book, and it should not be explained away. Israel’s own law forbids putting children to death for their fathers’ sins (Deuteronomy 24:16), which means a reader who finds this troubling is standing on ground the Old Testament itself provides.

A great heap of stones. There are two monuments in the land now: one at Gilgal where a river opened, and this one over a man buried under the rocks, and the writer says to this day of both. Then, and only then, the LORD turns from his burning anger.

A door of hope. The name Trouble is the last word of the chapter, but not the last word about the valley. Hosea, describing how God will win back an unfaithful nation, promises to “make the Valley of Achor a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15). God takes the worst place in Israel’s early history, a heap of stones over a thief, and hands it back as the entrance to the future. Centuries later he took the instrument of a criminal’s execution and made it the sign under which the world is saved. Achan, of the tribe of Judah, brought trouble on Israel and died under it for his own sin. Another son of Judah would take his people’s trouble on himself and die for sins that were not his (2 Corinthians 5:21), so that the valley of trouble could become a door of hope.

Where Christians differ. Were Achan’s children put to death for his sin? Some think only Achan was stoned, with his goods and animals destroyed, and that the family was brought to the valley to witness it. Others note that “all Israel stoned him” and “burned them with fire” (v. 25), and that the stolen goods were buried in the family tent, which suggests the household shared the theft and its concealment.

This commentary’s view. The likeliest reading is that his family died with him and were complicit in the concealment, so the law that children must not die for a father’s sin (Deuteronomy 24:16) was not broken. The text does not spell out what they knew, and the view should be held with care rather than used to make the scene feel easy.
verseByVerse.note: “Achor” means “trouble” (ESV note).

7.theology:
Sin is never private. God treats a body as a body: a church, a family, a nation is not a collection of separate units whose choices stay inside them. The teaching that offends here, that one person’s act counts for many, is the same teaching that saves in Romans 5.

Yesterday's victory is not today's permission. Nobody in verses 2-3 does anything wicked. Presumption in this chapter is not arrogance; it is the quiet assumption that because God helped last time he will help this time, without being asked.

The condition on the promise. Verse 12 attaches a condition to the promise of 1:5, and no amount of prayer substitutes for dealing with the thing itself.

The Valley of Trouble as a door of hope. The place of a nation's shame becomes, in Hosea, the way back in (Hos. 2:15), as the cross later became the sign of salvation.
7.examples: Achan buried a coat and some silver under his tent, and nothing happened to him for days while others paid for it. The four verbs run in order and each one is small, and most of us are somewhere in that sequence about something. The counsel is not to feel worse but to dig the thing up, and we can, because the trouble it deserves has already fallen on Christ, who obeyed where we took and hid. Bring it into the light: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9), and his Spirit gives the strength to put away what we have been hiding. The word spoken to the confessing sinner is my son.

keyVerse.quote: I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.
keyVerse.note: Everything since chapter 1 has rested on God’s promise to be with his people, and here he says his help can be withdrawn. Hidden sin is never private, and there is no way round it but to bring it out and put it away; the gospel answers that need in the one who bore our sin.

7.reflection:
God counted Achan’s secret sin as Israel’s sin (v. 1), and thirty-six men died for it. How does this challenge the idea that sin is a private matter, in a family or a church?

Israel went up against Ai without asking God (vv. 2–3). After a success, where are you most tempted to stop praying and start counting?

Achan said, “I coveted them and took them”, then hid them (v. 21). Where do you recognise the pattern of seeing, wanting, taking and hiding in your own temptations, and where is the best place to break it?

God promised to make “the Valley of Achor a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15). What would it look like for you to bring a hidden thing into the light, trusting that Christ has borne its judgment?

8.title: Ai Defeated and Covenant Renewal at Mount Ebal
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land.<sup>2</sup>And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. Only its spoil and its livestock you shall take as plunder for yourselves. Lay an ambush against the city, behind it."<sup>3</sup>So Joshua and all the fighting men arose to go up to Ai. And Joshua chose 30,000 mighty men of valor and sent them out by night.<sup>4</sup>And he commanded them, "Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind it. Do not go very far from the city, but all of you remain ready.<sup>5</sup>And I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. And when they come out against us just as before, we shall flee before them.<sup>6</sup>And they will come out after us, until we have drawn them away from the city. For they will say, 'They are fleeing from us, just as before.' So we will flee before them.<sup>7</sup>Then you shall rise up from the ambush and seize the city, for the LORD your God will give it into your hand.<sup>8</sup>And as soon as you have taken the city, you shall set the city on fire. You shall do according to the word of the LORD. See, I have commanded you."<sup>9</sup>So Joshua sent them out. And they went to the place of ambush and lay between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai, but Joshua spent that night among the people.<sup>10</sup>Joshua arose early in the morning and mustered the people and went up, he and the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai.<sup>11</sup>And all the fighting men who were with him went up and drew near before the city and encamped on the north side of Ai, with a ravine between them and Ai.<sup>12</sup>He took about 5,000 men and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, to the west of the city.<sup>13</sup>So they stationed the forces, the main encampment that was north of the city and its rear guard west of the city. But Joshua spent that night in the valley.<sup>14</sup>And as soon as the king of Ai saw this, he and all his people, the men of the city, hurried and went out early to the appointed place toward the Arabah to meet Israel in battle. But he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city.<sup>15</sup>And Joshua and all Israel pretended to be beaten before them and fled in the direction of the wilderness.<sup>16</sup>So all the people who were in the city were called together to pursue them, and as they pursued Joshua they were drawn away from the city.<sup>17</sup>Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel. They left the city open and pursued Israel.<sup>18</sup>Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand." And Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city.<sup>19</sup>And the men in the ambush rose quickly out of their place, and as soon as he had stretched out his hand, they ran and entered the city and captured it. And they hurried to set the city on fire.<sup>20</sup>So when the men of Ai looked back, behold, the smoke of the city went up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that, for the people who fled to the wilderness turned back against the pursuers.<sup>21</sup>And when Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had captured the city, and that the smoke of the city went up, then they turned back and struck down the men of Ai.<sup>22</sup>And the others came out from the city against them, so they were in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side. And Israel struck them down, until there was left none that survived or escaped.<sup>23</sup>But the king of Ai they took alive, and brought him near to Joshua.<sup>24</sup>When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the open wilderness where they pursued them, and all of them to the very last had fallen by the edge of the sword, all Israel returned to Ai and struck it down with the edge of the sword.<sup>25</sup>And all who fell that day, both men and women, were 12,000, all the people of Ai.<sup>26</sup>But Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin until he had devoted all the inhabitants of Ai to destruction.<sup>27</sup>Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as their plunder, according to the word of the LORD that he commanded Joshua.<sup>28</sup>So Joshua burned Ai and made it forever a heap of ruins, as it is to this day.<sup>29</sup>And he hanged the king of Ai on a tree until evening. And at sunset Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city and raised over it a great heap of stones, which stands there to this day.<sup>30</sup>At that time Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal,<sup>31</sup>just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded the people of Israel, as it is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, "an altar of uncut stones, upon which no man has wielded an iron tool." And they offered on it burnt offerings to the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings.<sup>32</sup>And there, in the presence of the people of Israel, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.<sup>33</sup>And all Israel, sojourner as well as native born, with their elders and officers and their judges, stood on opposite sides of the ark before the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, half of them in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded at the first, to bless the people of Israel.<sup>34</sup>And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the Book of the Law.<sup>35</sup>There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them.
8.overview:
Where we are. Achan’s sin has been exposed and judged, and the LORD has turned from his burning anger (7:26). Israel is still camped below Ai, with thirty-six fresh graves behind it.

The message. When sin has been dealt with, God restores his people with the same promise he gave at the start and leads them to victory by his own plan. Then he halts the campaign to bring the whole nation, native and foreigner, old and young, before his altar and his word, standing between blessing and curse. The land is held by a people who worship God and hear him.

Why it was said. The first hearers needed to know that defeat need not be final when sin is put away, and that the conquest was for covenant life, not merely territory, as Moses had commanded (Deuteronomy 27). Later readers, living under the covenant’s curses, could see where blessing and curse were first set before them (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God renews his commission: do not fear, take the whole army, lay an ambush, and this time keep the spoil (vv. 1–2). Joshua sets a trap that uses Israel’s earlier flight as bait (vv. 3–13). Ai’s army chases the decoy, the ambush takes the empty city at Joshua’s signal, and the men of Ai are caught between two forces (vv. 14–23). The city is destroyed, its spoil taken at God’s command, and its king hanged and buried under stones at the gate (vv. 24–29). At Mount Ebal Joshua builds an altar, writes the law on stones and reads every word of it to the whole assembly (vv. 30–35).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. The king of Ai, hanged on a tree and taken down at sunset as the law required (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), foreshadows another King hanged on a tree and taken down before evening, who became “a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The altar stands on Ebal, the mountain of the curse, because that is where atonement had to be made. And the law written on stones, which Israel would break, points to the new covenant in which God writes his law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), sealed in Christ’s blood.

For us. Failure is not the end for those who deal honestly with their sin: God gives back the same promises, unreduced. And victory is never the goal in itself. God’s people are won in order to worship, gathered around his whole word, with the outsider and the child standing among them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Same Words, After the Failure
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God restores his people after their failure with the very words of Joshua’s first commission. Before Joshua asks anything, the LORD says, “Do not fear and do not be dismayed” (v. 1), sends the whole army this time, not a detachment, and speaks of Ai as already given: king, people, city and land. Two new instructions follow (v. 2). The spoil and livestock of Ai, unlike Jericho’s, may be kept, so the whole difference between the two cities lies in what God says. And Israel is to lay an ambush behind the city. Grace after failure is not a reduced promise but the same promise, given back whole.
verseByVerse.theology: The words of chapter 1 are given back almost unaltered. God does not re-commission a chastened man on reduced terms or with a warning attached; the sentence he had used before the failure is the sentence he uses after it.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, this guards against two opposite mistakes. One is to turn a particular no from God into a permanent law for every case; the other is to think that because God later says yes, his earlier no did not matter. Achan's sin and Israel's freedom here rest on the same thing: what God has actually said.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land. And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. Only its spoil and its livestock you shall take as plunder for yourselves. Lay an ambush against the city, behind it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Joshua asks, God renews his first commission, promises Ai into his hand, and corrects two things without reproach: take the whole army, and this time keep the spoil.

Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Joshua has not asked. After Achan, after thirty-six funerals, after a day face down in the dust, God opens the conversation with almost the words of the original commission (1:9). The promise never rested on Joshua’s record, so Joshua’s record has not altered it.

Take all the fighting men with you. The first correction: last time three thousand went, because the scouts had done the arithmetic. And God says again I have given into your hand, as a thing already done.

Its spoil and its livestock. The second is a permission that ought to stop the reader cold: take the plunder, as the law allowed in ordinary war (Deuteronomy 20:14). Days earlier a man was executed for taking a coat and some silver. The difference was never the goods. Jericho was the firstfruits and belonged wholly to God; the goods of Ai are given to Israel. What changed is what God said, and Achan died because he treated a command about property as a suggestion.

The same call, given back. Jesus did the same with Peter after his denials: no lecture, but the original call given back, “Follow me” (John 21:15–19). God’s promises do not shrink after his people’s failures, because they rest on his faithfulness, not theirs.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The trap is God’s instruction, carried out with care, and its bait is Israel’s own earlier humiliation. Joshua sends a large force by night to hide west of the city, close and ready (vv. 3–4). The main army will approach, pretend to be beaten and run, because the men of Ai will say, “They are fleeing from us, just as before” (vv. 5–6). When the city is empty the hidden force will take it and burn it, “according to the word of the LORD” (vv. 7–8). The ambush is set overnight (v. 9). At dawn the army camps in plain view north of Ai across a ravine, a further force waits to the west, and Joshua spends the night in the valley (vv. 10–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Jericho fell to a shout and no tactics at all. Ai falls to reconnaissance, a night march, a concealed force and a feigned retreat, and God is the one who says lay an ambush. Both victories are entirely his. What changes is the means God uses, and nothing in this book lets a reader turn either method into a rule.
verseByVerse.examples: The bait is Israel's own humiliation. The plan works precisely because Ai has beaten them once and will believe it is happening again, just as before. The defeat that shamed the nation a chapter ago is the thing God uses to take the city.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua and all the fighting men arose to go up to Ai. And Joshua chose 30,000 mighty men of valor and sent them out by night. And he commanded them, "Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind it. Do not go very far from the city, but all of you remain ready. And I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. And when they come out against us just as before, we shall flee before them. And they will come out after us, until we have drawn them away from the city. For they will say, 'They are fleeing from us, just as before.' So we will flee before them. Then you shall rise up from the ambush and seize the city, for the LORD your God will give it into your hand. And as soon as you have taken the city, you shall set the city on fire. You shall do according to the word of the LORD. See, I have commanded you." So Joshua sent them out. And they went to the place of ambush and lay between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai, but Joshua spent that night among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua sets a careful ambush, as much God’s command as the trumpets at Jericho, and the bait in the trap is Israel’s own earlier flight.

You shall lie in ambush against the city. A night march, a concealed force, a decoy, a feigned retreat, a signal and a coordinated turn: competent soldiering. This is not Joshua falling back on human wisdom after the miracles ran out; the ambush is God’s instruction (v. 2). God works by wonders and by ordinary means, and both are his.

Just as before. The plan depends on the men of Ai saying, “They are fleeing from us, just as before” (v. 6). Once the sin is put away, God turns the defeat it brought into the bait for victory.

Joshua spent that night among the people. The commander does not withdraw to wait. He sleeps among the men who will be doing the running in the morning.

Is it right for God to command a deception? A feigned retreat in open war is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids: an enemy in battle is not owed the truth about one’s plans (compare Rahab, 2:4–6).

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua arose early in the morning and mustered the people and went up, he and the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai. And all the fighting men who were with him went up and drew near before the city and encamped on the north side of Ai, with a ravine between them and Ai. He took about 5,000 men and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, to the west of the city. So they stationed the forces, the main encampment that was north of the city and its rear guard west of the city. But Joshua spent that night in the valley.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The army camps in plain view north of Ai while a hidden force waits to the west, and Joshua spends the night in the valley between the armies.

Joshua arose early in the morning. Up early again, the fifth time the writer has said so (3:1; 6:12, 15; 7:16). Israel camps across a ravine where the whole city can count them, while the force to the west also blocks the road from Bethel.

Joshua spent that night in the valley. Not behind the lines, but on the low ground between two armies, the night before a battle in which he himself is the decoy.

Uncertain wording. Is the “about 5,000 men” of verse 12 the same ambush as the thirty thousand of verse 3? Some think there were two forces; others that one figure has suffered in copying, or that the word for thousand here means a military unit rather than an exact count. Nothing in the story depends on settling it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ai is defeated by trusting what it thought it knew. The king sees Israel and hurries out at dawn, not knowing there is an ambush behind the city (v. 14). Israel feigns defeat and runs toward the wilderness, and every man in Ai and Bethel pours out after them, leaving the city open (vv. 15–17). At God’s word Joshua stretches out his javelin, and the ambush rises, takes the city and sets it alight (vv. 18–19). The men of Ai look back and see the smoke, the fleeing army turns, and they are caught between two forces with nowhere to run (vv. 20–22). Not one escapes, and the king is brought to Joshua alive (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Their confidence was built on a real memory. Ai had beaten Israel, and the men running out of the gates that morning were reasoning from evidence. Overconfidence is rarely senseless; it usually reasons soundly from what happened last time.
verseByVerse.examples: The outstretched javelin is the gesture Moses made with his staff over the sea and with his hands at Rephidim (Ex. 14:16; 17:11). It has no power in itself. It is a man standing in plain view with his arm up, so that nobody watching can mistake whose victory this is.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as the king of Ai saw this, he and all his people, the men of the city, hurried and went out early to the appointed place toward the Arabah to meet Israel in battle. But he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city. And Joshua and all Israel pretended to be beaten before them and fled in the direction of the wilderness. So all the people who were in the city were called together to pursue them, and as they pursued Joshua they were drawn away from the city. Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel. They left the city open and pursued Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king of Ai rushes out, trusting his last victory, and empties his city to chase a retreat that is only pretended.

Hurried and went out early. He has beaten these people once and watched them run, and the evidence he trusts is about to destroy him. He is making Israel’s mistake of chapter 7: reading the future from the last result without reckoning with God. He can see everything in front of him and nothing behind (v. 14).

They left the city open. Every man of Ai, and of neighbouring Bethel, is out on the hillside chasing a defeat that is not happening, and the gates shut against Israel stand wide.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand." And Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city. And the men in the ambush rose quickly out of their place, and as soon as he had stretched out his hand, they ran and entered the city and captured it. And they hurried to set the city on fire. So when the men of Ai looked back, behold, the smoke of the city went up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that, for the people who fled to the wilderness turned back against the pursuers. And when Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had captured the city, and that the smoke of the city went up, then they turned back and struck down the men of Ai. And the others came out from the city against them, so they were in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side. And Israel struck them down, until there was left none that survived or escaped. But the king of Ai they took alive, and brought him near to Joshua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At God’s word Joshua stretches out his javelin, the hidden force takes and burns the empty city, and the men of Ai, caught between two forces, are destroyed.

Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand. The signal comes from God. A raised spear kills nobody at that distance, but the ambush rose “as soon as he had stretched out his hand” (v. 19). As with Moses’ uplifted hands against Amalek (Exodus 17:11), the outstretched arm of God’s servant marks the work of God.

The smoke of the city went up to heaven. When the pursuers look back, the city is gone and the road home is burning. An army caught between the men it was chasing and the men who took its houses is defeated not by superior force but by having believed something false. Only the king is taken alive (v. 23).

Uncertain wording. The weapon translated “javelin” (kidon) is not certainly identified: perhaps a throwing spear, perhaps a curved sword. Either way it is held out as a signal and kept outstretched until the end (v. 26).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–29 — A King on a Tree, Taken Down by Sunset
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The judgment on Ai is complete, and the narrator records it soberly. Israel strikes down the people of Ai in the open country and then in the city: twelve thousand men and women fall that day (vv. 24–25). Joshua keeps his javelin stretched out until the city is wholly devoted to destruction (v. 26). This time the livestock and spoil are taken as plunder, as the LORD commanded (v. 27). Ai is burned and left a heap of ruins (v. 28). Its king is hanged on a tree until evening, then taken down at sunset as the law required and buried under a great heap of stones at the city gate (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 29 is written to the letter of the law. A body was not to remain on a tree overnight, because a hanged man is cursed by God and would defile the land (Deut. 21:22-23). Israel executes a Canaanite king and then observes, to the hour, a commandment about how to handle the cursed.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul takes that exact law and puts it on Christ: he redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Gal. 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the open wilderness where they pursued them, and all of them to the very last had fallen by the edge of the sword, all Israel returned to Ai and struck it down with the edge of the sword. And all who fell that day, both men and women, were 12,000, all the people of Ai. But Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin until he had devoted all the inhabitants of Ai to destruction. Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as their plunder, according to the word of the LORD that he commanded Joshua. So Joshua burned Ai and made it forever a heap of ruins, as it is to this day. And he hanged the king of Ai on a tree until evening. And at sunset Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city and raised over it a great heap of stones, which stands there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
