Ai is wholly destroyed and its spoil taken at God’s word, and its king is hanged on a tree and taken down at sunset as the law required, a scene the New Testament sees answered at the cross.

All who fell that day. Twelve thousand people, stated as a number and not dressed up. The book neither celebrates this nor hides it (on the hard question, see 6:17–19). Joshua’s arm stayed out the whole time, as Moses’ hands were held up until Amalek was beaten (Exodus 17:12).

According to the word of the LORD. The plunder is taken at God’s word: the same action that condemned one man in chapter 7 is right when God commands it.

He hanged the king of Ai on a tree. The king was probably put to death first and his body then hung up for display, as the five kings are at 10:26. It comes down at sunset in obedience to the law, “for a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23), and is buried under stones at the gate he had led his army out of.

Another King hanged on a tree. Another King was hanged on a tree outside a city gate, taken down before evening because the law required it (John 19:31), and laid behind a stone. The curse that fell on a Canaanite king because he was God’s enemy fell on this one although he was not, so that his enemies could be freed from it: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

Was it just to destroy Ai? As at Jericho, this was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Leviticus 18:24–28). It was a unique command, no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is “not of this world” (John 18:36).

Twelve thousand at a small town? Ai’s people were joined by the men of Bethel (v. 17), and some read “thousand” here as a military unit rather than an exact count, as in verses 3 and 12.

A heap of ruins, as it is to this day. Ai means “the ruin”. Where it stood is uncertain (see on 7:2–5): if the usual site, et-Tell, is the wrong one, the main archaeological objection loses its force.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The campaign stops so that the nation can worship and hear God’s word, as Moses had commanded. Joshua builds an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal, and burnt offerings and peace offerings are made on it (vv. 30–31). He writes a copy of the law on stones before the people (v. 32). All Israel, sojourners as well as native-born, stands on either side of the ark, half facing Gerizim and half facing Ebal (v. 33), and Joshua reads every word of the law, the blessing and the curse, to the whole assembly, women and children included (vv. 34–35). The Greek Old Testament places these verses after 9:2, and one Dead Sea Scroll seems to set the altar just after the Jordan crossing; the Hebrew order, which our Bibles follow, puts it here.
verseByVerse.theology: Ebal and Gerizim are twenty miles north of Ai, in country nobody had taken. Israel broke off a war, marched the entire nation, women, children and foreigners, deep into unconquered territory, and held a service. This is not a pause between campaigns. It is a claim staked in the middle of the land.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 35 is exact about who was there: the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them. Not a word was left out and nobody was left outside. The foreigners standing in that assembly show what became of Rahab’s household, and of everyone since who has come in from outside: they stand with God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded the people of Israel, as it is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, "an altar of uncut stones, upon which no man has wielded an iron tool." And they offered on it burnt offerings to the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings. And there, in the presence of the people of Israel, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua builds the altar Moses commanded on Mount Ebal, offers sacrifice and writes the law on stones: Israel’s first building in the land is a place of worship under God’s word.

On Mount Ebal. Ebal stands above Shechem, some twenty miles north of Ai, in unconquered country. How the nation got there safely the text does not say, and many think the writer places the scene here for its meaning as much as its date. What matters is that it was done “just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded” (v. 31; Deuteronomy 27:1–8).

An altar of uncut stones. No iron tool was to touch it (Exodus 20:25; Deuteronomy 27:5–6). The one place where human skill is forbidden is the place where atonement is made: a man may not improve the way back to God.

Burnt offerings and peace offerings. Burnt offerings went up entirely, nothing kept back. Peace offerings ended in a shared meal, the sign that the quarrel was over. Sin is dealt with first, then the meal, and the gospel keeps the same order: Christ offered himself once for all, and his people eat at his table in peace.

A copy of the law of Moses. A nation that had spent forty years being carried and fed takes its first act of settled ownership, and the act is to put God’s words up where the country can read them.

verseByVerse.quote: And all Israel, sojourner as well as native born, with their elders and officers and their judges, stood on opposite sides of the ark before the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, half of them in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded at the first, to bless the people of Israel. And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the Book of the Law. There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole nation, foreigners, women and children included, stands between the mountains of blessing and curse while Joshua reads every word of the law: God’s people are gathered by his word and placed under its promises and warnings.

In front of Mount Gerizim and … Mount Ebal. The valley between the ridges is a natural amphitheatre. Moses had assigned their parts: Gerizim the mountain of blessing, Ebal the mountain of curse (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:12–13). The altar was built on Ebal. Any dealing with God has to happen where the curse is, because that is what stands in the way.

Sojourner as well as native born. The writer twice mentions the foreigners (vv. 33, 35). Rahab’s household, so lately outside the camp (6:23), may well have stood there. Whoever joined himself to Israel’s God stood under the same word.

There was not a word … that Joshua did not read. The whole law was read in one sitting, including the parts that indict the listeners, and the women and little ones stood through it with everyone else (Deuteronomy 31:10–13). A church that wants God’s blessing must be willing to hear the whole of his word.

Between blessing and curse. So the first great assembly in the land stands between a mountain of blessing and a mountain of curse, with an altar smoking on the mountain of curse, and hears a law it will in time break. Centuries later God promised through Jeremiah, who watched Israel break it and lose the land, “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). That is the Spirit’s work in believers now (Ezekiel 36:27), and where we still fall short, Christ has kept every word in our place and borne the curse for us.

Textual note. In Deuteronomy 27:4, where Moses commands this altar, the Samaritan Pentateuch (the Samaritans’ own copy of the five books of Moses) reads Gerizim, their holy mountain, instead of Ebal. The Hebrew text reads Ebal, and Joshua follows it.

8.theology:
Restoration on the original terms. The words God gives Joshua after the disaster are the words he gave him before it. Nothing is withheld and no conditions are added, because the promise never rested on Joshua's record in the first place. Jesus restored Peter the same way on the beach after his denials: he did not ask how Peter could have done it, but whether Peter loved him (John 21:15-17).

Miracle and means are both his. The shout at Jericho and the ambush at Ai were both commanded by God. Christians divide into those who think faith waits and those who think faith works, and each side has a favourite chapter here. The question in Joshua is never which approach is holier; it is what God has actually said.

The same act, damned and commanded. Achan died for taking spoil; Israel is ordered to take spoil, and the writer notes that they did it according to the word of the LORD (v. 27). What made the act right or wrong was God’s command, not the goods themselves, which is the thing to remember wherever Christians build permanent rules out of God's particular instructions.

Hanged on a tree, taken down by sunset. The king of Ai's body is removed before nightfall because a hanged man is cursed by God (Deut. 21:22-23), and Paul applies that same law to the cross (Gal. 3:13). And the altar in this chapter is built on Ebal, the mountain of cursing, not on Gerizim. Atonement is always made where the curse is.
8.examples:
Then: A defeated army went back to the town that had beaten it, won by pretending to run away again, and then walked twenty miles into enemy country with its wives and children to stand in a valley and listen to the whole law read out, every word, including the parts about what would happen if they broke it.

Now: The word to take from this chapter is the first one. God opened the conversation after the failure, and used the sentence he had used before it. If you are carrying something you assume has permanently changed the terms (a collapse, a disqualifying failure, a year you would not repeat), notice what God did not say to Joshua. He did not review the incident. He said do not be afraid, take the whole army, and go back to the place where it went wrong. The failure was real and had been dealt with; the promise had never rested on Joshua in the first place, and it does not rest on you.

keyVerse.quote: Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land.
keyVerse.note: After defeat, sin exposed and judgment carried out, God speaks first and gives back the words of Joshua’s original commission (1:9). His promise never rested on his servant’s record, so failure that has been dealt with does not reduce it; that is the grace believers know in Christ.

8.reflection:
After the defeat at Ai, God opened the conversation with almost the same words he used at the start (v. 1; 1:9). What does this tell you about how God treats his people after a failure that has been confessed and dealt with?

Ai was defeated because it trusted what had happened “just as before” (v. 6). Where are you tempted to read the future from your last success or failure rather than from God’s word?

The king of Ai was hanged on a tree and taken down at sunset (v. 29). Read Galatians 3:13 together. What does it mean for you that Christ took that curse?

Joshua read every word of the law to everyone, women, children and foreigners included (vv. 34–35). How does your church let the whole of Scripture be heard by the whole of God’s people, and what part could you play in that?

9.title: The Gibeonite Deception
9.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as all the kings who were beyond the Jordan in the hill country and in the lowland all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, heard of this,<sup>2</sup>they gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.<sup>3</sup>But when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai,<sup>4</sup>they on their part acted with cunning and went and made ready provisions and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins, worn-out and torn and mended,<sup>5</sup>with worn-out, patched sandals on their feet, and worn-out clothes. And all their provisions were dry and crumbly.<sup>6</sup>And they went to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, "We have come from a distant country, so now make a covenant with us."<sup>7</sup>But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you live among us; then how can we make a covenant with you?"<sup>8</sup>They said to Joshua, "We are your servants." And Joshua said to them, "Who are you? And where do you come from?"<sup>9</sup>They said to him, "From a very distant country your servants have come, because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt,<sup>10</sup>and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon the king of Heshbon, and to Og king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth.<sup>11</sup>So our elders and all the inhabitants of our country said to us, 'Take provisions in your hand for the journey and go to meet them and say to them, "We are your servants. Come now, make a covenant with us."'<sup>12</sup>Here is our bread. It was still warm when we took it from our houses as our food for the journey on the day we set out to come to you, but now, behold, it is dry and crumbly.<sup>13</sup>These wineskins were new when we filled them, and behold, they have burst. And these garments and sandals of ours are worn out from the very long journey."<sup>14</sup>So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore to them.<sup>16</sup>At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them.<sup>17</sup>And the people of Israel set out and reached their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim.<sup>18</sup>But the people of Israel did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders.<sup>19</sup>But all the leaders said to all the congregation, "We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them.<sup>20</sup>This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath that we swore to them."<sup>21</sup>And the leaders said to them, "Let them live." So they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, just as the leaders had said of them.<sup>22</sup>Joshua summoned them, and he said to them, "Why did you deceive us, saying, 'We are very far from you,' when you dwell among us?<sup>23</sup>Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you shall never be anything but servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God."<sup>24</sup>They answered Joshua, "Because it was told to your servants for a certainty that the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you—so we feared greatly for our lives because of you and did this thing.<sup>25</sup>And now, behold, we are in your hand. Whatever seems good and right in your sight to do to us, do it."<sup>26</sup>So he did this to them and delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel, and they did not kill them.<sup>27</sup>But Joshua made them that day cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, to this day, in the place that he should choose.
9.overview:
Where we are. Jericho and Ai have fallen, and at Mount Ebal Israel has just renewed the covenant and heard the whole law read (8:30–35). The news has spread through Canaan, and the danger now changes shape: not an assault but a confidence trick.

The message. God’s people are not only threatened by enemies who attack them but by decisions they make without him, and the most dangerous decisions are the ones that look obvious. Yet the chapter does not end in disaster. A promise made in the LORD’s name must be kept, even when it was obtained by fraud, and God takes Israel’s prayerless blunder and the Gibeonites’ lie and turns them into a place of service at his altar.

Why it was said. Israel’s law allowed terms of peace only with cities “very far from you” (Deuteronomy 20:15). A nation about to settle among the peoples of the land needed to learn that careful checking is no substitute for asking God, and that his name, once sworn by, binds (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The kings of the land unite to fight (vv. 1–2), but Gibeon chooses another way and arrives at Gilgal in costume, worn sandals and mouldy bread, claiming to come from far away (vv. 3–6). Israel is suspicious and is talked round by a speech of true statements with one fact left out (vv. 7–13). They examine the evidence but do not ask counsel from the LORD, and the leaders swear an oath (vv. 14–15). Three days later the truth is out; the congregation grumbles, but the leaders keep the oath (vv. 16–21). Joshua curses the deceivers with a sentence that turns out to be a mercy: they will cut wood and draw water for the house of God, and he delivers them from Israel’s anger (vv. 22–27).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God and by pattern. The leaders kept an oath sworn to deceivers because God’s name was on it; how much more will God keep the oath he swore to his own people, for “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). And the Gibeonites, outsiders who came “because of the name of the LORD your God” (v. 9), end up serving at his altar: a picture of strangers brought near. They had to come with a lie; no one needs to come to Christ that way, for he says, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

For us. Pray about the decisions that look easy as well as the hard ones, and keep your word when it costs you. God can make good even out of our failures to consult him, though that is no reason to repeat them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — Three Ways of Hearing the Same News
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The same news about Jericho and Ai reaches the whole land, and it drives the kings together. Six nations, from the hill country to the coast, hear what Israel’s God has done (v. 1), and instead of seeking peace they combine to fight Joshua and Israel (v. 2). They have heard enough to know that Israel’s God is at work, and they conclude that he can be resisted. Their response sets the stage for Gibeon’s very different one, and shows that information alone never changes a heart.
verseByVerse.theology: Three groups in this book hear the same reports and do three different things. Rahab heard and asked for mercy. These kings hear and form a coalition. The Gibeonites, in the next verse, hear and start sewing patches onto sandals. The news was identical every time.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as all the kings who were beyond the Jordan in the hill country and in the lowland all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, heard of this, they gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two burned towns unite the kings of Canaan against Israel.

They gathered together as one. Six nations, from every region of the country, act together for the first time. Canaan had been a patchwork of small rival city-kingdoms (see the introduction); the fall of Jericho and Ai has done what nothing else could and made them one.

The same news, different responses. Nobody in Canaan is short of information. What separates its people is what they do with it, one of the oldest patterns in Scripture: the same word softens one heart and hardens another. Rahab heard and believed (2:9–11); these kings hear and fight; Gibeon hears and schemes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–13 — Worn Sandals and Mouldy Bread
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gibeon hears the same reports and tries a third way: survival by deception. They dress the part of travellers from far away, with split wineskins, patched sandals, worn clothes and dry, crumbly bread, and ask for a covenant (vv. 3–6). Israel suspects they may be neighbours (v. 7), so the Gibeonites talk: they speak of the name of the LORD, of Egypt, Sihon and Og (vv. 9–10), quote their elders (v. 11), and show their exhibits, bread that was warm when they left home and wineskins that were new (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Every fact in their speech is chosen. They mention Egypt and the two Amorite kings, old news that would have reached a distant country, and say nothing whatever about Jericho and Ai, which happened last month and only a neighbour would know. The gaps in the story are as carefully made as the story.
verseByVerse.examples: Their disguise is also aimed at a clause of Israel’s own law. Deuteronomy permits terms of peace with a city that is very far and forbids it absolutely with the cities of Canaan (Deut. 20:10-18). The Gibeonites are not improvising a lie; they have worked out precisely which provision of Israel’s law they need to come under, and then dressed for it.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai, they on their part acted with cunning and went and made ready provisions and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins, worn-out and torn and mended, with worn-out, patched sandals on their feet, and worn-out clothes. And all their provisions were dry and crumbly. And they went to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, "We have come from a distant country, so now make a covenant with us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gibeon decides it cannot win, and sets out to survive by a carefully staged lie.

Acted with cunning. Someone in Gibeon worked out what a man would look like after weeks on the road and produced a whole wardrobe, down to the state of the bread. The disguise is aimed at a specific sentence of Israel’s law, which allowed terms of peace only with cities “very far from you” (Deuteronomy 20:15). They have studied the God they fear more closely than the kings up the road have.

In the camp at Gilgal. They walk into Gilgal, where the stones from the Jordan stand, where the nation was circumcised and the Passover kept, and open with the lie: “We have come from a distant country.”

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew verb in verse 4 is rare and its spelling uncertain. The ESV, reading a word that differs by one letter, has “made ready provisions”, as in verse 12; the other spelling means that they disguised themselves as envoys (so the KJV). Either way the meaning is clear: the whole journey was a costume.
verseByVerse.note: Gibeon lay about six miles north-west of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you live among us; then how can we make a covenant with you?" They said to Joshua, "We are your servants." And Joshua said to them, "Who are you? And where do you come from?" They said to him, "From a very distant country your servants have come, because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt, and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon the king of Heshbon, and to Og king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth. So our elders and all the inhabitants of our country said to us, 'Take provisions in your hand for the journey and go to meet them and say to them, "We are your servants. Come now, make a covenant with us."' Here is our bread. It was still warm when we took it from our houses as our food for the journey on the day we set out to come to you, but now, behold, it is dry and crumbly. These wineskins were new when we filled them, and behold, they have burst. And these garments and sandals of ours are worn out from the very long journey."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel asks exactly the right question, and is then talked out of its suspicion by a speech of true statements with the one vital fact left out.

Perhaps you live among us. Israel very nearly catches it. Someone in that meeting had read Deuteronomy and knew what to ask. That makes what follows worse: they saw the danger, named it aloud, and were then talked out of it.

We are your servants. They mention Egypt, Sihon and Og, all far away and long ago, and are carefully silent about Jericho and Ai, which verse 3 says is exactly what they had heard. The most effective lies are usually built from true statements.

Because of the name of the LORD your God. One clause in the whole performance is entirely true. They had heard the report of Israel’s God and were terrified, and that part needed no invention at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–15 — They Did Not Ask Counsel from the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Careful checking without prayer leads Israel into a covenant God had forbidden. The men examine the provisions, and the evidence seems sound (v. 14), but the chapter turns on one phrase: they “did not ask counsel from the LORD”. Joshua makes peace, grants them their lives, and the leaders of the congregation swear to the covenant (v. 15). The danger was not that Israel was careless, for they checked the evidence, but that they trusted their own judgment in a case that looked obvious.
verseByVerse.theology: The failure is not laziness and it is not wickedness. They investigated competently and reached a reasonable conclusion from real evidence. What they did not do was ask the one party who knew where these men lived.
verseByVerse.examples: The means were standing in the camp. The high priest carried the Urim and Thummim, the sacred lots, for exactly this: so that Israel could put a question to God and get an answer (Num. 27:21). It was not that God was silent. Nobody asked him.

verseByVerse.quote: So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD. And Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel examines the evidence carefully but does not ask God, and so makes a covenant he had forbidden.

Took some of their provisions. They tested the story against the bread and found it dry, exactly as it had been prepared to be found. The failure was not carelessness but checking without asking God, and the means of asking was at hand: Eleazar the priest, who could put the question to the LORD (Numbers 27:21), was in the camp.

Why they did not ask. The case looked closed. When the evidence is ambiguous we pray; when it looks obvious we act. The Gibeonites’ whole strategy was to make the case look obvious, and it will work again on anyone who only prays about the decisions that are difficult. God gives wisdom generously to those who ask him (James 1:5).

The leaders of the congregation swore to them. Nobody thinks the oath matters much when it is sworn. It is about to become the most important thing in the chapter.

Must every oath be kept? Israel kept this one, and God later held Saul’s house guilty for breaking it (2 Samuel 21:1). A Christian should keep his word even when it costs him (Psalm 15:4), unless keeping it would mean sin. Better still, make fewer and more careful promises: “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An oath sworn in the LORD’s name holds, even when it was obtained by fraud. Three days later Israel learns that these men are neighbours, and reaches their four cities, Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim (vv. 16–17). The army does not attack, because the leaders had sworn by the LORD, and the whole congregation grumbles (v. 18). The leaders hold firm: we have sworn by the LORD, and breaking it would bring wrath (vv. 19–20). So the Gibeonites live, as woodcutters and water-carriers (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The treaty was obtained by fraud, and everybody knows it. Israel could have cancelled it on those grounds in ten seconds, and the congregation clearly wanted to. The leaders hold to it because of whose name was invoked, not because of who deserved it.
verseByVerse.examples: That the oath was genuinely binding was proved centuries later, and expensively. Saul broke it and killed Gibeonites, and a three-year famine came on Israel in David's reign with the reason given plainly: there is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death (2 Sam. 21:1).

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them. And the people of Israel set out and reached their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim. But the people of Israel did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lie is exposed within three days, yet Israel does not attack, because the leaders had sworn by the LORD.

At the end of three days. The lie survives three days, and Israel reaches their cities in three days more: the truth was a short walk away the whole time. The army stands outside four towns it was under orders to destroy and does not attack, for one reason, a name: the leaders had sworn “by the LORD, the God of Israel”.

All the congregation murmured. The word is the one used all through the wilderness years. The old sin surfaces in a new situation, and this time the people grumble in favour of obeying a command about the Canaanites: a bad instinct can easily find a good text to stand on.

verseByVerse.quote: But all the leaders said to all the congregation, "We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them. This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath that we swore to them." And the leaders said to them, "Let them live." So they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, just as the leaders had said of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders keep their oath at their own cost, because breaking a promise sworn in God’s name would make him the sponsor of a lie.

We have sworn to them by the LORD. To swear in God’s name is to call him as guarantor of what you say. Breaking it does not merely make a man a liar; it drags God’s name into the lie. That is what the third commandment forbids in taking his name in vain, and it reaches far wider than swearing in the street.

Lest wrath be upon us. They are not being sentimental about promises, and Saul’s reign would prove them right: an oath sworn by deceived men to lying men still bound Israel generations later (2 Samuel 21:1–9).

Swearing to one’s own hurt. A deceived nation kept its word to its deceivers, at its own expense, because of whose name was on it. This is the man of Psalm 15, “who swears to his own hurt and does not change” (Psalm 15:4). The world keeps its promises while they remain convenient; here a whole nation, furious and within its rights, kept one that was not.

God keeps his oath. If men kept a promise made to deceivers because God’s name was on it, God will not break the oath he swore to his own people (Hebrews 6:17–18), and every one of his promises is Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment and mercy meet in the sentence on Gibeon. Joshua names the deception (v. 22) and pronounces a curse: they will always be servants, cutting wood and drawing water “for the house of my God” (v. 23). The Gibeonites answer honestly at last: they believed what God had commanded and feared for their lives (v. 24), and they put themselves in Joshua’s hands (v. 25). He delivers them from the people (v. 26) and attaches them permanently to the altar of the LORD, at the place God would choose (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The sentence Joshua passes is a curse, and the reader should feel how strange a curse it is. It condemns a Canaanite people to spend the rest of their history carrying firewood and water to the altar of the God of Israel. Every other Canaanite city in this book is destroyed; these men are sentenced to live out their lives beside the sacrifices.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what the Gibeonites' work was: wood for the fire and water for the washing, unglamorous, endless and absolutely necessary. No sacrifice was offered in Israel without somebody having carried the fuel, and no priest washed without somebody having drawn the water. The Gibeonites do not preach, prophesy or lead. They keep the altar supplied, and Scripture troubles to record it. Much faithful service in a church still looks like this, and God sees it.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua summoned them, and he said to them, "Why did you deceive us, saying, 'We are very far from you,' when you dwell among us? Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you shall never be anything but servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God." They answered Joshua, "Because it was told to your servants for a certainty that the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you—so we feared greatly for our lives because of you and did this thing. And now, behold, we are in your hand. Whatever seems good and right in your sight to do to us, do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua names the deception and passes sentence, and the Gibeonites, honest at last, put themselves in his hands.

Why did you deceive us? Joshua does not pretend nothing happened. The lie is named, a sentence is passed, and it is called a curse.

For the house of my God. But look at what the curse actually is: wood and water “for the house of my God”. Gibeon is put on the sanctuary’s staff.

So we feared greatly for our lives. Their first honest words are not an excuse but a statement of fact: we were told what your God had ordered, we believed it, and we were terrified. The six nations of verse 1 heard the same thing and decided they could fight; Gibeon decided they could not, and everything they did, the lying included, followed from taking God at his word.

We are in your hand. They do not argue that the treaty binds Israel, though it does. They put themselves in Joshua’s hand and stop negotiating.

Is this slavery? The Gibeonites became permanent servants at the sanctuary, a lower and lasting status, but not property to be bought and sold, and they were protected by an oath in God’s name that even a king was punished for breaking (2 Samuel 21:1). Many think the temple servants of later centuries were partly their descendants (Ezra 2:43; 8:20). Scripture records the arrangement as the merciful outcome of a deception, not as a model for society, and the gospel goes further: in Christ “there is neither slave nor free” (Galatians 3:28).

verseByVerse.quote: So he did this to them and delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel, and they did not kill them. But Joshua made them that day cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, to this day, in the place that he should choose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua shields the Gibeonites from Israel’s anger and binds them for good to the altar of the LORD, where God would later meet his people.

Delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel. The danger to the Gibeonites now is not the Canaanite kings but the congregation of Israel, still grumbling and ready to finish them. Joshua stands between an angry nation and the men who fooled it.

In the place that he should choose. This is Deuteronomy’s language for the future sanctuary (Deuteronomy 12:5). Joshua attaches these men permanently to whatever God is going to do next.

What Gibeon became. It went further than Joshua could have known. Centuries later the tabernacle stood at Gibeon, with Zadok the priest before it (1 Chronicles 16:39), and there Solomon went to sacrifice and God said to him, “Ask what I shall give you” (1 Kings 3:4–5; 2 Chronicles 1:3). The town that lied to save its life ended up with the tent of meeting standing in it.

Outsiders brought near. God took a prayerless blunder, a wardrobe of stage props and a nation’s fury, and made of them a place where he met people; the poor quality of the material has never stopped him. Strangers who came trembling “because of the name of the LORD” ended up serving at his altar, a small picture of what Christ does for outsiders: he brings near those who were far off (Ephesians 2:13), and they need no disguise to come.

9.theology:
Prayerlessness is not laziness. Israel investigated, and the evidence was real. What they did not do was ask the only party who knew where these men lived (Num. 27:21).

An oath in God's name binds even when it was obtained by fraud. The leaders refused to cancel it because the name of the LORD had been invoked. Behind this stands a God who keeps his own oath to his people (Heb. 6:17-18).

Same news, three responses. What divided Rahab, the kings of Canaan and Gibeon was not knowledge but what each did with it. The Gibeonites, for all their lying, had the truer view of God: they believed what God had said about the land, and the kings did not.

What God did with the blunder. The deceivers are sentenced to serve the altar, and centuries later the tent of meeting itself stood in their town. A prayerless decision and an elaborate lie ended in a place where God met his people.
9.examples:
Then: Four Canaanite towns survived the conquest because they dressed up in old clothes, carried stale bread on a journey of a few days, and told a story with the recent news left out of it. Israel checked the evidence, found it convincing, and signed. Three days later they were standing outside the towns of the people they had sworn to protect.

Now: The verse to take away is the eight words in the middle of verse 14, and the reason they are frightening is that nothing else in the chapter went wrong. There was no rebellion, no laziness, no obvious sin, only a sensible decision made on good evidence without asking God, because the case looked clear. Think of the last significant decision you did not pray about: almost certainly the answer seemed obvious. The God who invites us to ask gives wisdom generously and without reproach (James 1:5), and, as Gibeon shows, he is not defeated by the blunders we make when we forget to.

keyVerse.quote: So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this verse. Israel’s failure was not carelessness but careful checking without prayer, in a case that looked obvious. It warns every believer that the decisions we feel no need to pray about are often the ones where we are most easily deceived.

9.reflection:
The Gibeonites’ evidence was carefully prepared and Israel checked it carefully, but “did not ask counsel from the LORD” (v. 14). What kinds of decisions do you tend not to pray about because the answer seems obvious? How might you change that habit?

The leaders kept their oath even though it had been obtained by a lie (vv. 19–20). When is it right to keep a promise that has become costly, and when would keeping it be wrong? What does this teach us about how seriously to make promises in the first place?

The Gibeonites’ “curse” was to serve at the house of God, and Gibeon later became the place where the tabernacle stood (vv. 23, 27). What does this show you about how God can work even through human failure and sin?

The Gibeonites came “because of the name of the LORD” but had to come in disguise. How is coming to Christ different, and what does that mean for the way we invite outsiders to him?

10.title: The Sun Stands Still
10.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua had captured Ai and had devoted it to destruction, doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them,<sup>2</sup>he feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were warriors.<sup>3</sup>So Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, to Piram king of Jarmuth, to Japhia king of Lachish, and to Debir king of Eglon, saying,<sup>4</sup>"Come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon. For it has made peace with Joshua and with the people of Israel."<sup>5</sup>Then the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered their forces and went up with all their armies and encamped against Gibeon and made war against it.<sup>6</sup>And the men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal, saying, "Do not relax your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who dwell in the hill country are gathered against us."<sup>7</sup>So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands. Not a man of them shall stand before you."<sup>9</sup>So Joshua came upon them suddenly, having marched up all night from Gilgal.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD threw them into a panic before Israel, who struck them with a great blow at Gibeon and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon and struck them as far as Azekah and Makkedah.<sup>11</sup>And as they fled before Israel, while they were going down the ascent of Beth-horon, the LORD threw down large stones from heaven on them as far as Azekah, and they died. There were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.<sup>12</sup>At that time Joshua spoke to the LORD in the day when the LORD gave the Amorites over to the sons of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon."<sup>13</sup>And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stopped in the midst of heaven and did not hurry to set for about a whole day.<sup>14</sup>There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel.<sup>15</sup>So Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.<sup>16</sup>These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah.<sup>17</sup>And it was told to Joshua, "The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah."<sup>18</sup>And Joshua said, "Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them,<sup>19</sup>but do not stay there yourselves. Pursue your enemies; attack their rear guard. Do not let them enter their cities, for the LORD your God has given them into your hand."<sup>20</sup>When Joshua and the sons of Israel had finished striking them with a great blow until they were wiped out, and when the remnant that remained of them had entered into the fortified cities,<sup>21</sup>then all the people returned safe to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. Not a man moved his tongue against any of the people of Israel.<sup>22</sup>Then Joshua said, "Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me from the cave."<sup>23</sup>And they did so, and brought those five kings out to him from the cave, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon.<sup>24</sup>And when they brought those kings out to Joshua, Joshua summoned all the men of Israel and said to the chiefs of the men of war who had gone with him, "Come near; put your feet on the necks of these kings." Then they came near and put their feet on their necks.<sup>25</sup>And Joshua said to them, "Do not be afraid or dismayed; be strong and courageous. For thus the LORD will do to all your enemies against whom you fight."<sup>26</sup>And afterward Joshua struck them and put them to death, and he hanged them on five trees. And they hung on the trees until evening.<sup>27</sup>But at the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down from the trees and threw them into the cave where they had hidden themselves, and they set large stones against the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.<sup>28</sup>As for Makkedah, Joshua captured it on that day and struck it, and its king, with the edge of the sword. He devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. And he did to the king of Makkedah just as he had done to the king of Jericho.<sup>29</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah.<sup>30</sup>And the LORD gave it also and its king into the hand of Israel. And he struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it; he left none remaining in it. And he did to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho.<sup>31</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Libnah to Lachish and laid siege to it and fought against it.<sup>32</sup>And the LORD gave Lachish into the hand of Israel, and he captured it on the second day and struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it, as he had done to Libnah.<sup>33</sup>Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish. And Joshua struck him and his people, until he left none remaining.<sup>34</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Lachish to Eglon. And they laid siege to it and fought against it.<sup>35</sup>And they captured it on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword. And he devoted every person in it to destruction that day, as he had done to Lachish.<sup>36</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron. And they fought against it<sup>37</sup>and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword, and its king and its towns, and every person in it. He left none remaining, as he had done to Eglon, and devoted it to destruction and every person in it.<sup>38</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him turned back to Debir and fought against it<sup>39</sup>and he captured it with its king and all its towns. And they struck them with the edge of the sword and devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. Just as he had done to Hebron and to Libnah and its king, so he did to Debir and to its king.<sup>40</sup>So Joshua struck the whole land, the hill country and the Negeb and the lowland and the slopes, and all their kings. He left none remaining, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, just as the LORD God of Israel commanded.<sup>41</sup>And Joshua struck them from Kadesh-barnea as far as Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, as far as Gibeon.<sup>42</sup>And Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel.<sup>43</sup>Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
10.overview:
Where we are. Gibeon has tricked Israel into a treaty, and the leaders have kept their oath (chapter 9). Now the treaty Israel should never have made becomes the occasion of the greatest day in the whole campaign, and of the conquest of the south.

The message. The LORD fights for his people, and he listens to them. He keeps faith with Gibeon through an army that marches all night, throws the enemy into panic, hurls hailstones from heaven, and in answer to Joshua’s prayer lengthens the day. The chapter’s one-sentence reason for everything is its own: “because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel” (v. 42).

Why it was said. Israel faced the walled cities and allied kings of the southern hill country, and later generations faced enemies of their own. Both needed to know that victory had never rested on Israel’s numbers or skill, and that the God of the covenant hears the cry of those who call on him (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Five Amorite kings, led by Adoni-zedek of Jerusalem, besiege Gibeon for changing sides (vv. 1–5). Gibeon appeals to the treaty, and God promises Joshua victory before he sets out (vv. 6–8). After a night march, the LORD routs the coalition, and his hailstones kill more than Israel’s swords (vv. 9–11). Joshua prays publicly for the sun and moon to stand still, and the LORD heeds the voice of a man (vv. 12–15). The five kings are found in a cave, brought out, and put under the feet of Israel’s officers as a sign of what God will do to all their enemies (vv. 16–27). Then city after city in the south falls in the same repeated words, until the summary gives the reason (vv. 28–43).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by promise. The kings under the officers’ feet echo the promise that God will make the Messiah’s enemies his footstool (Psalm 110:1), and Paul tells ordinary Christians that God “will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). The kings hanged on trees bore the curse of the law; Christ became “a curse for us” on a tree (Galatians 3:13). And the man whose voice the LORD heeded for one afternoon points to the Son whom the Father always hears, who “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. The battles that matter are won by God, not by us, yet he invites us to pray boldly and works through ordinary obedience, even a march through the night. Take courage from the defeated enemies of Christ, and pray as those whose voice God hears for his Son’s sake.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Coalition Against the Traitors
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joining God’s people brings their enemies down on you, and Gibeon learns it within days. Adoni-zedek of Jerusalem hears about Ai and Gibeon’s peace with Israel and is afraid, for Gibeon is a great city full of warriors (vv. 1–2). He summons four other kings, of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon (v. 3), and names the target: “let us strike Gibeon” (v. 4). Five armies march and besiege not Israel but the city that changed sides (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's blunder in chapter 9 has just drawn the entire southern coalition out of five fortified cities and concentrated it in one place in open country. Nothing Joshua could have planned would have done that.
verseByVerse.examples: The name of the king of Jerusalem is Adoni-zedek. Centuries earlier a king of Salem, which most identify with Jerusalem (Ps. 76:2), met Abram and blessed him, and his name was Melchizedek, king of righteousness (Gen. 14:18; Heb. 7:2), the man Hebrews takes as the pattern of Christ's priesthood. Melchizedek came out of probably the same city to bless Abram with bread and wine; a later king with a name very like his raises an army to destroy Abram's descendants. Jerusalem has been capable of both since the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua had captured Ai and had devoted it to destruction, doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them, he feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were warriors. So Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, to Piram king of Jarmuth, to Japhia king of Lachish, and to Debir king of Eglon, saying, "Come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon. For it has made peace with Joshua and with the people of Israel." Then the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered their forces and went up with all their armies and encamped against Gibeon and made war against it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five kings turn on Gibeon for making peace with Israel: those who join God’s people inherit their enemies.

He feared greatly. What frightens the king of Jerusalem is not so much the fall of Ai as the defection of Gibeon, a great city, “greater than Ai, and all its men were warriors” (v. 2).

Let us strike Gibeon. The reasoning is military. While Gibeon stood with the Canaanites it was part of their line of defence; now it is a gap in that line, with fighting men in it. So the five kings march on Gibeon first: punishing the traitor comes before fighting the invader.

Inheriting the enemies. Gibeon lied its way into this covenant, and within days it is besieged by its old allies. Those who join God’s people inherit their enemies (John 15:18), but they also inherit their God.
verseByVerse.note: Adoni-zedek probably means “my lord is righteous,” a name like that of Melchizedek, king of Salem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God fights for those under his covenant, through his people’s costly obedience and by his own direct hand. Gibeon calls on the treaty: “Come up to us quickly and save us” (v. 6). Joshua takes the whole army (v. 7), and the LORD promises the victory before the march begins (v. 8). After climbing all night from Gilgal, Israel strikes at dawn (v. 9). The LORD throws the enemy into panic, Israel chases them down the pass of Beth-horon (v. 10), and the LORD throws down hailstones that kill more than the sword (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel marches all night to rescue the people who tricked them a chapter earlier. The oath they got by fraud is now costing them a forced march up a mountain, and nobody reopens the question of whether it was binding.
verseByVerse.examples: Gilgal is in the Jordan valley, several hundred feet below sea level; Gibeon sits over three thousand feet higher, some twenty miles away. This is a night climb of more than three thousand feet by an army that then fought a battle at the top of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal, saying, "Do not relax your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who dwell in the hill country are gathered against us." So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor. And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands. Not a man of them shall stand before you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gibeon claims the protection of the treaty, Joshua answers at once, and God promises the victory before the march begins.

Do not relax your hand from your servants. In the language of the treaty, “your servants”, they claim what was sworn to them, with real nerve, for the last time they spoke to Joshua he called them cursed. He goes, with no recorded debate about whether an oath obtained by fraud is really binding.

I have given them into your hands. Then God says what he always says in this book: do not fear; I have given. The victory is spoken of as already won before the march has started. Israel is going into battle to honour a treaty God was never consulted about, and he does not leave them to live with their mistake alone: his grace meets us even in the consequences of our failures.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua came upon them suddenly, having marched up all night from Gilgal. And the LORD threw them into a panic before Israel, who struck them with a great blow at Gibeon and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon and struck them as far as Azekah and Makkedah. And as they fled before Israel, while they were going down the ascent of Beth-horon, the LORD threw down large stones from heaven on them as far as Azekah, and they died. There were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel marches all night and attacks at dawn, but it is the LORD who breaks the enemy, with panic and with hailstones from heaven.

Having marched up all night from Gilgal. Joshua took an entire army up the long climb from the Jordan valley in the dark, arrived before dawn and attacked at once. At Jericho Israel walked round a city for a week and shouted; here they climb a mountain all night. There is no formula in this book for what obedience will require on a given day.

The LORD threw them into a panic. Yet the writer gives the credit elsewhere. Whatever the brilliance of the night march, what actually broke the coalition was terror sent from God.

Large stones from heaven. The descent at Beth-horon is a steep, rocky pass where running men could not scatter or shelter. The hail killed more than Israel did, and it was aimed: Israelites were in that pass too, and the stones fell on one side of a running battle and not the other. On the greatest day of the southern campaign, the army that marched all night was outdone by the weather, because the weather belongs to God (Psalm 148:8).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wonder of this day is that the LORD heeded the voice of a man. In front of the whole army Joshua speaks to the LORD and commands the sun and moon to stand still over Gibeon and Aijalon (v. 12). The narrator quotes the Book of Jashar and adds that the sun did not hurry to set for about a whole day (v. 13). There has never been another day like it, for the LORD fought for Israel (v. 14), and the army returns to Gilgal (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 does not say that the astonishing thing was the astronomy. It says the astonishing thing was that God listened to a man. The change in the heavens is the smaller wonder of the two.
verseByVerse.examples: Sun and moon were not neutral objects to anybody watching. They were worshipped as gods across Canaan and its neighbours. Joshua gave them orders in the name of the LORD, in public, and they did as they were told.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Joshua spoke to the LORD in the day when the LORD gave the Amorites over to the sons of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon." And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stopped in the midst of heaven and did not hurry to set for about a whole day. There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel. So Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In answer to Joshua’s public prayer God lengthened the day, and the wonder the writer stresses is that the LORD heeded the voice of a man.

In the sight of Israel. Joshua “spoke to the LORD”, and then said this “in the sight of Israel”. The command to the sun is a prayer said aloud in front of the army. Whatever happened next, he had committed himself publicly, and there was no quiet way back.

Sun, stand still. The words describe the sun as it appears from the ground, as we still speak of sunrise and sunset; they make no claim about whether the earth or the sun moves.

The Book of Jashar. The narrator cites a source: a collection of Hebrew verse, now lost, quoted again when David laments Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:18). So the words about the sun and moon are poetry from a song Israel already knew. Poetry can describe a real event with complete accuracy and still describe it as poetry does, and the narrator’s own comment that the sun “did not hurry to set for about a whole day” is written as plain report.

When the LORD heeded the voice of a man. The God who set the sun in its place listened to a soldier standing in a field and did what he asked. The chapter’s main question is not what happened to the light but what kind of God grants such a request. He is the same God who answered Elijah, and James, wanting ordinary Christians to pray, reminds them that “Elijah was a man with a nature like ours” (James 5:17).

His intercession has no sunset. No day before or since was like that one. But one Man’s voice the Father always hears: “I knew that you always hear me” (John 11:42), and he still speaks for his people at God’s right hand (Hebrews 7:25). The day at Gibeon lasted one afternoon; his intercession has no sunset.

Where Christians differ. Some take the words as poetic language for a great victory, the sun seeming to linger over a day of triumph. Some suggest a darkening, the hail cloud shielding Israel through the heat of the day. Others read a real miracle of prolonged daylight, by the earth’s rotation slowed or halted or by light lengthened in some other way. What no honest reading can do is remove God from the middle of it, for that is what both the poem and the narrator are for.

This commentary’s view. The text presents it as a real event: “There has been no day like it before or since” (v. 14). The best reading is a real miracle of prolonged daylight. How God did it Scripture does not say, and the God who made the sun is not limited by it.

Uncertain wording. The verb Joshua uses for the sun (v. 12) usually means “be still” or “wait”, but it can also mean “be silent” or “cease”, which is why some read a darkening rather than lengthened light; the verb for the moon (v. 13) means “stand” or “stop”. The phrase “about a whole day” is also imprecise, and need not mean exactly twenty-four extra hours. The ESV’s “stand still” is the most natural sense, supported by the narrator’s comment that the sun “did not hurry to set”.
verseByVerse.note: The Valley of Aijalon runs west from Gibeon towards the coastal plain, along the line of Israel's pursuit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–27 — Feet on the Necks of Kings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s victory over the kings is made visible so that his people will not fear. The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah (v. 16), and Joshua seals it and keeps the army chasing the enemy until they are crushed and no one dares speak against Israel (vv. 17–21). Then the kings are brought out, and Joshua has his commanders put their feet on their necks, with a word of courage: this is what the LORD will do to all your enemies (vv. 22–25). The kings are put to death, hanged until sunset, and buried in the cave they chose (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology: The foot on the neck is the oldest picture of total defeat there is. It is hard to read, and Scripture does not soften it; instead it carries the image all the way to Christ's final victory over every enemy, and to his people's share in it.
verseByVerse.examples: Note what Joshua says over the kings in verse 25. It is his own commissioning, almost word for word from 1:9, handed on to the men under him. What God said to him on the day Moses died, he now says to his officers with the evidence lying at their feet.

verseByVerse.quote: These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah. And it was told to Joshua, "The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah." And Joshua said, "Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them, but do not stay there yourselves. Pursue your enemies; attack their rear guard. Do not let them enter their cities, for the LORD your God has given them into your hand." When Joshua and the sons of Israel had finished striking them with a great blow until they were wiped out, and when the remnant that remained of them had entered into the fortified cities, then all the people returned safe to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. Not a man moved his tongue against any of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua seals the kings in their cave and keeps the army pursuing, until the enemy is broken and the land falls silent before Israel.

Pursue your enemies. The kings are not going anywhere, but their armies are, and every soldier who reaches a walled town will have to be besieged there later.

Returned safe. After a night march and a day of battle, the writer takes care to say it.

Not a man moved his tongue. A country with nothing left to say. The kings who were sending each other messages at the start of the chapter are in a cave, and everyone else has stopped talking.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua said, "Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me from the cave." And they did so, and brought those five kings out to him from the cave, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon. And when they brought those kings out to Joshua, Joshua summoned all the men of Israel and said to the chiefs of the men of war who had gone with him, "Come near; put your feet on the necks of these kings." Then they came near and put their feet on their necks. And Joshua said to them, "Do not be afraid or dismayed; be strong and courageous. For thus the LORD will do to all your enemies against whom you fight." And afterward Joshua struck them and put them to death, and he hanged them on five trees. And they hung on the trees until evening. But at the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down from the trees and threw them into the cave where they had hidden themselves, and they set large stones against the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The defeated kings are put under the feet of Israel’s officers, a sign that the LORD will do the same to all his people’s enemies.

Put your feet on the necks of these kings. The gesture is not cruelty for its own sake but a formal act before the whole army, meaning total and final conquest.

Be strong and courageous. Joshua hands on his own commission (1:9), and can point at the kings on the ground while he says it. Courage in this book keeps travelling outward: from God to Joshua in chapter 1, from the people back to Joshua at the end of that chapter, and now from Joshua to his officers with the evidence under their boots.

At the time of the going down of the sun. Once again the bodies come down at sunset, as the law required (Deuteronomy 21:22–23; compare 8:29). They are thrown into the cave they chose as a hiding place, behind the stones that kept them in that morning. The place a man picks to hide from God has a way of becoming the place he stays.

Under your feet. Scripture keeps the image of feet on enemies’ necks and never softens it. God tells the Messiah, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool” (Psalm 110:1), the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most often. Paul says Christ must reign until the last enemy, death, is under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25–26), and tells a small, quarrelling congregation, “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). Under theirs: what the chiefs of Israel did at Makkedah is promised to ordinary Christians.

Hanged on a tree. The law said that “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23). These kings hung under that curse for their own wickedness. Paul saw the same law fulfilled another way: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us”, for “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Galatians 3:13). The kings bore their own curse; Christ bore ours, and so our enemies end under our feet and not we under his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The conquest of the south is told as one repeated sentence, because it is one work of God. Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron and Debir fall in turn, each in the same words: captured, struck with the sword, none remaining, as he had done to the city before (vv. 28–39); only Lachish holds out a second day, and Horam of Gezer falls coming to its help (vv. 32–33). Verses 40–41 sum up the whole south, from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza, taken just as the LORD commanded. Verse 42 gives the reason in one clause, “because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel”, and the army returns to Gilgal (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: The flat repetition of set phrases is the writer’s method, not laziness. City after city falls in identical language, and the effect is of something advancing that nothing in the country can turn aside or slow. The morality of it is faced at Jericho (6:17-19), and answered briefly again in the commentary below.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 42 is the sentence the whole book exists to say: because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel. Every campaign in the chapter is credited to the LORD, not to any soldier.

verseByVerse.quote: As for Makkedah, Joshua captured it on that day and struck it, and its king, with the edge of the sword. He devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. And he did to the king of Makkedah just as he had done to the king of Jericho. Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah. And the LORD gave it also and its king into the hand of Israel. And he struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it; he left none remaining in it. And he did to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho. Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Libnah to Lachish and laid siege to it and fought against it. And the LORD gave Lachish into the hand of Israel, and he captured it on the second day and struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it, as he had done to Libnah. Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish. And Joshua struck him and his people, until he left none remaining. Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Lachish to Eglon. And they laid siege to it and fought against it. And they captured it on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword. And he devoted every person in it to destruction that day, as he had done to Lachish. Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron. And they fought against it and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword, and its king and its towns, and every person in it. He left none remaining, as he had done to Eglon, and devoted it to destruction and every person in it. Then Joshua and all Israel with him turned back to Debir and fought against it and he captured it with its king and all its towns. And they struck them with the edge of the sword and devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. Just as he had done to Hebron and to Libnah and its king, so he did to Debir and to its king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
City after city of the south falls in the same repeated words, recorded without boasting as the steady work of God’s judgment.

He left none remaining. A writer who wanted to celebrate would vary the telling and name the heroes; this one uses one repeated formula without a word of triumph. Two details break the pattern. Lachish takes two days (v. 32), the only city in the list said to have held out into a second day: a small honest note in a chapter that could easily have rounded everything off. And when Horam king of Gezer marches out to help Lachish, he is dealt with in a single verse and his city is never taken (v. 33; 16:10). He came to the aid of a doomed ally and lost his army for it.

Was it just? As at Jericho, this was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries, “for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), sin that included child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31). Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Leviticus 18:24–28). It was a unique command, carried out through Israel at one moment in the history of redemption, and no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is “not of this world” (John 18:36), and “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4). In the end, judgment fell at the cross on the one man who did not deserve it (see the introduction).

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua struck the whole land, the hill country and the Negeb and the lowland and the slopes, and all their kings. He left none remaining, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, just as the LORD God of Israel commanded. And Joshua struck them from Kadesh-barnea as far as Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, as far as Gibeon. And Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel. Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole south is taken, as God commanded, and the writer gives one reason for it all: the LORD fought for Israel.

Just as the LORD God of Israel commanded. Nothing in these chapters is Israel’s own initiative. At Ai the plunder was right because God allowed it; at Jericho it had been fatal because he forbade it. The map in verse 41 runs from Kadesh-barnea in the far south to Gaza on the coast; the Goshen named here is a district of Judah’s southern hill country (15:51), not the Goshen in Egypt where Israel had once lived.

Because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel. Not because Joshua marched at night, though he did, nor because the coalition blundered, though it did, but because the LORD fought. The army walks home to Gilgal, to the twelve stones and the place where the reproach of Egypt was rolled away (5:9). The God who threw hail down a mountain pass, who granted a man’s request about the length of an afternoon, and who put five kings under the feet of five ordinary officers, had done all of it for a people who had been slaves within living memory.

What “left none remaining” means. Canaanites survive in later chapters. This is the summary language of ancient war: the armies were broken and the kings killed, not every person in every place. Joshua itself says that much land remained to be taken (13:1), and Judges 1 tells of tribes still driving out the inhabitants. Hebron and Debir, struck here, have to be taken again by Caleb and Othniel (15:13–17). Many think this summary style, common in ancient war reports, also means the killing was less total than the phrases sound; that does not remove the moral question, but it is part of reading the text honestly.

10.theology:
Covenant faithfulness when it costs. Israel marches through the night to rescue the men who deceived them, and the narrative records no debate about it. The oath was obtained by fraud and it is kept anyway, uphill, at night, at risk, and God meets the army on the way with do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands (v. 8). Keeping your word to people who do not deserve it is not naivety in this book; it is an imitation of God.

The long day, and where the miracle is. Verses 12-13 are quoted poetry from the Book of Jashar, and the narrator names his source. This commentary takes the event as a real miracle of prolonged daylight, while Scripture does not say how God did it. And verse 14 does not locate the marvel in the sky at all: what had never happened before or since was that the LORD heeded the voice of a man.

The gods of Canaan take orders. Sun and moon were worshipped throughout the country Israel was invading. Joshua addresses them out loud, in front of the army, in the name of the LORD, and they do as they are told. The truth underneath the miracle is the one the whole book teaches: the LORD is not a local god competing for territory. He is the Lord of all the earth, and the things Canaan worshipped as gods are his servants.

Feet on the necks of kings. The image is the ancient world's picture of final conquest, and Scripture carries it to Christ, who reigns until every enemy is under his feet, death last of all (1 Cor. 15:25-26). Then Paul hands it to an ordinary congregation (Rom. 16:20).
10.examples:
Then: An army climbed more than three thousand feet of hill road in the dark to save the people who had swindled it, arrived at dawn, watched the sky kill more of the enemy than they did, and stayed on the field so long that the day itself became a national memory. Then five kings were pulled out of a cave and buried in it, behind the stones they had chosen for shelter.

Now: Two things apply directly to us. The first is the march: a promise made carelessly is still a promise, and God met Israel on the road they took to keep it rather than lecturing them about how they got there. The second is verse 14. Before you decide what you think happened to the sun, notice what the writer thought was remarkable: that God listened to a man. Whatever you were about to conclude about the size of your own requests, he heard a soldier ask for more daylight.

keyVerse.quote: There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel.
keyVerse.note: The narrator tells us where the wonder of the long day lies: not chiefly in the sun, but in the LORD listening to a man and fighting for his people. The verse joins the two great truths of the chapter, God’s power and his willingness to hear, and points to the Son whose prayers the Father always hears.

10.reflection:
Gibeon came under attack because it had joined Israel (vv. 4–5). Have you found that following Christ has brought you opposition you did not have before? How does it help to know that you have also gained his protection?

Israel marched all night, yet the writer says the victory came because “the LORD threw them into a panic” and sent the hail (vv. 9–11). How do you hold together hard work and complete dependence on God in your own life?

Joshua prayed a bold, public prayer, and “the LORD heeded the voice of a man” (vv. 12–14). What keeps you from praying boldly? How does Jesus’ ongoing intercession for you (Hebrews 7:25) change the way you pray?

The officers put their feet on the necks of defeated kings (v. 24), and Paul promises that God “will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). Which enemies of your faith seem strongest to you, and how does Christ’s victory give you courage to face them?

11.title: The Northern Campaign Completed
11.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jabin, king of Hazor, heard of this, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph,<sup>2</sup>and to the kings who were in the northern hill country, and in the Arabah south of Chinneroth, and in the lowland, and in Naphoth-dor on the west,<sup>3</sup>to the Canaanites in the east and the west, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites in the hill country, and the Hivites under Hermon in the land of Mizpah.<sup>4</sup>And they came out with all their troops, a great horde, in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots.<sup>5</sup>And all these kings joined their forces and came and encamped together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire."<sup>7</sup>So Joshua and all his warriors came suddenly against them by the waters of Merom and fell upon them.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD gave them into the hand of Israel, who struck them and chased them as far as Great Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh.
