And they struck them until he left none remaining.<sup>9</sup>And Joshua did to them just as the LORD said to him: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.<sup>10</sup>And Joshua turned back at that time and captured Hazor and struck its king with the sword, for Hazor formerly was the head of all those kingdoms.<sup>11</sup>And they struck with the sword all who were in it, devoting them to destruction; there was none left that breathed. And he burned Hazor with fire.<sup>12</sup>And all the cities of those kings, and all their kings, Joshua captured, and struck them with the edge of the sword, devoting them to destruction, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded.<sup>13</sup>But none of the cities that stood on mounds did Israel burn, except Hazor alone; that Joshua burned.<sup>14</sup>And all the spoil of these cities and the livestock, the people of Israel took for their plunder. But every person they struck with the edge of the sword until they had destroyed them, and they did not leave any who breathed.<sup>15</sup>Just as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>16</sup>So Joshua took all that land, the hill country and all the Negeb and all the land of Goshen and the lowland and the Arabah and the hill country of Israel and its lowland<sup>17</sup>from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon. And he captured all their kings and struck them and put them to death.<sup>18</sup>Joshua made war a long time with all those kings.<sup>19</sup>There was not a city that made peace with the people of Israel except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle.<sup>20</sup>For it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle, in order that they should be devoted to destruction and should receive no mercy but be destroyed, just as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>21</sup>And Joshua came at that time and cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah, and from all the hill country of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction with their cities.<sup>22</sup>There was none of the Anakim left in the land of the people of Israel. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain.<sup>23</sup>So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments. And the land had rest from war.
11.overview:
Where we are. The south has fallen (chapter 10). Now the north does what the south could not, and gathers every king from the hill country to the coast under Jabin of Hazor. This is the last great battle of the conquest.

The message. The LORD gives his people the whole land and rest from war, and he will not let them trust in anything but himself. Against the largest army in the book, with horses and chariots Israel did not have, God promises victory “tomorrow at this time” and then orders the captured horses hamstrung and the chariots burned. Joshua obeys completely, “he left nothing undone” (v. 15), and the giants who once terrified Israel are cut off.

Why it was said. Israel was a nation of foot soldiers facing the most feared weapon of its day, and its later kings would be tempted to build their security on horses and alliances. Every generation needed to hear that the land was God’s gift, won by his power and held by trusting obedience (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Jabin summons the northern kings, who gather at the waters of Merom with a horde like the sand of the sea and very many chariots (vv. 1–5). God promises victory, Israel attacks suddenly, and Joshua hamstrings the horses and burns the chariots as he was told (vv. 6–9). Hazor, head of the northern kingdoms, is burned, and Joshua does everything the LORD commanded Moses (vv. 10–15). The summary covers the whole land and a long war: no city sought peace except Gibeon, because God hardened their hearts (vv. 16–20). The Anakim are cut off, a few remain in Philistine towns, and the land has rest (vv. 21–23).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need it exposes. Joshua “left nothing undone”, yet the rest he gave did not last, and Hebrews says that “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). The only servant who left nothing undone in the fullest sense is Jesus, who could say to his Father, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). He is the king who comes humble, cutting off the chariot (Zechariah 9:9–10), and he gives the true rest: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

For us. Our chariots are whatever we trust to keep us safe instead of God: name them and hold them loosely. Obey fully, and find rest in Christ, who has finished the work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Chariots at the Waters of Merom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives victory over the strongest army in the land and forbids his people to trust in its weapons. Jabin of Hazor summons the kings of the north, from the hill country to the coast and six nations named (vv. 1–3). They gather at the waters of Merom, a horde like the sand of the seashore, with very many horses and chariots (vv. 4–5). God tells Joshua not to fear: “tomorrow at this time” he will give them all over, and Israel is to hamstring their horses and burn their chariots (v. 6). Israel attacks suddenly, routs them, and Joshua does exactly as he was told (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel has no chariots. The enemy's advantage is not numbers alone but technology, and God's answer is not to give Israel better technology but to destroy the enemy's and forbid his people to keep any of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The phrase in verse 4, like the sand that is on the seashore, is the promise God made to Abraham about his own descendants (Gen. 22:17). Here it describes the army coming to kill them. The echo is deliberate: the countless army will fall, and the promise of countless descendants will stand.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jabin, king of Hazor, heard of this, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph, and to the kings who were in the northern hill country, and in the Arabah south of Chinneroth, and in the lowland, and in Naphoth-dor on the west, to the Canaanites in the east and the west, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites in the hill country, and the Hivites under Hermon in the land of Mizpah. And they came out with all their troops, a great horde, in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots. And all these kings joined their forces and came and encamped together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole north gathers against Israel with the largest army in the book and the most feared weapon of the age, and in doing so gathers itself into one place for God to judge.

Like the sand that is on the seashore. The size of this army is described in the very words of God’s promise to Abraham, that his offspring would be “as the sand that is on the seashore” (Genesis 22:17). Now it is the enemy who looks like the fulfilment of that promise.

Very many horses and chariots. A chariot was the decisive weapon of that world, expensive, fast and terrifying, and foot soldiers usually broke in front of it. Israel has none. They are a nation of foot soldiers who were slaves within living memory, looking at massed chariots.

Encamped together at the waters of Merom. They camp together, which is their mistake and God’s arrangement. Every king in the north is now in one place, and the whole northern war will be settled in a single morning.
verseByVerse.note: Hazor, north of the Sea of Galilee, was the largest city in Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire." So Joshua and all his warriors came suddenly against them by the waters of Merom and fell upon them. And the LORD gave them into the hand of Israel, who struck them and chased them as far as Great Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh. And they struck them until he left none remaining. And Joshua did to them just as the LORD said to him: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names the hour of victory and forbids Israel to keep the enemy’s horses and chariots, so that his people will trust him and not their weapons.

Tomorrow at this time. The same promise as always, and this time with a clock on it. God does not merely promise the outcome; he names the hour, in front of an army that has just seen what is camped at Merom.

You shall hamstring their horses. To hamstring a horse is to cut the tendon of its hind leg, so that it can never be used in war again. Militarily it makes no sense. Chariots and trained horses were the most valuable plunder on any ancient battlefield, and Israel could have become the strongest power in the region by nightfall. God will not have it, not because technology is wicked, but because a nation that owns chariots will sooner or later trust them. Moses had written it into the law of the king before Israel had a king: “he must not acquire many horses for himself” (Deuteronomy 17:16). The psalmist puts it in a sentence: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7).

Burned their chariots with fire. Joshua obeyed: standing on a won field with the best military hardware in Canaan around him, he set fire to it. Israel did not keep the rule for long. Solomon gathered fourteen hundred chariots and imported horses from Egypt (1 Kings 10:26–29), buying back at great expense precisely what Joshua was ordered to burn.

Our chariots. A chariot was security you could see, stable and count. Ours are subtler: the savings that mean we need nobody, the expertise that means nothing is left to chance, the technology that promises to keep every risk in hand. None of these is wicked, any more than a horse is. The danger is what they quietly become. Whatever we trust to keep us safe soon starts telling us what we may risk, whom we may love and how far we may obey, and it never tells us we have enough. God was not taking away Israel’s safety; he was refusing to let them move it somewhere else.

The King without chariots. Zechariah foresaw a king, humble and mounted on a donkey, who would “cut off the chariot from Ephraim” (Zechariah 9:9–10). The King who came won his victory by being weak, on a cross, and his word to a church that owns very little is the word of Merom in another key: “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua’s obedience is complete. He turns back and captures Hazor, “the head of all those kingdoms”, kills its king and burns the city (vv. 10–11). The other royal cities are taken but, unlike Hazor, not burned (vv. 12–13), and the spoil is kept as plunder (v. 14). Then comes the verdict on Joshua’s whole career: as the LORD commanded Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did; “he left nothing undone” (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is not reluctance; it is plain good sense. Israel is about to live in these towns. They burn the capital that organised the war and leave standing the houses they will move into, the houses Moses had promised them, which they did not build (Deut. 6:10-11).
verseByVerse.examples: The chain in verse 15 has four links and none of them fails: the LORD commanded Moses; Moses commanded Joshua; Joshua did it; nothing was left out. It is the sentence the writer wants on Joshua's record, and it is the exact opposite of what will be said about the generation in the book of Judges.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua turned back at that time and captured Hazor and struck its king with the sword, for Hazor formerly was the head of all those kingdoms. And they struck with the sword all who were in it, devoting them to destruction; there was none left that breathed. And he burned Hazor with fire. And all the cities of those kings, and all their kings, Joshua captured, and struck them with the edge of the sword, devoting them to destruction, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded. But none of the cities that stood on mounds did Israel burn, except Hazor alone; that Joshua burned. And all the spoil of these cities and the livestock, the people of Israel took for their plunder. But every person they struck with the edge of the sword until they had destroyed them, and they did not leave any who breathed. Just as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua burns Hazor, the capital of the north, and carries out every command God gave through Moses: he left nothing undone.

The head of all those kingdoms. Hazor was the largest and most important city in the north. Defeating the coalition in the field was the battle; burning its capital is the end of the war. Excavations at Hazor have uncovered a great Canaanite city destroyed by an intense fire in the Late Bronze Age. Scholars debate who burned it and when, partly depending on how the exodus is dated, but the burned city fits verse 11 well.

All the spoil of these cities. The plunder is taken by permission, as at Ai (8:2).

He left nothing undone. Verse 15 is the summit of Joshua’s career, and its last clause goes further than the rest. Almost every failure in Israel’s later history is of exactly the opposite kind: not open defiance but things left undone, tribes that did not drive out the inhabitants, commands obeyed in the parts that suited. The book of Judges opens with a list of them (Judges 1:27–36).

Having accomplished the work. In the fullest sense this can be said of only one servant, Jesus, who could tell his Father, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). Our own obedience is always partial; his is complete and counted to those who trust him, and the Spirit he gives finishes in us what God began (Philippians 1:6).

Another Jabin. Judges 4 has another Jabin, king of Hazor. Jabin seems to have been a royal name, and Hazor was rebuilt in the generations between.

Was it just? As in the south, this was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), including child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Leviticus 18:24–28). It was a unique command at one moment in the history of redemption, no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is “not of this world” (John 18:36), and “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4) (see the note on 10:28–39 and the introduction).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God completes what he promised, and the land has rest from war. The summary covers the whole country, from Mount Halak in the south to Baal-gad under Hermon, and admits that it took a long time (vv. 16–18). No city made peace except Gibeon, because the LORD hardened their hearts to fight (vv. 19–20). The Anakim, the giants who had frightened a generation into the wilderness, are cut off, with a few left in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod (vv. 21–22). Joshua takes the whole land and gives it to the tribes, “and the land had rest from war” (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 20 is hard, and verse 19 keeps us from misreading it. Peace was available: the text says so by noting the one city that took it. The hardening is a judge’s sentence: God gives a people over to what they have already chosen, exactly as with Pharaoh (Ex. 9:16; Rom. 9:17-18), and in the same book he takes a prostitute and four Gibeonite towns out of the same judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: The Anakim were the reason Israel spent forty years in a desert. Ten spies had come back saying we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers (Num. 13:33), and the nation believed them. Here one verse disposes of the giants.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua took all that land, the hill country and all the Negeb and all the land of Goshen and the lowland and the Arabah and the hill country of Israel and its lowland from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon. And he captured all their kings and struck them and put them to death. Joshua made war a long time with all those kings. There was not a city that made peace with the people of Israel except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle. For it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle, in order that they should be devoted to destruction and should receive no mercy but be destroyed, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole land is taken over long years, and behind the Canaanites’ refusal to seek peace stood God’s judgment, hardening hearts already set against him.

Joshua made war a long time. The narrative has been moving fast, a city a verse, and here the writer stops to say it took years.

Except the Hivites. Gibeon got its treaty by fraud, but it need not have been fraud; mercy was there to be sought. Rahab needed no treaty at all, only belief. What the country did, almost without exception, was fight.

It was the LORD’s doing to harden their hearts. This is one of the hardest sentences in the book: behind their resistance stood God, hardening. Scripture says the same of Pharaoh, who had first hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15; 9:16; Romans 9:17–18). Hardening in Scripture is an act of judgment, God confirming people in the direction they have already chosen. It is not arbitrary cruelty: the same God had taken a Canaanite prostitute out of a burning city and put her in the family of the Messiah (Matthew 1:5), and hardening is never the whole story of what he was doing in that country.

What it does mean. The outcome was never in the balance. The kings gathering at Merom believed they were making a decision. They were being gathered.
verseByVerse.note: The conquest took “a long time” (v. 18): about seven years, judging from Caleb’s ages (14:7, 10).

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua came at that time and cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah, and from all the hill country of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction with their cities. There was none of the Anakim left in the land of the people of Israel. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain. So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments. And the land had rest from war.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The giants who once frightened Israel into the wilderness are cut off, and God gives his people the whole land and rest, a real rest that still points beyond itself.

Cut off the Anakim. One verse settles a question that had cost the nation forty years. Joshua was one of the two spies who did not believe the frightened report of the other ten (Numbers 13:33; 14:6–9); now an old man, he cuts those same giants out of those same hills. The giants were as big as the spies had said. What changed was that Israel now measured them against God.

Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod. A remnant survived in three Philistine cities on the coast, and one of them is Gath. Centuries later a champion came out of the Philistine camp, nearly ten feet tall in the Hebrew text (the Greek Old Testament and a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel give about six and a half feet, still a giant to the men of that day), and the text is careful to say where he came from: Goliath of Gath (1 Samuel 17:4). An army of Israelites was paralysed by him, as their ancestors had been, and a shepherd boy, David, killed him with a stone.

And the land had rest from war. Behind these words stand four hundred years in Egypt, blood on the doorframes, a sea, forty years of wandering, a river, a walled city and years of fighting. The rest was real, but it did not last, and Hebrews puts it exactly: “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on”, so “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:8–9).

I will give you rest. The rest under Joshua was a copy. The one who gives the real thing carries the same name, and made the offer in the plainest words ever used about it: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The land had rest from war because God fought for it. So does the soul that comes to Christ.

The whole land, yet much remains? Joshua broke the organised power of the Canaanite coalitions, so Israel was at rest from war, but local pockets remained for each tribe to take (13:1). Both statements are true.
verseByVerse.note: The three Philistine towns where Anakim survived were Gaza, Gath and Ashdod (v. 22).

11.theology:
Burning the chariots. God destroys the enemy's technology and forbids his people to keep any of it (v. 6), because what we own we soon rely on (Ps. 20:7; Deut. 17:16). Every generation has its own version of the captured chariot: the thing that would make the church formidable, and would quietly make God unnecessary.

Nothing left undone. Verse 15 is the high-water mark of the book. Partial obedience is the ordinary form disobedience takes among religious people, because from a distance it looks like the real thing.

The hardening, and its control. Verse 20 is not softened, but the hardening is a just sentence, not a whim: peace was available, and one city took it (v. 19).

Rest, and the rest that remains. The rest that closes the conquest did not last, and Hebrews draws the conclusion that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God (Heb. 4:8-9). The rest under Joshua was real and it was a copy; the one who gives the original, Jesus, carries the same name (Matt. 11:28).
11.examples:
Then: A nation of foot soldiers walked towards massed chariots at Merom, won, and then spent the evening crippling horses and burning the best military equipment in the country because God had told them to. Years of fighting later, an old man cut the giants out of the hills that had terrified his own generation when he was young, and the land was quiet.

Now: Two questions come straight out of this chapter. The first is what your chariots are: the resource, position or security that would make you formidable and would quietly make God optional. Joshua stood on a won field and set fire to his. The second is verse 15: not whether you have disobeyed anything, but whether anything has been left undone. That is where Israel actually lost the land, and it never felt like rebellion at the time. The question is asked by a God who fought every battle in this chapter for them, and the one who left nothing undone for us gives his Spirit for what remains.

keyVerse.quote: So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments. And the land had rest from war.
keyVerse.note: This verse closes the story of the conquest and opens the story of the inheritance. Everything happened “according to all that the LORD had spoken”, and the goal was not war but rest. That rest was real but temporary, and it points to the lasting rest God gives his people in Christ (Hebrews 4:8–9).

11.reflection:
God ordered Israel to hamstring the horses and burn the chariots rather than keep them (vv. 6, 9). What are the “chariots” in your life, the things you are tempted to trust for security instead of God? What would it look like to hold them loosely?

Joshua “left nothing undone” (v. 15), while later Israel failed by leaving things undone. Is there an area where you obey God partly, in the ways that suit you? How does Jesus’ finished work encourage you to keep going rather than despair?

The Anakim had terrified a whole generation, yet Joshua cut them off (v. 21). What fears have loomed large in your life, and how does measuring them against God change the way they look?

“The land had rest from war” (v. 23), but Hebrews says a greater rest remains (Hebrews 4:8–9). What does it mean for you to enter the rest Christ gives, and how does that rest show in the way you live and work?

12.title: The Roll Call of Defeated Kings
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the kings of the land whom the people of Israel defeated and took possession of their land beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, with all the Arabah eastward:<sup>2</sup>Sihon king of the Amorites who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the middle of the valley as far as the river Jabbok, the boundary of the Ammonites, that is, half of Gilead,<sup>3</sup>and the Arabah to the Sea of Chinneroth eastward, and in the direction of Beth-jeshimoth, to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, southward to the foot of the slopes of Pisgah;<sup>4</sup>and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei<sup>5</sup>and ruled over Mount Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan to the boundary of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and over half of Gilead to the boundary of Sihon king of Heshbon.<sup>6</sup>Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the people of Israel defeated them. And Moses the servant of the LORD gave their land for a possession to the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.<sup>7</sup>And these are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the people of Israel defeated on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, that rises toward Seir (and Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotments,<sup>8</sup>in the hill country, in the lowland, in the Arabah, in the slopes, in the wilderness, and in the Negeb, the land of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites):<sup>9</sup>the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one;<sup>10</sup>the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one;<sup>11</sup>the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one;<sup>12</sup>the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one;<sup>13</sup>the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one;<sup>14</sup>the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one;<sup>15</sup>the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one;<sup>16</sup>the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;<sup>17</sup>the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one;<sup>18</sup>the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one;<sup>19</sup>the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one;<sup>20</sup>the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one;<sup>21</sup>the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one;<sup>22</sup>the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one;<sup>23</sup>the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Galilee, one;<sup>24</sup>the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.
12.overview:
Where we are. The conquest is over: chapter 11 ended with “the land had rest from war” (11:23). Before the land is shared out in chapters 13–21, the writer pauses to take stock, and the stock-taking is a list of defeated kings.

The message. Every throne that stood against God’s people has been counted out, one at a time, and the whole victory, east and west of the Jordan, under Moses and under Joshua, is one work of one faithful God. The list is a record of promises kept: what God said he would give, he has given.

Why it was said. For the tribes about to receive their inheritance, this roll was a title deed: every family could see whose land they were being given and how it had been won. For later Israel, it was a reminder that the land was a gift, not an achievement (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The roll begins east of the Jordan with Sihon and Og, beaten under Moses, whose land went to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh (vv. 1–6). Then it turns west, maps Joshua’s conquests across every kind of country and all six nations (vv. 7–8), and lists thirty-one kings, each followed by the single word “one” (vv. 9–24). The early names retrace the book; most of the later ones have no story at all.

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern. Paul describes the cross as God’s victory over every hostile power: “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). The roll of defeated kings anticipates the day when Christ “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet”, and “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). Even the king of Jerusalem is on the list, though his city was not yet taken: Jerusalem waited for David, and in the end for the Son of David.

For us. God keeps count of his faithfulness even when we do not. Look back over what he has done, including the victories nobody wrote up, and trust him with the ground still to be taken.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Two Kings East of the Jordan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tally of victories begins with what God did under Moses, because the conquest is one work across two leaders. East of the Jordan, from the Arnon to Mount Hermon, Israel defeated Sihon king of the Amorites at Heshbon, whose territory is mapped from the Arnon to the Jabbok (vv. 1–3), and Og king of Bashan, one of the last of the Rephaim (vv. 4–5). Moses, the servant of the LORD, defeated them and gave their land to Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The tally of the conquest begins with two victories Joshua had nothing to do with. The writer will not let the book be about Joshua: what was begun under one leader and finished under another is counted as one work, and it was God’s.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses is called the servant of the LORD twice in verse 6, which is the title the book opened with in its first sentence (1:1). Joshua does not get it here; the book gives him that title only at his death (24:29), and until then the honour of it is left where it was.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the kings of the land whom the people of Israel defeated and took possession of their land beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, with all the Arabah eastward: Sihon king of the Amorites who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the middle of the valley as far as the river Jabbok, the boundary of the Ammonites, that is, half of Gilead, and the Arabah to the Sea of Chinneroth eastward, and in the direction of Beth-jeshimoth, to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, southward to the foot of the slopes of Pisgah; and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei and ruled over Mount Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan to the boundary of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and over half of Gilead to the boundary of Sihon king of Heshbon. Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the people of Israel defeated them. And Moses the servant of the LORD gave their land for a possession to the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roll begins with Sihon and Og, beaten under Moses, because the whole conquest is one work of God across two generations.

Sihon and Og. Both kings were formidable. Sihon had refused Israel passage and come out to fight (Numbers 21:21–35); Og was one of the last of the Rephaim, the giant peoples, and Deuteronomy records the size of his iron bed as a matter of public curiosity: nine cubits, something over thirteen feet (Deuteronomy 3:11).

Beaten before the Jordan. These two were defeated before Israel ever saw the Jordan. Rahab had heard about them and named them in her list of what God had done (2:10); the Gibeonites cited them in their sales pitch (9:10). They are the reason the whole country was frightened before the invasion started.

Moses, the servant of the LORD. The writer starts the tally not at chapter 6 but with a dead man’s victories: what Moses began and could not finish, Joshua completed, and neither of them gets the credit. One God took the land across two generations and two leaders, so the victories are counted in one list.

Uncertain wording. “Rephaim” (v. 4) is used in the Old Testament both for an ancient people remembered for their great size (Deuteronomy 2:11; 3:11) and, in poetry, for the shades of the dead (Isaiah 14:9). How the two uses are related is not known. Here it plainly means the people, of whom Og was one of the last.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–24 — Thirty-One, Counted One at a Time
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every king west of the Jordan is counted, because God gave the whole land. The list sets the bounds, from Baal-gad in the north to Mount Halak in the south, through hill country, lowland, Arabah, slopes, wilderness and Negeb, the land of six nations (vv. 7–8). Then come the kings one by one, Jericho, Ai, Jerusalem, Hebron and the rest, each entered with the single word “one”, ending with the north and the total: “in all, thirty-one kings” (vv. 9–24).
verseByVerse.theology: About fifteen of these kings have no battle and no story anywhere in the book: Geder, Hormah, Arad, Adullam, Tappuah, Hepher, Aphek, Lasharon, Taanach, Megiddo, Kedesh, Jokneam, Dor (named only in passing at 11:2), Goiim, Tirzah. The list is longer than the narrative.
verseByVerse.examples: The king of Jerusalem is counted in verse 10, and Jerusalem was not taken (see the note on vv. 9-16). The very next verse of this book says what that means: there remains yet very much land to possess (13:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And these are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the people of Israel defeated on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, that rises toward Seir (and Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotments, in the hill country, in the lowland, in the Arabah, in the slopes, in the wilderness, and in the Negeb, the land of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites):
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land Joshua conquered covers every kind of country and all six nations, and it is already being given away as an inheritance.

Joshua gave their land to the tribes. The clause in brackets is doing quiet work. The conquest is already spoken of as an inheritance being distributed, which is what the next nine chapters are about. The war is finished; the paperwork is not.

Six kinds of country. Each had its own way of being difficult. Hill country favours the defender. The lowland is chariot country. The Arabah is furnace-hot below sea level. The Negeb is desert. A nation of former slaves who had spent forty years in one kind of terrain has now fought in all six, and the geography is listed so that the reader can see the size of what was given.

verseByVerse.quote: the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one; the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one; the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one; the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one; the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one; the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one; the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one; the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each defeated king is entered with a single word, “one”: the thrones that terrified a generation have become an inventory.

The king of Jericho, one. The roll has a sound: Jericho, one. Ai, one. It is written as a storekeeper writes a stock list, and the flatness is the point. Each name is a walled city with a court, an army and a god, and each is entered in a ledger with a single digit beside it. What terrified a generation is now stock-taking.

Names that recall the book. The early names walk the reader back through the story. Jericho, where the wall fell flat. Ai, where thirty-six men died because Achan had buried stolen plunder in his tent. Then Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon in a row: the five kings of the southern coalition, in the order they came out of the cave at Makkedah (10:23).

The king of Jerusalem, one. Its king, Adoni-zedek, is dead, but Jerusalem itself is not taken. The Jebusites went on living there alongside Benjamin (Judges 1:21), and the city was not held until David took it generations later (2 Samuel 5:6–9). Judges 1:8, where Judah sets the city on fire, is no contradiction: a raid that burns a town is not a garrison that holds it, and the Jebusites stayed or returned. The list quietly admits the gap between victory and possession, and the next verse says it aloud (13:1).

verseByVerse.quote: the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one; the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one; the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one; the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one; the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one; the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one; the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Galilee, one; the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roll runs on through kings whose defeat is never told, to the total: thirty-one thrones, all counted out by God.

Untold campaigns. If the stories of the conquest were all we had, we would assume Israel fought about eight battles. They fought at least thirty-one, and chapter 11 has told us it took a long time (11:18). There is no chapter for the king of Lasharon, and he is on the list. Most of what God does never gets written down.

The king of Megiddo, one. Hazor, the head of all those kingdoms, gets the same single digit as everyone else. So does Megiddo, the town on the pass that controlled the road across the plain of Jezreel. Its name most likely lies behind Armageddon (in Greek Harmagedon, probably ‘mountain of Megiddo’), the name John hears in his vision for the place where the kings of the whole world are gathered for the last battle (Revelation 16:16). Here the king of Megiddo is number twenty-six on Joshua’s inventory.

In all, thirty-one kings. Not one of the thirty-one thrones is standing. The LORD God of Israel counted them out, one at a time, and gave the ground they had sat on to a nation of former slaves who could not have taken a single city on their own.

The last one on his list. Paul, describing the cross, uses the language of a Roman victory parade: God disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in Christ (Colossians 2:15). God is still counting off defeated enemies, and the last one on his list has a name too: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26).

Textual note. In verse 23 the Hebrew text reads “Goiim in Gilgal”; the ESV follows the ancient Greek translation, “in Galilee”, which suits a list that has reached the north.

12.theology:
One work, two leaders. The roll begins with Moses' victories east of the Jordan, which Joshua had no part in, and the title the servant of the LORD is given to Moses twice in the verse that closes them (v. 6). The conquest is presented as a single act of God spanning two generations and two leaders. It was begun under Moses, who could not enter the land, and finished under Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of the name Jesus (see 1:1 and Heb. 4:8).

The list is longer than the story. Most of what God did in those years was never written up, which is a fair description of most faithful work in most centuries.

Victory is not yet possession. Jerusalem's king is counted while Jerusalem stands (Judg. 1:21). The whole Christian life is lived in that gap: Christ has won the decisive battle, and we are still taking possession of what he won.

The accounting continues. Paul pictures the cross as God's triumph over the rulers and authorities (Col. 2:15), and the last entry on that ledger is already named: death (1 Corinthians 15:26).

Why count the dead? A reader may flinch at a page that tallies slain kings. The book has given its reasons in the battle chapters: this was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin he had borne with for centuries (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:5), commanded for this land at this moment, and never a licence for any later war. The list records that God kept his word to Abraham, through a people who could not have taken one city alone, and it waits for the King who wins his war by dying rather than by killing.
12.examples:
Then: Somebody sat down and wrote out the names of thirty-one kings with the word one after each, and added them up at the bottom. It is the least dramatic page in the book and it is the receipt for everything in the eleven chapters before it.

Now: Two things to take from a list. Many of these kings have no story, and they are still counted, which is worth remembering for anyone whose work nobody writes up. And the king of Jerusalem is on the list while the city is still occupied, which is the shape of the Christian life exactly: the decisive victory is a matter of record, and there is a great deal of ground you have not yet walked on. The next verse of the book says so, and says it to a man who was old and tired.

keyVerse.quote: the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.
keyVerse.note: The list ends with a total, and the total is the point: every king who stood against Israel has been counted out, one at a time, by the God who promised the land. It is a record of faithfulness, and a foretaste of the day when every enemy of Christ, death last of all, will be under his feet.

12.reflection:
The roll of kings begins with victories won under Moses, not Joshua (vv. 1–6). What does it teach us that one leader began what another finished, and that neither gets the credit? How might that shape the way we serve in the church?

Most of the kings in verses 9–24 have no story in the book, only a name. What do you make of the fact that most of what God does is never written down? What unrecorded mercies of God can you name in your own life?

The king of Jerusalem was defeated, but the city was not taken for generations (v. 10). Where do you see a gap in your own life between what Christ has won and what you have actually taken hold of?

Paul says Christ triumphed over every hostile power at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and that the last enemy is death (1 Corinthians 15:26). How does it change the way you face death, and the enemies of your faith, to know they are already on God’s list?

13.title: Land Still to Be Possessed
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Joshua was old and advanced in years, and the LORD said to him, "You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess.<sup>2</sup>This is the land that yet remains: all the regions of the Philistines, and all those of the Geshurites<sup>3</sup>(from the Shihor, which is east of Egypt, northward to the boundary of Ekron, it is counted as Canaanite; there are five rulers of the Philistines, those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron), and those of the Avvim,<sup>4</sup>in the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that belongs to the Sidonians, to Aphek, to the boundary of the Amorites,<sup>5</sup>and the land of the Gebalites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath,<sup>6</sup>all the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, even all the Sidonians. I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and half the tribe of Manasseh."<sup>8</sup>With the other half of the tribe of Manasseh the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond the Jordan eastward, as Moses the servant of the LORD gave them:<sup>9</sup>from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland of Medeba as far as Dibon;<sup>10</sup>and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the boundary of the Ammonites;<sup>11</sup>and Gilead, and the region of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan to Salecah;<sup>12</sup>all the kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei (he alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim); these Moses had struck and driven out.<sup>13</sup>Yet the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, but Geshur and Maacath dwell in the midst of Israel to this day.<sup>14</sup>To the tribe of Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance. The offerings by fire to the LORD God of Israel are their inheritance, as he said to him.<sup>15</sup>And Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of the people of Reuben according to their clans.<sup>16</sup>So their territory was from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland by Medeba;<sup>17</sup>with Heshbon, and all its cities that are in the tableland; Dibon, and Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon,<sup>18</sup>and Jahaz, and Kedemoth, and Mephaath,<sup>19</sup>and Kiriathaim, and Sibmah, and Zereth-shahar on the hill of the valley,<sup>20</sup>and Beth-peor, and the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth,<sup>21</sup>that is, all the cities of the tableland, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses defeated with the leaders of Midian, Evi and Rekem and Zur and Hur and Reba, the princes of Sihon, who lived in the land.<sup>22</sup>Balaam also, the son of Beor, the one who practiced divination, was killed with the sword by the people of Israel among the rest of their slain.<sup>23</sup>And the border of the people of Reuben was the Jordan as a boundary. This was the inheritance of the people of Reuben, according to their clans with their cities and villages.<sup>24</sup>Moses gave an inheritance also to the tribe of Gad, to the people of Gad, according to their clans.<sup>25</sup>Their territory was Jazer, and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, to Aroer, which is east of Rabbah,<sup>26</sup>and from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the territory of Debir,<sup>27</sup>and in the valley Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, having the Jordan as a boundary, to the lower end of the Sea of Chinnereth, eastward beyond the Jordan.<sup>28</sup>This is the inheritance of the people of Gad according to their clans, with their cities and villages.<sup>29</sup>And Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was allotted to the half-tribe of the people of Manasseh according to their clans.<sup>30</sup>Their region extended from Mahanaim, through all Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all the towns of Jair, which are in Bashan, sixty cities,<sup>31</sup>and half Gilead, and Ashtaroth, and Edrei, the cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. These were allotted to the people of Machir the son of Manasseh for the half of the people of Machir according to their clans.<sup>32</sup>These are the inheritances that Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan east of Jericho.<sup>33</sup>But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance; the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance, just as he said to them.
13.overview:
Where we are. The war is over: “the land had rest from war” (11:23), and chapter 12 has counted the defeated kings. Chapters 13 to 21 are a land registry, and it opens not with a celebration but with an old man being told that he is old and that much of the work remains.

The message. God’s gift is certain before it is complete. He treats land still full of Philistines as Israel’s to share out, because he has promised to drive its people out himself; Israel’s part is to take him at his word. And the chapter frames all the fields with one tribe that receives none: Levi, whose inheritance is the LORD himself.

Why it was said. Joshua’s generation needed to know that the work did not depend on his lifespan, and later readers needed to see where many of their troubles began: with peoples left in the land “to this day” (v. 13; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God tells Joshua plainly that he is old and lists the regions still unconquered, from the Philistine coast to Lebanon (vv. 1–5); then he promises to drive them out himself and orders the land allotted anyway (vv. 6–7). He reviews the eastern land Moses had already given to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh (vv. 8–12), notes in passing that Geshur and Maacath were never driven out (v. 13), and sets Levi apart (v. 14). He then walks through the three eastern territories (vv. 15–32), stopping only to record the death of Balaam (v. 22), and closes where he began with Levi: “the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance” (v. 33).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern. Joshua grows old with the work unfinished; the greater Joshua, whose name he shares, cannot fail to finish his, for he “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25). Meanwhile the church lives where Israel stands in this chapter, blessed “in Christ with every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3) and still told to put on the armour of God and stand (6:11). The land itself was a pledge of something greater: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were looking for “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16). And Levi’s portion becomes the portion of every believer, a royal priesthood whose inheritance is God himself (1 Peter 2:9).

For us. You may be like Joshua, aware that time is short and much is unfinished. The work is God’s, and he does not grow old. Take hold of what he has already given, fight for the ground still held against him, and learn with Levi that having God is better than having anything he gives.
13.theology:
Given and not yet taken. Chapter 1 says God has given the land; chapter 13 says very much of it remains to be possessed; and verse 6 holds both together. That is the position of every Christian: in possession of every spiritual blessing and still required to put on the armour and stand.

Whose land, and for how long? A reader today will ask what these boundaries mean now, and Christians answer in more than one way. Many in the Reformed tradition hold that the land promise is fulfilled and enlarged in Christ: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), and the patriarchs were looking for a better, heavenly country (Hebrews 11:16). Others, including many Reformed and Puritan writers, expect God still to show great mercy to Abraham’s physical descendants, because the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29), and some of them expect a future for Israel in this land. Faithful Christians differ here and should do so kindly. All agree that no one inherits anything from God except through Christ, the true offspring of Abraham (Galatians 3:16, 29).

What is not driven out does not stay still. The failure at verse 13 is not defiance and it costs nothing that year. Centuries later it becomes David’s marriage to a princess of Geshur, their son Absalom’s flight to Geshur, and then Absalom’s rebellion (2 Sam. 3:3; 13:37-38; 15:8). Scripture keeps records of this kind, and what a generation tolerates because it is tired is inherited by people who did not choose it.

A name in a list of fields. Balaam is named in the register among the slain (v. 22), and what he did should be remembered. He could not curse Israel, because blessings came out every time he tried, so he taught Balak to seduce them instead, and twenty-four thousand died at Peor (Num. 25:9; 31:16). The danger to God's people was never chiefly military.

Levi's portion. The other tribes walked away from the allotment holding a map. Levi was handed nothing at all, and the explanation is one sentence: the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance. The rest of Scripture treats that as the richest outcome of the day, in surveyor's language: the LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot; the lines have fallen for me in pleasant places (Ps. 16:5-6). Everything else in this chapter has since changed hands. And Levi’s portion is no longer one tribe’s: in Christ every believer is made part of a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9) and is given an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4), which is God himself, possessed through his Son.
13.examples:
Then: An old soldier was told there was more to do than he had time for, and Israel was ordered to divide up a country it did not yet hold. The tribes were read their allotments one by one, and when the reading finished the men of Levi were still standing there with nothing in their hands.

Now: Two things to take. The first is verse 13, and the question it asks is not whether you have rebelled against God but what sin you have simply stopped fighting, and allowed to go on living in the middle of your life because the fight got long. Geshur looked like a small compromise for about four hundred years, until Absalom. The God who says I myself will drive them out (v. 6) has not left that work to your willpower: his Spirit is given to put to death what we have let stay (Rom. 8:13), and what we confess he forgives (1 John 1:9). The second is the test at the end: if everything you own were taken away tomorrow, what would you still have? The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God opens the land registry with honesty and a promise. Joshua is old, and very much land remains to be taken (v. 1). The LORD lists it: the whole Philistine coast with its five rulers at Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron, the Geshurites and the Avvim in the south, and in the north the Sidonian coast, the land of the Gebalites and all Lebanon as far as Lebo-hamath (vv. 2–6a). Then come two sentences that belong together: “I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance” (v. 6). Joshua is to divide land not yet conquered among the nine and a half tribes, because God’s promise makes it as good as theirs (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The land was given in chapter 1 and most of it is still occupied in chapter 13. That is not a contradiction the book is embarrassed by; it states both facts in one verse. The inheritance is legally theirs, by God’s gift, and not yet theirs in practice.
verseByVerse.examples: The first item on the unconquered list is the Philistines, with all five of their cities named. They are about to be Israel's chief enemy for generations: through Samson, through the loss of the ark, through Saul's death on Gilboa, until David finally breaks them. Centuries of trouble are listed here as unfinished business.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joshua was old and advanced in years, and the LORD said to him, "You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess. This is the land that yet remains: all the regions of the Philistines, and all those of the Geshurites (from the Shihor, which is east of Egypt, northward to the boundary of Ekron, it is counted as Canaanite; there are five rulers of the Philistines, those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron), and those of the Avvim, in the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that belongs to the Sidonians, to Aphek, to the boundary of the Amorites, and the land of the Gebalites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath, all the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, even all the Sidonians. I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you. Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and half the tribe of Manasseh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Joshua that his time is running out with much land untaken, then promises to drive out its people himself and has him share it out as if it were already won.

You are old and advanced in years. God tells an old man that he is old, and there is nothing cruel in it: it is plain honesty to a man who has fought for years and is not going to finish. Among the Philistine cities still untaken is Gath, where some of the giants were left standing two chapters ago (11:22).

I myself will drive them out. Then two sentences that ought to pull against each other and do not. God will drive them out, and meanwhile Israel is to allot territory still full of Philistines: to draw the boundaries of fields nobody has walked on and hand out title deeds to towns somebody else still holds. That is exactly the position the church lives in. Paul writes to people who already have every spiritual blessing in Christ and tells them, before the letter ends, to put on the armour and stand (Ephesians 1:3; 6:11).

Did Joshua take the whole land? In the summary language of ancient war, yes (11:23): the armies were broken and the kings killed. But not every town was occupied: this verse says much land remained, and Judges 1 shows tribes still driving out the inhabitants. The Canaanite kingdoms were broken; the long work of settling had only begun.

Uncertain wording. Some names in verses 3–5 cannot be placed with certainty. The Shihor (v. 3) is probably the Brook of Egypt, the dry riverbed on Canaan’s southern edge, though the name can also mean a branch of the Nile. Lebo-hamath (v. 5) is either a town called Lebo or “the entrance of Hamath”; either way it marks the northern limit of the promised land (Numbers 34:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — What Was Not Driven Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The eastern land is written into the same deed as the west, and two notes are added that will matter. Moses had already given Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh the country beyond the Jordan: the tableland from the Arnon, the cities of Sihon, Gilead, and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, the last of the Rephaim (vv. 8–12). Then, without comment, verse 13 records that Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, who were still there “to this day”. And verse 14 sets one tribe apart: Levi received no territory, because the offerings made to the LORD were its inheritance.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is the first of a series that will run through the next few chapters and then open the book of Judges: the towns that were not taken. Nobody rebelled. The war simply stopped somewhere short of the orders, and the writer keeps a list.
verseByVerse.examples: Geshur did not stay quiet. Centuries later David married Maacah, daughter of the king of Geshur; their son Absalom murdered his half-brother and fled to his grandfather's kingdom for three years, and came home to raise the revolt that nearly ended David's reign (2 Sam. 3:3; 13:37-38; 15:8). What was left in the midst of Israel here came back as David's in-laws.

verseByVerse.quote: With the other half of the tribe of Manasseh the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond the Jordan eastward, as Moses the servant of the LORD gave them: from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland of Medeba as far as Dibon; and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the boundary of the Ammonites; and Gilead, and the region of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan to Salecah; all the kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei (he alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim); these Moses had struck and driven out. Yet the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, but Geshur and Maacath dwell in the midst of Israel to this day. To the tribe of Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance. The offerings by fire to the LORD God of Israel are their inheritance, as he said to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes are written into the same deed as the rest, and the record notes, without comment, peoples Israel never drove out.

Why repeat Moses’ allotment? The eastern land had been settled under Moses (Numbers 32). The writer records it so that the tribes beyond the river are written into the same deed as the rest: one land, given by one God, to one people. Chapter 22 will show how quickly the river could make that unity look doubtful.

Geshur and Maacath dwell in the midst of Israel. Verse 13 is dropped into a property list without comment: no command refused, just two small kingdoms on the edge of Bashan left where they were, still there to this day. The same note will sound through the next chapters (15:63; 16:10; 17:12–13), and Judges opens by counting the cost. Geshur’s bill came due under David: its princess bore him Absalom, who fled there after murdering his brother and whose rebellion later drove the king barefoot out of Jerusalem (2 Samuel 3:3; 13:37–38; 15:30).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–33 — Fields for Eleven Tribes, and God for One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The eastern territories are surveyed tribe by tribe, and the chapter ends by naming the best inheritance of all. Reuben receives the tableland around Heshbon and Medeba, the old kingdom of Sihon (vv. 15–23); Gad receives Jazer, the towns of Gilead and the Jordan valley up to the Sea of Chinnereth (vv. 24–28); and half of Manasseh receives Bashan with the sixty towns of Jair (vv. 29–31). One man is named among the place-names: Balaam, the diviner, killed with the sword (v. 22). Verse 32 closes the eastern register, and verse 33 returns to Levi, saying more plainly what verse 14 said: “the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance.”
verseByVerse.theology: The lists are dull on purpose: they are a receipt. Every boundary and village in them goes back to God’s promise of this land to Abraham while he was still childless (Gen. 15:18), and here it is surveyed, divided and handed over. God’s promises do not stay as warm words; they end as real places with names.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter is framed by the tribe that got none of it. Verse 14 and verse 33 sit at either end of the survey like bookends, and both say the same thing in different words: Levi has no fields, and Levi has the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of the people of Reuben according to their clans. So their territory was from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland by Medeba; with Heshbon, and all its cities that are in the tableland; Dibon, and Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon, and Jahaz, and Kedemoth, and Mephaath, and Kiriathaim, and Sibmah, and Zereth-shahar on the hill of the valley, and Beth-peor, and the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth, that is, all the cities of the tableland, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses defeated with the leaders of Midian, Evi and Rekem and Zur and Hur and Reba, the princes of Sihon, who lived in the land. Balaam also, the son of Beor, the one who practiced divination, was killed with the sword by the people of Israel among the rest of their slain. And the border of the people of Reuben was the Jordan as a boundary. This was the inheritance of the people of Reuben, according to their clans with their cities and villages.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among the towns of Reuben the writer records one death: Balaam, the hired diviner who could not curse Israel but taught its enemies how to ruin it.

Balaam also, the son of Beor. In the middle of a chapter about fields stands a man. Balaam was the prophet for hire who could not curse Israel, the great comic failure of Numbers 22–24. What he did afterwards was not comic: he advised Israel’s enemies to ruin them from the inside, and it worked at Peor when cursing had not (Numbers 31:8, 16). The risen Christ names the danger in a compromising church as “the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel” (Revelation 2:14). Nobody could curse them from outside. They had to be talked into sinning.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses gave an inheritance also to the tribe of Gad, to the people of Gad, according to their clans. Their territory was Jazer, and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, to Aroer, which is east of Rabbah, and from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the territory of Debir, and in the valley Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, having the Jordan as a boundary, to the lower end of the Sea of Chinnereth, eastward beyond the Jordan. This is the inheritance of the people of Gad according to their clans, with their cities and villages. And Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was allotted to the half-tribe of the people of Manasseh according to their clans. Their region extended from Mahanaim, through all Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all the towns of Jair, which are in Bashan, sixty cities, and half Gilead, and Ashtaroth, and Edrei, the cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. These were allotted to the people of Machir the son of Manasseh for the half of the people of Machir according to their clans. These are the inheritances that Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan east of Jericho. But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance; the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance, just as he said to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern register closes on the tribe that receives no land, because the LORD himself is its inheritance.

In the plains of Moab. The distribution was made on the plains of Moab, by Moses, who never crossed the river (v. 32).

The LORD God of Israel is their inheritance. Picture the day. Men hear the names of places they will farm, and each family walks away holding something it can stand on. Levi is handed nothing: no fields, no boundary stones, no town with a wall round it (see Priests and Levites). Having the LORD instead of land could look like a consolation prize, and the rest of the Bible will not allow that. Asaph gets to the bottom of it: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:25–26).

What could be lost. Everything Reuben was given could be taken away, and eventually was: Assyria carried those eastern tribes off first (1 Chronicles 5:26). Levi’s portion could not be taken, and in Christ every believer shares it: an inheritance “kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4).

keyVerse.quote: I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you.
keyVerse.note: These two sentences hold the chapter together. God’s promise to finish the work is so sure that Israel can share out land it has not yet taken. The church lives the same way, already given everything in Christ and still called to take hold of it.

13.reflection:
God tells Joshua plainly that he is old and that much remains undone (v. 1). How do you respond when you realise you will not finish everything you hoped to? What comfort is there in knowing the work is God’s?

Israel was told to allot land not yet taken, trusting God’s promise to drive out its inhabitants (v. 6). Where are you called to act now on promises God has not yet fully worked out in your life?

Geshur and Maacath were quietly left in place, and years later trouble came from Geshur into David’s own family (v. 13). What small compromises have you left standing, and what might they cost later?

Levi received no land because “the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance” (v. 33). In what ways do you treat God as a consolation prize rather than the best portion? How does Christ make God himself your inheritance?

14.title: Caleb's Inheritance
14.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the inheritances that the people of Israel received in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel gave them to inherit.<sup>2</sup>Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses for the nine and one-half tribes.<sup>3</sup>For Moses had given an inheritance to the two and one-half tribes beyond the Jordan, but to the Levites he gave no inheritance among them.<sup>4</sup>For the people of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. And no portion was given to the Levites in the land, but only cities to dwell in, with their pasturelands for their livestock and their substance.<sup>5</sup>The people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses; they allotted the land.<sup>6</sup>Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. And Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God in Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me.<sup>7</sup>I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him word again as it was in my heart.<sup>8</sup>But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; yet I wholly followed the LORD my God.<sup>9</sup>And Moses swore on that day, saying, 'Surely the land on which your foot has trodden shall be an inheritance for you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.'<sup>10</sup>And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years since the time that the LORD spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old.<sup>11</sup>I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming.<sup>12</sup>So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said."<sup>13</sup>Then Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance.<sup>14</sup>Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>15</sup>Now the name of Hebron formerly was Kiriath-arba. (Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim.) And the land had rest from war.
14.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 13 recorded the land east of the Jordan, settled under Moses. Now the western allotment begins at Gilgal, and before a single tribal boundary is drawn the register stops for one man: Caleb, eighty-five years old, the last survivor with Joshua of the generation that refused to enter the land.

The message. God keeps his word to those who trust it, even across forty-five years. Caleb believed God when everyone else was afraid, lived for decades with the consequences of other people’s unbelief, and now claims exactly what was promised, the hardest ground in the country, because he is still counting on the God who promised it.

Why it was said. Israel was about to divide a land still partly held by enemies, and later chapters show how tempted the tribes were to settle for what was easy (see the introduction). Caleb stands at the head of the allotments as the model of how to receive an inheritance: by faith, wholeheartedly, and unafraid of giants.

How the chapter makes its case. The method is laid down first: Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the tribal heads divide the land by lot, as the LORD commanded, with Joseph counted as two tribes and Levi given towns but no territory (vv. 1–5). Then Caleb recalls Kadesh-barnea, where ten spies made the people’s heart melt while he “wholly followed the LORD” (vv. 6–9). He counts the forty-five years God has kept him alive and asks for the hill country of the Anakim (vv. 10–12). Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron, and the writer repeats the reason: “because he wholly followed the LORD” (vv. 13–15).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need it exposes. Wholehearted following was rare: out of a whole generation only two men had it, and even they were not sinless. What Caleb showed in part, Jesus showed in full. He alone trusted his Father perfectly, finished the work he was given (John 17:4), and won the inheritance not for himself but for people who had not wholly followed. Caleb also shows what faith looks like in those who belong to Christ: it holds a promise for decades and goes up against giants in the strength of God.

For us. Faith does not retire. Whatever your age, God’s promises in Christ are still to be taken hold of, and the strength to do it is his. And when following him costs you years you did not deserve to lose, remember Caleb: the LORD was keeping count too.
14.theology:
The lot, and who is really deciding. Land drawn by lot looks like chance, but it is the opposite: God decides. Every family that ends up on hard ground knows exactly whose decision it was: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov. 16:33).

Wholly followed. The phrase is repeated three times over one man (vv. 8, 9, 14): he went after the LORD with nothing held back. It is the exact opposite of the verdict the rest of these chapters keep recording about the tribes: they did not drive out, they could not drive out, they left them living in the midst.

Did Caleb earn his hill? No. Hebron was a promise kept, sworn by God at Kadesh, not wages paid. Caleb’s wholehearted following was the shape his faith took, and God himself calls him my servant who had a different spirit (Numbers 14:24). Only one man ever followed the LORD wholly with no lapse at all: Christ, faithful to him who appointed him (Hebrews 3:2) and obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:8). His people inherit because he followed wholly; then, made new, they begin to follow him with something of Caleb’s undivided heart.

Faithfulness is not exempted from other people's consequences. Caleb was right at forty and it bought him thirty-eight years in a wilderness he had argued against, burying men who had been wrong. God kept him alive through all of it and gave him the ground at eighty-five. A believer who was right still has to live among the people who chose wrongly, and shares what their choice brings.

Asking for the giants. The request in verse 12 is for the hardest terrain on the map, named with its difficulties attached, and it ends it may be that the LORD will be with me: certainty about the promise and humility about himself, in one sentence. This is what faith and patience look like at eighty-five (Heb. 6:12).
14.examples:
Then: An old man walked up to the man dividing the country and asked for the one district everybody else was avoiding, because God had promised it to him forty-five years earlier and he had not forgotten.

Now: Two questions come out of this chapter, and the second is the harder. What promise of God are you still waiting for, year after year, and would you recognise it if it arrived? Caleb knew the number of years exactly. And then: what would you ask God for if you were sure he had already granted it? Most requests get smaller with age. Caleb's got steeper, and he still would not say more than it may be that the LORD will be with me. And if your own strength has not lasted like his, the promise never rested on his strength either; it rested on the God who kept him alive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The western allotment is God’s work, done his way. The writer names who carried it out, Eleazar the priest first, then Joshua and the heads of the tribes (v. 1), and how: “Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses” (v. 2). Then he explains the arithmetic. Two and a half tribes are already settled beyond the Jordan (v. 3); Joseph counts as two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim; and Levi receives no territory, only towns to live in with pasturelands for their animals (v. 4). Verse 5 sums it up: Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses and allotted the land.
verseByVerse.theology: Drawing lots takes the decision out of human hands: no tribe can lobby, no elder can trade a favour, the strongest tribe cannot argue its way to the best ground, and the smallest cannot be quietly cheated.
verseByVerse.examples: Levi is dealt with in half a verse: no portion, only cities to live in and grazing for the animals. The tribe that carried the ark across the Jordan ends the day with somewhere to sleep and nowhere to farm.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the inheritances that the people of Israel received in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel gave them to inherit. Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses for the nine and one-half tribes. For Moses had given an inheritance to the two and one-half tribes beyond the Jordan, but to the Levites he gave no inheritance among them. For the people of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. And no portion was given to the Levites in the land, but only cities to dwell in, with their pasturelands for their livestock and their substance. The people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses; they allotted the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land is divided by lot, so that each tribe receives its share from God, not from human favour.

Their inheritance was by lot. The lot left no room for lobbying: no tribe could push for better ground and no family could be quietly cheated, for “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). And the priest is named before the general. This is not soldiers sharing out the spoils of war; it is God assigning his land.

No portion was given to the Levites. Levi’s half verse is the third such note in two chapters (13:14, 33), and it will come round again in chapters 18 and 21.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — I Wholly Followed the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the lot falls on Judah, one man of Judah steps forward with a claim forty-five years old. Caleb comes to Joshua at Gilgal and reminds him what the LORD said at Kadesh-barnea about the two of them (v. 6).
