He tells the story: he was forty when Moses sent him to spy out the land, and he reported honestly what he believed (v. 7). His fellow spies made the people’s heart melt, but he “wholly followed the LORD my God” (v. 8). So Moses swore that the ground Caleb’s foot had trodden would belong to him and his children for ever (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The phrase runs through the chapter three times and it is Caleb's whole testimony: he wholly followed the LORD, going after God with nothing held back.
verseByVerse.examples: Twice he is called the Kenizzite (vv. 6, 14), and Kenaz is an Edomite clan name (Gen. 36:11, 15). The most single-minded Israelite in the book may not have been born an Israelite at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. And Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God in Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me. I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him word again as it was in my heart. But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; yet I wholly followed the LORD my God. And Moses swore on that day, saying, 'Surely the land on which your foot has trodden shall be an inheritance for you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caleb recalls Kadesh-barnea, where ten spies frightened a nation and he trusted God, and the promise Moses swore to him there.

Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite. The Kenizzites were a people of Canaan (Genesis 15:19), so Caleb’s family may have joined Israel from outside: the man who followed Israel’s God most wholly may not have been an Israelite by birth.

Concerning you and me. He opens with the two of them, because Joshua and Caleb are the only two left of the men counted and condemned at Kadesh-barnea (Numbers 14:29–30). Most of those listening were children then, or unborn. The rest of that generation is buried in the desert behind them.

Made the heart of the people melt. His account of the worst day in Israel’s history is brief and spares no one. Ten men came back and made a nation’s heart melt, the same word used for the terror of Jericho and of the kings of Canaan (2:11; 5:1). What frightened Israel out of the land was not the Anakim. It was a report.

I wholly followed the LORD my God. It was God’s own verdict on him: he “has followed me fully” (Numbers 14:24). And it cost him. Telling the truth did not get Caleb the land at forty; it got him thirty-eight more years in a desert with the people who had been wrong.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — Give Me This Hill Country
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Caleb’s request rests on God’s faithfulness, not his own fitness. The LORD has kept him alive for forty-five years, just as he said (v. 10), and at eighty-five Caleb is as strong for war as he was at forty (v. 11). So he asks for the hardest ground in the land, the hill country where the Anakim live in great fortified cities. And he ends not with a boast but with dependence: “It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said” (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: He asks for the hardest ground on the map. The giants that had frightened ten men into a forty-year detour are still living in those hills, and the eighty-five-year-old who brought back the minority report is asking for that particular address.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause keeps the whole speech from being bravado. Not “the LORD will be with me”, but it may be. Forty-five years of waiting had not made him presumptuous about God; he asks for giants and does not tell God what to do about them.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years since the time that the LORD spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old. I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming. So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At eighty-five Caleb credits his strength to God and spends it on the hardest ground in the land.

These forty-five years. He has been counting, as a man waiting on a specific promise does: thirty-eight years watching the men who made the decision die one funeral at a time, then seven years of war. He was forty when God swore it and is eighty-five now. Most men at eighty-five are taking an inventory of what they can no longer do. Caleb is applying for work.

So now give me this hill country. He does not ask for a quiet valley near water but for the giants’ country that had terrified the spies (Numbers 13:28, 33). It may be that the LORD will be with me is humility, not doubt: his confidence is in God’s presence, not his own strength.

Shouldn’t old age be a long rest? Our culture hands the old two scripts. One treats age as a decline to be hidden: keep up, look younger, pretend. The other treats it as a reward to be spent on ourselves, the well-earned holiday at the end of the working life. Both quietly assume that our worth lay in what we could produce. Caleb lives by neither. He is still holding a promise, and a promise does not retire. Rest is a good gift, and Scripture never despises the frail; but Caleb puts his strength down to the LORD who kept him alive, and spends it on the hardest hill in the country. The gospel gives every ageing Christian the same freedom: “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). A life hidden with Christ is not winding down. It is getting nearer to its inheritance.

Had the Anakim not been cut off? Joshua broke their power in the campaign (11:21–22); they held on or came back, and Caleb finished the occupation (15:13–14). Judges 1:10 gives the same victory to Judah, because Caleb fought as a leader of Judah.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The promise is kept. Joshua blesses Caleb and gives him Hebron as his inheritance (v. 13), and the writer adds that it has been his family’s “to this day”, giving the reason a third time: he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel (v. 14). Verse 15 records the town’s old name, Kiriath-arba, after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim, so that the giants’ city becomes the home of the man who was not afraid of them. The chapter ends with the words that closed the conquest: “And the land had rest from war.”
verseByVerse.theology: Of all the ground in Canaan, Hebron is the one place already thick with promise. Abraham lived there under the oaks, and bought the cave of Machpelah there as the only piece of the land he ever owned: the grave where he, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah are buried (Gen. 23; 49:31). Caleb asks for the ground where the fathers of Israel are buried.
verseByVerse.examples: The town's old name honoured a giant, for Arba was the greatest of the Anakim. The name that once frightened the spies became the address of the one man among them who was not afraid.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance. Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel. Now the name of Hebron formerly was Kiriath-arba. (Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim.) And the land had rest from war.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua blesses Caleb and gives him Hebron, the giants’ city, because he wholly followed the LORD.

He gave Hebron to Caleb. Two old men, the last of a generation, settle a promise made in the desert nearly half a century before. Abraham had pitched his tent by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron, and he, Sarah, Isaac and Jacob were buried there (Genesis 13:18; 23:19; 50:13): Caleb asked for the place where the men who first received the promise lay. Hebrews tells sluggish Christians to imitate “those who through faith and patience inherit the promises” (Hebrews 6:12), and it could have named Caleb. He believed God at forty, said so when it was unpopular, paid for it with thirty-eight years in the desert, and at eighty-five walked up to the hardest hill in the country and asked for it by name.
verseByVerse.note: “Kiriath-arba” means “the city of Arba”; 15:13 calls Arba the father of Anak.

keyVerse.quote: So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said.
keyVerse.note: Caleb asks for the hardest ground in the land, at eighty-five, because God promised it. His confidence rests not on his own strength but on the LORD being with him. It is faith in a sentence: bold about the promise, humble about himself.

14.reflection:
Caleb told the truth at Kadesh-barnea, and it cost him thirty-eight years in the desert (vv. 7–8). When has being faithful cost you something? How does Caleb’s story help you wait?

Caleb “wholly followed the LORD” (vv. 8, 9, 14). What would it look like for you to follow him wholly, with nothing held back? Where is your following only partial?

At eighty-five Caleb asked for the hardest ground in the land (v. 12). How should God’s promises shape the way older Christians spend their later years, and what can younger Christians learn from them?

Caleb’s faithfulness was real but partial; Jesus trusted his Father perfectly and won the inheritance for people who had not. How does that change the way you read Caleb’s story, and your own?

15.title: The Allotment of Judah
15.text: <sup>1</sup>The allotment for the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans reached southward to the boundary of Edom, to the wilderness of Zin at the farthest south.<sup>2</sup>And their south boundary ran from the end of the Salt Sea, from the bay that faces southward.<sup>3</sup>It goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, turns about to Karka,<sup>4</sup>passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Brook of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary.<sup>5</sup>And the east boundary is the Salt Sea, to the mouth of the Jordan. And the boundary on the north side runs from the bay of the sea at the mouth of the Jordan.<sup>6</sup>And the boundary goes up to Beth-hoglah and passes along north of Beth-arabah. And the boundary goes up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben.<sup>7</sup>And the boundary goes up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, and so northward, turning toward Gilgal, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim, which is on the south side of the valley. And the boundary passes along to the waters of En-shemesh and ends at En-rogel.<sup>8</sup>Then the boundary goes up by the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the southern shoulder of the Jebusite (that is, Jerusalem). And the boundary goes up to the top of the mountain that lies over against the Valley of Hinnom, on the west, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>9</sup>Then the boundary extends from the top of the mountain to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, and from there to the cities of Mount Ephron. Then the boundary bends around to Baalah (that is, Kiriath-jearim).<sup>10</sup>And the boundary circles west of Baalah to Mount Seir, passes along to the northern shoulder of Mount Jearim (that is, Chesalon), and goes down to Beth-shemesh and passes along by Timnah.<sup>11</sup>The boundary goes out to the shoulder of the hill north of Ekron, then the boundary bends around to Shikkeron and passes along to Mount Baalah and goes out to Jabneel. Then the boundary comes to an end at the sea.<sup>12</sup>And the west boundary was the Great Sea with its coastline. This is the boundary around the people of Judah according to their clans.<sup>13</sup>According to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, he gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh a portion among the people of Judah, Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron (Arba was the father of Anak).<sup>14</sup>And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the descendants of Anak.<sup>15</sup>And he went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir. Now the name of Debir formerly was Kiriath-sepher.<sup>16</sup>And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife."<sup>17</sup>And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, captured it. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.<sup>20</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans.<sup>21</sup>The cities belonging to the tribe of the people of Judah in the extreme south, toward the boundary of Edom, were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur,<sup>22</sup>Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah,<sup>23</sup>Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan,<sup>24</sup>Ziph, Telem, Bealoth,<sup>25</sup>Hazor-hadattah, Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor),<sup>26</sup>Amam, Shema, Moladah,<sup>27</sup>Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, Beth-pelet,<sup>28</sup>Hazar-shual, Beersheba, Biziothiah,<sup>29</sup>Baalah, Iim, Ezem,<sup>30</sup>Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah,<sup>31</sup>Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah,<sup>32</sup>Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon: in all, twenty-nine cities with their villages.<sup>33</sup>And in the lowland, Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah,<sup>34</sup>Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, Enam,<sup>35</sup>Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah,<sup>36</sup>Shaaraim, Adithaim, Gederah, Gederothaim: fourteen cities with their villages.<sup>37</sup>Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad,<sup>38</sup>Dilean, Mizpeh, Joktheel,<sup>39</sup>Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon,<sup>40</sup>Cabbon, Lahmam, Chitlish,<sup>41</sup>Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah: sixteen cities with their villages.<sup>42</sup>Libnah, Ether, Ashan,<sup>43</sup>Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib,<sup>44</sup>Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah: nine cities with their villages.<sup>45</sup>Ekron, with its towns and its villages;<sup>46</sup>from Ekron to the sea, all that were by the side of Ashdod, with their villages.<sup>47</sup>Ashdod, its towns and its villages; Gaza, its towns and its villages; to the Brook of Egypt, and the Great Sea with its coastline.<sup>48</sup>And in the hill country, Shamir, Jattir, Socoh,<sup>49</sup>Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir),<sup>50</sup>Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim,<sup>51</sup>Goshen, Holon, and Giloh: eleven cities with their villages.<sup>52</sup>Arab, Dumah, Eshan,<sup>53</sup>Janim, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah,<sup>54</sup>Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior: nine cities with their villages.<sup>55</sup>Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah,<sup>56</sup>Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah,<sup>57</sup>Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah: ten cities with their villages.<sup>58</sup>Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor,<sup>59</sup>Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon: six cities with their villages.<sup>60</sup>Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), and Rabbah: two cities with their villages.<sup>61</sup>In the wilderness, Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah,<sup>62</sup>Nibshan, the City of Salt, and Engedi: six cities with their villages.<sup>63</sup>But the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.
15.overview:
Where we are. The western allotment opened with Caleb’s claim (chapter 14). Now the lot falls first on Judah, and this is the longest allotment in the book: a boundary walked landmark by landmark, a family story in the middle, more than a hundred towns, and a last verse that admits failure.

The message. God gives his people a real place, measured and named down to the last spring and village, and he gives Judah first and most because of what he will do through Judah. Yet the chapter ends honestly: the one city that would matter most, Jerusalem, stayed in enemy hands. The gift is God’s, the taking was incomplete, and the story was not over.

Why it was said. The register was Judah’s title deed, kept for families who wanted to know where they belonged (see the introduction). The note that the Jebusites were still in Jerusalem “to this day” (v. 63) shows it was written before David took the city, and later readers would have heard in it a waiting that ended with him.

How the chapter makes its case. The boundary is traced: south from the Salt Sea past Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Egypt, east along the Salt Sea, north through the Valley of Achor and below Jerusalem in the Valley of Hinnom, and west to the Mediterranean (vv. 1–12). The register stops for a family: Caleb drives the sons of Anak out of Hebron, Othniel takes Debir and wins Achsah, and Achsah asks her father for springs of water (vv. 13–19). Then the towns are counted region by region, the far south, the lowland, the hill country and the wilderness (vv. 20–62). The last word is that Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem (v. 63).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise. Judah comes first because Jacob had promised that “The scepter shall not depart from Judah” (Genesis 49:10), and from Judah came David and then Jesus, “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5). The city Judah could not take became David’s capital, and outside its gate the Son of David was crucified (Hebrews 13:12) and rose again. Achsah, asking boldly and receiving more than she asked, also illustrates what Jesus taught about asking our Father (Luke 11:9–13).

For us. God knows your place in his purposes as exactly as he knew Judah’s villages. Ask him boldly for what makes his gifts fruitful, as Achsah did. And do not be surprised that some strongholds stand a long time: the one who conquered the city Judah could not take will finish his work.
15.theology:
Promises kept in real places. Forty verses of town names are the keeping of a promise made to Abraham, a childless man who was told to count the stars (Gen. 15:5, 18). God does not fulfil his word in the abstract; he fulfils it in Kabzeel and Jagur and Adadah, until somebody has to count them in batches. Talk of inheritance can become vague, little more than a feeling; this chapter ties it to a map.

Two valleys on one boundary. Achor is where Achan of Judah was stoned and buried (7:24-26); Hinnom becomes Gehenna, the New Testament’s word for hell. Yet through Hosea God promised to make the Valley of Achor a door of hope (Hos. 2:15): he can turn the place of his people’s worst day into a place of hope.

Asking well. Achsah has land and no water, so she gets down off her donkey and says give me a blessing and then names the thing she actually needs (vv. 18-19). Her father, who waited forty-five years for one promise and then asked for a mountain full of giants, gives her both the upper and the lower springs. The man who knew how to ask raised a daughter who knew how to ask, and neither of them was refused. Jesus argues from the same kind of father: if earthly fathers know how to give good gifts, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

Could not. More than a hundred towns were delivered exactly as promised, and one was not, and the one was the city where the temple would stand and, outside its wall, the hill where Christ, the Lion of Judah, would be crucified.
15.examples:
Then: Surveyors walked a boundary past a heap of stones over a thief and along a ravine that would one day give hell its name, counted more than a hundred towns into batches, and finished by writing down the name of the one city they could not take.

Now: Take the two verses in the middle. Achsah had been given something real that was useless without one more thing, and she asked for it directly and got more than she named. Many Christians pray in general terms and never name the one thing they actually need. And take the last verse with it, for honesty: a great deal given, and one thing still standing that will not move yet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah’s inheritance is a real, measured land, and its borders carry memories. The writer traces the south boundary from the tip of the Salt Sea past Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Egypt and the Mediterranean (vv. 1–4), and the east boundary along the Salt Sea to the mouth of the Jordan (v. 5). The north boundary is walked landmark by landmark: Beth-hoglah, the stone of Bohan, the Valley of Achor, En-shemesh and En-rogel (vv. 6–7), up the Valley of the Son of Hinnom past the shoulder of the Jebusite city, Jerusalem (v. 8), then west by Kiriath-jearim, Beth-shemesh and Ekron to the sea (vv. 9–11). The Great Sea is the western boundary (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Two names on this boundary are not neutral. The line runs through the Valley of Achor, where a man of Judah was buried under stones for stealing from God (7:24-26); and it runs along the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, which the New Testament knows as Gehenna. Judah's title deeds are drawn through the valley of its own worst day and past the valley that became a word for hell.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 puts Jerusalem on the boundary and calls it the Jebusite. The city that will one day be the centre of everything is at this point a foreign town on the edge of somebody's farmland, and verse 63 says what happened when Judah tried to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: The allotment for the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans reached southward to the boundary of Edom, to the wilderness of Zin at the farthest south. And their south boundary ran from the end of the Salt Sea, from the bay that faces southward. It goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, turns about to Karka, passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Brook of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary. And the east boundary is the Salt Sea, to the mouth of the Jordan. And the boundary on the north side runs from the bay of the sea at the mouth of the Jordan. And the boundary goes up to Beth-hoglah and passes along north of Beth-arabah. And the boundary goes up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben. And the boundary goes up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, and so northward, turning toward Gilgal, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim, which is on the south side of the valley. And the boundary passes along to the waters of En-shemesh and ends at En-rogel. Then the boundary goes up by the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the southern shoulder of the Jebusite (that is, Jerusalem). And the boundary goes up to the top of the mountain that lies over against the Valley of Hinnom, on the west, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim. Then the boundary extends from the top of the mountain to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, and from there to the cities of Mount Ephron. Then the boundary bends around to Baalah (that is, Kiriath-jearim). And the boundary circles west of Baalah to Mount Seir, passes along to the northern shoulder of Mount Jearim (that is, Chesalon), and goes down to Beth-shemesh and passes along by Timnah. The boundary goes out to the shoulder of the hill north of Ekron, then the boundary bends around to Shikkeron and passes along to Mount Baalah and goes out to Jabneel. Then the boundary comes to an end at the sea. And the west boundary was the Great Sea with its coastline. This is the boundary around the people of Judah according to their clans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s boundary is walked landmark by landmark: God’s gift is a real place, and some of its landmarks recall sin and judgment.

The allotment for the tribe of the people of Judah. Judah is dealt with first and at greatest length, the writer’s way of showing how much this tribe will matter: it is the tribe of David, and of Christ. Most names on this circuit meant a great deal to an ancient reader: a spring, a ridge, a stone somebody had set up.

Achor and Hinnom. Achan, buried in the Valley of Achor, was a man of Judah (7:1, 18, 26), and every generation of surveyors after this walked past the stones. Gehenna, the Greek form of the name Hinnom, is the word Jesus uses more than anyone else in the New Testament for final judgment (Matthew 10:28); in Joshua’s day it is simply a ravine outside a Canaanite town, later the place where children were burned to Molech (2 Kings 23:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the property register stands a family that takes God at his word. As the LORD commanded, Caleb receives Hebron (v. 13) and drives out the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai (v. 14). He moves against Debir and promises his daughter Achsah to the man who captures it (vv. 15–16). Othniel, his kinsman, takes it and marries her (v. 17). Then Achsah gets down from her donkey and asks her father herself: “Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water.” Caleb gives her the upper springs and the lower springs (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: The three giants of verse 14 are named: Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. These are the names the spies brought back from Hebron forty-five years earlier, on the journey that ended with the spies feeling like grasshoppers (Num. 13:22, 33). An eighty-five-year-old took their town, and the writer troubles to give their names because they had been a legend and now they are a line in a property record.
verseByVerse.examples: Othniel goes on to become the first of the judges, the man God raises up to deliver Israel when the nation collapses in the next book (Judg. 3:9-11). Israel's first deliverer is introduced here as a young man who captured a town to win a wife.

verseByVerse.quote: According to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, he gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh a portion among the people of Judah, Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron (Arba was the father of Anak). And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the descendants of Anak. And he went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir. Now the name of Debir formerly was Kiriath-sepher. And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife." And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife. When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caleb takes what God promised, and his daughter Achsah asks boldly for what makes her land fruitful.

Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak. An old man does what he said he would do. The giants who had been a legend for two generations are cleared out of Hebron in half a verse, and the writer records their names the way an estate agent records a previous owner.

I will give him Achsah my daughter. Caleb is still fighting and still recruiting. In that world a father arranged his daughter’s marriage, and here the bride-price was courage (compare 1 Samuel 17:25): he wants a son-in-law with nerve, and the test is a walled town. Othniel takes it, the future first judge of Israel.

Give me also springs of water. The best scene in the chapter takes two verses. A field in the dry Negeb without water is a farm in name only. So Achsah gets down from her donkey and asks her father herself, not for more land but for the one thing that makes the land she has worth having. Scripture records the custom and then shows that Achsah was no mere prize: she speaks for herself and is heard. Caleb does not haggle with his daughter; he gives more than she asked for.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 17 can make Othniel Caleb’s younger brother or his nephew (Leviticus 18 forbade neither marriage). The verb translated dismounted (v. 18) is rare, used elsewhere only in Judges 1:14 and of a tent peg going into the ground (Judges 4:21); “got down” is the likely sense.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–63 — More Than a Hundred Towns, and One That Would Not Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the chapter counts Judah’s towns and ends with the one it could not take. The list is grouped by region: twenty-nine towns in the far south towards Edom (vv. 21–32); the lowland in groups, including the Philistine cities of Ekron, Ashdod and Gaza, still to be won (vv. 33–47); the hill country in five groups (vv. 48–60); and six towns in the wilderness by the Salt Sea, ending at Engedi (vv. 61–62). Many of these names will return in the stories of David. Then the last verse admits what Judah could not do: drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem, where they still lived alongside Judah “to this day” (v. 63).
verseByVerse.theology: The list is better read aloud once than studied: a deed of property running to more than a hundred addresses, promised to Abraham, who owned nothing in this country but a burial cave.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends on a failure, and the wording has shifted. Earlier the writer said Israel did not drive out Geshur and Maacath (13:13). Here he says Judah could not drive out the Jebusites. Judah will burn Jerusalem early in Judges, but the Jebusites stay, and it is still a Jebusite city generations later, when David, the shepherd from Bethlehem, takes it (Judg. 1:8, 21; 2 Sam. 5:6-9).

verseByVerse.quote: This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans. The cities belonging to the tribe of the people of Judah in the extreme south, toward the boundary of Edom, were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur, Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah, Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan, Ziph, Telem, Bealoth, Hazor-hadattah, Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor), Amam, Shema, Moladah, Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, Beth-pelet, Hazar-shual, Beersheba, Biziothiah, Baalah, Iim, Ezem, Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah, Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah, Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon: in all, twenty-nine cities with their villages. And in the lowland, Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah, Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, Enam, Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah, Shaaraim, Adithaim, Gederah, Gederothaim: fourteen cities with their villages. Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad, Dilean, Mizpeh, Joktheel, Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon, Cabbon, Lahmam, Chitlish, Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah: sixteen cities with their villages. Libnah, Ether, Ashan, Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib, Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah: nine cities with their villages. Ekron, with its towns and its villages; from Ekron to the sea, all that were by the side of Ashdod, with their villages. Ashdod, its towns and its villages; Gaza, its towns and its villages; to the Brook of Egypt, and the Great Sea with its coastline.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s towns are counted region by region, every one a real place, including Philistine cities Judah did not yet hold.

The cities belonging to the tribe. The Philistine coast is listed as Judah’s, though Judah does not yet hold it (13:2–3). Every name here is a real place with real people in it: a well, a threshing floor, a few dozen families, somebody’s grandmother. Ziklag is on the list, where David will live as an outlaw; Beersheba, where Abraham planted a tamarisk tree (Genesis 21:33); Adullam, where David hid in a cave (1 Samuel 22:1).

Why do the totals not match the names? Verse 32 says twenty-nine, after about thirty-six names. Some pairs are probably one place (Ain and Rimmon are En-rimmon in Nehemiah 11:29), and some southern towns later went to Simeon (19:1–9), so the totals may come from another stage of the list.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the hill country, Shamir, Jattir, Socoh, Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir), Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim, Goshen, Holon, and Giloh: eleven cities with their villages. Arab, Dumah, Eshan, Janim, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah, Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior: nine cities with their villages. Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah, Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah, Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah: ten cities with their villages. Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor, Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon: six cities with their villages. Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), and Rabbah: two cities with their villages. In the wilderness, Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah, Nibshan, the City of Salt, and Engedi: six cities with their villages. But the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list ends in the wilderness, and the chapter ends not with a total but with the one city Judah could not take: Jerusalem.

In the wilderness. The list ends out by the Salt Sea with six towns that are barely towns. The last is Engedi, the oasis where David will one day spare Saul and cut off only the corner of his robe (1 Samuel 24).

The people of Judah could not drive out. The counting is meticulous to the end, and then the chapter stops counting. The greatest tribe, with more than a hundred towns, could not take the one city on its boundary that mattered. Judah once burned the city (Judges 1:8), but the Jebusites held on (Judges 19:11–12) until David took it (2 Samuel 5:6–9).

The city left standing. This whole section of the book is honest like that: much given, something not yet taken. Judah did not know what was on that ridge. The tribe whose boundary ran through Achor, the Valley of Trouble, and along the ravine that would give hell its name could not take the city outside whose wall the Lamb of God would be crucified. It was left standing, in foreign hands, on the border of the tribe out of which the Lion of Judah would come.

Textual note. After verse 59 some ancient copies add a further group of towns, including Tekoa and Bethlehem, which are otherwise missing from the list; it may have dropped out of the Hebrew by accident.
verseByVerse.note: Achor means “trouble” (cf. 7:26); Engedi (v. 62) is the oasis of 1 Samuel 24.

keyVerse.quote: But the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.
keyVerse.note: After a hundred towns counted, the chapter ends with the one city Judah could not take. It is an honest admission that the gift was not yet fully possessed. And the city left standing would become David’s capital and the place where the Son of David died and rose.

15.reflection:
Judah’s boundary ran past the Valley of Achor, where Achan was buried (v. 7; 7:26). What reminders of past sin are part of your story, and how has God turned trouble into “a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15)?

Achsah asked her father for springs of water to make her land fruitful, and received more than she asked (vv. 18–19). What would it look like to ask God boldly for what you need to make good use of what he has already given you?

The chapter names more than a hundred ordinary towns and villages (vv. 20–62). How does it encourage you that God knows your place in his purposes just as exactly?

Judah could not take Jerusalem (v. 63), yet that city became the place where Christ died and rose. Where do strongholds still stand in your life, and how does Christ’s victory give you hope about them?

16.title: The Allotment of Ephraim
16.text: <sup>1</sup>The allotment of the people of Joseph went from the Jordan by Jericho, east of the waters of Jericho, into the wilderness, going up from Jericho into the hill country to Bethel.<sup>2</sup>Then going from Bethel to Luz, it passes along to Ataroth, the territory of the Archites.<sup>3</sup>Then it goes down westward to the territory of the Japhletites, as far as the territory of Lower Beth-horon, then to Gezer, and it ends at the sea.<sup>4</sup>The people of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance.<sup>5</sup>The territory of the people of Ephraim by their clans was as follows: the boundary of their inheritance on the east was Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon,<sup>6</sup>and the boundary goes from there to the sea. On the north is Michmethath. Then on the east the boundary turns around toward Taanath-shiloh and passes along beyond it on the east to Janoah,<sup>7</sup>then it goes down from Janoah to Ataroth and to Naarah, and touches Jericho, ending at the Jordan.<sup>8</sup>From Tappuah the boundary goes westward to the brook Kanah and ends at the sea. Such is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Ephraim by their clans,<sup>9</sup>together with the towns that were set apart for the people of Ephraim within the inheritance of the Manassites, all those towns with their villages.<sup>10</sup>However, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor.
16.overview:
Where we are. Judah has received its land (chapter 15). Now the lot falls to the house of Joseph, the second great block of territory, across the middle of the country. Chapter 16 gives Joseph’s southern boundary and Ephraim’s portion; chapter 17 will give Manasseh’s.

The message. God keeps his word across the generations: the brother once sold into slavery receives, through his two sons, a double share of the land his fathers were promised. But the last verse shows how God’s gifts are spoiled, not by defeat but by profitable compromise. Ephraim left the Canaanites in Gezer and put them to work, and what it kept for its own use, it never drove out.

Why it was said. Later Israel lived with the consequences of the peoples left in the land, and Judges explains them (Judges 2:1–3). This chapter shows one place where it started, and asks every reader what they are keeping that God told them to end (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The lot of Joseph runs from the Jordan at Jericho up through the hill country by Bethel and down past Beth-horon and Gezer to the sea (vv. 1–3), and both sons of Joseph receive it (v. 4). Ephraim’s own borders are then traced east, north and west, with towns set apart for it inside Manasseh (vv. 5–9). The last verse records that the Canaanites of Gezer were not driven out but made to do forced labour, “to this day” (v. 10).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need it exposes. Joseph, rejected by his brothers and raised up to save them, ends with a double portion; Jesus, rejected by his own and exalted by his Father, shares his inheritance with the people who rejected him. And Ephraim’s half-heartedness exposes what every human heart is like. Only Christ obeyed his Father with nothing held back, and he gives his people the Spirit by whom they “put to death the deeds of the body” (Romans 8:13).

For us. Compromise rarely feels like rebellion; it feels sensible. Ask what you are keeping because it is useful, though God has told you to be done with it. Christ was not half-hearted in saving you, and he gives the strength to be wholehearted in following him.
16.theology:
Compromise is usually profitable. Ephraim's practical decision paid better than obedience would have. That is what makes verse 10 worth more attention than the nine boundary verses before it: it is what disobedience usually looks like among people who would be shocked to be called disobedient.

What is kept because it is useful does not stay in its place. The book of Judges opens by collecting all these verses into one list and then delivering its verdict (Judg. 2:3), and Israel finished up worshipping the gods of the labour force.

Unfinished business gets finished by somebody else. Gezer was never taken by Israel; an Egyptian king settled the matter centuries later (1 Kings 9:16). What God's people leave undone does not quietly disappear; it is settled eventually, by other hands and on other terms.

Was forced labour the sin? Not in the writer’s eyes. God had ordered the Canaanite cults removed from his land (Deuteronomy 7:1-5), and a labour force was a way of keeping the people and their gods within reach. Forced labour was common in that world and Scripture records it without commending it; Israel later felt its weight from its own king (1 Kings 5:13; 9:20-21; 12:4). The fault named here is that a clear command was traded for a profit.

The rejected brother’s portion. The map gives Joseph, the brother who was sold, a double share. Stephen tells Joseph’s story as the first of a pattern in which God’s people reject the deliverer God sends and are then saved by him (Acts 7:9-14, 35, 52). Its last and greatest instance is Christ, handed over by his own brothers and raised to God’s right hand, from where he holds out forgiveness and an inheritance to the very people who rejected him (Acts 2:36-39).
16.examples:
Then: A tribe looked at a fortified town full of people it had been told to remove, weighed the cost, and put them to work instead. It looked the sensible decision, and the Canaanites were still there when the book was written.

Now: The test in this chapter is not whether there is open sin in your life. It is whether there is something God told you to end that you have instead made useful: the arrangement that is easier to keep than to break, and that happens to pay. Ephraim's Canaanites were not rebels in the camp. They were the workforce. The land was a gift before it was a task, and the same is true for the believer: Christ has already won the ground, and his Spirit gives the strength to put away what we have kept because it was useful (Gal. 5:16), with mercy for every time we have not (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joseph’s inheritance comes first as a single boundary line, because the two tribes descended from him share a southern border. The lot runs from the Jordan by Jericho up through the wilderness into the hill country to Bethel (v. 1), on to Luz and Ataroth in the territory of the Archites (v. 2), then down westward past the Japhletites and Lower Beth-horon to Gezer and the sea (v. 3). Verse 4 names the heirs: the people of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance. The son who was sold into slavery has become two tribes in the heart of the land.
verseByVerse.theology: Joseph counts as two tribes because Jacob adopted his two sons as his own on his deathbed, crossing his hands to put the younger in front (Gen. 48:5, 14). The boy who was sold into Egypt gets a double share of the country his brothers sold him out of.

verseByVerse.quote: The allotment of the people of Joseph went from the Jordan by Jericho, east of the waters of Jericho, into the wilderness, going up from Jericho into the hill country to Bethel. Then going from Bethel to Luz, it passes along to Ataroth, the territory of the Archites. Then it goes down westward to the territory of the Japhletites, as far as the territory of Lower Beth-horon, then to Gezer, and it ends at the sea. The people of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jacob adopted Joseph’s two sons, the brother once sold into slavery receives a double share of the land.

The allotment of the people of Joseph. The territory runs right across the middle of the country, from the Jordan to the Mediterranean, and it is given to Joseph, who has been dead for a very long time.

Manasseh and Ephraim. Jacob, dying, said “Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are” (Genesis 48:5), and would not be corrected about the crossed hands (48:17–19). Nobody in this chapter says what that meant for Joseph, the brother who was thrown into a pit. The map shows it: he receives two tribes’ share of the land.

Uncertain wording. “From Bethel to Luz” (v. 2) is puzzling, because elsewhere Luz is Bethel’s older name (Genesis 28:19; Joshua 18:13). Here they seem to be two places, perhaps the holy site of Bethel and the town of Luz nearby.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim’s own portion is traced, and the two sons of Joseph are bound together. The boundary runs on the east from Ataroth-addar to Upper Beth-horon (v. 5), north by Michmethath, round by Taanath-shiloh and on to Janoah (v. 6), down to Ataroth and Naarah, touching Jericho and ending at the Jordan (v. 7), and west from Tappuah along the brook Kanah to the sea (v. 8). Verse 9 adds that some of Ephraim’s towns lay inside Manasseh’s territory, so that the lands of the two brothers’ tribes were woven together.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is a small administrative kindness with a long history behind it. Ephraim gets towns inside his brother's allotment, which means the two tribes of Joseph are deliberately kept living among each other rather than cleanly separated.

verseByVerse.quote: The territory of the people of Ephraim by their clans was as follows: the boundary of their inheritance on the east was Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon, and the boundary goes from there to the sea. On the north is Michmethath. Then on the east the boundary turns around toward Taanath-shiloh and passes along beyond it on the east to Janoah, then it goes down from Janoah to Ataroth and to Naarah, and touches Jericho, ending at the Jordan. From Tappuah the boundary goes westward to the brook Kanah and ends at the sea. Such is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Ephraim by their clans, together with the towns that were set apart for the people of Ephraim within the inheritance of the Manassites, all those towns with their villages.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim receives the central hill country, its land woven into Manasseh’s.

The territory of the people of Ephraim. The perimeter walk again: ridges, brooks, towns and a coastline. Ephraim gets the central hill country, which is good ground and defensible, and it will hold the tabernacle at Shiloh (18:1) for generations, until the days of Eli.

Towns within Manasseh. Whatever the practical reason for verse 9, the effect is that the sons of Joseph cannot forget each other: their fields touch. The next chapter shows what these two tribes do when they have a grievance, which is to come to Joshua together (17:14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse closes the chapter, and it is the chapter’s point. Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer. The verse does not say they could not; it says they did not, and that the Canaanites lived on in the midst of the tribe “to this day”, made to do forced labour. It is a quiet record of disobedience dressed as good sense, and it prepares for the verdict of Judges: the peoples left in the land would become thorns in Israel’s sides, and their gods a snare (Judges 2:3).
verseByVerse.theology: The failure is not that Ephraim lost a battle. It is that they found an arrangement: the command was replaced by a labour policy, and everybody did rather well out of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Gezer never became Israelite by conquest. Centuries later Pharaoh king of Egypt captured it, burned it and killed the Canaanites living in it, and handed it over as a dowry when his daughter married Solomon (1 Kings 9:16). Ephraim's unfinished business was eventually settled by a foreign king, as a wedding present.

verseByVerse.quote: However, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim kept the Canaanites of Gezer as forced labour instead of driving them out, a profitable compromise with what God had told them to remove.

They did not drive out the Canaanites. Everything before this verse is a boundary description; this is a policy decision. Somebody weighed the cost of removing an entrenched population from a fortified town against the value of a permanent labour supply, and made the sensible decision. The law allowed forced labour from distant cities that surrendered, not from the cities of Canaan, lest their gods teach Israel their ways (Deuteronomy 20:10–18). Ephraim never did take Gezer: centuries later a pharaoh captured it and gave it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon’s wife (1 Kings 9:16).

How compromise happens. It is the ordinary form spiritual compromise takes. Nobody in Ephraim decided to disobey God; they decided to be practical about something God had told them to end. And what a person keeps against God’s command because it is useful will not stay under control. Judges, the sequel to all these verses, gives the verdict in advance: the peoples left in the land would become “thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you” (Judges 2:3).

What it does not mean. The command to drive out the Canaanites was God’s unique judgment on persistent wickedness, never a pattern or licence for violence today. What carries over is the call to deal decisively with sin in ourselves: “Put to death therefore what is earthly in you” (Colossians 3:5).

keyVerse.quote: However, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor.
keyVerse.note: After a chapter of boundaries, this verse records a choice. Ephraim kept what God had told it to remove because it was useful, and so began the long trouble that Judges records. It is the shape of most compromise: not open rebellion, but disobedience made to look sensible.

16.reflection:
Joseph, once sold by his brothers, received a double share of the land through his sons (vv. 1–4; Genesis 48:5). How does God’s faithfulness across many generations encourage you when you cannot see the end of what he is doing?

Ephraim kept the Canaanites of Gezer because they were useful (v. 10). What do you keep in your life because it is convenient or profitable, though you know God wants you to be done with it?

Compromise rarely feels like rebellion; it feels sensible. How can you recognise it in yourself, and how can your church family help one another to see it?

Christ was not half-hearted in saving us. How does his wholehearted love give you both the reason and the strength to put to death what you would rather keep (Colossians 3:5)?

17.title: The Allotment of Manasseh and the Complaint of Joseph
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Then allotment was made to the people of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. To Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, were allotted Gilead and Bashan, because he was a man of war.<sup>2</sup>And allotments were made to the rest of the people of Manasseh by their clans, Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These were the male descendants of Manasseh the son of Joseph, by their clans.<sup>3</sup>Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, but only daughters, and these are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.<sup>4</sup>They approached Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the leaders and said, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers." So according to the mouth of the LORD he gave them an inheritance among the brothers of their father.<sup>5</sup>Thus there fell to Manasseh ten portions, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan, which is on the other side of the Jordan,<sup>6</sup>because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance along with his sons. The land of Gilead was allotted to the rest of the people of Manasseh.<sup>7</sup>The territory of Manasseh reached from Asher to Michmethath, which is east of Shechem. Then the boundary goes along southward to the inhabitants of En-tappuah.<sup>8</sup>The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah on the boundary of Manasseh belonged to the people of Ephraim.<sup>9</sup>Then the boundary went down to the brook Kanah. These cities, to the south of the brook, among the cities of Manasseh, belong to Ephraim. Then the boundary of Manasseh goes on the north side of the brook and ends at the sea,<sup>10</sup>the land to the south being Ephraim's and that to the north being Manasseh's, with the sea forming its boundary. On the north Asher is reached, and on the east Issachar.<sup>11</sup>Also in Issachar and in Asher Manasseh had Beth-shean and its villages, and Ibleam and its villages, and the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of En-dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of Taanach and its villages, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages; the third is Naphath.<sup>12</sup>Yet the people of Manasseh could not take possession of those cities, but the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land.<sup>13</sup>Now when the people of Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not utterly drive them out.<sup>14</sup>Then the people of Joseph spoke to Joshua, saying, "Why have you given me but one lot and one portion as an inheritance, although I am a numerous people, since all along the LORD has blessed me?"<sup>15</sup>And Joshua said to them, "If you are a numerous people, go up by yourselves to the forest, and there clear ground for yourselves in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you."<sup>16</sup>The people of Joseph said, "The hill country is not enough for us. Yet all the Canaanites who dwell in the plain have chariots of iron, both those in Beth-shean and its villages and those in the Valley of Jezreel."<sup>17</sup>Then Joshua said to the house of Joseph, to Ephraim and Manasseh, "You are a numerous people and have great power. You shall not have one allotment only,<sup>18</sup>but the hill country shall be yours, for though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders. For you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong."
17.overview:
Where we are. The land is being shared out by lot (chapters 13–19). Judah has received its portion (chapters 14–15) and Ephraim its own (chapter 16); now comes the other half of Joseph’s house, Manasseh, whose eastern clans already hold Gilead and Bashan under Moses’ grant (13:29–31).

The message. God keeps his word to the weak, and he expects his people to act on it when they are strong. Five fatherless women receive their land simply by pointing to what the LORD had said. A tribe that grows strong settles for profit instead of obedience. And a tribe that asks for more is told that what God has given is enough, if they will clear the forest and trust him against the iron chariots.

Why it was said. Later Israel lived with Canaanite cities in the middle of its land, Megiddo and Beth-shean among them, and with the gods those cities worshipped. This chapter told them why: not because God’s promise failed, but because his people stopped halfway (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The register of Manasseh opens with Machir the warrior and then stops for Zelophehad’s daughters, who claim and receive the inheritance God had granted them (vv. 1–6). The boundary is traced and the great towns of the north are listed, followed by two hard verses: Manasseh could not take them, and when it grew strong it did not drive the Canaanites out (vv. 7–13). Finally the house of Joseph complains that its portion is too small, and Joshua sends them to the forest with a promise that the chariots will not stop them (vv. 14–18).

Where it leads. To Christ, in two ways. The God who heard five women when the custom of the day would have passed them by is the God revealed in Christ, in whom believing women are, with their brothers, “heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). And the chapter exposes a need: a people who obey only as far as it suits them. Christ did not stop halfway. He finished the work his Father gave him, and he now works in his people “both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

For us. Take God at his word, as the daughters did, and claim what he has promised in Christ. Then look honestly at the arrangements made in a weak season and kept because they became comfortable, and let God’s promise, not the size of the obstacle, decide what you do next.
17.theology:
Five women in a land register. The daughters of Zelophehad are named one by one every time Scripture mentions them, and the reason is a case they argued and won. The gospel carries their case to its end: in Christ the Father’s inheritance is no longer held through sons alone, for all who belong to him are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:26-29), and husbands are told to honour their wives as heirs with them of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7).

When the excuse expires. Could not in verse 12 is stated as fact, not blamed. Verse 13 is the sting: once Israel grew strong, the arrangement made in weakness was kept because by then it paid, and that is a different matter from the first failure.

Blessing as a claim. The house of Joseph argues that because God has blessed them they are owed more room (v. 14). Joshua takes the argument seriously and turns it round: if you are numerous, behave like it, and he gives them a forest to clear. Being many and blessed does not entitle anyone to easier ground.

He refuses his own tribe. Joshua gives his own kinsmen nothing but work and a promise, and he does not pretend the iron chariots are not there: he names them, adds that the enemy is strong, and repeats the instruction anyway. Honest leadership tells people the size of the difficulty and sends them at it.

Was God beaten by iron? A reader meets the iron chariots again in Judges 1:19 and may wonder whether they were too much for God. Chariots were the heavy armour of that world and could not be matched on flat ground. But Joshua’s answer settles the question: you shall drive them out, though they have chariots of iron (v. 18). The limit was never the LORD’s strength; it was Israel’s readiness to trust him on the plain.
17.examples:
Then: Five sisters asked Israel’s new leaders to honour a ruling given under Moses, and got their fields. A tribe that already held a broad band across the middle of the country came to complain that it was not enough, and went away with permission to cut down a forest.

Now: Verse 13 is the searching one. Most people can name something they could not deal with at the time, and the honest question is not whether the excuse was true then, but whether it is still true. Israel grew strong and kept the arrangement. And when the house of Joseph finally said what was really wrong, it was not the size of the land but the iron chariots on the part of it worth having. Joshua's answer named the chariots and did not change the instruction, and it came with a promise: you shall drive out the Canaanites (v. 18). For a Christian that promise is the Spirit's work, God at work in us to will and to do (Phil. 2:13), and the arrangement we kept too long is forgiven when it is confessed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Five Women in a Land Register
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word secures an inheritance for those the custom of the day would have left out. Manasseh’s allotment begins with Machir, a firstborn and a man of war, who has Gilead and Bashan (v. 1), and the clans of the rest (v. 2). Then the register stops: Zelophehad had no sons, only daughters, and all five are named: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah (v. 3). They come to Eleazar, Joshua and the leaders and cite what the LORD commanded Moses, and they are given land at once (v. 4). So Manasseh receives ten portions west of the Jordan, because the daughters inherited alongside the sons (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: These five had already been to court once, and won (see below). They are now standing in front of a new administration, asking only that the ruling be honoured, and it is.
verseByVerse.examples: Their names are given in full here for the fourth time in Scripture (Num. 26:33; 27:1; 36:11, and this). In a section of the Bible made of place names, five women are named and named again.

verseByVerse.quote: Then allotment was made to the people of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. To Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, were allotted Gilead and Bashan, because he was a man of war. And allotments were made to the rest of the people of Manasseh by their clans, Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These were the male descendants of Manasseh the son of Joseph, by their clans. Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, but only daughters, and these are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. They approached Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the leaders and said, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers." So according to the mouth of the LORD he gave them an inheritance among the brothers of their father. Thus there fell to Manasseh ten portions, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan, which is on the other side of the Jordan, because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance along with his sons. The land of Gilead was allotted to the rest of the people of Manasseh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word protects those the custom of the day would pass over: five fatherless women receive land simply by citing what the LORD had commanded.

Had no sons, but only daughters. The register opens with Machir, a firstborn and a soldier, then stops for five women, in a culture where land passed through sons (see inheritance and the firstborn). With no son, their father’s name and portion would have vanished. They had put their case to Moses: “Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son?” Moses took it to God, who answered, “The daughters of Zelophehad are right”, and made it law (Numbers 27:1–11).

The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance. Now, with Moses dead, they do not plead their merits. They cite the ruling, and it is granted at once. Most likely Hepher’s share passed to them, so the five other clans and the five women make the ten portions (vv. 5–6).

Heirs according to promise. This is faith at prayer: bringing not our worthiness but what God has said. The God who heard these women is the God revealed in Christ, in whom believing women with their brothers are “heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — Could Not, and Would Not
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manasseh received rich land and stopped short of possessing it. The boundary runs from Asher to Michmethath, down past En-tappuah and the brook Kanah to the sea, with Ephraim to the south (vv. 7–10). Verse 11 lists the strongest towns of the north, Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor, En-dor, Taanach and Megiddo, all assigned to Manasseh. Then come two hard verses. At first the tribe could not take those cities (v. 12); later, when Israel grew strong, it put the Canaanites to forced labour but did not drive them out (v. 13). Weakness was excused; profitable compromise was not.
verseByVerse.theology: The two verbs in two verses are the whole story of this half of the book: first could not, then, once it was possible, did not. The excuse expired and the arrangement stayed.
verseByVerse.examples: The six towns are the best real estate in the north: Beth-shean commanding the Jordan valley road, Megiddo commanding the pass into the plain of Jezreel. Manasseh had the title and never got the keys, and those towns will be trouble to Israel for centuries.

verseByVerse.quote: The territory of Manasseh reached from Asher to Michmethath, which is east of Shechem. Then the boundary goes along southward to the inhabitants of En-tappuah. The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah on the boundary of Manasseh belonged to the people of Ephraim. Then the boundary went down to the brook Kanah. These cities, to the south of the brook, among the cities of Manasseh, belong to Ephraim. Then the boundary of Manasseh goes on the north side of the brook and ends at the sea, the land to the south being Ephraim's and that to the north being Manasseh's, with the sea forming its boundary. On the north Asher is reached, and on the east Issachar. Also in Issachar and in Asher Manasseh had Beth-shean and its villages, and Ibleam and its villages, and the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of En-dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of Taanach and its villages, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages; the third is Naphath. Yet the people of Manasseh could not take possession of those cities, but the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land. Now when the people of Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not utterly drive them out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manasseh could not take the great towns of the north at first, and when it grew strong it chose profit over obedience and left the Canaanites in place.

Cities Manasseh never held. After the boundary walk come six towns Manasseh held only on paper, the best sites in the north: Beth-shean, where the Jordan valley meets the plain, and Taanach and Megiddo, guarding the pass every ancient army used to cross the country.

Could not take possession. The first verb is could not. Manasseh was not yet strong enough, and Scripture states it as a fact, without scolding. Some things are genuinely beyond us for a season.

When the people of Israel grew strong. Then the second sentence changes everything. The weakness passed, and when the task became possible, Manasseh did not do it. Forced labour was profitable, and they left it there, though God had said to drive them out (Deuteronomy 7:2). Judges repeats these verses (Judges 1:27–28) and gives the result: the Canaanites’ gods became “a snare” to Israel (Judges 2:3).

Megiddo. Solomon will fortify it and Josiah will die there (1 Kings 9:15; 2 Kings 23:29), and its name probably lies behind Armageddon (Revelation 16:16).

In everyday life. The excuse is often true when first offered. What matters is whether the arrangement made in weakness is dismantled once strength arrives, or quietly kept because it now suits everybody. Christ did not stop halfway; the one who began a good work in his people “will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6), and that gives hope to finish the fight.

Uncertain wording. “The third is Naphath” (v. 11) is obscure. Naphath probably means “height”; the phrase may mean “the three heights” or point to Dor, called Naphath-dor in 12:23. The general sense is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — Ask for More, Get a Forest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s blessing is not a reason to demand easier ground but the strength to take the hard ground he has given. The house of Joseph complains that one lot is too little for a people the LORD has blessed (v. 14). Joshua answers with an axe: if you are numerous, clear the forest (v. 15). Then the real objection comes out: the hill country is not enough, and the plain is full of iron chariots (v. 16). Joshua repeats their own claim back to them with God’s promise attached: you are numerous and strong, the forest shall be yours, and you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron and though they are strong (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua is himself an Ephraimite (Num. 13:8, 16). These are his own people asking their own kinsman for a better deal, and he gives them nothing but work and a promise. Favouring his own family would have been easy and nobody would have objected.
verseByVerse.examples: Their two complaints pull against each other. In verse 14 they are a great people who need more room; in verse 16 they are too weak, they say, to take the ground the chariots hold. A people large enough to need more room is large enough to take it, and Joshua says so in almost those words.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Joseph spoke to Joshua, saying, "Why have you given me but one lot and one portion as an inheritance, although I am a numerous people, since all along the LORD has blessed me?" And Joshua said to them, "If you are a numerous people, go up by yourselves to the forest, and there clear ground for yourselves in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you." The people of Joseph said, "The hill country is not enough for us. Yet all the Canaanites who dwell in the plain have chariots of iron, both those in Beth-shean and its villages and those in the Valley of Jezreel." Then Joshua said to the house of Joseph, to Ephraim and Manasseh, "You are a numerous people and have great power. You shall not have one allotment only, but the hill country shall be yours, for though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders. For you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph’s tribes ask for more land because God has blessed them, and Joshua answers that the blessing is their strength: clear the forest and trust God against the chariots.

Why have you given me but one lot? They have not been treated unjustly; they hold a broad band across the middle of the country. They want more, and their argument is that God has blessed them. Joshua is an Ephraimite himself (Numbers 13:8), so this is his own tribe asking for a favour.

Go up by yourselves to the forest. Joshua gives them an axe and a forest instead: you say you are numerous, so behave like it.

Chariots of iron. Then the real objection surfaces, the one honest sentence in the exchange. They wanted the plain, flat and fertile, and did not want to fight the people on it. Chariots with iron fittings were the terror of open ground (compare Judges 1:19).

You shall drive out the Canaanites. Joshua neither softens nor sneers, and shows his tribe no favour. He gives them back their own words with the promise attached: you are numerous and strong, the hill country shall be yours, and you shall drive them out. The difficulty is real, he says it twice, and it does not change the instruction.

Work out what God works in. The promise does not remove the axe; it makes it worth lifting. “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). The fault here is not asking God for things but asking for an easier inheritance than he has given.

Uncertain wording. Where the forest “in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim” lay (v. 15) is uncertain: most likely the wooded hills of Joseph’s own allotment, as verse 18 suggests; some think of Gilead east of the Jordan. The point is the same either way.

keyVerse.quote: but the hill country shall be yours, for though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders. For you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong.
keyVerse.note: Joshua’s answer turns a complaint into a commission. The difficulty is real and he names it twice, but God’s promise, not the size of the obstacle, decides what his people are to do. It is the pattern of the Christian life: Christ gives the inheritance, and his people clear the ground in his strength.

17.reflection:
Zelophehad’s daughters received their inheritance by citing what the LORD had commanded (v. 4). What promises of God could you bring to him in prayer in the same way, and why is that better than bringing our own worthiness?

Manasseh first could not drive out the Canaanites, and then, when strong, did not (vv. 12–13). Is there an arrangement you made in a weak season that you have kept because it now suits you? What would it mean to dismantle it?

The house of Joseph used God’s blessing as an argument for easier ground (v. 14). How do we sometimes do the same, and how does Joshua’s answer correct us?

Read Philippians 2:12–13. How does knowing that God works in you change the way you approach the ‘forest’ and the ‘chariots’ in your own life?

18.title: Shiloh and the Remaining Allotments
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the whole congregation of the people of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the tent of meeting there. The land lay subdued before them.<sup>2</sup>There remained among the people of Israel seven tribes whose inheritance had not yet been apportioned.<sup>3</sup>So Joshua said to the people of Israel, "How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?<sup>4</sup>Provide three men from each tribe, and I will send them out that they may set out and go up and down the land. They shall write a description of it with a view to their inheritances, and then come to me.<sup>5</sup>They shall divide it into seven portions. Judah shall continue in his territory on the south, and the house of Joseph shall continue in their territory on the north.<sup>6</sup>And you shall describe the land in seven divisions and bring the description here to me. And I will cast lots for you here before the LORD our God.<sup>7</sup>The Levites have no portion among you, for the priesthood of the LORD is their heritage. And Gad and Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan eastward, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave them."<sup>8</sup>So the men arose and went, and Joshua charged those who went to write the description of the land, saying, "Go up and down in the land and write a description and return to me. And I will cast lots for you here before the LORD in Shiloh."<sup>9</sup>So the men went and passed up and down in the land and wrote in a book a description of it by towns in seven divisions. Then they came to Joshua to the camp at Shiloh,<sup>10</sup>and Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh before the LORD. And there Joshua apportioned the land to the people of Israel, to each his portion.<sup>11</sup>The lot of the tribe of the people of Benjamin according to its clans came up, and the territory allotted to it fell between the people of Judah and the people of Joseph.<sup>12</sup>On the north side their boundary began at the Jordan. Then the boundary goes up to the shoulder north of Jericho, then up through the hill country westward, and it ends at the wilderness of Beth-aven.<sup>13</sup>From there the boundary passes along southward in the direction of Luz, to the shoulder of Luz (that is, Bethel), then the boundary goes down to Ataroth-addar, on the mountain that lies south of Lower Beth-horon.<sup>14</sup>Then the boundary goes in another direction, turning on the western side southward from the mountain that lies to the south, opposite Beth-horon, and it ends at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), a city belonging to the people of Judah. This forms the western side.<sup>15</sup>And the southern side begins at the outskirts of Kiriath-jearim. And the boundary goes from there to Ephron, to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah.<sup>16</sup>Then the boundary goes down to the border of the mountain that overlooks the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, which is at the north end of the Valley of Rephaim. And it then goes down the Valley of Hinnom, south of the shoulder of the Jebusites, and downward to En-rogel.<sup>17</sup>Then it bends in a northerly direction going on to En-shemesh, and from there goes to Geliloth, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim. Then it goes down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben,<sup>18</sup>and passing on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-arabah it goes down to the Arabah.<sup>19</sup>Then the boundary passes on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-hoglah. And the boundary ends at the northern bay of the Salt Sea, at the south end of the Jordan: this is the southern border.<sup>20</sup>The Jordan forms its boundary on the eastern side. This is the inheritance of the people of Benjamin, according to their clans, boundary by boundary all around.<sup>21</sup>Now the cities of the tribe of the people of Benjamin according to their clans were Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz,<sup>22</sup>Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel,<sup>23</sup>Avvim, Parah, Ophrah,<sup>24</sup>Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, Geba—twelve cities with their villages:<sup>25</sup>Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth,<sup>26</sup>Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah,<sup>27</sup>Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah,<sup>28</sup>Zela, Haeleph, Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeah and Kiriath-jearim —fourteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the people of Benjamin according to its clans.
18.overview:
Where we are. Judah and Joseph have their land (chapters 14–17), but seven tribes still have none. The camp now moves from Gilgal in the Jordan valley up to Shiloh in the hills, and the distribution resumes there.

The message. God has already given his people everything he promised, and he will not let them leave it untaken. The first thing built in the subdued land is not a fort but the tent where God dwells, and from his presence comes both a rebuke for delay and a practical way forward. Even the smallest tribe receives a portion chosen by God, and it holds places that will shape the whole story of redemption.

Why it was said. The first hearers needed to know that the land was theirs by God’s gift and by his lot, not by negotiation or strength, and that the sin of a settled people is often not rebellion but inertia (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The tent of meeting is set up at Shiloh, at the centre of the land (v. 1). Joshua asks seven tribes how long they will put off taking what God has given, and sets out a plan: three men from each tribe, a written survey, seven divisions, and lots cast before the LORD (vv. 2–7). The men walk the land and write it in a book, and Joshua casts lots at Shiloh (vv. 8–10). Benjamin’s lot comes up first: a narrow strip between Judah and Joseph that holds Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon and Jerusalem (vv. 11–28).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by promise. The tent at the centre of the land points to the one in whom God came to live among his people: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The land already given but not yet taken is a picture of every believer’s position, blessed “in Christ with every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3). And Benjamin’s little strip holds Jerusalem, where the Son of David would die and rise.

For us. The question “how long will you put off…?” is put to Christians who possess more in Christ than they have ever taken up. The answer is not a better feeling but a first concrete step, taken in God’s presence and in dependence on the one who gives every portion.
18.theology:
Worship first, and then everything else. The land is subdued and the tent goes up before a single fort or granary. And the tent points beyond itself. The Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us (John 1:14), and the place where God meets his people is now a person: not Shiloh, not even Jerusalem, but the Son, in whom the Father is worshipped in spirit and truth (John 4:21-24). Shiloh could fall. He cannot.

The sin that feels like nothing. Joshua confronts a failure in which nothing dramatic happened at all: seven tribes who have not gone in.
