The clause that makes it a rebuke is which the LORD... has given you. Delay is treated here as something to answer for, and the rebuke is itself a reminder of the gift.

The remedy is the gift already given. Joshua does not wait for God to do something new. For the Christian the same Spirit who has given us everything in Christ is the one who moves us to take it up, through his word, prayer and the company of his people. At Shiloh the deadlock broke not because anyone's feelings changed but because there was something specific to do.

Work and lot together. The men measure, describe and write a book; God assigns by lot (vv. 9-10). Every mile was walked by somebody with sore feet, and not one boundary was decided by the men who walked it. It is the same pattern as at the Jordan and Jericho, where Israel walked and God did what decided the day; only here it is a survey instead of a battle.
18.examples:
Then: Seven tribes sat comfortably in camp with a country waiting for them, and were asked how long they intended to put it off. The answer they were given was not a sermon but a job: three men each, go and walk it, write it down, bring the book back.

Now: The question in verse 3 is the one to sit with, because it is aimed at people who have done nothing wrong. Name the thing you already have in Christ and have not taken up: the promise not yet rested on, the conversation not had, the discipline not begun. Then notice Joshua's remedy. He did not wait for some new gift. He appointed people, set a task and named the day it was due, and the Spirit who lives in believers is given for exactly that kind of plain obedience (Gal. 5:25).

verseByVerse.ref: v. 1 — The Tent Goes Up at Shiloh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Once the land is subdued, Israel puts God’s dwelling at its centre. The whole congregation leaves Gilgal and gathers at Shiloh in the hill country of Ephraim, and there sets up the tent of meeting. The writer adds the reason it was now possible: the land lay subdued before them (v. 1). Shiloh will remain the place of God’s presence for generations, until the ark is lost there in the days of Eli.
verseByVerse.theology: The first structure Israel raises once the fighting stops is not a fort, a palace or a granary. It is the tent. Worship is not what the nation does when the practical work is finished; it is the first practical decision made.
verseByVerse.examples: Shiloh holds the tabernacle for generations, and it ends in ruins. Centuries later God tells Jerusalem to go and look at them: go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel (Jer. 7:12-14).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the whole congregation of the people of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the tent of meeting there. The land lay subdued before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once the land is subdued, Israel’s first act is to set God’s dwelling at the centre of it.

Assembled at Shiloh. The camp moves up from Gilgal in the Jordan valley into the hill country of Ephraim. The word “subdued” is the one used when God tells Adam and Eve to “subdue” the earth (Genesis 1:28): life in the land is meant to be a fresh start under God.

Shiloh in Israel’s story. Shiloh is where Hannah prayed so desperately that Eli thought she was drunk, and where Samuel first heard his name called in the night. It ended badly: the ark was carried into battle and lost (1 Samuel 4:3–11), and Jeremiah later pointed to its ruins as a warning (Jeremiah 7:12).

The tent at the centre. The tent pointed beyond itself to the day when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14): Christ is the true meeting place of God and his people. But no place is safe merely because God once lived there. A church can have the tent at its centre and still lose it, if God’s presence becomes a heritage rather than a living reliance.
verseByVerse.note: Shiloh lay north of Bethel, east of the road from Bethel to Shechem (Judg. 21:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–7 — How Long Will You Put Off?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people are rebuked for failing to take what he has already given, and then given a way to do it. Seven tribes still have no inheritance (v. 2), and Joshua asks them how long they will put off taking the land the LORD has given (v. 3). He then sets out a procedure: three men from each tribe, a written description, seven divisions, and lots cast before the LORD (vv. 4–6). He also notes who is already provided for: Levi, whose heritage is the priesthood, and the two and a half tribes east of the Jordan (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Both halves of the question matter. The land has been given, and they have not gone in. Nobody here is rebelling; they are simply not moving, and Joshua treats that as a thing that needs answering for.
verseByVerse.examples: There is no suggestion that they need more from God. They need to go. The remedy for this kind of delay is never another gift; the gift is the thing lying unclaimed.

verseByVerse.quote: There remained among the people of Israel seven tribes whose inheritance had not yet been apportioned. So Joshua said to the people of Israel, "How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you? Provide three men from each tribe, and I will send them out that they may set out and go up and down the land. They shall write a description of it with a view to their inheritances, and then come to me. They shall divide it into seven portions. Judah shall continue in his territory on the south, and the house of Joseph shall continue in their territory on the north. And you shall describe the land in seven divisions and bring the description here to me. And I will cast lots for you here before the LORD our God. The Levites have no portion among you, for the priesthood of the LORD is their heritage. And Gad and Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan eastward, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven tribes had been given land they had not taken, and Joshua calls their delay what it is.

Seven tribes. Seven tribes out of twelve have not taken their land. Not lost it, not been driven out of it: simply not gone.

Which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you. The sting is in the last clause, and it is also the comfort: there is no obstacle in heaven and no further permission required. A country sits there with their names on it.

The priesthood of the LORD is their heritage. Levi is mentioned again, in the middle of a rebuke about land. The tribe with nothing to claim is the one tribe that has never held anything up (see priests and Levites).

In everyday life. This is the commonest condition in the Christian life. A believer possesses more in Christ than he has ever taken up. The forgiveness is granted and not enjoyed; the prayer is available and not made; the reconciliation is possible and postponed another year. Nothing is refused; nothing is done.

How do I go in and take it? Name one piece of land. Pick one thing God has given that you have not taken up: the forgiveness you keep asking for again as if it were not granted, the prayer you keep meaning to start, the brother you have not spoken to since the funeral. Give it a task and a date. Joshua sent surveyors with a job to do; make yours as concrete: ten minutes of prayer before work this week, the phone call on Thursday. Start from the gift, not the effort. “His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness” (2 Peter 1:3), so you are not climbing towards something withheld but walking onto ground already deeded to you. Take someone with you. Joshua sent men in threes; tell a friend and ask them to hold you to it. Every one of these gifts was secured by Christ, for the Father “has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3). Nothing remains to be won; it remains to be entered.

Is casting lots a model today? Here God himself appointed the lot to divide a land he had already promised (Numbers 26:55; Proverbs 16:33). The last lot in Scripture came before Pentecost (Acts 1:26); believers now seek God’s will through his word, prayer and wise counsel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — A Survey, a Book, and a Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paralysis is broken by obedience to a clear task, and the outcome is left to God. Joshua charges the men to walk the land and write a description (v. 8). They go up and down the country and write it in a book, town by town, in seven divisions, and bring it back to the camp at Shiloh (v. 9). There Joshua casts lots before the LORD and gives each tribe its portion (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The cure for passivity here is a task, a team, a method and a deadline: a few men from each tribe walking the hills with a pen.
verseByVerse.examples: The survey is human work done thoroughly, and the allocation is still by lot before the LORD. Israel measures and describes; God assigns. Both halves are needed, and the book they carried back to Shiloh did not decide a single boundary.

verseByVerse.quote: So the men arose and went, and Joshua charged those who went to write the description of the land, saying, "Go up and down in the land and write a description and return to me. And I will cast lots for you here before the LORD in Shiloh." So the men went and passed up and down in the land and wrote in a book a description of it by towns in seven divisions. Then they came to Joshua to the camp at Shiloh, and Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh before the LORD. And there Joshua apportioned the land to the people of Israel, to each his portion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men walk the land and write it down, and Joshua divides it by lot before the LORD: obedience to a plain task, with the outcome left to God.

Write a description. The job is specific and unglamorous: a survey compiled on foot and written in a book. That is how paralysis is usually broken, not by a change of feeling but by a defined task: who goes, what they do, what they bring back, and when. Nothing suggests the tribes became enthusiastic. They were given something concrete to do and a man who expected it done.

Before the LORD in Shiloh. The survey is human work; the decision is God’s (Proverbs 16:33). So a believer can say of his place and calling, “you hold my lot. The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places” (Psalm 16:5–6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives the smallest tribe a narrow portion that holds some of the most important places in Israel’s future. Benjamin’s lot comes up first, and its land falls between Judah to the south and Joseph to the north (v. 11). The boundary is walked: north from the Jordan past Jericho and Bethel, west to Kiriath-jearim, south past the Valley of Hinnom below the Jebusite city, and back to the Salt Sea (vv. 12–20). Then the towns are listed, twelve and then fourteen, ending with Jebus, that is, Jerusalem, Gibeah and Kiriath-jearim (vv. 21–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Benjamin is the smallest tribe and gets the most consequential few square miles in the country. Jericho is in it. Bethel, where Jacob saw the ladder, is on its border. Gibeon is in it. And Jerusalem is in the list.
verseByVerse.examples: Two men named Saul came out of this tribe. The first was Israel's first king, the people's choice, who ended on Gilboa. The second was a Pharisee from Tarsus who described himself as of the tribe of Benjamin twice in his letters (Rom. 11:1; Phil. 3:5), and who took the gospel to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: The lot of the tribe of the people of Benjamin according to its clans came up, and the territory allotted to it fell between the people of Judah and the people of Joseph. On the north side their boundary began at the Jordan. Then the boundary goes up to the shoulder north of Jericho, then up through the hill country westward, and it ends at the wilderness of Beth-aven. From there the boundary passes along southward in the direction of Luz, to the shoulder of Luz (that is, Bethel), then the boundary goes down to Ataroth-addar, on the mountain that lies south of Lower Beth-horon. Then the boundary goes in another direction, turning on the western side southward from the mountain that lies to the south, opposite Beth-horon, and it ends at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), a city belonging to the people of Judah. This forms the western side. And the southern side begins at the outskirts of Kiriath-jearim. And the boundary goes from there to Ephron, to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah. Then the boundary goes down to the border of the mountain that overlooks the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, which is at the north end of the Valley of Rephaim. And it then goes down the Valley of Hinnom, south of the shoulder of the Jebusites, and downward to En-rogel. Then it bends in a northerly direction going on to En-shemesh, and from there goes to Geliloth, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim. Then it goes down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben, and passing on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-arabah it goes down to the Arabah. Then the boundary passes on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-hoglah. And the boundary ends at the northern bay of the Salt Sea, at the south end of the Jordan: this is the southern border. The Jordan forms its boundary on the eastern side. This is the inheritance of the people of Benjamin, according to their clans, boundary by boundary all around. Now the cities of the tribe of the people of Benjamin according to their clans were Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz, Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel, Avvim, Parah, Ophrah, Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, Geba—twelve cities with their villages: Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth, Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah, Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah, Zela, Haeleph, Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeah and Kiriath-jearim —fourteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the people of Benjamin according to its clans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin, the smallest tribe, draws the narrow strip between Judah and Joseph, and it holds some of the most important places in Israel’s future, Jerusalem among them.

Between the people of Judah and the people of Joseph. The small tribe drawn first lands in the narrowest strip on the map, wedged between Judah and the house of Joseph.

The youngest son. Benjamin was the youngest son, born on the road to Bethlehem as his mother Rachel died naming him (Genesis 35:16–19). His tribe was nearly wiped out in the civil war at the end of Judges, down to six hundred men (Judges 20:47). What it has is position: Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, Ramah and Mizpeh are all in this list.

Jebus (that is, Jerusalem). Jerusalem is on Benjamin’s list and on Judah’s, and neither tribe took it. Judah could not (15:63); Benjamin did not (Judges 1:21). The city that will hold the temple sits on the boundary between two tribes, and both file it under unfinished business until David takes it (2 Samuel 5:6–9). There, centuries later, the Son of David would be crucified outside the walls and rise again.

Gibeah. The very next name is Gibeah, which will be the most shameful town in Israel: its crime starts the civil war that almost ends this tribe (Judges 19–20).

Two men named Saul. Two men named Saul came from Benjamin. The first, Israel’s first king, began by hiding among the baggage and ended by falling on his sword on Gilboa (1 Samuel 10:22; 31:4). The second, the apostle Paul, named his tribe once to show that God had not rejected Israel (Romans 11:1), and once in the list of what he counted as loss for the sake of Christ (Philippians 3:5).

The smallest tribe. The smallest tribe, in the narrowest strip of land, produced the king who lost the kingdom and the apostle who carried the gospel from Israel to the ends of the earth. God’s portions are not measured by size.

keyVerse.quote: How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?
keyVerse.note: The land is already given; what is missing is the will to go in. Joshua’s question exposes the quiet sin of a settled people, and it still searches Christians who have every spiritual blessing in Christ and have taken up little of it.

18.reflection:
The first thing Israel builds in the subdued land is the tent of meeting (v. 1). What does it look like for God’s presence to be at the centre of a church or a home, and how could it become merely a heritage, as Shiloh did?

Joshua asks, “How long will you put off going in?” (v. 3). What has God given you in Christ that you have not yet taken up? What would be one concrete first step?

The survey team broke the deadlock with a plain, practical task (vv. 8–9). Why do we often wait for a change of feeling before we obey, and what does this passage suggest instead?

Benjamin, the smallest tribe, received a narrow strip that held Jerusalem (v. 28). How does God’s choice of small things and small people encourage you?

19.title: The Remaining Tribes and Joshua's Own Inheritance
19.text: <sup>1</sup>The second lot came out for Simeon, for the tribe of the people of Simeon, according to their clans, and their inheritance was in the midst of the inheritance of the people of Judah.<sup>2</sup>And they had for their inheritance Beersheba, Sheba, Moladah,<sup>3</sup>Hazar-shual, Balah, Ezem,<sup>4</sup>Eltolad, Bethul, Hormah,<sup>5</sup>Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susah,<sup>6</sup>Beth-lebaoth, and Sharuhen—thirteen cities with their villages;<sup>7</sup>Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan—four cities with their villages,<sup>8</sup>together with all the villages around these cities as far as Baalath-beer, Ramah of the Negeb. This was the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Simeon according to their clans.<sup>9</sup>The inheritance of the people of Simeon formed part of the territory of the people of Judah. Because the portion of the people of Judah was too large for them, the people of Simeon obtained an inheritance in the midst of their inheritance.<sup>10</sup>The third lot came up for the people of Zebulun, according to their clans. And the territory of their inheritance reached as far as Sarid.<sup>11</sup>Then their boundary goes up westward and on to Mareal and touches Dabbesheth, then the brook that is east of Jokneam.<sup>12</sup>From Sarid it goes in the other direction eastward toward the sunrise to the boundary of Chisloth-tabor. From there it goes to Daberath, then up to Japhia.<sup>13</sup>From there it passes along on the east toward the sunrise to Gath-hepher, to Eth-kazin, and going on to Rimmon it bends toward Neah,<sup>14</sup>then on the north the boundary turns about to Hannathon, and it ends at the Valley of Iphtahel;<sup>15</sup>and Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem—twelve cities with their villages.<sup>16</sup>This is the inheritance of the people of Zebulun, according to their clans—these cities with their villages.<sup>17</sup>The fourth lot came out for Issachar, for the people of Issachar, according to their clans.<sup>18</sup>Their territory included Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem,<sup>19</sup>Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath,<sup>20</sup>Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez,<sup>21</sup>Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, Beth-pazzez.<sup>22</sup>The boundary also touches Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth-shemesh, and its boundary ends at the Jordan—sixteen cities with their villages.<sup>23</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Issachar, according to their clans—the cities with their villages.<sup>24</sup>The fifth lot came out for the tribe of the people of Asher according to their clans.<sup>25</sup>Their territory included Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph,<sup>26</sup>Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal. On the west it touches Carmel and Shihor-libnath,<sup>27</sup>then it turns eastward, it goes to Beth-dagon, and touches Zebulun and the Valley of Iphtahel northward to Beth-emek and Neiel. Then it continues in the north to Cabul,<sup>28</sup>Ebron, Rehob, Hammon, Kanah, as far as Sidon the Great.<sup>29</sup>Then the boundary turns to Ramah, reaching to the fortified city of Tyre. Then the boundary turns to Hosah, and it ends at the sea; Mahalab, Achzib,<sup>30</sup>Ummah, Aphek and Rehob—twenty-two cities with their villages.<sup>31</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Asher according to their clans—these cities with their villages.<sup>32</sup>The sixth lot came out for the people of Naphtali, for the people of Naphtali, according to their clans.<sup>33</sup>And their boundary ran from Heleph, from the oak in Zaanannim, and Adami-nekeb, and Jabneel, as far as Lakkum, and it ended at the Jordan.<sup>34</sup>Then the boundary turns westward to Aznoth-tabor and goes from there to Hukkok, touching Zebulun at the south and Asher on the west and Judah on the east at the Jordan.<sup>35</sup>The fortified cities are Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth,<sup>36</sup>Adamah, Ramah, Hazor,<sup>37</sup>Kedesh, Edrei, En-hazor,<sup>38</sup>Yiron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh—nineteen cities with their villages.<sup>39</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Naphtali according to their clans—the cities with their villages.<sup>40</sup>The seventh lot came out for the tribe of the people of Dan, according to their clans.<sup>41</sup>And the territory of its inheritance included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh,<sup>42</sup>Shaalabbin, Aijalon, Ithlah,<sup>43</sup>Elon, Timnah, Ekron,<sup>44</sup>Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Baalath,<sup>45</sup>Jehud, Bene-berak, Gath-rimmon,<sup>46</sup>and Me-jarkon and Rakkon with the territory over against Joppa.<sup>47</sup>When the territory of the people of Dan was lost to them, the people of Dan went up and fought against Leshem, and after capturing it and striking it with the sword they took possession of it and settled in it, calling Leshem, Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor.<sup>48</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Dan, according to their clans—these cities with their villages.<sup>49</sup>When they had finished distributing the several territories of the land as inheritances, the people of Israel gave an inheritance among them to Joshua the son of Nun.<sup>50</sup>By command of the LORD they gave him the city that he asked, Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim. And he rebuilt the city and settled in it.<sup>51</sup>These are the inheritances that Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel distributed by lot at Shiloh before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. So they finished dividing the land.
19.overview:
Where we are. At Shiloh the lots are being cast for the seven tribes still without land (18:1–10). Benjamin has received its portion (18:11–28); now the last six lots are drawn, and the whole distribution is completed.

The message. God finishes what he begins: every tribe receives its inheritance, by his lot and in his presence, and then the man who led them is served last. Yet the lists also carry warnings and promises. Old words spoken over a tribe come true, a tribe loses what it was given and settles for an easier prize, and obscure northern ground is quietly handed out where the light of the world will one day shine.

Why it was said. These were title deeds for every clan, and later Israel could read in them both God’s faithfulness and its own failures, such as Simeon’s fading and Dan’s idolatry in the north (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Simeon receives towns inside Judah but no border of its own (vv. 1–9). Four northern tribes follow, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher and Naphtali, each in the same orderly form (vv. 10–39). Dan receives good land on the Philistine border, loses it, and moves north to seize Leshem (vv. 40–48). Last of all, Israel gives Joshua the town he asks for, and the distribution is sealed before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting (vv. 49–51).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise and by pattern. Zebulun and Naphtali are the lands where Isaiah promised a great light, and where Jesus began to preach (Matthew 4:13–16). Simeon’s and Levi’s story shows how a curse can be turned into a calling, which is what Christ does by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). And Joshua, served last after all the people, foreshadows the greater Joshua, who “came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45) and goes to prepare a place for his people (John 14:2).

For us. Our portion comes from God’s hand, and no one is too obscure for his purposes. Do not trade the hard ground he gives for an easier prize, and let the servant-hearted Joshua, and the greater Joshua, shape how you lead.
19.theology:
One curse, two histories. Simeon and Levi received the same sentence from their dying father for the same crime, and both were scattered exactly as he said. Levi ended up teaching in forty-eight towns across every tribe; Simeon ended up largely absorbed. The words spoken over them were identical, and for Levi God turned the scattering into a calling.

The map of the Gospels is drawn here. Zebulun and Naphtali are two entries in a property register here and two names in a prophecy about light in Isaiah 9, the region where Jesus would live and preach. God was preparing the place where his Son would live as a man while a clerk at Shiloh was writing down town names.

Leaving the hard place. Dan is the only tribe recorded as losing its inheritance, and its allotment faced the Philistines. They went north and took an easier town, and did not stop being religious when they moved: they set up a stolen idol with a hired priest (Judg. 18:31). A tribe that leaves the ground God assigned does not become irreligious. It builds a religion of its own.

Served last. Joshua distributes the entire country for seven chapters and receives his own portion only when the register is closed (v. 49). He asks for one town, and has to rebuild it before he can live in it. The man who bore the name Jesus would bear is served last, and the greater Joshua went further: he came not to be served but to serve and to give his life (Mark 10:45), and had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20) while he won an inheritance for others.
19.examples:
Then: One tribe got no border and eventually no identity. One lost its land to the Philistines and went north to easier neighbours, taking a stolen idol with it. And the general who had taken the whole country waited until every family was housed, then asked for a town that needed rebuilding.

Now: Dan is the warning and Joshua the model. Dan left the assigned ground because the opposition on it was relentless; Joshua kept his place and was served last. Ask which describes the way you have handled the hardest thing God has actually given you. The ground was a gift before it was a battlefield, and the God who gave it gives his Spirit to hold it. Where you have walked away, the greater Joshua stayed at his post to the cross for you, and the way back is open.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Simeon’s inheritance shows God’s word coming true: the tribe receives no border of its own, only towns inside Judah. The second lot falls to Simeon, whose inheritance lay in the midst of Judah’s (v. 1): thirteen towns with their villages, Beersheba among them, and four more (vv. 2–8). The writer gives the practical reason: Judah’s portion was too large for them (v. 9). But behind the adjustment lies Jacob’s old word that Simeon would be scattered in Israel (Genesis 49:7).
verseByVerse.theology: Of the twelve tribes, Simeon is the one that stops being a place on the map.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer gives a practical reason in verse 9, Judah's share was too large; a reader of Genesis also remembers Jacob’s words that Simeon would be scattered in Israel (Gen. 49:7).

verseByVerse.quote: The second lot came out for Simeon, for the tribe of the people of Simeon, according to their clans, and their inheritance was in the midst of the inheritance of the people of Judah. And they had for their inheritance Beersheba, Sheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, Balah, Ezem, Eltolad, Bethul, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susah, Beth-lebaoth, and Sharuhen—thirteen cities with their villages; Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan—four cities with their villages, together with all the villages around these cities as far as Baalath-beer, Ramah of the Negeb. This was the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Simeon according to their clans. The inheritance of the people of Simeon formed part of the territory of the people of Judah. Because the portion of the people of Judah was too large for them, the people of Simeon obtained an inheritance in the midst of their inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon receives towns inside Judah but no border of its own, and so Jacob’s dying word that Simeon would be scattered begins to come true.

In the midst of the inheritance of the people of Judah. The writer explains it as a practical adjustment: Judah’s allotment was too big. That is true, and not the whole story. Simeon was already the smallest tribe at the second census (Numbers 26:14), is left out of Moses’ blessing (Deuteronomy 33), and within a few generations had largely merged into Judah.

Jacob’s word over Simeon and Levi. Simeon and Levi had taken swords into Shechem and killed every man in the town (Genesis 34), and their father never forgot it. His dying word was a curse on their anger: “Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel! I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7; see Jacob).

Two kinds of scattering. Both were scattered, exactly as he said, and the outcomes could not be less alike. Levi’s scattering became the priesthood, a tribe with no land, placed throughout Israel to teach the law. Simeon was absorbed into Judah. Scripture shows where Levi’s story turned: at the golden calf, when Moses cried, “Who is on the LORD’s side? Come to me”, the sons of Levi came (Exodus 32:26–29).

A curse turned into a calling. The same sentence fell on both, and God made one of them a blessing. That is the gospel in miniature: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), and in him the sentence that hung over a life can be turned into a calling.
verseByVerse.note: Several of Simeon’s towns, Beersheba among them, appear in Judah’s list as well (15:26-32).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hands out the northern lands in orderly, unremarkable lists, and that ground will matter far beyond them. Four lots follow in the same form: Zebulun in the hills of Lower Galilee with twelve towns (vv. 10–16), Issachar in the Jezreel valley with sixteen (vv. 17–23), Asher along the coast towards Tyre and Sidon with twenty-two (vv. 24–31), and Naphtali in the high country west of the lake with nineteen (vv. 32–39). Each entry repeats the pattern: the lot came out, the boundary ran, the cities with their villages, the inheritance by clans.
verseByVerse.theology: These four tribes get the north, and the north is where the Gospels happen.
verseByVerse.examples: Read quickly, the list is a register of villages. Read with the Gospels open, it is the stage being set: the towns of the ministry of Jesus are entered in this register more than a thousand years early.

verseByVerse.quote: The third lot came up for the people of Zebulun, according to their clans. And the territory of their inheritance reached as far as Sarid. Then their boundary goes up westward and on to Mareal and touches Dabbesheth, then the brook that is east of Jokneam. From Sarid it goes in the other direction eastward toward the sunrise to the boundary of Chisloth-tabor. From there it goes to Daberath, then up to Japhia. From there it passes along on the east toward the sunrise to Gath-hepher, to Eth-kazin, and going on to Rimmon it bends toward Neah, then on the north the boundary turns about to Hannathon, and it ends at the Valley of Iphtahel; and Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem—twelve cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the people of Zebulun, according to their clans—these cities with their villages. The fourth lot came out for Issachar, for the people of Issachar, according to their clans. Their territory included Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem, Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath, Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez, Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, Beth-pazzez. The boundary also touches Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth-shemesh, and its boundary ends at the Jordan—sixteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Issachar, according to their clans—the cities with their villages. The fifth lot came out for the tribe of the people of Asher according to their clans. Their territory included Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph, Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal. On the west it touches Carmel and Shihor-libnath, then it turns eastward, it goes to Beth-dagon, and touches Zebulun and the Valley of Iphtahel northward to Beth-emek and Neiel. Then it continues in the north to Cabul, Ebron, Rehob, Hammon, Kanah, as far as Sidon the Great. Then the boundary turns to Ramah, reaching to the fortified city of Tyre. Then the boundary turns to Hosah, and it ends at the sea; Mahalab, Achzib, Ummah, Aphek and Rehob—twenty-two cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Asher according to their clans—these cities with their villages. The sixth lot came out for the people of Naphtali, for the people of Naphtali, according to their clans. And their boundary ran from Heleph, from the oak in Zaanannim, and Adami-nekeb, and Jabneel, as far as Lakkum, and it ended at the Jordan. Then the boundary turns westward to Aznoth-tabor and goes from there to Hukkok, touching Zebulun at the south and Asher on the west and Judah on the east at the Jordan. The fortified cities are Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth, Adamah, Ramah, Hazor, Kedesh, Edrei, En-hazor, Yiron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh—nineteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Naphtali according to their clans—the cities with their villages.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four northern tribes receive their land in plain, orderly lists, and in the land of two of them, Zebulun and Naphtali, Jesus would one day begin his ministry.

Four tribes. Four tribes in thirty verses, each in the same form. No line is meant to stand out; together they show a country handed over in order to families who will farm it.

Names with a future. Some names matter later. Gath-hepher (v. 13) was the prophet Jonah’s home (2 Kings 14:25). The Bethlehem of verse 15 is in Zebulun, not Judah’s Bethlehem where Jesus was born. Chinnereth (v. 35) gave its name to the lake later called the Sea of Galilee. And the prophetess Anna, who greeted the infant Jesus in the temple, was “of the tribe of Asher” (Luke 2:36).

Zebulun and Naphtali. Keep hold of the first and last names. Centuries later, after Assyria had ravaged the north, Isaiah picked out these two tribes: “In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali… The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone” (Isaiah 9:1–2).

In a list nobody reads. When Jesus left Nazareth for Capernaum to begin preaching, Matthew quoted that promise (Matthew 4:13–16). Nazareth is in the hills of Zebulun’s allotment; Capernaum is on Naphtali’s shore. Neither town is mentioned here, but the ground they would stand on is being handed out, by lot, in a list nobody reads.

Uncertain wording. Verse 34 says Naphtali’s border touched “Judah on the east at the Jordan”, though Judah lay far to the south. No explanation is certain. Some think the text has suffered in copying; others think of a place by the Jordan with a similar name, or of towns east of the river held by Jair, a descendant of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:21–22). The rest of the boundary is clear.
verseByVerse.note: Both tribes lay in the region later called Galilee.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–48 — The Tribe That Lost Its Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dan lost the land God gave it and went after an easier prize. The seventh lot gives Dan fertile lowland west of Benjamin, running down to the coast near Joppa, with Zorah, Eshtaol, Aijalon and Ekron in its list (vv. 40–46). Then a sentence unlike anything else in these chapters: the territory was lost to them, so they went north, captured Leshem and renamed it Dan (v. 47). The summary still calls the first allotment their inheritance (v. 48).
verseByVerse.theology: Dan is the one tribe that could not hold what it was given. The Amorites pressed them back into the hill country (Judg. 1:34), so they left the land God assigned them and took land he had not.
verseByVerse.examples: The book of Judges tells that migration in full (Judg. 18), and it is not a proud story.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventh lot came out for the tribe of the people of Dan, according to their clans. And the territory of its inheritance included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh, Shaalabbin, Aijalon, Ithlah, Elon, Timnah, Ekron, Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Baalath, Jehud, Bene-berak, Gath-rimmon, and Me-jarkon and Rakkon with the territory over against Joppa. When the territory of the people of Dan was lost to them, the people of Dan went up and fought against Leshem, and after capturing it and striking it with the sword they took possession of it and settled in it, calling Leshem, Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Dan, according to their clans—these cities with their villages.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dan could not hold the good land God gave it against the Philistines, and moved north to take an easier target instead.

The seventh lot came out for the tribe of the people of Dan. On paper Dan’s is one of the better allotments: fertile lowland west of Benjamin, running down towards the coast near Joppa. It also sits directly against the Philistines, and that turns out to be the whole story. Zorah and Eshtaol, on Dan’s list, are where Samson will be born and buried: the strong man who fought that border single-handed and never cleared it (Judges 13:2, 25; 16:31).

The territory of the people of Dan was lost to them. Other tribes failed to take part of what they were given. Dan could not hold what it had. Rather than trust God for that ground, the tribe marched about a hundred miles north, attacked a quiet, unsuspecting town at the far frontier, Leshem, also called Laish, and renamed it after themselves (Judges 18:27–29).

What Judges adds. The details in Judges are worse. On the way north the Danites steal a household idol and persuade a hired Levite to become priest to a whole tribe, a better career, they tell him (Judges 18:19); he turns out to be a grandson of Moses (Judges 18:30). They set up the stolen image at Laish, and it stood “as long as the house of God was at Shiloh” (Judges 18:31). Centuries later Jeroboam put one of his golden calves in the same town (1 Kings 12:29).

Set his face. Dan turned from hard ground to an easy prize, and false worship followed. Christ did the opposite: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51). He did not retreat from the hardest ground of all, and his people follow him, not the Danites.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “was lost to them” (v. 47) reads literally “went out from them”. Most take it, as the ESV does, to mean the land slipped out of their control; others read it as “went out beyond them”, that is, their land was too small. Judges 1:34 and chapter 18 support the ESV: the Amorites pressed Dan back into the hills.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–51 — The Man Who Was Served Last
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who led the conquest and the division is served last, and the whole distribution is sealed before the LORD. When every tribe has its land, Israel gives Joshua an inheritance among them (v. 49). By the LORD’s command they give him the town he asked for, Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, and he rebuilds it and lives there (v. 50). Verse 51 closes the distribution: Eleazar, Joshua and the heads of the tribes, by lot at Shiloh, before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. So they finished dividing the land.
verseByVerse.theology: The man who conquered the country is given somewhere to live only after every tribe has its portion. He had the authority to take whatever he wanted at any point in seven chapters, and he waited until the register was closed.
verseByVerse.examples: Caleb asked for a mountain full of giants. Joshua asks for one town, and has to rebuild it. The two old men who alone trusted God at Kadesh each choose a portion that fits the man.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had finished distributing the several territories of the land as inheritances, the people of Israel gave an inheritance among them to Joshua the son of Nun. By command of the LORD they gave him the city that he asked, Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim. And he rebuilt the city and settled in it. These are the inheritances that Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel distributed by lot at Shiloh before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. So they finished dividing the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua, who led the conquest and the division, takes his own inheritance last, asks for a modest town, and has to rebuild it before he can live there.

When they had finished distributing. Every tribe has been provided for, and Levi is about to receive its forty-eight towns. Only then does anyone give the commander-in-chief anywhere to live.

The city that he asked. Joshua has run this distribution for seven chapters. He casts the lots, he has the ear of the priest and the confidence of the nation, and he could have taken a valley without anyone objecting. He asks for one town in his own tribal hills, and apparently not a good one, because he had to rebuild it. Like Caleb, the other faithful spy (Numbers 14:30), he receives his portion by asking, and he asks modestly.

Before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. The whole distribution is signed off in one verse: by lot, at Shiloh, before the LORD, at the door of the tent. Not by negotiation or by the size of anyone’s army. A nation of former slaves now holds a country town by town, and the man who led them lives in a rebuilt house in the hills, served last.

The greater Joshua. Jesus bears the same name, and the pattern is his: “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Joshua gave others their land before he took his own; Christ goes ahead to prepare a place for his people: “In my Father’s house are many rooms” (John 14:2). Leaders in his church are to serve the same way.

Uncertain wording. The town is called Timnath-serah here and in 24:30, but Timnath-heres in Judges 2:9. The two names use the same letters in a different order. Heres means “sun”; serah may mean “extra” or “remainder”. Whether one form is a copying slip or a deliberate change is not known; it is plainly the same place.

keyVerse.quote: These are the inheritances that Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers’ houses of the tribes of the people of Israel distributed by lot at Shiloh before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. So they finished dividing the land.
keyVerse.note: The long distribution ends where it belongs: before the LORD, at the door of his tent. Every inheritance came from his hand, by his lot, and the closing words record a finished work, a promise to Abraham kept to the last family.

19.reflection:
Simeon and Levi were both scattered as Jacob said, but Levi’s scattering became a calling (vv. 1–9; Exodus 32:26–29). How does Christ’s becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13) give hope to someone who feels their past has defined them?

The lists of the northern tribes seem dull, yet God was preparing the ground where Jesus would preach (vv. 10–39; Matthew 4:13–16). What ordinary, unnoticed parts of your life might God be using for purposes you cannot yet see?

Dan lost its land and went after an easier target, and idolatry followed (v. 47; Judges 18). Where are you tempted to swap the hard place God has given you for an easier one?

Joshua took his own inheritance last and asked modestly (vv. 49–50). How does his example, and Christ’s (Mark 10:45), challenge the way we lead and serve?

20.title: The Cities of Refuge
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>2</sup>"Say to the people of Israel, 'Appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses,<sup>3</sup>that the manslayer who strikes any person without intent or unknowingly may flee there. They shall be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood.<sup>4</sup>He shall flee to one of these cities and shall stand at the entrance of the gate of the city and explain his case to the elders of that city. Then they shall take him into the city and give him a place, and he shall remain with them.<sup>5</sup>And if the avenger of blood pursues him, they shall not give up the manslayer into his hand, because he struck his neighbor unknowingly, and did not hate him in the past.<sup>6</sup>And he shall remain in that city until he has stood before the congregation for judgment, until the death of him who is high priest at the time. Then the manslayer may return to his own town and his own home, to the town from which he fled.'"<sup>7</sup>So they set apart Kedesh in Galilee in the hill country of Naphtali, and Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah.<sup>8</sup>And beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, they appointed Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland, from the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead, from the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan, from the tribe of Manasseh.<sup>9</sup>These were the cities designated for all the people of Israel and for the stranger sojourning among them, that anyone who killed a person without intent could flee there, so that he might not die by the hand of the avenger of blood, till he stood before the congregation.
20.overview:
Where we are. The land has been divided (19:51). Before the Levites receive their towns (chapter 21), God speaks to Joshua again, and what he asks for is not a fort or a shrine but six towns of refuge, as he had commanded through Moses (Numbers 35; Deuteronomy 19).

The message. God takes both justice and mercy seriously. A death must be answered, and a man who killed by accident must not be killed in hot blood. So God provides public places of refuge, a fair hearing, and a release that comes only with the death of the high priest. The law protects the innocent, restrains vengeance, and opens its gates even to the foreigner.

Why it was said. In a world with no police, the dead man’s nearest relative, the avenger of blood, was expected to pursue the killer. Israel, now settled, needed a way to tell murder from accident before grief took a life that was not owed.

How the chapter makes its case. God commands the cities and states their purpose: refuge for the one who kills without intent (vv. 1–3). The procedure follows: the manslayer states his case at the gate, the elders take him in and refuse to hand him over, and he stays until he has stood trial and until the death of the high priest (vv. 4–6). Six towns are named, three west and three east of the Jordan, open to Israelite and stranger alike (vv. 7–9).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern, and the letter to the Hebrews draws the line itself, describing believers as those “who have fled for refuge” (Hebrews 6:18). The manslayer’s exile ended only with the death of the high priest; Christ is the High Priest whose death sets his people free. Yet the picture also falls short: Christ shelters not only the unlucky but the guilty, and his death does not merely end an exile but puts away sin.

For us. Run to Christ, the refuge open to all who come. Then, having been sheltered, be people who slow the pursuit of others, weigh what was meant, and keep the gate open.
20.theology:
Justice and mercy in the same statute. The law does not pretend the killing did not happen and does not treat the avenger as a criminal. It builds a distinction into the legal system, between a murderer and a man who has killed someone, and then builds six towns so that the man can stay alive while a court decides which he is. Israel is given a trial and a place to wait for it.

Freedom by the death of the high priest. Verse 6 is where Christian preachers have long seen Christ. The refugee's exile ends at one moment only: when the high priest dies. A death he had nothing to do with opens the gate and gives him his home back. Hebrews describes Christians in this language, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us (Heb. 6:18), in the letter that spends four chapters on a high priest who died. Hebrews does not cite this law by name, so Scripture does not itself call this law a picture of Christ, but the pattern fits the gospel closely.

Refuge that a frightened man can reach. Three cities west and three east, spaced north, middle and south. Mercy in Scripture is characteristically practical: not a principle announced but a road built, near enough to be reached by somebody running.

The stranger, again. A foreigner with no tribe, no land and no clan to protect him gets the same gate on the same terms (v. 9), one more outsider this book quietly brings inside the covenant.
20.examples:
A man whose axe-head killed his neighbour ran for a town he had probably never visited, stood at the gate in front of strangers and told them what he had done, and lived there among people who all knew, waiting, for years perhaps, on the health of an old man in Shiloh he had never met.

For a Christian the picture is close to exact. Everything that decided that man’s position lay outside himself. He could not buy his way home, earn it or appeal. He was safe and not yet free, and his freedom came through a death that was nothing to do with him. For those who have fled to Christ, that death has already happened.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — A City to Run To
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God provides a place of safety where justice can be done without vengeance. The LORD tells Joshua to have Israel appoint the cities of refuge he had commanded through Moses (vv. 1–2). Their purpose is stated exactly: a manslayer who kills without intent or unknowingly may flee there, and be safe from the avenger of blood (v. 3). The law neither ignores the death nor lets grief decide the verdict.
verseByVerse.theology: The law is drawing a line that every legal system since has had to draw, and drawing it carefully. There is a difference between a murderer and a man who has killed somebody, and a society without that distinction will either execute the innocent or let the guilty walk.
verseByVerse.examples: The avenger was family, not a vigilante, and these cities exist to keep a grieving man from killing a man who did not deserve death.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Say to the people of Israel, 'Appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses, that the manslayer who strikes any person without intent or unknowingly may flee there. They shall be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands places of refuge so that a man who has killed by accident is not killed in turn before justice can be done.

Without intent or unknowingly. Deuteronomy gives the example this law exists for: a man is chopping wood, the axe-head slips from the handle, and his neighbour is dead (Deuteronomy 19:5). Nobody meant anything, and somebody is dead. Deliberate murder is not covered; Numbers makes clear that a murderer was to be handed over (Numbers 35:16–21).

The avenger of blood. In a world with no police force and no public prosecutor, the dead man’s nearest relative came for the killer. The avenger was not a vigilante; he was family, doing a duty society expected. The word is go’el, used in Leviticus and Ruth of the kinsman who buys back a relative’s land, and by Isaiah of God himself as Israel’s Redeemer. The nearest relative did for a helpless family member what he could not do for himself, and when a relative was killed, that included answering for his blood.

Justice and refuge. So God does two things at once. He does not abolish the avenger, because the loss is real and the demand for justice is not wicked. And he provides a place to run, because grief is in no condition to judge whether a death was meant. A society that will not distinguish murder from accident ends by executing the innocent; one that makes the distinction too easily ends by releasing the guilty. Israel is given six towns and a trial.

A refuge for the guilty. The gospel goes further than this law, because it offers refuge to the guilty as well as the unlucky: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

A culture with no cities of refuge. Ours is a society that has rediscovered the avenger of blood. A careless remark, an old post, one bad evening caught on a phone, and the pursuit begins, carried on by people who never met the accused and do not ask whether he meant it. There is no gate to run to, because the record never forgets, and many live with a keen sense of guilt and no idea how anyone is ever released from it. Israel’s law took the demand for justice seriously and still gave the hunted man a road, a gate, a hearing and a date on which his exile would end. People who have fled to Christ themselves should be the first to slow a pursuit down, to ask what someone meant, and to keep the gate open.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Until the Death of the High Priest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The refuge is public, protective and fair, and its release waits on the death of the high priest. The manslayer runs to one of the cities, stands at the entrance of the gate, and explains his case to the elders, who take him in and give him a place (v. 4). If the avenger pursues him, they must not hand him over, because he did not hate his neighbour beforehand (v. 5). He stays until he has stood before the congregation for judgment, and until the death of the high priest then in office; then he may go home (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: He does not sneak in; he explains himself in the open, and the elders have to keep him against an angry family. Refuge in Israel was a decision made by a whole town.
verseByVerse.examples: Two hearings are in view: the elders at the gate decide whether to take him in, and the congregation later tries the case. Refuge was shelter until a verdict, not an acquittal in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall flee to one of these cities and shall stand at the entrance of the gate of the city and explain his case to the elders of that city. Then they shall take him into the city and give him a place, and he shall remain with them. And if the avenger of blood pursues him, they shall not give up the manslayer into his hand, because he struck his neighbor unknowingly, and did not hate him in the past. And he shall remain in that city until he has stood before the congregation for judgment, until the death of him who is high priest at the time. Then the manslayer may return to his own town and his own home, to the town from which he fled.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The manslayer is received publicly, protected from the avenger, given a fair trial, and set free only when the high priest dies.

At the entrance of the gate of the city. The procedure is public from the first minute. He does not slip in at night and hide. He stands at the gate, where the elders sat and business was done (see the gate of the city), and states his case aloud. They take him in and give him a place: not a cell, but somewhere to live and work in a town that now knows what he has done.

They shall not give up the manslayer. Then the town has to stand between him and the family. A grieving relative arrives with a right everyone recognises, and the elders have to say no and mean it. The reason given is that he did not hate him in the past: motive is weighed by asking what the relationship had been, as a competent court still does.

Until the death of him who is high priest. Then the strangest and best clause in the chapter. Even after the trial clears him, the man does not go home until the death of him who is high priest at the time. His freedom does not depend on compensation, on the family relenting, on a term of years, or on anything he can do. He is safe but not home, and only the death of a man he may never have met will end his exile. When it comes, the gate opens: no payment, no further verdict. He goes back to his own town and his own home.

Why a high priest’s death? The law does not say. Many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, have connected it with Numbers 35:33, where blood that is shed can be atoned for only “by the blood of the one who shed it”: the death of the high priest, “anointed with the holy oil” (Numbers 35:25), stood in its place and closed the case. Others see it more simply as the end of an era, like an amnesty at a change of reign. Either way, nobody who ran to one of those six gates could have explained why somebody else’s funeral should set him free.

We who have fled for refuge. The letter to the Hebrews reaches for this picture when it describes Christians as those “who have fled for refuge” to “hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18), and it is the same letter that spends four chapters on a High Priest who dies.

Where the picture fails. The picture does not fit at one point, and the misfit is good news. The manslayer was innocent of murder, and the high priest’s death only ended his exile. Those who flee to Christ are not innocent, and their High Priest’s death does more: he came “to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26), and “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Their refuge is not a town they wait in but the Priest himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God places refuge within reach of everyone, Israelite and foreigner alike. On the west of the Jordan Israel sets apart Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Hebron in Judah (v. 7). On the east it appoints Bezer on the tableland, Ramoth in Gilead and Golan in Bashan (v. 8). Verse 9 states who they are for: all the people of Israel and the stranger sojourning among them, so that anyone who killed without intent need not die before he stood trial.
verseByVerse.theology: North, middle and south on each side, so that no one was much more than a day's run from a gate. The mercy is within reach of a frightened man on foot.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 9 names the foreigner alongside the Israelite, on exactly the same terms.

verseByVerse.quote: So they set apart Kedesh in Galilee in the hill country of Naphtali, and Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah. And beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, they appointed Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland, from the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead, from the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan, from the tribe of Manasseh. These were the cities designated for all the people of Israel and for the stranger sojourning among them, that anyone who killed a person without intent could flee there, so that he might not die by the hand of the avenger of blood, till he stood before the congregation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six cities, spread across the land on both sides of the Jordan, put refuge within reach of everyone, Israelite and foreigner alike.

Six cities. Three towns west of the Jordan, north, middle and south, and three on the east matching them. That spacing turns a merciful principle into a merciful provision. A frightened man on foot, with a relative behind him, does not need a doctrine of asylum. He needs to know which way to run and that he can get there before dark. Moses had already named the three eastern towns (Deuteronomy 4:41–43).

Hebron and Shechem. Two of the names are old friends. Hebron is Caleb’s town and holds Abraham’s grave. Shechem is where Joseph’s bones will be buried (24:32) and near where the nation heard the law read between two mountains (8:30–35). The places thickest with Israel’s history are set aside for people running for their lives. All six were also Levite towns (chapter 21), so the refugee lived among those who taught God’s law.

For the stranger sojourning among them. The last clause does what this book keeps doing. The foreigner, with no clan to protect him, is named in the statute alongside everybody else. Rahab walked out of Jericho, the Gibeonites carried water for the altar, Caleb the Kenizzite received Hebron, and now the law of refuge is written with the outsider inside it. So is the gospel: Christ’s refuge is open to anyone who runs to him (John 6:37).

keyVerse.quote: And he shall remain in that city until he has stood before the congregation for judgment, until the death of him who is high priest at the time. Then the manslayer may return to his own town and his own home, to the town from which he fled.
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the law of refuge: safety now, a fair hearing, and freedom that comes only through the death of the high priest. It prepares for the High Priest whose death sets his people free and who becomes their refuge for ever.

20.reflection:
God did not abolish the avenger of blood, but he did provide a place to run (vv. 1–3). How does this law hold justice and mercy together, and how does the cross do the same?

The manslayer’s release came only with the death of the high priest (v. 6). Read Hebrews 6:18–20 and 9:24–26. What does it mean for you that Christ is both your refuge and your High Priest?

Our culture often pursues people without asking what they meant, and never lets them go. How can Christians, who have been sheltered themselves, be people who slow the pursuit and keep the gate open?

The cities were open to the stranger as well as the Israelite (v. 9). Who are the outsiders near you, and how could your church make the refuge of the gospel easy for them to reach?

21.overview:
Where we are. Every tribe has received its land (chapters 13–19), the cities of refuge have been set apart (chapter 20), and one tribe is still without a home. Levi, which was to have no territory of its own, comes last to ask for the towns Moses had promised it. Then the narrator steps back and sums up the whole division of the land in three verses.

The message. God keeps every word he speaks. He houses the tribe that had nothing, he plants teachers of his law in every corner of the country, and he gives Israel the land, the possession and the rest he had sworn to their fathers. Whatever is still unfinished in Israel’s story, it is not God’s side: “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass” (v. 45).

Why it was said. Israel would live for centuries with Canaanite towns still in its land and with hard questions about whether God had really done what he said (see the introduction). This chapter answers that God had kept faith completely, and that the gaps lay in Israel’s possessing, not in his giving.

How the chapter makes its case. The Levites ask, citing only what the LORD commanded through Moses, and are given towns out of the other tribes’ inheritance (vv. 1–3). The towns are then shared out by lot among the priests and the three Levite clans, forty-eight in all, spread through every tribe and including all six cities of refuge (vv. 4–42). Finally the whole story since chapter 1 is gathered into one confession: the land given, the rest granted, not one promise fallen (vv. 43–45).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise. The land and the rest were real gifts and true fulfilments, yet Hebrews notes that if Joshua had given Israel final rest, God would not have spoken later of another day (Hebrews 4:8). The God who kept every word to Israel has made his greatest promises in his Son, and “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

For us. Do not blame God for the ground you have not yet taken; he has not failed in a single word. Plead his promises as the Levites did, treasure those he has given to teach his word, and rest your whole hope on the one in whom every promise has already been kept.
21.theology:
Citing the promise. Three times in these chapters somebody comes to the leadership appealing to something God had said rather than to a grievance: Caleb with an oath from Kadesh-barnea, the daughters of Zelophehad with a ruling from Moses, and now the Levites. Every time the answer is immediate. Prayer in Scripture often works this way: it does not so much inform God of a need as plead what he has promised.

A curse turned into a calling. Levi and Simeon received the same sentence for the same crime. Simeon largely disappeared into Judah; Levi became the teaching order of Israel. Nothing in Jacob’s words explains the difference; God made it.

Mercy administered by the landless. The elders who had to stand at the gate and refuse to hand a man over to a grieving family were from the tribe that owned nothing and belonged to no faction. God put the cities of refuge in the hands of the only people in Israel with nothing to gain by an unjust verdict.

Not one word failed, and Gezer was not taken. Both are true and neither may be softened: God gave everything he promised, and Israel did not take everything he gave (13:6). And the faithfulness in verse 45 cuts another way too, as Joshua says two chapters later: the God who kept every good word will keep his warnings just as surely (23:15).
21.examples:
The tribe that had carried the ark across the Jordan waited until everybody else was housed, then came and quoted a promise, and the other tribes handed back forty-eight of their own towns.

Verse 45 is the verse to carry home, and the honest way to carry it is where the book puts it, immediately after the list of what was never taken. Not one of God’s promises to you has failed. A good deal of ground in your life is still occupied. This chapter refuses to let you use either sentence to excuse the other. The possessing is not done by willpower: the God who gave the land gives his Spirit to those who are his, and where you have left ground untaken, the record that stands for you is Christ's, not yours, and the way back is to come to him and take the next town.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last tribe asks for its home and pleads God’s word, not its need. The heads of the Levites come to Eleazar, Joshua and the tribal leaders at Shiloh (v. 1), and their whole case is one sentence: the LORD commanded through Moses that they be given towns to live in, with pasturelands for their livestock (v. 2). The answer is immediate. By command of the LORD the people of Israel give them towns, and they give them out of their own inheritance (v. 3), so that the teachers of the law are housed at the cost of the people they serve.
verseByVerse.theology: Levi comes last, after every other tribe is housed, and asks with a promise rather than a need.
verseByVerse.examples: Every Levite house stood on ground some other tribe gave up: Israel paid for its own teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites came to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel. And they said to them at Shiloh in the land of Canaan, "The LORD commanded through Moses that we be given cities to dwell in, along with their pasturelands for our livestock." So by command of the LORD the people of Israel gave to the Levites the following cities and pasturelands out of their inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites, the only tribe still without a home, ask for the towns God had promised them, and Israel gives them out of its own land at once.

The Levites came. Everyone else has been housed, down to Joshua (19:50). Levi has been mentioned four times since the register began, always to say that it receives no territory (13:14, 33; 14:3–4; 18:7), and now the heads of the tribe come and ask (see priests and Levites).

The LORD commanded through Moses. Notice what they ask with. Not “we have nowhere to live”, which was true, and not “we carried the ark across the Jordan”, which was also true, but the word God had already spoken (Numbers 35:1–8). Caleb did the same at eighty-five, citing an oath from Kadesh-barnea (14:6–12), and the daughters of Zelophehad did it, citing a ruling Moses had brought back from God (17:3–4). Each time the answer is immediate. This is prayer at its strongest: pleading what God has promised.

Out of their inheritance. These towns were not spare land. Every one came off some other tribe’s allotment, already surveyed, drawn by lot and handed over. The men who taught Israel the law were housed at Israel’s expense, as God’s people have always been asked to provide for those who teach them (Galatians 6:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God scatters Levi through all Israel, so that no family lives far from those called to teach his law. The lot first assigns towns by groups: thirteen to the priests, the descendants of Aaron, from Judah, Simeon and Benjamin (v. 4); ten to the rest of Kohath (v. 5); thirteen to Gershon (v. 6); twelve to Merari (v. 7), all as the LORD commanded through Moses (v. 8). Then the towns are named one by one, beginning with Hebron for the priests (vv. 9–19) and ending with Merari east of the Jordan (vv. 34–40). The total is forty-eight cities with their pasturelands (vv. 41–42).
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob’s curse becomes a calling: the scattering he foretold now puts a teacher of the law within reach of every family in Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: Six of the forty-eight are the cities of refuge of chapter 20.

verseByVerse.quote: The lot came out for the clans of the Kohathites. So those Levites who were descendants of Aaron the priest received by lot from the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin, thirteen cities. And the rest of the Kohathites received by lot from the clans of the tribe of Ephraim, from the tribe of Dan and the half-tribe of Manasseh, ten cities. The Gershonites received by lot from the clans of the tribe of Issachar, from the tribe of Asher, from the tribe of Naphtali, and from the half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan, thirteen cities. The Merarites according to their clans received from the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the tribe of Zebulun, twelve cities. These cities and their pasturelands the people of Israel gave by lot to the Levites, as the LORD had commanded through Moses. Out of the tribe of the people of Judah and the tribe of the people of Simeon they gave the following cities mentioned by name, which went to the descendants of Aaron, one of the clans of the Kohathites who belonged to the people of Levi; since the lot fell to them first. They gave them Kiriath-arba (Arba being the father of Anak), that is Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, along with the pasturelands around it. But the fields of the city and its villages had been given to Caleb the son of Jephunneh as his possession. And to the descendants of Aaron the priest they gave Hebron, the city of refuge for the manslayer, with its pasturelands, Libnah with its pasturelands, Jattir with its pasturelands, Eshtemoa with its pasturelands, Holon with its pasturelands, Debir with its pasturelands, Ain with its pasturelands, Juttah with its pasturelands, Beth-shemesh with its pasturelands—nine cities out of these two tribes; then out of the tribe of Benjamin, Gibeon with its pasturelands, Geba with its pasturelands, Anathoth with its pasturelands, and Almon with its pasturelands—four cities. The cities of the descendants of Aaron, the priests, were in all thirteen cities with their pasturelands. As to the rest of the Kohathites belonging to the Kohathite clans of the Levites, the cities allotted to them were out of the tribe of Ephraim. To them were given Shechem, the city of refuge for the manslayer, with its pasturelands in the hill country of Ephraim, Gezer with its pasturelands, Kibzaim with its pasturelands, Beth-horon with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the tribe of Dan, Elteke with its pasturelands, Gibbethon with its pasturelands, Aijalon with its pasturelands, Gath-rimmon with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Taanach with its pasturelands, and Gath-rimmon with its pasturelands—two cities. The cities of the clans of the rest of the Kohathites were ten in all with their pasturelands. And to the Gershonites, one of the clans of the Levites, were given out of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Golan in Bashan with its pasturelands, the city of refuge for the manslayer, and Beeshterah with its pasturelands—two cities; and out of the tribe of Issachar, Kishion with its pasturelands, Daberath with its pasturelands, Jarmuth with its pasturelands, En-gannim with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the tribe of Asher, Mishal with its pasturelands, Abdon with its pasturelands, Helkath with its pasturelands, and Rehob with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the tribe of Naphtali, Kedesh in Galilee with its pasturelands, the city of refuge for the manslayer, Hammoth-dor with its pasturelands, and Kartan with its pasturelands—three cities. The cities of the several clans of the Gershonites were in all thirteen cities with their pasturelands. And to the rest of the Levites, the Merarite clans, were given out of the tribe of Zebulun, Jokneam with its pasturelands, Kartah with its pasturelands, Dimnah with its pasturelands, Nahalal with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the tribe of Reuben, Bezer with its pasturelands, Jahaz with its pasturelands, Kedemoth with its pasturelands, and Mephaath with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the tribe of Gad, Ramoth in Gilead with its pasturelands, the city of refuge for the manslayer, Mahanaim with its pasturelands, Heshbon with its pasturelands, Jazer with its pasturelands—four cities in all. As for the cities of the several Merarite clans, that is, the remainder of the clans of the Levites, those allotted to them were in all twelve cities. The cities of the Levites in the midst of the possession of the people of Israel were in all forty-eight cities with their pasturelands. These cities each had its pasturelands around it. So it was with all these cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God spreads the Levites through every tribe in Israel, so that the tribe with no land of its own becomes a teacher within reach of every family.

Thirteen cities. The arithmetic matters. The thirteen priestly towns come from Judah, Simeon and Benjamin, clustered in the south around the place where the temple will one day stand, so the men who will serve the altar are settled within reach of it centuries before it exists. One of them, Anathoth, will be the home town of Jeremiah, a priest’s son (Jeremiah 1:1). The other Levite towns are spread everywhere else, and no tribe is without them.

Hebron and its fields. Hebron, the first town named, goes to the descendants of Aaron, while its fields and villages stay with Caleb (vv. 11–12): nobody is dispossessed.

Scattered in Israel. This fulfils the second half of what Jacob said over Simeon and Levi after their violence at Shechem: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7). Simeon’s scattering was absorption into Judah (19:1, 9). Levi’s is forty-eight towns in every corner of the country, among people whose duty Moses had already described: “They shall teach Jacob your rules and Israel your law” (Deuteronomy 33:10). A judgment has become a calling. The tribe sentenced to have no territory ends up living among every tribe in Israel, and its loss of land is Israel’s gain.

The cities of refuge. Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron, Bezer, Ramoth and Golan are all on this list (chapter 20). The towns that took in a frightened man were held by the tribe with no land, no faction and no stake in anybody’s feud: the people in Israel with nothing to gain by being unfair.

A teacher near every home. God did not gather his teachers into one holy city; he placed them among the people. The risen Christ still gives pastors and teachers to his church (Ephesians 4:11), and Paul had elders appointed “in every town” (Titus 1:5).

Textual note. Verses 36–37, which list Reuben’s four towns, are missing from some Hebrew manuscripts, though they are found in others and in the ancient Greek translation. The same towns appear in 1 Chronicles 6:78–79, and the twelve towns of Merari (v. 7) and the total of forty-eight (v. 41) require them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The division of the land closes with the summit of the book: God has kept every word. The LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to their fathers, and they took possession of it and settled there (v. 43). He gave them rest on every side, and none of their enemies withstood them, because he had given them into Israel’s hands (v. 44). Then comes the sentence the whole book has been building towards: not one word of all the good promises the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass (v. 45).
verseByVerse.theology: Read against nine chapters of unfinished business, this looks impossible. How can the writer say that not one word failed?
verseByVerse.examples: The answer lies in who had undertaken what: God to give, and Israel to possess. It is Israel's part that is incomplete.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the LORD gave to Israel all the land that he swore to give to their fathers. And they took possession of it, and they settled there. And the LORD gave them rest on every side just as he had sworn to their fathers. Not one of all their enemies had withstood them, for the LORD had given all their enemies into their hands. Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Israel the land, the possession and the rest he had sworn to their fathers: on his side not one word failed.

Thus the LORD gave to Israel all the land. Everything since chapter 1 is gathered up here: the land sworn to the fathers, given; the possession, taken; the rest, granted on every side. Then comes the sentence of verse 45, and it must be faced honestly, not merely admired.

The apparent contradiction. The reader has just come through nine chapters that seem to say the opposite. Judah could not take Jerusalem (15:63). Ephraim did not drive out Gezer (16:10). Manasseh left the best towns of the north in Canaanite hands (17:12–13). Dan lost its first allotment (19:47). The phrase to this day has been used again and again about ground never occupied. How can a writer who recorded all of that say that not one word failed?

How both are true. Because God had already said who was doing what: “I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel.
