Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you” (13:6). Every promise on his side was kept, at the Jordan, at Jericho, at Merom, on the day the sun stood still. What was unfinished was not his giving but Israel’s possessing. Read as a statement about God’s record, verse 45 is exact.

All came to pass. A nation of former slaves, who could not have taken a single walled city, now lived in houses it had not built, with the tent of meeting at Shiloh and Levi among the tribes. God had promised it centuries earlier to Abraham, a childless man in a foreign country (Genesis 12:7; 15:18). He did it.

A down payment on a greater one. Every one of those promises was a down payment on a greater one. “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The rest on every side in verse 44 was real, and it was not final: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later of another day (Hebrews 4:8). God kept his word about the land; the greater rest that remains for his people is secured by his Son, whose name, Jesus, is Joshua’s name.

In everyday life. That is the shape of the Christian life too. No promise of God has failed. The blood was shed, the tomb was emptied, the Spirit was given, and the inheritance is ours. What is patchy is our possessing. This book will not let a reader blame God for Gezer, and it will not let him pretend Gezer was taken.

Where Christians differ. The boundaries promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18) were reached, for a time, under Solomon (1 Kings 4:21), and Joshua says God kept every word. Christians differ over whether a land promise to Israel is still to be fulfilled. Dispensational and some other premillennial believers expect one, because the land was sworn to Abraham’s offspring as “an everlasting possession” (Genesis 17:8). Many Reformed Christians think the New Testament widens the promise rather than repeating it: Abraham is “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs desired “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16). Both sides honour the promise and differ over its final shape, and they should differ as brothers.

This commentary’s view. The land promise was truly fulfilled in Joshua’s day, as this verse says, and it points beyond itself to the whole new earth that Christ’s people will inherit (Matthew 5:5).

keyVerse.quote: Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass.
keyVerse.note: This is the summit of the book, written by someone who has just listed nine chapters of unfinished business. It is a statement about God’s record: every word on his side was kept. It invites every reader to trust the God whose promises all find their Yes in Christ.

21.reflection:
The Levites asked for their towns by pointing to what the LORD had commanded (v. 2), as Caleb and Zelophehad’s daughters had done. Which promises of God could you plead in prayer this week, and why is that a stronger way to pray than describing our need?

Jacob’s word of judgment on Levi (Genesis 49:7) became a calling that put teachers of God’s law near every family in Israel. How has God brought good out of loss or failure in your life or your church?

Israel gave the Levites towns out of its own inheritance (v. 3). What does this teach about how a church should value and provide for those who teach it God’s word?

Verse 45 says that not one of God’s promises failed, though much of the land was still not possessed. Where are you tempted to blame God for ground you have not yet taken, and how does 2 Corinthians 1:20 encourage you?

22.title: The Eastern Tribes Return and the Altar of Witness
22.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Joshua summoned the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh,<sup>2</sup>and said to them, "You have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you and have obeyed my voice in all that I have commanded you.<sup>3</sup>You have not forsaken your brothers these many days, down to this day, but have been careful to keep the charge of the LORD your God.<sup>4</sup>And now the LORD your God has given rest to your brothers, as he promised them. Therefore turn and go to your tents in the land where your possession lies, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you on the other side of the Jordan.<sup>5</sup>Only be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, to love the LORD your God, and to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments and to cling to him and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul."<sup>6</sup>So Joshua blessed them and sent them away, and they went to their tents.<sup>7</sup>Now to the one half of the tribe of Manasseh Moses had given a possession in Bashan, but to the other half Joshua had given a possession beside their brothers in the land west of the Jordan. And when Joshua sent them away to their homes and blessed them,<sup>8</sup>he said to them, "Go back to your tents with much wealth and with very much livestock, with silver, gold, bronze, and iron, and with much clothing. Divide the spoil of your enemies with your brothers."<sup>9</sup>So the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh returned home, parting from the people of Israel at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan, to go to the land of Gilead, their own land of which they had possessed themselves by command of the LORD through Moses.<sup>10</sup>And when they came to the region of the Jordan that is in the land of Canaan, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh built there an altar by the Jordan, an altar of imposing size.<sup>11</sup>And the people of Israel heard it said, "Behold, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built the altar at the frontier of the land of Canaan, in the region about the Jordan, on the side that belongs to the people of Israel."<sup>12</sup>And when the people of Israel heard of it, the whole assembly of the people of Israel gathered at Shiloh to make war against them.<sup>13</sup>Then the people of Israel sent to the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest,<sup>14</sup>and with him ten chiefs, one from each of the tribal families of Israel, every one of them the head of a family among the clans of Israel.<sup>15</sup>And they came to the people of Reuben, the people of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, and they said to them,<sup>16</sup>"Thus says the whole congregation of the LORD, 'What is this breach of faith that you have committed against the God of Israel in turning away this day from following the LORD by building yourselves an altar this day in rebellion against the LORD?<sup>17</sup>Have we not had enough of the sin at Peor from which even yet we have not cleansed ourselves, and for which there came a plague upon the congregation of the LORD,<sup>18</sup>that you too must turn away this day from following the LORD? And if you too rebel against the LORD today then tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel.<sup>19</sup>But now, if the land of your possession is unclean, pass over into the LORD's land where the LORD's tabernacle stands, and take for yourselves a possession among us. Only do not rebel against the LORD or make us as rebels by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God.<sup>20</sup>Did not Achan the son of Zerah break faith in the matter of the devoted things, and wrath fell upon all the congregation of Israel? And he did not perish alone for his iniquity.'"<sup>21</sup>Then the people of Reuben, the people of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh said in answer to the heads of the families of Israel,<sup>22</sup>"The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD! He knows; and let Israel itself know! If it was in rebellion or in breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today<sup>23</sup>for building an altar to turn away from following the LORD. Or if we did so to offer burnt offerings or grain offerings or peace offerings on it, may the LORD himself take vengeance.<sup>24</sup>No, but we did it from fear that in time to come your children might say to our children, 'What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?<sup>25</sup>For the LORD has made the Jordan a boundary between us and you, you people of Reuben and people of Gad. You have no portion in the LORD.' So your children might make our children cease to worship the LORD.<sup>26</sup>Therefore we said, 'Let us now build an altar, not for burnt offering, nor for sacrifice,<sup>27</sup>but to be a witness between us and you, and between our generations after us, that we do perform the service of the LORD in his presence with our burnt offerings and sacrifices and peace offerings, so your children will not say to our children in time to come, "You have no portion in the LORD."'<sup>28</sup>And we thought, 'If this should be said to us or to our descendants in time to come, we should say, "Behold, the copy of the altar of the LORD, which our fathers made, not for burnt offerings, nor for sacrifice, but to be a witness between us and you."'<sup>29</sup>Far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD and turn away this day from following the LORD by building an altar for burnt offering, grain offering, or sacrifice, other than the altar of the LORD our God that stands before his tabernacle!"<sup>30</sup>When Phinehas the priest and the chiefs of the congregation, the heads of the families of Israel who were with him, heard the words that the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the people of Manasseh spoke, it was good in their eyes.<sup>31</sup>And Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest said to the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the people of Manasseh, "Today we know that the LORD is in our midst, because you have not committed this breach of faith against the LORD. Now you have delivered the people of Israel from the hand of the LORD."<sup>32</sup>Then Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, and the chiefs, returned from the people of Reuben and the people of Gad in the land of Gilead to the land of Canaan, to the people of Israel, and brought back word to them.<sup>33</sup>And the report was good in the eyes of the people of Israel. And the people of Israel blessed God and spoke no more of making war against them to destroy the land where the people of Reuben and the people of Gad were settled.<sup>34</sup>The people of Reuben and the people of Gad called the altar Witness, "For," they said, "it is a witness between us that the LORD is God."
22.overview:
Where we are. The land has been divided and the Levites housed, and the book has just declared that not one of God’s promises failed (21:45). Now the two and a half tribes whose land lay east of the Jordan, who had crossed the river to fight for their brothers, are sent home.

The message. God’s people belong together around one Lord and one altar, and they must guard that unity both by faithfulness and by fairness. An altar the eastern tribes build nearly starts a civil war, which is avoided because Israel asks before it strikes and listens to the answer. What looked like rebellion turns out to be a fear of being cut off from the LORD, and the altar becomes a witness that both sides of the river belong to him.

Why it was said. The Jordan lay between these tribes and the sanctuary for the rest of Israel’s history, and later generations would ask whether those across the river were truly part of the LORD’s people (see the introduction). Israel also needed to learn to handle suspected unfaithfulness without ignoring it or destroying brothers on a rumour.

How the chapter makes its case. Joshua commends the eastern tribes, releases them with a charge to love, walk, keep, cling and serve, and sends them home to share their spoil (vv. 1–9). They build a great altar by the Jordan; Israel musters for war, then sends Phinehas and ten chiefs, who accuse them of breach of faith and offer them land on the western side (vv. 10–20). The eastern tribes answer under oath that the altar is only a copy, built so that their children would never be told they had no portion in the LORD (vv. 21–29). The delegation accepts it gladly, war is called off, and the altar is named Witness (vv. 30–34).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and the pattern it sets. Israel had one altar, and Christians too have one sacrifice and one way to God, Christ himself (Hebrews 10:12–14; 13:10). And the eastern tribes’ fear, being told “You have no portion in the LORD”, is answered for good in him: those who were far off “have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13), and in him there is no far side of the river.

For us. Love the Lord with your whole heart and cling to him, especially when life is comfortable. Guard the church’s faithfulness, but ask before you accuse and listen before you act. And make the gospel’s welcome visible, so that no child of the church and no believer far off is ever left wondering whether they belong.
22.theology:
Inquire before you accuse. Israel gathered for war on a conclusion drawn about a structure nobody had gone to see. What averted the disaster was a delegation, and its leader was the most zealous man in the nation. Zeal and enquiry are not opposites here. Jesus gives the church the same order: go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone (Matt. 18:15).

The offer inside the accusation. Verse 19 keeps this from being a story about religious hotheads: if your land is unclean, come and take a possession among us. The western tribes offered to give up part of their own allotments rather than lose their brothers. That is what zeal for God looks like when it is not merely zeal for being right.

The fear of being written out. The eastern tribes understood that if their children were to know they belonged to God’s people, there had to be something they could see, and so they built something that could be pointed at.

One altar, and one sacrifice. The western tribes were right that there could be only one altar, and the gospel shows why the oneness mattered so much. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and one offering, made once for all (Hebrews 10:10-14). Every quarrel in this chapter was about how far a family might live from the one place of sacrifice; in Christ that sacrifice has been made, and those once far off are brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13).
22.examples:
A nation that had just finished a war mustered to fight its own brothers over a structure nobody had inspected, and the men on the far bank turned out to be terrified of being told one day that they did not belong.

Two things apply to us directly. The first is the procedure: go and ask before drawing a sword, as the man with the strongest convictions in Israel did. The second is the fear. A great deal of what looks like awkwardness or defensiveness in other Christians is the same quiet dread of being told they have no portion in the LORD. Find that out before you decide what you are looking at. Those who have themselves been welcomed in Christ, and given his Spirit of gentleness, can afford to ask first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Sent Home with a Blessing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The eastern tribes are sent home with praise for their faithfulness and a charge to keep loving the LORD. Joshua commends them without reserve: they have kept Moses’ commands, obeyed Joshua, and not forsaken their brothers for many years (vv. 2–3). Since their brothers now have rest, they may go home (v. 4), but with one charge that packs the law into five verbs: love the LORD, walk in his ways, keep his commandments, cling to him and serve him with all their heart and soul (v. 5). Joshua blesses them (vv. 6–7), tells them to share their great spoil with the brothers who stayed behind (v. 8), and they part from Israel at Shiloh (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: They promised this in chapter 1 and they have just finished paying for it: years of somebody else's war, fought by men who already had their land.
verseByVerse.examples: The fourth verb in verse 5 is cling, the word Genesis uses when a man holds fast to his wife (Gen. 2:24). Joshua's last word to men going home to a comfortable settlement is a word about attachment.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Joshua summoned the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and said to them, "You have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you and have obeyed my voice in all that I have commanded you. You have not forsaken your brothers these many days, down to this day, but have been careful to keep the charge of the LORD your God. And now the LORD your God has given rest to your brothers, as he promised them. Therefore turn and go to your tents in the land where your possession lies, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you on the other side of the Jordan. Only be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, to love the LORD your God, and to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments and to cling to him and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul." So Joshua blessed them and sent them away, and they went to their tents.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua honours the eastern tribes for keeping faith with their brothers, then sends them home with a charge to love and cling to the LORD with all their heart.

You have not forsaken your brothers. It is a commendation with nothing held back, earned over about seven years of war. These men already had their land east of the Jordan, and they left their families and herds on the far side of the river to fight for other people’s inheritance until everybody else was home (Numbers 32:16–32).

Rest to your brothers. The condition of their service had been “until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you” (1:15). Joshua now certifies that it is met. Nobody had to argue about when it was over.

Only be very careful. The charge comes after “the LORD your God has given rest” (v. 4): the land and the kept promise are already theirs, and the five verbs describe life with the God who gave them. One verb stands out. Cling is a word of attachment, not of duty, the word used of a man holding fast to his wife (Genesis 2:24), and Joshua puts it between keeping commandments and wholehearted service, as though the outward things will not survive without it.

Where the danger lies. These are not soldiers facing an enemy but men going home with money in their packs. Joshua knows the danger is not on the road. It is in the third year of prosperity, across the river from Shiloh, when nothing whatever is going wrong.

To love the LORD your God. Centuries later a lawyer asked which commandment was the greatest, and the answer was this verse’s first verb: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37). Nobody has kept it with all the heart but the one who gave that answer, and he kept it for those who have not. The clinging asked of the Christian is the work of his Spirit, who holds us fast to Christ before we learn to hold fast ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to the one half of the tribe of Manasseh Moses had given a possession in Bashan, but to the other half Joshua had given a possession beside their brothers in the land west of the Jordan. And when Joshua sent them away to their homes and blessed them, he said to them, "Go back to your tents with much wealth and with very much livestock, with silver, gold, bronze, and iron, and with much clothing. Divide the spoil of your enemies with your brothers." So the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh returned home, parting from the people of Israel at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan, to go to the land of Gilead, their own land of which they had possessed themselves by command of the LORD through Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes go home rich, under orders to share the spoil with those who stayed behind, and they part from Israel at the place where God dwells.

Divide the spoil of your enemies with your brothers. The wives, the older boys and the men too old to march had run the farms for seven years and never lifted a sword. Joshua rules that the spoil is theirs too. David will later make the same principle a statute: “as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage. They shall share alike” (1 Samuel 30:24).

Parting at Shiloh. The last thing they see of the rest of Israel is the tent of meeting, where God dwells among his people (18:1). Then they walk east towards a river that will lie between them and the sanctuary for the rest of their history.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — An Altar, and an Army
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zeal for God’s honour nearly turns into war against brothers, until Israel decides to ask first. At the Jordan the eastern tribes build an altar of imposing size (v. 10). The news reaches the other tribes, and the whole assembly gathers at Shiloh to make war on them (vv. 11–12). Before marching they send Phinehas the priest with ten chiefs, one from each tribe (vv. 13–14). The charge is blunt: breach of faith and rebellion (v. 16). They recall Peor, whose sin still clings to Israel (vv. 17–18), and Achan, who did not perish alone (v. 20). In the middle comes a generous offer: if your land is unclean, come and share ours (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The alarm is not paranoia. Sacrifice was to be offered at one place only (Deut. 12), and the two examples they cite are both cases where the sin of a few brought wrath on everybody.
verseByVerse.examples: The delegation is ten chiefs, one from each tribe, with a priest at their head: the whole nation comes to ask, not one faction.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the region of the Jordan that is in the land of Canaan, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh built there an altar by the Jordan, an altar of imposing size. And the people of Israel heard it said, "Behold, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built the altar at the frontier of the land of Canaan, in the region about the Jordan, on the side that belongs to the people of Israel." And when the people of Israel heard of it, the whole assembly of the people of Israel gathered at Shiloh to make war against them. Then the people of Israel sent to the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, and with him ten chiefs, one from each of the tribal families of Israel, every one of them the head of a family among the clans of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes build a great altar by the Jordan, and Israel, fearing a rival altar, prepares for war but first sends Phinehas to confront them.

An altar of imposing size. The writer records two facts: it is an altar, and it is big. Both are about to cause a war. Israel had one altar, at the tent of meeting, and Deuteronomy is emphatic that burnt offerings are to be made only “at the place that the LORD will choose” (Deuteronomy 12:13–14). A second altar was not a local convenience. It was a rival.

To make war against them. The response takes one verse, with no debate recorded: the whole assembly gathers to fight. Men who finished a seven-year war together are mustering against the brothers they fought it with, over a structure by a river that nobody has been to look at.

Phinehas the son of Eleazar. Then somebody has a better idea: talk first. The choice of leader is deliberate. At Peor, Phinehas had killed an Israelite and the Midianite woman he brought into the camp during a plague, and the plague stopped (Numbers 25:7–8). He is the most zealous man in Israel, the last person you would send to smooth things over. Israel sends its hardest man, with ten tribal chiefs behind him, and he goes to talk before anyone fights.

Uncertain wording. Where the altar stood is not certain. Verse 10 places it in “the region of the Jordan that is in the land of Canaan”, which suggests the west bank, and verse 11 says it was built “at the frontier of the land of Canaan” and “on the side that belongs to the people of Israel”, but the Hebrew of verse 11 can also mean “opposite” or “facing” the land of Canaan, which would put it on the east bank. The word translated “region” may also be a place name, Geliloth (compare 18:17). Either way, it stood where it could be seen and pointed to.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to the people of Reuben, the people of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, and they said to them, "Thus says the whole congregation of the LORD, 'What is this breach of faith that you have committed against the God of Israel in turning away this day from following the LORD by building yourselves an altar this day in rebellion against the LORD? Have we not had enough of the sin at Peor from which even yet we have not cleansed ourselves, and for which there came a plague upon the congregation of the LORD, that you too must turn away this day from following the LORD? And if you too rebel against the LORD today then tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel. But now, if the land of your possession is unclean, pass over into the LORD's land where the LORD's tabernacle stands, and take for yourselves a possession among us. Only do not rebel against the LORD or make us as rebels by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God. Did not Achan the son of Zerah break faith in the matter of the devoted things, and wrath fell upon all the congregation of Israel? And he did not perish alone for his iniquity.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The delegation charges the eastern tribes with treason against God, recalls past sins that brought judgment on all Israel, and offers to share its own land rather than lose them.

What is this breach of faith? The charge is not softened. It is treason against God, said to the men’s faces.

Peor and Achan. Both examples fit. At Peor, where Israel joined in the worship of Baal, twenty-four thousand died in the plague (Numbers 25:9), and one of the men speaking here had stopped it. At Ai, Achan hid plunder in his tent, thirty-six men fell in battle and his own family died with him (7:5, 24–25). “He did not perish alone for his iniquity” is not superstition; it is the lesson of chapter 7, learned at funerals. One man’s or one tribe’s sin affects the whole people of God. So the alarm is reasonable. The mistake is one of order: they raised an army before they had the facts.

Take for yourselves a possession among us. Then, in the middle of an accusation of treason, the most unexpected sentence in the chapter: if your side of the river feels far from God, come and live on ours. The western tribes, who have just divided the country into carefully surveyed allotments, offer to cut their own portions again rather than lose their brothers.

In everyday life. Zeal for God’s honour is right, and so is being willing to confront. But “If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (Proverbs 18:13). Christians who suspect a brother or a church of unfaithfulness should go and ask, say plainly what they fear, and be ready to be wrong (Matthew 18:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — We Were Afraid of Your Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The eastern tribes answer under oath that the altar was built not in rebellion but out of fear for their children’s faith. They call on God by three names, twice over, and invite judgment if they are lying (vv. 22–23). Their reason is that one day the western tribes’ children might tell theirs that the Jordan is a boundary and they have no portion in the LORD, and so make them stop worshipping him (vv. 24–25). So they built a copy of the LORD’s altar, not for sacrifice but as a witness that they too serve him at his sanctuary (vv. 26–28). They end by confessing the one true altar before the tabernacle (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The answer turns the accusation inside out: the altar at the frontier was built out of loyalty, not rebellion.
verseByVerse.examples: Both sides are frightened of the same thing from opposite ends. The west fears a rival altar splitting the worship of God; the east fears a river splitting the people of God. Nobody in the chapter is indifferent, and that is why it nearly ended in a battle.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Reuben, the people of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh said in answer to the heads of the families of Israel, "The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD! He knows; and let Israel itself know! If it was in rebellion or in breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today for building an altar to turn away from following the LORD. Or if we did so to offer burnt offerings or grain offerings or peace offerings on it, may the LORD himself take vengeance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes answer under the most solemn oath that they have not rebelled, and call on God himself to judge them if they are lying.

The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The answer begins with three names of God said twice over, El, Elohim, YHWH, about as emphatic as Hebrew gets, and then invites death if the charge is true. Nobody takes offence at being asked; they answer under oath.

He knows; and let Israel itself know! They appeal first to God, who sees the heart, and only then to Israel, which can judge only by what it is told. The order is right for anyone falsely accused: the case rests first with the one who cannot be deceived (1 Samuel 16:7).

Burnt offerings or grain offerings or peace offerings. These are the main kinds of offering in the law (Leviticus 1–3), and they disown every one: the altar was not built for sacrifice at all, which was exactly what the delegation feared. “May the LORD himself take vengeance” hands the judgment to God: if they are lying, Israel need not shed their blood.

verseByVerse.quote: No, but we did it from fear that in time to come your children might say to our children, 'What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel? For the LORD has made the Jordan a boundary between us and you, you people of Reuben and people of Gad. You have no portion in the LORD.' So your children might make our children cease to worship the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The altar was built out of fear that the western tribes’ children would one day tell the eastern tribes’ children that they had no part in the LORD, and so turn them from him.

You have no portion in the LORD. They were afraid, not of the Canaanites or of Israel’s army, but of a sentence not yet spoken, to be said by children not yet born, to children not yet born.

The Jordan a boundary. The fear had something to stand on. When Moses drew the borders of Canaan, its eastern edge was the Jordan (Numbers 34:12), and the land beyond it was given to these tribes only because they asked for it (Numbers 32:1–5). A later generation on the west bank could argue from the law itself that Gilead lay outside the promised land, and its people outside the LORD’s inheritance. Add distance from the sanctuary and the ordinary drift of two or three generations, and their grandchildren could become strangers.

Cease to worship the LORD. The Hebrew is literally “cease to fear the LORD”, the reverent worship by which Israel belonged to him. What frightened them was not a quarrel between tribes but a slow loss of faith: children told often enough that they did not belong would stop coming to the LORD’s house, and in the end would stop believing.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we said, 'Let us now build an altar, not for burnt offering, nor for sacrifice, but to be a witness between us and you, and between our generations after us, that we do perform the service of the LORD in his presence with our burnt offerings and sacrifices and peace offerings, so your children will not say to our children in time to come, "You have no portion in the LORD."' And we thought, 'If this should be said to us or to our descendants in time to come, we should say, "Behold, the copy of the altar of the LORD, which our fathers made, not for burnt offerings, nor for sacrifice, but to be a witness between us and you."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The altar was a copy, never to be used, built as a witness that the eastern tribes also worship the LORD at his sanctuary.

The copy of the altar of the LORD. It is a copy, shaped like the real thing and deliberately never lit, standing at the river as an exhibit for a conversation that would happen after everyone present was dead.

That we do perform the service of the LORD in his presence. The altar was never meant to replace the journey to the tent of meeting at Shiloh but to defend their right to make it. “In his presence” means at the sanctuary, where they would go on bringing their offerings like every other tribe. In Israel an object could serve as a witness, as the heap of stones Jacob and Laban set up was “a witness between you and me” (Genesis 31:48).

In everyday life. They understood that belonging has to be visible to survive a generation. Their grandchildren would not share their memories, and children are told who they are by other children. So they put up something that could be pointed at, as Israel set up the twelve stones from the Jordan for the day “when your children ask in time to come” (4:6). Churches and families still need visible signs and spoken reminders, so that the next generation knows it is welcome among the Lord’s people and is called to trust him for itself.

verseByVerse.quote: Far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD and turn away this day from following the LORD by building an altar for burnt offering, grain offering, or sacrifice, other than the altar of the LORD our God that stands before his tabernacle!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes end by confessing that there is only one true altar, the one before the LORD’s tabernacle.

Far be it from us. This is the strongest form of denial in Hebrew, built on a word meaning something profane. They end where they began, under oath: they have no thought of rebelling against the LORD or turning away from following him.

Other than the altar of the LORD our God. They accept the very law the western tribes feared they had broken: one altar, at the place God chooses (see the note on vv. 10–14). Their copy points away from itself to the real altar across the river and has meaning only because that altar exists. Their last word is not a defence of themselves but a confession of where God is to be worshipped.

One altar. Christians too have one place of sacrifice: Christ, who “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:12). Every sign in the church, from the Lord’s Supper to the cross on a wall, is at best a copy that points to him, and has meaning only because his sacrifice is real.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The quarrel ends in gladness, worship and a name that tells the truth. Phinehas and the chiefs are satisfied by the explanation (v. 30), and Phinehas declares that the LORD is in their midst, since the eastern tribes have kept faith and so delivered Israel from judgment (v. 31). The delegation reports back, Israel blesses God, and the talk of war ends (vv. 32–33). The eastern tribes name the altar Witness, because it testifies between them that the LORD is God (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody in this chapter has to be humiliated for it to end well. The west does not have to admit it was hysterical and the east does not have to apologise for building anything. The delegation asked, the answer was true, and both sides went home believing better of each other than they had that morning.

verseByVerse.quote: When Phinehas the priest and the chiefs of the congregation, the heads of the families of Israel who were with him, heard the words that the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the people of Manasseh spoke, it was good in their eyes. And Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest said to the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the people of Manasseh, "Today we know that the LORD is in our midst, because you have not committed this breach of faith against the LORD. Now you have delivered the people of Israel from the hand of the LORD." Then Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, and the chiefs, returned from the people of Reuben and the people of Gad in the land of Gilead to the land of Canaan, to the people of Israel, and brought back word to them. And the report was good in the eyes of the people of Israel. And the people of Israel blessed God and spoke no more of making war against them to destroy the land where the people of Reuben and the people of Gad were settled. The people of Reuben and the people of Gad called the altar Witness, "For," they said, "it is a witness between us that the LORD is God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The delegation gladly accepts the explanation, Israel blesses God instead of going to war, and the altar is named Witness, a testimony that the LORD is God on both sides of the river.

It was good in their eyes. There is no grudging here, and no face-saving. The delegation came convinced of treason, heard the explanation, and accepted it completely.

Today we know that the LORD is in our midst. The verdict from the hardest man in Israel is more generous than it needed to be. His brothers’ faithfulness is taken as evidence that God is present, and “you have delivered the people of Israel from the hand of the LORD”: the accused end the interview as Israel’s deliverers. The army that gathered in one verse disperses in one, and blesses God.

Called the altar Witness. The name is the whole point. Not “Peace”, and not anything about the quarrel: Witness, standing at the river to testify that the men on the far side belong to the LORD. What almost destroyed Israel was not wickedness on either side but two parties both zealous for the honour of the same God.

The frontier is gone. The fear beneath it all has been answered since, in terms the eastern tribes could not have known. There is “one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:4–5), and those once furthest off, with no portion and no claim, “have been brought near by the blood of Christ” and are “no longer strangers and aliens” but “members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:13, 19). Nobody in Christ is on the far side of anything. No copy of an altar is needed at the frontier, because the frontier is gone.

Textual note. The Hebrew text as usually printed does not actually give the altar’s name; it reads literally “called the altar, for it is a witness between us”. Translations supply the name “Witness” (Hebrew Ed) from the rest of the sentence, as a few Hebrew manuscripts and ancient translations do. The meaning is not in doubt.

keyVerse.quote: Only be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, to love the LORD your God, and to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments and to cling to him and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.
keyVerse.note: Joshua’s charge gathers the whole law into love, obedience and clinging to the LORD, and everything that follows in the chapter turns on whether the eastern tribes have kept it. Jesus named this love the greatest commandment, and he alone kept it with all his heart, for those who have not.

22.reflection:
Joshua charged the eastern tribes, as they went home prosperous, to love the LORD and cling to him (v. 5). Why is comfort sometimes more dangerous to faith than hardship, and what helps you cling to Christ when life is going well?

Israel gathered for war before it knew the facts, but then sent a delegation to ask (vv. 12–16). How should Christians respond when they suspect a brother, sister or church of unfaithfulness? Read Proverbs 18:13 and Matthew 18:15.

The eastern tribes feared their children would be told, “You have no portion in the LORD” (v. 25). What makes people today feel they do not belong among God’s people, and what could your church do to make the gospel’s welcome visible?

The altar of Witness was only a copy that pointed to the real altar (vv. 28–29). How does Christ’s one sacrifice, and his bringing near of those far off (Ephesians 2:13–19), answer the fears in this chapter?

23.title: Joshua's Farewell Charge
23.text: <sup>1</sup>A long time afterward, when the LORD had given rest to Israel from all their surrounding enemies, and Joshua was old and well advanced in years,<sup>2</sup>Joshua summoned all Israel, its elders and heads, its judges and officers, and said to them, "I am now old and well advanced in years.<sup>3</sup>And you have seen all that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, for it is the LORD your God who has fought for you.<sup>4</sup>Behold, I have allotted to you as an inheritance for your tribes those nations that remain, along with all the nations that I have already cut off, from the Jordan to the Great Sea in the west.<sup>5</sup>The LORD your God will push them back before you and drive them out of your sight. And you shall possess their land, just as the LORD your God promised you.<sup>6</sup>Therefore, be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, turning aside from it neither to the right hand nor to the left,<sup>7</sup>that you may not mix with these nations remaining among you or make mention of the names of their gods or swear by them or serve them or bow down to them,<sup>8</sup>but you shall cling to the LORD your God just as you have done to this day.<sup>9</sup>For the LORD has driven out before you great and strong nations. And as for you, no man has been able to stand before you to this day.<sup>10</sup>One man of you puts to flight a thousand, since it is the LORD your God who fights for you, just as he promised you.<sup>11</sup>Be very careful, therefore, to love the LORD your God.<sup>12</sup>For if you turn back and cling to the remnant of these nations remaining among you and make marriages with them, so that you associate with them and they with you,<sup>13</sup>know for certain that the LORD your God will no longer drive out these nations before you, but they shall be a snare and a trap for you, a whip on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from off this good ground that the LORD your God has given you.<sup>14</sup>"And now I am about to go the way of all the earth, and you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed.<sup>15</sup>But just as all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you have been fulfilled for you, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things, until he has destroyed you from off this good land that the LORD your God has given you,<sup>16</sup>if you transgress the covenant of the LORD your God, which he commanded you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them. Then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and you shall perish quickly from off the good land that he has given to you."
23.overview:
Where we are. Years have passed since the land was divided and the eastern tribes went home (chapter 22). Israel has rest, and Joshua is old. He calls the leaders of the nation together for the first of two farewells; the second, the covenant renewal at Shechem, follows in chapter 24.

The message. The God who has fought for you will go on keeping his word, so cling to him and love him. His faithfulness cuts both ways: every good word he promised has come true, and every warning will come true just as surely if his people turn to other gods. The safety of Israel’s future does not lie in its leader, who is about to die, but in the LORD, and in whether Israel holds fast to him.

Why it was said. Israel was about to lose the man who had led it since Moses died, while Canaanite peoples and their gods still lived among the tribes (see the introduction). The next generation would face the slow pull of those neighbours without Joshua, and the book of Judges shows how quickly it gave way.

How the chapter makes its case. Joshua points to what they have seen: the LORD has fought for them, and he will drive out the nations that remain (vv. 1–5). He repeats the charge God gave him on his first day, warns them away from even speaking the names of other gods, and calls them to cling to the LORD and love him (vv. 6–11). Then he sets out the other path: cling to the nations instead, and they will become a snare and a trap; and as surely as every good word has come true, so will every warning (vv. 12–16).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by covenant. Israel needed a leader who would not die and a people who would not let go, and it had neither: Joshua went the way of all the earth, and Israel did not cling. Christ “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24), and he took on himself the curse that Joshua warned of, “becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), so that the God who keeps every word can keep only good words towards those who are in him.

For us. Remember what the Lord has done for you, and let that memory keep your love for him warm. Watch the small beginnings of drift, the borrowed words and easy friendships with what he hates. And rest your future not in any human leader but in the Saviour who will never leave you.
23.theology:
Cling, with two possible objects. The Hebrew dabaq is the verb Genesis uses of a man holding fast to his wife, and Joshua uses it twice here: cling to the LORD (v. 8), or cling to the remnant of these nations, the peoples still left in the land (v. 12). The choice is not between devotion and indifference. It is a choice of what to hold on to, because everyone holds on to something.

The guard rail is set a long way back. Verse 7 forbids serving and bowing down, which anybody would call idolatry, and before those it forbids mixing, and even to make mention of the names of their gods. Joshua has watched a nation fall away before, and knows the slide begins with shared talk and easy friendship, years before anybody kneels to an idol.

The same faithfulness, both directions. Not one word has failed of all the good things, and just as those were fulfilled, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things. Both sentences say one thing about God: what he says, happens. His faithfulness is not a kindly mood that can only bless; he keeps his warnings as surely as his promises, and the exile proved it.

Where the two kinds of word met. A believer who trembles at verses 15-16 should follow the story to its end. The evil words did fall, on Israel at the exile, and then once more on the one Israelite who had kept every word: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The God whose warnings are as sure as his promises has made both sure in his Son. For those who are in Christ there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1), and the faithfulness that makes the warning terrible is the same faithfulness that makes the gospel safe.

The last instruction is the first one. What Joshua tells the nation at the end of his life is what God told him at the beginning of his command. And the summary of the whole charge is not vigilance but affection: Be very careful, therefore, to love the LORD your God (v. 11), an odd thing to be careful about, until you notice that love is precisely what people lose without noticing.
23.examples:
An old man who had watched a river open and a wall fall flat gathered the leaders of a settled, comfortable nation and warned them, not about armies, but about marriages, conversation and the names people use for things.

In everyday life. Verse 7 is the practical one. The question is not whether you are about to bow down to anything, because you are not. It is whether the vocabulary, the assumptions and the friendships of a world that does not know God have become so normal to you that you no longer notice them, which is where the descent starts and where it is still easy to stop. And verse 11 is the one to keep: be very careful to love him. Love is not manufactured by trying harder; it is answered love, kindled by the God who fought for you, and kept alive by his Spirit through his word, prayer and his people. Where you find it has cooled, Christ loved the Father perfectly in your place, and the way back is open today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The LORD Has Fought for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD who has fought for Israel will finish what he began, even after Joshua is gone. A long time has passed, Israel has rest, and Joshua is old (v. 1). He summons all Israel’s leaders (v. 2) and sums up the conquest in one clause: the LORD your God has fought for you, and you have seen it (v. 3). He has allotted the land as an inheritance, both the nations already cut off and those that remain (v. 4). The LORD himself will push those remaining nations back and drive them out, and Israel will possess their land as he promised (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: He argues from their own lifetime, and in every sentence God is the one who acts. Every command that follows rests on what he has done.
verseByVerse.examples: Nations still remain, and they have been allotted anyway. The promise of verse 5 is future tense, given to men who are about to bury the only leader they have known.

verseByVerse.quote: A long time afterward, when the LORD had given rest to Israel from all their surrounding enemies, and Joshua was old and well advanced in years, Joshua summoned all Israel, its elders and heads, its judges and officers, and said to them, "I am now old and well advanced in years. And you have seen all that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, for it is the LORD your God who has fought for you. Behold, I have allotted to you as an inheritance for your tribes those nations that remain, along with all the nations that I have already cut off, from the Jordan to the Great Sea in the west. The LORD your God will push them back before you and drive them out of your sight. And you shall possess their land, just as the LORD your God promised you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua, old and near death, reminds Israel’s leaders that the LORD has fought for them and promises that he will go on driving out the nations after Joshua is gone.

I am now old and well advanced in years. The old man calls the leaders together to say goodbye and begins with his own age, without embarrassment. Nothing in this chapter pretends he has long to live.

You have seen. Then the whole conquest in one clause, and the one who does everything in it is God: “it is the LORD your God who has fought for you” (v. 3). Joshua argues from what they saw with their own eyes. They were at the Jordan, at Jericho, on the hillside at Gibeon when the day would not end. They cannot say they have no evidence.

Those nations that remain. He is entirely honest about the state of the country. Nations are still standing, allotted anyway, with deeds written for ground still occupied, exactly as in chapter 13.

The LORD your God will push them back. The promise of verse 5 is in the future tense. He is telling men who are about to bury him that God will go on doing what they watched him do, when the man who led them is not there.

A leader who does not die. The church never has to hear a farewell like this from its leader. Its true Joshua died once and lives, “he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24), and he has promised, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s safety lies in clinging to the LORD and loving him, not in its own strength. Joshua repeats the charge God gave him at the start: be very strong to keep all that is written in the Book of the Law, turning neither right nor left (v. 6). He warns them not to mix with the nations, or even mention their gods’ names, swear by them, serve them or bow to them (v. 7), but to cling to the LORD as they have done (v. 8). The evidence is plain: the LORD drove out great nations, and one Israelite puts a thousand to flight because the LORD fights for them (vv. 9–10). So be very careful to love him (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 lists steps downward, and it begins with the smallest.
verseByVerse.examples: Joshua hands the nation the words once spoken over him (1:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, turning aside from it neither to the right hand nor to the left, that you may not mix with these nations remaining among you or make mention of the names of their gods or swear by them or serve them or bow down to them, but you shall cling to the LORD your God just as you have done to this day. For the LORD has driven out before you great and strong nations. And as for you, no man has been able to stand before you to this day. One man of you puts to flight a thousand, since it is the LORD your God who fights for you, just as he promised you. Be very careful, therefore, to love the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua calls Israel to keep God’s law, to refuse even the first small steps towards other gods, and above all to cling to the LORD and love him, because it is the LORD who fights for them.

Be very strong. These are the words God spoke to Joshua just after Moses died: “Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law” and “do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left” (1:7). Decades later Joshua hands them on without updating them or qualifying them with anything he has learned.

Make mention of the names of their gods. Read verse 7 in order, because it is a descent. The last items are what anybody would call idolatry; the first are conversational. Joshua puts the guard rail a long way back from the cliff. Nobody begins by bowing down. They begin by borrowing the words, then find them convenient, then use them in an oath because everyone else does, and kneeling comes last.

Cling to the LORD your God. The positive command is one verb, cling, the word Joshua used to the eastern tribes as they went home (22:5). Verse 10 says one man puts a thousand to flight and gives the reason in the same breath: not that Israelites are formidable, but that the LORD fights for them, as he promised (compare Leviticus 26:8). The strength they are told to be strong in is his, given before it is asked for.

Be very careful, therefore, to love. The summary is not vigilance about the Canaanites but care about affection, the thing people lose without noticing.

How do I keep my love for him from cooling? Love for God seldom dies in a crisis; it cools in a busy, comfortable stretch when nothing seems wrong. So be careful in the ordinary places. Keep the first thing first. Before the phone and the inbox, give the first minutes of the day to his word and to prayer, even when it feels dry. Notice the rivals. Ask what your mind drifts to when it is free, what you spend on without a second thought, what would most upset you to lose. Those are the loves competing with him, named so that they can be handed back. Rehearse what he has done. Joshua’s whole speech is memory (vv. 3, 9, 14). Keep a list of God’s kindnesses to you and read it when your heart feels cold. Stay with his people. Love grows in company and withers alone, which is why Hebrews warns against “neglecting to meet together” (Hebrews 10:25). But the motive is never to earn his love by keeping ours warm: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Christ loved the Father without a lapse in our place, and when our love has cooled, the cure is to look again at his love for us, which never has.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — The Same Faithfulness, the Other Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s faithfulness cuts both ways: his warnings are as sure as his promises. If Israel turns back and clings to the remaining nations, marrying among them (v. 12), the LORD will stop driving them out, and they will become a snare, a trap, a whip and thorns, until Israel perishes from the good land (v. 13). Joshua, about to die, calls them to witness that not one of God’s good words has failed (v. 14). Just as surely, the LORD will bring every evil thing he has warned of, if they break his covenant and serve other gods (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 12 uses the same verb as verse 8: one word, two possible objects.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 14 and 15 are joined by just as, and must not be read apart.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you turn back and cling to the remnant of these nations remaining among you and make marriages with them, so that you associate with them and they with you, know for certain that the LORD your God will no longer drive out these nations before you, but they shall be a snare and a trap for you, a whip on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from off this good ground that the LORD your God has given you. "And now I am about to go the way of all the earth, and you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed. But just as all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you have been fulfilled for you, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things, until he has destroyed you from off this good land that the LORD your God has given you, if you transgress the covenant of the LORD your God, which he commanded you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them. Then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and you shall perish quickly from off the good land that he has given to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel clings to the nations instead of the LORD, those nations will become its ruin, because the God who has kept every good promise will keep every warning just as surely.

Cling to the remnant of these nations. Nobody wakes up and decides to stop holding on to God. What happens is that something else gets hold of the hands. The chapter names the process exactly: association, then marriage, then the slow merging of two peoples, and the gods come with the families.

A snare and a trap. Four images escalate from inconvenience to blindness. A snare catches a foot. A trap holds. A whip on the sides is constant and painful. Thorns in the eyes is the worst: the thing you failed to remove ends by taking your sight. These are the nations Israel did not drive out, Gezer, the towns of Manasseh, the Philistine coast: the people already living down the road. Judges repeats the warning almost word for word when Israel has ignored it (Judges 2:3).

Not one word has failed. He is dying, and he calls them as witnesses to God’s record. Not one word has failed, the writer’s verdict two chapters ago (21:45), now from the man who was there for every one of them. Then the sentence most readers would rather he had not said: God’s faithfulness means that his warnings come true as well as his promises.

Every syllable came true. Centuries later Jerusalem burned and the survivors walked to Babylon, and the prophets who watched it said what Joshua said here: God had kept his word. Yet the same prophets promised a new covenant, written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), so that judgment was never God’s last word to his people.

The curse carried. The faithfulness that brings the evil words is the same faithfulness that brought them down on Christ. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). For those who are in him, God’s consistency is no longer a threat but a guarantee: he will not punish twice what his Son has already borne.

Why this matters. The old man’s final argument is not that God is dangerous but that he is consistent: the God who gave them the fields, the towns and the rest is the God they must now trust without Joshua.

Was the ban racial? No. Rahab and Ruth joined Israel by faith and became ancestors of David and of Christ (Matthew 1:5). The danger was idolatry: “they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:4). The principle carries over: a Christian should marry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39).

What it does not mean. It does not tell a believer who is already married to an unbeliever to leave. Paul says the opposite: if the unbelieving spouse is willing to stay, the believer should not divorce (1 Corinthians 7:12–14).

keyVerse.quote: And now I am about to go the way of all the earth, and you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed.
keyVerse.note: The dying Joshua calls the whole nation to witness God’s perfect record. It is the ground of his appeal to cling to the LORD, and of his warning that God’s threats are as sure as his promises. For those in Christ, the same faithfulness guarantees every good word.

23.reflection:
Joshua grounds everything in what Israel had seen: “it is the LORD your God who has fought for you” (v. 3). What has God done in your life that you need to remember when your faith feels weak?

Verse 7 describes a descent from speaking the names of other gods to bowing down to them. What are the small, ‘conversational’ first steps by which Christians today drift towards the idols of their culture?

Joshua’s summary is “Be very careful, therefore, to love the LORD your God” (v. 11). Which of the suggestions for keeping love from cooling do you most need, and how could others in your group help?

God’s warnings are as sure as his promises (vv. 14–15). How does Galatians 3:13 change the way a Christian hears these warnings, without making them less serious?

24.title: The Covenant at Shechem
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem and summoned the elders, the heads, the judges, and the officers of Israel. And they presented themselves before God.<sup>2</sup>And Joshua said to all the people, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Long ago, your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates, Terah, the father of Abraham and of Nahor; and they served other gods.<sup>3</sup>Then I took your father Abraham from beyond the River and led him through all the land of Canaan, and made his offspring many. I gave him Isaac.<sup>4</sup>And to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. And I gave Esau the hill country of Seir to possess, but Jacob and his children went down to Egypt.<sup>5</sup>And I sent Moses and Aaron, and I plagued Egypt with what I did in the midst of it, and afterward I brought you out.<sup>6</sup>"'Then I brought your fathers out of Egypt, and you came to the sea. And the Egyptians pursued your fathers with chariots and horsemen to the Red Sea.<sup>7</sup>And when they cried to the LORD, he put darkness between you and the Egyptians and made the sea come upon them and cover them; and your eyes saw what I did in Egypt. And you lived in the wilderness a long time.<sup>8</sup>Then I brought you to the land of the Amorites, who lived on the other side of the Jordan. They fought with you, and I gave them into your hand, and you took possession of their land, and I destroyed them before you.<sup>9</sup>Then Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and fought against Israel. And he sent and invited Balaam the son of Beor to curse you,<sup>10</sup>but I would not listen to Balaam. Indeed, he blessed you. So I delivered you out of his hand.<sup>11</sup>And you went over the Jordan and came to Jericho, and the leaders of Jericho fought against you, and also the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. And I gave them into your hand.<sup>12</sup>And I sent the hornet before you, which drove them out before you, the two kings of the Amorites; it was not by your sword or by your bow.<sup>13</sup>I gave you a land on which you had not labored and cities that you had not built, and you dwell in them. You eat the fruit of vineyards and olive orchards that you did not plant.'<sup>14</sup>"Now therefore fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And if it is evil in your eyes to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."<sup>16</sup>Then the people answered, "Far be it from us that we should forsake the LORD to serve other gods,<sup>17</sup>for it is the LORD our God who brought us and our fathers up from the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and who did those great signs in our sight and preserved us in all the way that we went, and among all the peoples through whom we passed.<sup>18</sup>And the LORD drove out before us all the peoples, the Amorites who lived in the land. Therefore we also will serve the LORD, for he is our God."<sup>19</sup>But Joshua said to the people, "You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins.<sup>20</sup>If you forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, then he will turn and do you harm and consume you, after having done you good."<sup>21</sup>And the people said to Joshua, "No, but we will serve the LORD."<sup>22</sup>Then Joshua said to the people, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the LORD, to serve him." And they said, "We are witnesses."<sup>23</sup>He said, "Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the LORD, the God of Israel."<sup>24</sup>And the people said to Joshua, "The LORD our God we will serve, and his voice we will obey."<sup>25</sup>So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and put in place statutes and rules for them at Shechem.<sup>26</sup>And Joshua wrote these words in the Book of the Law of God. And he took a large stone and set it up there under the terebinth that was by the sanctuary of the LORD.<sup>27</sup>And Joshua said to all the people, "Behold, this stone shall be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words of the LORD that he spoke to us. Therefore it shall be a witness against you, lest you deal falsely with your God."<sup>28</sup>So Joshua sent the people away, every man to his inheritance.<sup>29</sup>After these things Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, being 110 years old.<sup>30</sup>And they buried him in his own inheritance at Timnath-serah, which is in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash.<sup>31</sup>Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and had known all the work that the LORD did for Israel.<sup>32</sup>As for the bones of Joseph, which the people of Israel brought up from Egypt, they buried them at Shechem, in the piece of land that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of money. It became an inheritance of the descendants of Joseph.<sup>33</sup>And Eleazar the son of Aaron died, and they buried him at Gibeah, the town of Phinehas his son, which had been given him in the hill country of Ephraim.
24.overview:
Where we are. This is Joshua’s second and last farewell. In chapter 23 he warned Israel’s leaders; now he gathers all the tribes at Shechem, where God first promised the land to Abram (Genesis 12:6–7), to renew the covenant before he dies. The book then closes with three burials.

The message. Everything Israel has is the gift of a God who chose them when their fathers served idols, and the only fitting answer is to put away every other god and serve him alone. That choice must be real, made with open eyes, because the LORD is holy and jealous and his people cannot serve him in their own strength. Yet the God who has kept every promise stands behind the covenant, and even the graves at the end of the book are full of hope.

Why it was said. Israel still had household idols in its tents, and the generation that had seen the Jordan open was passing (see the introduction). This chapter put the covenant on record, in writing and in stone, for generations that would not share his memories.

How the chapter makes its case. The LORD himself retells Israel’s history in the first person, from Terah’s idols to the vineyards they did not plant, so that every good thing is seen to be his doing (vv. 1–13). Joshua calls them to fear the LORD, put away their gods and choose whom they will serve, declaring that he and his house will serve the LORD; the people answer gladly (vv. 14–18). He refuses their quick answer, warns them that they are not able, makes them witnesses against themselves, writes the covenant down and sets up a stone (vv. 19–28). Joshua dies, Joseph’s bones are buried at Shechem, and Eleazar dies (vv. 29–33).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by pattern. “You are not able to serve the LORD” (v. 19) shows that Israel needed new hearts, which God would later promise to give (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Joshua, the servant of the LORD, brought the people in but could not keep them faithful beyond his generation; Hebrews says that “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). The greater Joshua, the Son over God’s house, gives that rest and keeps all whom the Father gives him.

For us. Remember that everything you have in Christ is given, not earned. Name the rivals in your own life and put them away, and choose today, with your household, to serve the Lord. Do it not in your own strength, but trusting the one who chose you first and who keeps those who come to him.
24.theology:
Grace before demand. Twelve verses of history precede a single word of requirement, and in that history God is the one who acts throughout, beginning with a family of idolaters (v. 2). Everything Israel has is on the list of things done to them, ending with a land they had not worked for and vineyards they had not planted (v. 13).

The choice is never between God and nothing. Joshua names the two alternatives and both are gods: the gods their ancestors served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites around them: the old family gods or the fashionable local ones (v. 15). Everyone at Shechem was going to serve something. The famous verse is a demand to say which god, out loud, today.

A refused profession. The people give a confession that is accurate, evidently sincere and immediate, and Joshua answers you are not able (v. 19). He had heard this nation promise everything at Sinai and break the promise before Moses came down the mountain. It is the method of the Lord who told an eager crowd to sit down and count the cost first (Luke 14:28-30). And you are not able is not the last word on it. The answer Scripture gives is not a stronger promise from the people but a better covenant, in which God writes his law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), enacted through a better mediator (Hebrews 8:6-10): the greater Joshua, who came to do God’s will (Hebrews 10:7) and did for his people what they could not do for themselves.

One generation. Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders who had known all the work that the LORD did for Israel (v. 31). Judges finishes the sentence: and there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done (Judg. 2:10). All the memorial stones in this book, set up so that children would ask what they meant, were there to carry the faith from one generation to the next, and still the next generation did not know the LORD. Which is why the rest for the people of God is still spoken of as future, and why there had to be another Joshua (Heb. 4:8-9).
24.examples:
Then: A nation stood where the promise had started, heard its history with God as the subject of every sentence, and was asked which god it would serve. It answered well and was told it could not do it. It insisted, and was sent home to throw out the idols it had been carrying since Mesopotamia.

Now: Verse 14 is the searching one, not verse 15. The famous verse gets hung in kitchens; the verse before it says the people making that fine confession still had the old gods in their houses. It is entirely possible to have seen God work, to be genuinely grateful, to be at the meeting and mean every word, and to have kept something on a shelf at home. Joshua would not let them leave with the decision in the air; he tied it to something they had to do: put the idols away. The order is the same for us: first what God has done, then the putting away, and the strength to do it is the Spirit who inclines the heart. And when we find we have kept idols again, the covenant does not rest on our record but on the one who kept it for us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Everything God Did, in the First Person
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD retells Israel’s history so that every good thing in it is seen to be his gift. Joshua gathers the tribes at Shechem, and they present themselves before God (v. 1). God speaks in the first person: their fathers beyond the Euphrates served other gods, but he took Abraham and led him through Canaan (vv. 2–3). He gave Isaac, Jacob and Esau, sent Moses and Aaron, plagued Egypt and brought Israel out (vv. 3–5). He drowned the Egyptians, gave them the Amorites, and would not listen to Balaam (vv. 6–10). He gave them Jericho and the nations, not by their sword or bow (vv. 11–12), and a land, cities and vineyards they had not worked for (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Count the verbs. In almost every sentence God acts and Israel is acted upon, and the only two things Israel is credited with are crying out at the sea and going over the Jordan.
verseByVerse.examples: Before the nation promises anything, it is reminded that its ancestors were idol-worshippers, so its ancestry gives it no claim on God.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem and summoned the elders, the heads, the judges, and the officers of Israel. And they presented themselves before God. And Joshua said to all the people, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Long ago, your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates, Terah, the father of Abraham and of Nahor; and they served other gods. Then I took your father Abraham from beyond the River and led him through all the land of Canaan, and made his offspring many. I gave him Isaac. And to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. And I gave Esau the hill country of Seir to possess, but Jacob and his children went down to Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Shechem, where the land was first promised, God reminds Israel that its story began with idol-worshippers and with his free choice of Abraham.

Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem. Shechem is not chosen at random. It is the first place Abram stopped when he came in from Mesopotamia, and where God first said the sentence everything since has depended on: “To your offspring I will give this land” (Genesis 12:7). It is where Jacob made his household hand over their foreign gods and hid them under the terebinth (Genesis 35:4). It lies between Ebal and Gerizim, where the nation heard the law read (8:33), and Joseph’s bones will be buried there before the chapter ends.

They served other gods. God’s speech begins not with a promise but with an embarrassing fact. Abraham’s father Terah is named, and the family religion is stated flatly in the opening line of a covenant renewal.

Then I took your father Abraham. Then the verbs start, and they do not stop for eleven verses: I took, I led, I made, I gave. Nothing is a response to anything Abraham did. He is taken out of a family of idol-worshippers by a God he was not looking for. The whole history of Israel begins with God’s choice, not man’s, as every believer’s story does (Ephesians 1:4).

The background. The shape of the ceremony would have been familiar in the ancient Near East. Treaties between a great king and a subject people commonly named the king, rehearsed what he had done for them, set out his demands, called witnesses and laid up a written copy. Joshua 24 follows much the same order: history (vv. 2–13), demand (vv. 14–15), witnesses (vv. 22, 27) and a written record (v. 26). Israel is told, in a form any subject people understood, that the LORD is their great King, and that his kindness comes before his claims.
verseByVerse.note: “The River” is the Euphrates (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And I sent Moses and Aaron, and I plagued Egypt with what I did in the midst of it, and afterward I brought you out. "'Then I brought your fathers out of Egypt, and you came to the sea. And the Egyptians pursued your fathers with chariots and horsemen to the Red Sea. And when they cried to the LORD, he put darkness between you and the Egyptians and made the sea come upon them and cover them; and your eyes saw what I did in Egypt. And you lived in the wilderness a long time. Then I brought you to the land of the Amorites, who lived on the other side of the Jordan. They fought with you, and I gave them into your hand, and you took possession of their land, and I destroyed them before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brought Israel out of Egypt, shielded them at the sea and gave them the land east of the Jordan, and he speaks to the present generation as though they had been there.

I brought you out. The exodus is told in three sentences, and each time God is the one acting. Notice who is addressed. The speech began with your fathers, centuries away. By verse 6 it is “I brought your fathers out of Egypt, and you came to the sea.” Most of the men at Shechem were children at the Red Sea or not yet born, and God speaks to them as though they had been there. That is how Israel was taught to remember, and how the church learns to: nobody reading this was at Golgotha, yet the New Testament speaks to Christians as people who were crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6).

He put darkness between you and the Egyptians. One clause is given to Israel’s own part: “they cried to the LORD”. Then a detail from Exodus that is easy to lose: the pillar moved round behind them and stood in the gap all night, darkness on one side and light on the other (Exodus 14:19–20). God did not only open a road; he stood in the doorway while they used it.

You lived in the wilderness a long time. Forty years in a single clause. God’s own summary of the wilderness is brief, and the brevity is a mercy; the details are in Numbers and they are not flattering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and fought against Israel. And he sent and invited Balaam the son of Beor to curse you, but I would not listen to Balaam. Indeed, he blessed you. So I delivered you out of his hand.
