And you went over the Jordan and came to Jericho, and the leaders of Jericho fought against you, and also the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. And I gave them into your hand. And I sent the hornet before you, which drove them out before you, the two kings of the Amorites; it was not by your sword or by your bow. I gave you a land on which you had not labored and cities that you had not built, and you dwell in them. You eat the fruit of vineyards and olive orchards that you did not plant.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turned Balaam’s curse into blessing and gave Israel the land by his own power, so that everything they now enjoy is an unearned gift.

I would not listen to Balaam. Israel very likely knew nothing about Balaam at the time: a king hiring a prophet to curse them while they sat in their tents in the valley below (Numbers 22–24). God’s account is one clause. The threat was real, the fee offered, the prophet willing, and nothing happened because God declined to hear him. Most believers have a stretch of life like that: danger arranged by people they never met, which came to nothing for reasons they learn only afterwards.

It was not by your sword or by your bow. Israel had swords and used them, at Jericho and Ai and Merom. God says the country was not taken by them. The weapons were real; the victory was his.

Cities that you had not built. The speech ends with an inventory of unearned things: land, cities, vineyards, olive trees. Every man listening stood on ground he had not cleared, near a house he had not built. Moses had warned what that does to a heart: “then take care lest you forget the LORD” (Deuteronomy 6:12). It is the last thing God says before asking for their allegiance: not a threat, not an argument, but a list of what they have been given. So it is with grace in Christ: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Uncertain wording. The meaning of “the hornet” (v. 12) is uncertain. It may mean the insect literally, or, as most interpreters think, the panic God sent ahead of Israel, as he had promised: “I will send my terror before you” and “I will send hornets before you” (Exodus 23:27–28). Some have suggested it stands for Egypt’s armies weakening Canaan beforehand, but that is a guess. Either way, the point is plain: “it was not by your sword or by your bow.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua calls Israel to choose the LORD and put away every rival, and the people answer gladly. Because of all God has done, they must fear him and serve him sincerely, and put away the gods their fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt (v. 14). If serving the LORD seems evil to them, let them choose today which gods they will have, the old ones or the Amorites’; but Joshua and his house will serve the LORD (v. 15). The people respond at once: far be it from them to forsake the LORD, who brought them out of slavery, did great signs, kept them on the way and drove out the nations. They too will serve him, for he is their God (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua declares for his own house before he has heard what anyone else will choose.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 asks for sincerity and faithfulness before it mentions idols: the inward and the outward together.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD. And if it is evil in your eyes to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua calls Israel to fear and serve the LORD alone and to put away the gods they still keep, and he declares that he and his household will serve the LORD whatever others choose.

Put away the gods. The second half of the demand should stop a reader. They still have the old gods. After the Jordan opened, after Jericho fell and the sun stood still, there are idols in Israelite houses, some from the old family religion beyond the River and some picked up in Egypt, carried across the desert into the promised land. It is the ordinary condition of religious people.

Choose this day whom you will serve. The most quoted sentence in the book is usually quoted without its setting. Both alternatives Joshua names are gods, the old ones beyond the River and the local ones of the Amorites, and his contempt for both is audible in the way he lists them. The choice is never between serving and not serving, only between masters.

As for me and my house. Then the last clause. He includes his household: a man declaring publicly what will be served under his roof, and taking responsibility for it.

What choosing looks like. Joshua’s choice was not a feeling but a set of acts, and ours is the same. Name the rival. Israel’s alternatives had names, and ours do too: a career that decides every move, the approval of a certain circle, comfort, money saved so that we need nobody. Choose today, not someday. This day means the decision in front of you now: the job offer that would swallow the Lord’s Day, the hard conversation you have been avoiding, the habit you would rather keep. Make it concrete. Choosing the LORD usually means getting rid of something, as Joshua will insist (v. 23). Choose with your household. Pray and read the Bible with the people under your roof, and let them see what you put first when it costs something. Choose with your eyes on the God who chose first. Joshua at once tells them they cannot keep this choice in their own strength (v. 19), and Jesus says, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). Our choosing answers his, and it is renewed each morning by grace, not secured by the strength of our resolve.

Does “choose” teach free will? The command is a real summons, and each must answer it. But Joshua at once warns, “You are not able to serve the LORD” (v. 19): the people cannot keep covenant in their own strength. The call to choose and God’s promise to change the heart belong together (Deuteronomy 30:6). And “as for me and my house” is a father’s resolve to lead his household in serving God, not a promise that every child will believe; it commits him to lead, teach and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people answered, "Far be it from us that we should forsake the LORD to serve other gods, for it is the LORD our God who brought us and our fathers up from the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and who did those great signs in our sight and preserved us in all the way that we went, and among all the peoples through whom we passed. And the LORD drove out before us all the peoples, the Amorites who lived in the land. Therefore we also will serve the LORD, for he is our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people promise at once to serve the LORD, giving the right reasons: he redeemed them, kept them and gave them the land.

Far be it from us. The answer comes back immediately, and it is a good one. It is not vague enthusiasm; they give reasons, and the reasons are right.

The reasons they give. They rehearse God’s own speech back to him. He brought us out of slavery. He did the signs where we could see them. He kept us on every road and among every people we passed through. He drove out the nations. Every clause is accurate, and it is offered as the ground of their commitment.

A sound confession. By any ordinary standard this is exactly the response the ceremony was designed to produce: the history recited, the demand made, and the nation answering with a confession that is theologically sound and evidently sincere. Joshua does not accept it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua will not let Israel promise lightly, and he makes the covenant solemn, written and witnessed. He tells them they are not able to serve the LORD, for he is holy and jealous, and will turn against them if they forsake him (vv. 19–20). They insist they will serve him (v. 21), so he makes them witnesses against themselves (v. 22) and tells them to put away their foreign gods and incline their hearts to the LORD (v. 23). They promise again to serve and obey (v. 24). Joshua makes a covenant, writes it in the Book of the Law, and sets up a large stone as a witness under the terebinth at the sanctuary (vv. 25–27), then sends the people home (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua is not being difficult; he is refusing a cheap yes. A commitment that has not been told what it will cost is not worth witnessing.
verseByVerse.examples: The stone is a witness because there is nobody else left to be one. Moses is dead, Joshua is going, and the generation that saw the Jordan will soon be buried. So a rock is stood up under a tree at Shechem, and told what it has heard.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joshua said to the people, "You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins. If you forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, then he will turn and do you harm and consume you, after having done you good." And the people said to Joshua, "No, but we will serve the LORD." Then Joshua said to the people, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the LORD, to serve him." And they said, "We are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua warns that Israel cannot serve the holy and jealous LORD in its own strength, and he makes the people bind themselves knowingly as witnesses against themselves.

You are not able to serve the LORD. This is the most startling thing anybody says in the book, said by a preacher to a congregation that has just made a good confession. He tells them to their faces that they cannot do what they have just promised.

Not cynical, but honest. He is doing what an honest man does when a promise is made too quickly by people who have not counted the cost. This nation said at Sinai, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (Exodus 19:8), and had a golden calf in the camp before Moses came down the mountain. Joshua himself was coming down with Moses when they heard the noise of it (Exodus 32:17).

A holy God, a jealous God. The two words he uses about God are the reason. Holy: utterly unlike us and not to be treated casually. Jealous: the word for a husband’s response to a rival, not for petty envy.

What it means that God is jealous. To modern ears jealousy is a flaw: the insecure partner checking the other’s phone. So a jealous God sounds small. But a husband who merely shrugged when his wife took a lover would not be showing a large heart; he would be showing that he did not love her. Timothy Keller often pointed out, borrowing from Rebecca Pippert, that the opposite of love is not anger but hate, and that the final form of hate is indifference. God’s jealousy is love refusing to be indifferent to what is destroying the beloved, and the gods Israel kept in their tents were doing exactly that. The cross shows how far this jealousy goes: Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), paying with his life to win back an unfaithful bride. In practice, ask what you would be most afraid to lose, and put it back in his hands. He will not share you with something that cannot love you back.

He will not forgive your transgressions. The hardest clause is the last. Read alongside the rest of Scripture, and alongside the God who has just described centuries of carrying this people, it is plainly not a denial that God forgives. It is a warning about betraying the covenant: he will not simply overlook a people who take his covenant and keep idols in the house. Forgiveness is not something the unfaithful can presume on; it is found only where God provides it, finally in Christ.

We are witnesses. They push back, and they are right to. This is what Joshua was after: not a smaller commitment but a considered one. So he makes them say it again as a legal act. As witnesses against yourselves, their own words are entered as evidence, and everyone knows which way it will point if the promise fails.

Counting the cost. Joshua makes it harder before he lets anybody agree, telling them what God is like before they say yes. Jesus does the same with a crowd of eager followers: sit down first and count the cost, like a man building a tower (Luke 14:28–30).

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the LORD, the God of Israel." And the people said to Joshua, "The LORD our God we will serve, and his voice we will obey." So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and put in place statutes and rules for them at Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua insists that their promise be made real by getting rid of their idols and turning their hearts to the LORD, and only then is the covenant made.

Then put away the foreign gods. Having accepted their word, he makes it concrete, with the same instruction as verse 14, because nothing has happened yet. The idols are still in the tents. Joshua will not let the decision remain fine words: go home and get rid of the things.

Incline your heart to the LORD. The second half is the inward half. Neither substitutes for the other. A man can throw out an idol and keep his heart where it was, or feel deeply about God and still have the thing on a shelf. The inclining they are commanded is what God himself would later promise to do: “I will give you a new heart” and “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:26–27).

Joshua made a covenant with the people. Only now is the covenant made. The whole ceremony has been an exercise in slowing a willing people down.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua wrote these words in the Book of the Law of God. And he took a large stone and set it up there under the terebinth that was by the sanctuary of the LORD. And Joshua said to all the people, "Behold, this stone shall be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words of the LORD that he spoke to us. Therefore it shall be a witness against you, lest you deal falsely with your God." So Joshua sent the people away, every man to his inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua writes the covenant down and sets up a great stone as a witness, so that the promise made at Shechem will outlast everyone who heard it.

Joshua wrote these words. Two things are done to make the day survive the people who were in it: it is written down in the Book of the Law of God, and a rock is stood up.

It has heard all the words. The stone “has heard”. It is a striking thing to say, and Joshua says it deliberately. A covenant needed witnesses, and soon he will not have any. Moses is dead, Eleazar is old, Joshua is near the end, and every man who saw the Jordan open will be buried within a generation. Nobody will be left to stand up in twenty years and say what was promised at Shechem.

A large stone. So he uses a stone, because stone outlives men. It is the last in a line of stone markers in the book: the twelve at Gilgal and the twelve in the riverbed, the stones over Achan, the heap at Ai’s gate, the law written on stones at Ebal, the stones over the cave at Makkedah, and now this. Israel’s history is marked in rock by people who knew how short memory is.

Every man to his inheritance. That is the last thing Joshua does. He sends them home, each to the land drawn for him by lot, in a country that had been a promise to Abram, the childless son of an idol-worshipper, centuries earlier.

What was “the sanctuary of the LORD” at Shechem? It was the sacred place where Abraham and Jacob had built altars (Genesis 12:6–7; 33:18–20), not a rival to the tabernacle at Shiloh.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book ends with three graves, each a sign that God keeps his word. Joshua, the servant of the LORD, dies at 110 and is buried in his own inheritance (vv. 29–30). Israel serves the LORD throughout his lifetime and the lifetime of the elders who had seen the LORD’s work (v. 31), a verdict with a time limit built in. Joseph’s bones, carried up from Egypt, are buried at Shechem in the field Jacob bought, so that a dying man’s faith in God’s promise is honoured (v. 32). Eleazar the priest dies and is buried in the hill country of Ephraim (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: The book ends with three funerals and no successor. There is no Joshua to follow Joshua, and the next book will open on a nation with no leader, going down the list of what each tribe failed to take.
verseByVerse.examples: Joshua dies at a hundred and ten, the age at which Joseph died (Gen. 50:26), whose bones are buried in the same passage.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, being 110 years old. And they buried him in his own inheritance at Timnath-serah, which is in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash. Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and had known all the work that the LORD did for Israel. As for the bones of Joseph, which the people of Israel brought up from Egypt, they buried them at Shechem, in the piece of land that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of money. It became an inheritance of the descendants of Joseph. And Eleazar the son of Aaron died, and they buried him at Gibeah, the town of Phinehas his son, which had been given him in the hill country of Ephraim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua dies as the servant of the LORD, Israel stays faithful only while his generation lives, and Joseph’s bones rest at last in the promised land: God’s word kept, and a greater Joshua still needed.

The servant of the LORD. The title has been withheld from Joshua for twenty-four chapters. From chapter 1 only Moses has been called that. Joshua enters the book as Moses’ assistant and is given the title in his obituary: not when the Jordan opened or the sun stood still, but when he is dead, in the town he asked for and rebuilt (19:49–50).

All the days of the elders. The verdict on the generation carries a warning. The nation held while there were men alive who had seen the river open, and Judges says what came next: “there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD” (Judges 2:10). One generation is the whole distance between Shechem and the collapse. Faith must be passed on, not assumed.

The bones of Joseph. The second grave is four centuries in the making. Joseph, dying in Egypt as the second man in the kingdom, made his brothers swear: “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here” (Genesis 50:25). Moses took the bones on the night of the exodus (Exodus 13:19), and for forty years, through the sea and the wilderness, somebody carried the bones of a man who had died before any of them were born. They bury him in the field his father bought, in the land God promised, where the nation has just renewed its covenant. Hebrews counts it as faith (Hebrews 11:22): an old man’s confidence in a promise, honoured four centuries later by people he never met.

Eleazar the son of Aaron died. The third grave is the priest who stood beside Joshua at every distribution. No new Joshua is named, no charge is given, nobody says “be strong and courageous”. The next book opens with a nation asking who will go up first (Judges 1:1).

Graves full of hope. Yet what has been buried here, and where, is full of hope. Joseph’s bones lie in Canaan because a dying man believed God would keep his promise. And a stone stands at Shechem, where Abram was told “To your offspring I will give this land”, and the offspring are in it.

Faithful over God’s house as a son. Servant is the highest title this book knows, and the New Testament names one higher. Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, “but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son” (Hebrews 3:6). Joshua earned the servant’s name by a lifetime and could not hold his people beyond his own generation; the Son keeps every one the Father gives him (John 6:37–39).

Another Joshua. Not one word had failed. The LORD had fought for Israel, and the man who bore the name later borne by Jesus had brought them in and could not keep them there, and the book knows it. There would have to be another day, another rest and another Joshua: “So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9).

Who bought the tomb at Shechem? Stephen says Abraham bought the tomb at Shechem (Acts 7:16). He is compressing two purchases, Abraham’s cave at Hebron and Jacob’s field here, into one sentence.

Uncertain wording. The value of “a hundred pieces of money” (v. 32; compare Genesis 33:19) is unknown. The Hebrew word, qesitah, is a rare unit of money or weight found only in the stories of Jacob and Job, and nobody now knows how much it was worth.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob had bought the field on his return to Canaan and set up an altar there (Gen. 33:19-20).

keyVerse.quote: And if it is evil in your eyes to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
keyVerse.note: This is the decision the whole book has been leading to. After God has told what he has given, Joshua calls Israel to choose between him and every rival, and leads the way with his own household. It is a choice that must be made again in every generation, and one that only God’s grace can keep.

24.reflection:
In verses 2–13 God tells Israel’s history with himself as the one acting in every sentence. Try telling your own story that way. What has God given you that you did not earn?

Israel still had other gods in its tents (vv. 14, 23). What rivals to the Lord are present in your life or home, and what would it mean to put them away concretely this week?

Joshua told the people, “You are not able to serve the LORD” (v. 19), even after a good confession. Why was this a kindness rather than discouragement, and how does Christ answer the inability Joshua exposed?

Israel served the LORD while the elders who had seen his work were alive (v. 31), but the next generation did not know him. What can your family and church do to pass on faith to those who come after you?
